statement: High IT (software delivery) performance correlates with strong organizational performance, boosting productivity, profitability, and market share.
There is a causal link, not merely a correlation, between good technical and management practices and business performance.

Speed and stability are not a trade-off in software delivery; speed depends on stability, so good delivery practices yield both rather than forcing a choice between them (refuting the bimodal-IT notion).

Twenty-four key capabilities drive improvements in software delivery performance, grouped into five categories: continuous delivery, architecture, product and process, lean management and monitoring, and cultural.
Teams can improve their organizational culture by implementing specific technical and management practices, rather than treating culture as a fixed prerequisite.
Improvement in software delivery performance is possible for every team and organization.
condition: leadership provides consistent support (time, actions, and resources) and team members commit to the work
exception: leadership support or team commitment is absent

statement: The capabilities and practices are methodology-agnostic and apply across waterfall, Agile, and DevOps contexts, and across greenfield, legacy, mainframe, packaged-software, and product teams.
The research findings are based on a large empirical dataset: over 23,000 survey responses from more than 2,000 organizations spanning startups to large enterprises and regulated industries.
The research uses cross-sectional study designs and snowball sampling, the same methodological family used in healthcare, workplace, and memory research.
Year over year, high performers keep improving while organizations that fail to improve fall further behind.

The highest-performing organizations move code from committed-to-mainline to running-in-production in about an hour and deploy many times per day, while lower performers take months and deploy far less frequently.
High performers' changes cause failures at a fraction of the rate of lower performers, and those failures are typically restored within the hour.

Treat all work as a single backlog rather than separate backlogs for features, technical debt, and operations, because non-functional requirements are features and reducing technical debt improves product stability.
Senior leadership support must be demonstrated through actions, not words: leaders must build trust so teams feel safe surfacing risks and so failure leads to inquiry rather than blame.
Limit the blast radius of a transformation by starting with one or two teams instead of attempting to change the whole organization at once.
The book's findings concern IT delivery (the journey from commit to production) and subjective survey perceptions, and warrant independent confirmation before being treated as universal.
condition: generalizing beyond IT delivery or treating survey-based results as definitive

statement: Organizations should focus on measuring and improving capabilities rather than on maturity models when seeking to accelerate software delivery.
Maturity models are the wrong tool for technology transformation because they treat improvement as arriving at a finished 'mature' state rather than as continuous improvement.
Maturity models are typically lock-step and linear, prescribing the same technologies and capabilities for every team, whereas teams have different contexts, systems, goals, and constraints.
Capability models are multidimensional, dynamic, and outcome-based, letting each part of the organization improve the capabilities that yield the most benefit for its current context.
Most maturity models measure technical proficiency or tooling install base without tying it to outcomes, producing vanity metrics that say nothing about business impact.
Transformation should be evidence-based, selecting capabilities by research evidence rather than by vendor product alignment, consultant background, or internal champions' skill sets.

Several commonly cited factors did not predict software delivery or organizational performance: application age and technology stack (mainframe vs greenfield), whether operations or development teams performed deployments, and whether a change approval board was implemented.

In 2017, high performers compared to low performers had 46 times more frequent code deployments, 440 times faster lead time from commit to deploy, 170 times faster mean time to recover, and a 5 times lower change failure rate.
The gap between high and low performers continues to grow over time.
From 2016 to 2017 the performance gap narrowed for tempo (deployment frequency and lead time) but widened for stability (mean time to recover and change failure rate).
Low-performing teams that increase tempo without investing in building quality in tend to suffer larger deployment failures that take longer to restore.
Strategic use of technology explains revenue and productivity gains more than mergers and acquisitions or entrepreneurship.
Executives, being further from the work, systematically overestimate their organization's DevOps progress relative to the practitioners actually doing the work.
Organizations should measure DevOps capabilities accurately and communicate the results to leaders so strategy is informed by the real technology posture rather than by executive estimates.

A valid, reliable measure of software delivery performance must be defined before performance can be improved, and such measurement is hard because software inventory is invisible and design and delivery happen simultaneously.
Productivity measures fail when they focus on outputs rather than outcomes and on individual or local measures rather than team or global ones.

Rewarding developers for lines of code leads to bloated software with higher maintenance and change costs; developers should instead be rewarded for solving business problems with the minimum necessary code.
exception: reducing code to a single unreadable line that no one else can maintain

statement: Velocity is designed as a relative, team-dependent capacity-planning tool and is invalid as a productivity metric because teams game it by inflating estimates, which also inhibits cross-team collaboration.

Utilization is a poor proxy for productivity because beyond a certain level there is no slack to absorb unplanned or improvement work, and as utilization approaches 100% lead times approach infinity per queue theory.
condition: utilization rises above the level where spare capacity remains

statement: Utilization should be managed and balanced against lead time in an economically optimal way rather than maximized.
A good performance measure must focus on a global outcome (so teams are not pitted against each other) and on outcomes rather than output (so busywork is not rewarded).
Software delivery performance should be measured with four metrics: delivery lead time, deployment frequency, time to restore service, and change fail rate.

Rewarding developers for throughput while rewarding operations for stability creates a 'wall of confusion' in which poor-quality code is thrown over to operations and operations imposes painful change-management to inhibit change.

Product delivery lead time should be measured as the time from code committed to code running successfully in production, because the delivery portion is lower-variability and easier to measure than the design 'fuzzy front end'.
Shorter product delivery lead times are better because they enable faster feedback and allow rapid, high-confidence delivery of fixes during defects or outages.
Reducing batch size reduces cycle time and flow variability, accelerates feedback, lowers risk and overhead, improves efficiency, and reduces cost and schedule growth.
Deployment frequency is used as a measurable proxy for batch size in software because software has no visible inventory.

Because failure is inevitable in rapidly changing complex systems, reliability should be measured by how quickly service can be restored (time to restore service) rather than by time between failures.
Change fail rate, the percentage of production changes that degrade service or require remediation (hotfix, rollback, fix-forward, patch), is a key quality metric for delivery.

Cluster analysis of the survey data, which carries no a-priori notion of good or bad responses, consistently identified statistically distinct high, medium, and low software-delivery performance groups every year across all four measures.
There is no trade-off between delivery performance and stability or quality: high performers do better on all four measures simultaneously.
When low performers increase tempo by simply working harder without addressing underlying obstacles such as rearchitecture, process improvement, and automation, they lose ground on stability.
High-performing organizations are about twice as likely as low performers to exceed goals for profitability, market share, and productivity.

High-performing organizations are about twice as likely as low performers to exceed non-commercial goals including quantity of goods and services, operating efficiency, customer satisfaction, quality, and mission attainment.
An organization's software delivery capability provides a competitive advantage to the business.

The ability to deliver in small batches is especially valuable because it enables fast user feedback through techniques such as A/B testing, and is correlated with the technical practices of continuous delivery.

Software that is strategic to the business should be developed in-house rather than outsourced, while non-strategic software such as office productivity and payroll should generally be acquired as software-as-a-service.
condition: the software is strategic to the business (vs. commodity/non-strategic)

statement: Change approval boards do not improve software delivery performance; they are negatively correlated with both tempo and stability.

Performance metrics must be used carefully: in a learning culture they are powerful, but in pathological or bureaucratic cultures measurement becomes a form of control and people hide information, so culture must be understood and developed first.
condition: the organization has a learning (generative) culture
exception: pathological or bureaucratic cultures where measurement is used as control

statement: It is possible to influence and improve organizational culture by implementing DevOps and continuous-delivery practices.

Ron Westrum's typology classifies organizational cultures as pathological (power-oriented), bureaucratic (rule-oriented), or generative (performance-oriented), and organizational culture predicts how information flows through the organization.
A generative culture is characterized by high cooperation, trained messengers, shared risk, encouraged bridging, failure leading to inquiry rather than scapegoating, and implemented novelty.
Good information flow is critical to safe and effective operation of high-tempo, high-consequence environments such as technology organizations.
The Westrum organizational-culture construct measuring trust and collaboration is statistically valid and reliable and can be measured with strongly-worded Likert items scored 1 to 7 and averaged.
Westrum organizational culture predicts software delivery performance, organizational performance, and job satisfaction.
Survey measures must be confirmed valid (discriminant and convergent validity) and reliable (internal consistency) as constructs before any correlation or prediction analysis is performed on them.

Bureaucracy is not inherently bad: rule-oriented structures can ensure fairness and consistency; the Westrum 'bureaucratic' pathology is specifically when following rules is treated as more important than achieving the mission.

Only lead time, deployment frequency, and time to restore service together form a statistically valid and reliable software-delivery-performance construct; change fail rate is excluded from the construct but is strongly correlated with it.
Who is on a team matters less than how team members interact, structure their work, and view their contributions, so team performance is driven by team dynamics rather than individual traits.

Failure in complex adaptive systems is emergent from many interacting factors rather than the fault of a single person, so accident investigations that stop at 'human error' are dangerous and human error should instead be the start of the investigation.
After an incident, the goal should be to improve information flow and tooling so people get better, more timely information, rather than to find a person to blame.
The way to change culture is to start by changing how people behave (what they do), not by first trying to change how they think.
Technical practices play a vital role in delivery outcomes and should not be treated as secondary to management and team practices, as many Agile adoptions have done.
Continuous delivery is a set of capabilities for getting changes of all kinds into production or users' hands safely, quickly, and sustainably.
Build quality in: cease dependence on end-stage inspection and instead build quality into the product so issues are detected and fixed quickly when they are cheap to resolve.

Work in small batches: split work into small chunks that deliver measurable business outcomes quickly to get feedback and avoid work that delivers zero or negative value, accepting modest added overhead.
Automate repetitive, time-consuming work such as regression testing and deployments so people are freed for higher-value problem-solving like improving system and process design.
Make continuous improvement part of everyone's daily work, since the defining characteristic of high-performing teams is that they are never satisfied and always strive to get better.

Everyone in the delivery process is responsible for system-level outcomes such as quality and stability, which can only be achieved through close collaboration rather than each function optimizing its own departmental goal.

Comprehensive configuration management means provisioning environments and building, testing, and deploying software in a fully automated way purely from information in version control, with manual approvals allowed but changes applied automatically once approved.

High-performing teams practice continuous integration by keeping branches short-lived (less than a day's work) and integrating into trunk frequently, with each change triggering a build and unit tests that developers fix immediately on failure.

Testing should be continuous: automated unit and acceptance tests run against every commit, developers able to run all automated tests on their workstations, testers performing ongoing exploratory testing, and no work called 'done' until all relevant automated tests pass.
Continuous delivery practices have a strong, statistically significant positive impact on software delivery performance and also decrease deployment pain and team burnout.
A loosely coupled, well-encapsulated architecture and letting teams choose their own tools are both strong, statistically significant drivers of a team's continuous-delivery capability.
Teams that do well at continuous delivery achieve higher software delivery performance, lower change fail rates, a generative culture, and stronger identification with their organization.
Continuous delivery makes work more sustainable, lowering deployment pain and team burnout, so investments in delivery technology are also investments in people.

Continuous delivery improves quality: it predicts lower change fail rates and statistically significantly lower levels of unplanned work and rework, with high performers spending ~49% of time on new work and ~21% on unplanned work versus ~38% and ~27% for low performers.
Unplanned work and rework are useful proxies for quality because they represent a failure to build quality in (failure demand from not doing the right thing the first time).

Keeping system and application configuration in version control is more strongly correlated with software delivery performance than keeping application code in version control, contradicting the view that configuration is a secondary concern.

Automated tests should be reliable so that passing tests mean the software is releasable and failures indicate real defects; unreliable, flaky tests should be moved to a separate quarantine suite or deleted.

Software delivery performance improves when developers, rather than QA or an outsourced party, primarily create and maintain acceptance tests, because writing tests produces more testable designs and developers maintain tests they own.
Test automation does not eliminate the need for testers, who perform essential manual exploratory, usability, and acceptance testing and help build and evolve automated suites alongside developers.
Successful teams manage test data so that adequate data is available on demand for fully automated test suites and test data is not a constraint on which tests can run.

Trunk-based development correlates with higher delivery performance: top teams keep fewer than three active branches, branch lifetimes under a day, and no code-freeze or stabilization periods, independent of team size, organization size, or industry.
exception: open-source projects with part-time contributors, where longer-lived branches (e.g. GitHub Flow) are appropriate

statement: Information security should be shifted left: infosec provides feedback integrated into the team's daily work at every step of the delivery lifecycle in a way that does not slow development and in fact contributes to delivery performance.

Adopting continuous delivery requires substantial investment in test and deployment automation combined with ongoing work to simplify systems architecture so the automation is not prohibitively expensive to maintain.

High delivery performance is achievable with any kind of system, including mainframe and legacy, provided the systems and the teams that build and maintain them are loosely coupled, which lets teams test and deploy independently as the organization scales.
condition: systems and teams are loosely coupled

statement: System type (greenfield, systems of engagement vs record, packaged, embedded, mainframe) is largely uncorrelated with delivery performance, except that low performers are more likely to be building or integrating against custom software developed by another company and to be working on mainframe systems.

High performance depends on architectural characteristics, not on the implementation technology or system type, so it is achievable with packaged or legacy mainframe systems while a microservices-on-containers stack is no guarantee of performance if those characteristics are ignored.

The two architectural characteristics that predict high performance are testability (being able to do most testing without an integrated environment) and deployability (being able to deploy or release independently of other applications and services).

The single biggest contributor to continuous delivery in 2017, larger than test and deployment automation, was whether a team could make large-scale design changes and deploy on demand without permission from, dependence on, or coordination with other teams.
Delivery teams should be cross-functional, containing all the skills to design, develop, test, deploy, and operate the system, so that the architecture and the teams are loosely coupled.

Organizations should apply the inverse Conway maneuver, evolving team and organizational structure to produce the desired loosely coupled architecture, so teams can work from design to deployment without high-bandwidth cross-team communication.

Service-oriented and microservices architectures only enable higher performance if teams are strict about being able to test and deploy services independently; many real-world SOAs do not permit this and therefore do not deliver the benefit.
condition: services can actually be tested and deployed independently of each other

statement: A loosely coupled architecture matched by organizational structure lets an engineering organization grow while increasing productivity linearly or better, measured as deploys per day per developer.

As developer count grows, high performers' deploys per day per developer increases, medium performers' stays constant, and low performers' decreases, refuting the orthodox view that individual productivity must fall as teams scale.
Letting teams choose their own tools contributes to software delivery performance and organizational performance because the practitioners pick tools best suited to their work and users.
There remains a place for standardization, particularly around infrastructure architecture and configuration and around preapproved security libraries, toolchains, and processes.
exception: infrastructure architecture/configuration and security tooling, where a standardized platform is beneficial

statement: Architects should focus on engineers and outcomes rather than on choosing specific tools or technologies, collaborating with the engineers who build and operate systems to enable teams to make changes without depending on other teams.
Building security into software development improves both delivery performance and security quality, with high performers spending about 50% less time remediating security issues than low performers.

Shifting left on security means conducting security reviews of all major features without slowing development, integrating infosec experts across the whole lifecycle (design, demos, automated tests), and giving developers easy-to-consume preapproved libraries, packages, toolchains, and processes.

Security should shift from infosec teams performing reviews themselves to giving developers the means to build security in, because it is cheaper to help builders do the right thing than to inspect near-complete systems, and infosec lacks capacity to review frequent deployments.
Information security is everyone's responsibility, not solely the infosec team's.

Lean management for software comprises limiting work in progress and using those limits to drive process improvement, maintaining visual displays of quality and productivity metrics and work status, and using application and infrastructure monitoring data to make business decisions daily.

Work-in-progress limits alone do not strongly predict delivery performance; they have a strong positive effect only when combined with visual displays and a feedback loop from production monitoring back to delivery teams or the business.
condition: WIP limits are combined with visual displays and a production-monitoring feedback loop

statement: WIP limits are only valuable if they make obstacles to flow visible and lead teams to remove those obstacles through process improvement that increases throughput.
Lean management practices decrease team burnout and foster a more generative culture in addition to improving delivery performance.

Requiring production changes to be approved by an external body such as a manager or change advisory board lowers delivery performance: it is negatively correlated with lead time, deployment frequency, and restore time and uncorrelated with change fail rate, making it worse than having no change-approval process.
Teams with no formal change-approval process or that rely on peer review achieve higher software delivery performance, and approval limited to high-risk changes is uncorrelated with performance.

Use a lightweight change-approval process based on peer review (such as pair programming or intrateam code review) combined with a deployment pipeline that detects and rejects bad changes, applied to all change types including code, infrastructure, and database.

Segregation of duties in regulated industries can be satisfied without a change advisory board or separate operations team by having an independent person review and record approval of each change and by applying all production changes through a fully automated deployment pipeline.
condition: a regulated environment requires segregation of duties

statement: A deployment pipeline gives auditors a complete record of which changes were applied to which environments, their version-control origin, the tests run, and who approved them, making it especially valuable in safety-critical or highly regulated industries.

External change approval is a form of risk-management theater because a body unfamiliar with a complex system's internals cannot accurately assess the impact of large code changes; risk management is better served by a governance role that helps teams adopt practices known to increase stability, quality, and speed.

Lean product development and the Lean startup approach test a product's design and business model through frequent user research from the start, building and validating prototypes, working in small batches, and pivoting early and often.

Lean product development comprises four capabilities: slicing work into small batches completable in under a week (including MVPs), making the flow of work from business to customer visible, actively gathering and incorporating customer feedback into design, and giving teams authority to create and change specifications without outside approval.
Lean product management practices statistically predict higher software delivery performance and organizational performance while improving culture and decreasing burnout.
Software delivery performance and Lean product management practices form a reciprocal virtuous cycle: each predicts and reinforces the other.

Working in small batches, including using MVPs (prototypes with just enough features for validated learning), produces short lead times and faster feedback loops and enables techniques like A/B testing.

A team's ability to try new ideas and create or update specifications during development without approval from outside the team predicts organizational performance in profitability, productivity, and market share.
Team experimentation is effective only when combined with working in small batches, making work flow visible, and incorporating customer feedback, not as unconstrained freedom to build anything.
condition: experimentation is combined with small batches, visible flow, and customer feedback

statement: Deployment pain, the fear and anxiety staff feel pushing code to production, is a useful signal: where deployments are most painful you find the poorest software delivery performance, organizational performance, and culture.

Teams having no visibility into what deployments are like is itself a warning sign of low delivery performance, because barriers that hide deployment work isolate developers from the downstream consequences of their work.

Improving technical capabilities (test and deployment automation, continuous integration with trunk-based development, shift-left security, test data management, loosely coupled architecture, version control of everything needed to reproduce environments) reduces deployment pain.

Needing to perform deployments outside normal business hours is a sign of architectural problems, since with sufficient investment large-scale distributed systems can support fully automated zero-downtime deployments.

Most deployment problems stem from a complex, brittle deployment process caused by software not written for deployability, manual changes to production environments (which cause errors and configuration drift), and multiple handoffs between siloed teams.

To reduce deployment pain, build systems that deploy easily into multiple environments, tolerate environmental failures, and allow components to be updated independently; reproduce production state automatically from version control (except production data); and build deployment intelligence into the application and platform.

Burnout is physical, mental, or emotional exhaustion that is correlated with pathological cultures and wasteful work, and its consequences for health and organizations are severe (stressful jobs can be as harmful as secondhand smoke and job stress costs the US economy around $300 billion per year).
Burnout can be prevented or reversed, and the conditions that cause it are organizational factors that management has the power to change.
Managers should fix the work environment rather than trying to fix the person, because changing the environment is far more effective for preventing burnout.

To avert burnout, managers should foster a respectful, supportive, blame-free environment that learns from failure, communicate a strong sense of purpose, invest in employee development, remove the obstacles employees identify, give time and space to experiment and learn, and give employees authority over decisions affecting their work.

Maslach's six organizational risk factors that predict burnout are work overload, lack of control, insufficient rewards, breakdown of community, absence of fairness, and value conflicts, all of which are within management's power to change.

The five factors most strongly correlated with burnout are a pathological organizational culture, deployment pain, ineffective leadership, lack of organizational investment in DevOps capability, and poor organizational performance.

Organizations should create space for employees to do new, creative, value-adding work during the work week rather than expecting extra after-hours effort (e.g., Google's 20% time, IBM's THINK Friday).
Burnout is reduced when an employee's values align with the organization's real, lived values (not merely its stated values), and a values mismatch is a strong contributor to burnout.
condition: the organization's actual lived values align with the individual's values

statement: Improving technical and Lean practices reduces feelings of burnout, so investments in technology also improve the work lives of technology professionals.
Employee engagement and satisfaction indicate loyalty and identity, help reduce burnout, and drive organizational outcomes such as profitability, productivity, and market share.

Employees in high-performing organizations are 2.2 times more likely to recommend their organization and 1.8 times more likely to recommend their team as a great place to work, measured by employee Net Promoter Score.

Employee engagement drives business outcomes: highly engaged workforces have been shown to grow revenue about 2.5 times as much as low-engagement ones, and high-trust companies' stocks outperformed market indexes threefold over 1997-2011.

When employees see the connection between their work and its positive impact on customers, they identify more strongly with the organization's purpose, which leads to better software delivery and organizational performance.
When leaders invest in their people and enable them to do their best work, employees identify more strongly with the organization and go the extra mile, yielding higher performance and productivity.

Teams that implement continuous delivery and an experimental approach to product development build better products and feel more connected to their organization, creating a virtuous cycle of higher delivery performance, faster idea validation, job satisfaction, and organizational performance.

A strong sense of organizational identity, which includes alignment of personal and organizational values, helps reduce burnout, so investments in continuous delivery and Lean management that strengthen identity may also reduce burnout.
Handing requirements down to teams to deliver in large batches leaves employees feeling little control or connection, which is demotivating and leads to worse organizational outcomes.

The extent to which people identify with their organization predicts a generative culture and organizational performance (productivity, market share, profitability), making strong employee identification a competitive advantage.

A culture of experimentation and learning, supported by investment in the technical and management capabilities that enable it, is the best thing an organization can do for its products, company, and people, and it aids hiring and retention.

Job satisfaction depends strongly on having the right tools and resources to do the work and on the job making good use of one's skills and abilities, and good DevOps technical practices predict job satisfaction.

Automation improves job satisfaction by handing rote tasks to computers so people can focus on weighing evidence, solving problems, and exercising judgment, which is a major source of work satisfaction.

Diverse teams (by gender and underrepresented minorities) are smarter and achieve better team performance and business outcomes, so teams seeking high performance should recruit and retain more women, underrepresented minorities, and people with disabilities.
Diversity alone is insufficient; organizations must also be inclusive, where all members feel welcome and valued, because inclusion must be present for diversity to take hold.

There is no significant difference between men and women in STEM ability, and the main barrier keeping women and underrepresented groups out of tech is the pervasive belief that innate brilliance is required, which drives women to leave tech at a 45% higher rate than men.
Leaders and peers should actively watch for and counter harassment, microaggressions, and unequal pay to retain women and underrepresented minorities.
Leadership has a powerful impact on results, but leadership means inspiring and motivating those around you rather than having direct reports on an org chart.

A good leader improves a team's ability to deliver code, architect good systems, and apply Lean principles, which measurably impacts profitability, productivity, and market share, but these effects are indirect, operating through the technical and Lean practices leaders support.

Transformational leadership is essential for establishing generative, high-trust cultural norms, enabling developer productivity, supporting team experimentation and innovation, and achieving strategic alignment across organizational silos.

Engaged leadership is essential to successful DevOps transformations because leaders have the authority and budget to make large-scale changes, provide air cover, change group incentives, and set and reinforce cultural norms.
Three things are highly correlated with software delivery performance and a strong team culture: cross-functional collaboration, a climate for learning, and good tools.

Cross-functional collaboration is best enabled by building trust with counterparts on other teams over time through kept promises, open communication, and predictable behavior under stress, plus encouraging lateral moves between departments and rewarding collaborative work.

Disaster-recovery testing exercises (game days) that deliberately simulate outages build cross-team working relationships and organizational learning, but only when the organization first accepts system and process failures as a means of learning.
condition: the organization accepts failure as a means of learning

statement: Create a climate of learning by funding a training budget, giving teams resources and space for informal learning and side projects, making it safe to fail, and setting up regular venues to share knowledge such as lightning talks, lunch-and-learns, and demo days.
Making it safe to fail through blameless postmortems lets people take reasonable risks and try new things, whereas punishing failure stops people from innovating.

Practitioners should choose their own tools unless there is a good reason not to, because tool autonomy increases investment in their work and predicts both job satisfaction and continuous delivery; when standardization is required, procurement and finance should act in the interests of the teams.
Make monitoring a priority: proactive infrastructure and application monitoring is strongly related to delivery performance and job satisfaction and is a key part of a strong technical foundation.

Organizations should treat leadership development as an investment in their teams, technology, and products, because technology transformations benefit from engaged, transformational leaders who amplify their teams' work.

Primary research (collecting new data) gives researchers more control and can reveal insights not in existing datasets, though it is more costly and time-intensive than secondary research that reuses others' data.

Correlation does not imply causation: two variables moving together can be due to a third variable or chance, so correlations belong only to the exploratory stage and must be followed by more complex analysis before claiming prediction or causation.

To avoid fishing for spurious correlations, hypotheses must be theory-driven: state a hypothesis grounded in well-supported theory, design research to test it, collect data, and test it, gaining confidence as supporting evidence accumulates.

Claims of 'impacting' or 'driving' results in the book rest on inferential predictive analysis (theory-driven hypothesis testing with multiple linear or partial least squares regression), not on full causal analysis, which would require randomized studies.

The high-, medium-, and low-performer groups were derived by hierarchical cluster analysis on the four performance variables, yielding statistically significant groups that differ on all four measures.
Survey data can be trustworthy, but well-designed survey questions must avoid leading questions, loaded questions, double-barreled questions that ask more than one thing, and unclear language.
Single-question 'quick surveys' such as Net Promoter Score are useful only for drawing narrow conclusions and only when the question is carefully developed and well understood.
condition: the single question is carefully developed and well understood

statement: Things that cannot be measured directly, such as organizational culture, should be measured as latent constructs through several manifest variables (survey items), each capturing one aspect of the underlying concept.

Using several measures rather than a single one to capture a concept safeguards against bad measures and bad actors, because it is harder for one rogue or changed data source to skew results; this applies to system data as well as survey data.
Always start measurement by clearly defining what you want to measure, because vague questions such as 'is your culture good?' are interpreted differently by respondents and yield meaningless data.

Westrum organizational culture is measured with seven team-level items: information is actively sought, messengers are not punished for bad news, responsibilities are shared, cross-functional collaboration is encouraged and rewarded, failure causes inquiry, new ideas are welcomed, and failures are treated as opportunities to improve the system.
Culture should be measured at the team level rather than the organization level because large organizations contain pockets of different cultures and people answer more accurately for their own team.
Latent constructs and measures should be periodically retested for good psychometric properties because the system or environment can change and shift what the items measure.

Proactive failure notification (alerts from logging and monitoring systems, plus threshold and rate-of-change warnings) is a distinct construct from externally sourced notification and is a technical capability predictive of software delivery performance.
All measures are proxies for an underlying idea, true of both system data and survey data, so relying on a single data point means a bad or silently changed measure will go undetected.

Surveys are a legitimate and often preferable data source because they let you collect and analyze data quickly across organizational boundaries, can capture things system data cannot, and, when built as well-tested psychometric constructs, can be trusted.

Teams must define their measurement terms precisely, because terms like 'lead time' (commit to deployable state) and 'cycle time' (start of work to deployable state) measure different things yet are frequently confused and used interchangeably.
Perceptions, feelings, and opinions such as how people experience organizational culture can often only be measured through surveys, by asking people directly.

Objective proxies like retention or turnover are poor measures of organizational culture because many unrelated factors drive whether people stay (pay offers, relocation, career changes) and the metric can be gamed by managers.
Survey data should be collected anonymously and with the intent to improve, not coercively, because pressuring respondents to answer positively yields the answers you want but meaningless data.

When assessing whether a team performs a practice, measure the core behaviors of that practice (e.g., whether automated tests run on code check-in) rather than asking directly whether they 'do continuous integration', because people claim practices they do not actually follow.

Foundational practices such as version control and automated testing are likely to yield positive results across DevOps, Agile, and even waterfall contexts, and a culture of transparency, trust, and innovation is likely beneficial regardless of software paradigm or industry.

Research conclusions should be triangulated against industry feedback, literature, and external subject-matter-expert review rather than relying on a single data source, revisiting hypotheses when discrepancies appear.
Team dynamics and psychological safety are the most important factors for understanding team performance, and organizational culture is predictive of technology and organizational performance.
A large, pooled, diverse survey sample protects against a handful of bad actors, since skewing results would require many people to lie about every item of a construct in a coordinated way.

Sustaining competitive advantage requires not only technical performance but also a lightweight, high-performance management framework that connects enterprise strategy to action, streamlines the flow of ideas to value, and enables rapid feedback and learning.
Leaders and teams must understand why a practice works rather than merely copying the behaviors of successful organizations.
Use visual management (an Obeya) to make strategic objectives, targets, gaps, progress, and problems immediately visible and color-coded, with each objective tied measurably to enterprise strategy.
Organize work along value streams into cross-functional, self-steering teams kept small (the two-pizza rule), each guided by a product owner and owning a distinct customer mission.
Organizational structure should be allowed to evolve and emerge from experience and learning rather than being fixed or fully planned up front.
Scale culture change by coaching the coaches: a small expert coaching group develops leaders and leads who in turn coach their teams, creating a leveraged effect across the organization.

Standardize team visuals to show goals, current performance and gaps, new and escalated problems, demand, work-in-progress, and done work, while letting each team tailor the rest, because visualizing demand helps keep the WIP load small.

Run short daily stand-ups (about 15 minutes) that report work, obstacles, and completed items; do not solve problems in the stand-up but route, escalate, and rapidly resolve them, keeping each problem visualized until resolved.

Use a catchball routine of vertical and horizontal communication so problems and learning flow rapidly between squads, chapters, centers of expertise, and tribes, implementing strategy deployment and a continuous PDCA feedback cycle.

Shift leaders from command-and-control to leaders-as-coaches who ask teams to help them understand problems and learning and how to better support the team, so that everyone's job becomes to do the work, improve the work, and develop the people.

Developing people is especially important as automation disrupts technology jobs, because people will only bring their best when they have complete faith that leaders value them for their ability to learn and improve, not just for their current work.

A courageous, supportive leader who gives teams permission and safety to put quality first helps them slow down to speed up, which over time improves speed, consistency, and capacity while reducing cost, delays, and rework and increasing customer trust.
Allocate a fixed percentage of each team's time to improvement work and treat improvement as regular work rather than an optional extra.

Solve problems by gathering people with real experience to rigorously examine the current condition so the root cause (not just symptoms) is found, forming a measurable improvement hypothesis, and on success making it standard work, sharing it, and monitoring to sustain it.

Establish standard work by having a team experiment and agree on the best current way to do the work and then spread it, re-evaluating as conditions change, rather than imitating a method prescribed in a book or used by another company.
Culture change cannot be implemented as a checklist or playbook; trying to mimic another company's specific behaviors and practices is by its nature counter to building a generative culture.

Do not outsource a transformation to a consulting firm to implement methodologies for you, because teams will feel the methods are being done to them and will not develop the capability to sustain, adapt, and improve on their own.

Develop your own internal coaches; outside coaching may help establish a foundation, but the organization must ultimately be the agent of its own change, since coaching depth is a key lever for sustaining and scaling.
Leaders at every level must change their own way of working and lead by example, because a generative culture starts with demonstrating new behaviors rather than delegating them.
Develop leader standard work (visual management, regular stand-ups, consistent coaching) to replace long meetings and firefighting, beginning by measuring how leaders currently spend their time.
Transformation requires discipline and patience, because an entrenched way of working took years to form and new behaviors become habit and then culture only through sustained, repeated practice.

High performance cannot be bought or copied; an organization must develop its own capabilities along a path that fits its particular context and goals, which takes sustained effort, investment, focus, and time.

Version control should cover all production artifacts, including application code, application configuration, system configuration, and build/configuration automation scripts, not just application code.

Continuous delivery means keeping software in a deployable state throughout its lifecycle and prioritizing that deployable state over new feature work, with fast feedback on deployability available to all and on-demand deployment.
Test data management should provide adequate data on demand and condition data in the pipeline, while teams should minimize the amount of test data needed to run automated tests wherever possible.

Monitoring should use application and infrastructure data to inform business decisions and proactively detect problems via threshold and rate-of-change warnings, going beyond merely paging people when things break.
Transformational leadership comprises five factors: vision, intellectual stimulation, inspirational communication, supportive leadership, and personal recognition.

A generative (Westrum) culture is predictive of IT performance and organizational performance and of decreased burnout, with hallmarks of good information flow, high cooperation and trust, bridging between teams, and conscious inquiry.
High performers had 50% higher market capitalization growth over three years than low performers among publicly traded companies analyzed.

Deploy frequency is highly correlated with continuous delivery and comprehensive version control, lead time with version control and automated testing, and mean time to restore with version control and monitoring.
There is a J-curve in rework: medium performers spend more of their time on unplanned work or rework (about 32%) than low performers (about 27%), while high performers spend the least (about 21%).

High performers do the least manual work across configuration management, testing, deployments, and change approval, but a J-curve appears where medium performers do more manual deployment and change-approval work than low performers.
Job satisfaction as a capability means doing challenging, meaningful work, being empowered to exercise skills and judgment, and being given the tools and resources to do the job well.

A construct should only be used in further analysis after it passes all measurement-validation tests for convergent validity, divergent validity, and reliability (i.e., it exhibits good psychometric properties).

Convergent validity requires average variance extracted (AVE) above 0.50, and divergent validity requires the square root of AVE to exceed cross-construct correlations and inter-construct correlations to be below about 0.85.

Internal-consistency reliability should meet a cutoff of about 0.70, and because Cronbach's alpha is biased against scales with few items, both Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability should be checked.
Report only correlations when no supporting theory exists for a predictive relationship, and test prediction only for hypotheses backed by theory and literature.
Partial least squares regression is a suitable method for exploratory predictive research because it optimizes for prediction of the outcome and does not assume multivariate normality.
Production monitoring should be designed for observability so teams can infer when, where, and why code fails after deployment rather than relying on late manual discovery.
Testing and pre-production environments do not expose all errors that users will encounter after release.
User reports are an unreliable primary detection mechanism because users may not report every issue and may not provide enough detail to reproduce the problem.
Automated monitoring systems are presented as the preferred way to identify high-priority production issues quickly enough to act without wasting time.
condition: when teams need to prioritize production failures from runtime signals

statement: Without automated observability, teams fall back on manual reports and log-based debugging that consume more time and provide a reactive view of failures.
Effective monitoring strategy starts by identifying what failure domain is being monitored and matching tools to that domain.
condition: when designing or revising a production monitoring stack

statement: The source frames production application failures as coming from three operational categories: infrastructure/availability, speed/performance, and functionality/reliability.
Infrastructure and availability monitoring should cover signals such as network health, response time, uptime, CPU, disk, and memory utilization.
condition: when the monitored failure mode is infrastructure or service availability

statement: Application performance monitoring is mainly suited to finding bottlenecks, unusually slow transactions, and methods responsible for latency.
condition: when the monitored failure mode is speed or performance

statement: Functionality and reliability failures require tooling beyond searchable logs when the needed diagnostic data was never logged.
condition: when debugging bugs, exceptions, or reliability failures in staging or production

statement: If diagnostic information is missing from logs, teams may need to add logging, redeploy, and wait for the problematic condition to recur.
condition: when log files lack the runtime details needed for diagnosis

statement: Production alerts should notify teams as soon as a new error is introduced so remediation can begin before severe user or business impact.
condition: when production applications or services are continuously running

statement: Alerts need enough context to identify the error, code location, occurrence count, urgency, first/last occurrence timing, ownership, and whether the error is new or recurring.
condition: when an alert is meant to guide investigation rather than merely signal that something happened

statement: Error dashboards are more useful when they summarize the small set of values that determine importance and urgency for each unique error.
condition: when teams must triage many runtime errors

statement: Root cause analysis should include the causal runtime state, source-code context, and variable values behind each exception, not only the fact that an exception occurred.
condition: when investigating production or staging exceptions

statement: For large systems that emit very high volumes of errors, manually searching logs is not a scalable way to find root causes.
condition: when applications generate hundreds of thousands or millions of errors per day

statement: Some production issues found in logs may still be difficult or impossible to reproduce, so diagnosis should not depend solely on reproduction from log evidence.
condition: when incidents are intermittent or environment-specific

statement: Alert handling should assign issues to the responsible person or team before or as alerts fire, rather than improvising ownership during an outage.
condition: when teams operate shared production systems

statement: Incident response is less effective when team members do not know who owns the affected code, what was deployed, or how alerts should be handled.
Automated alert routing should direct exception-handling tasks to the person responsible for maintaining the affected area.
condition: when ownership information is available for the relevant code or service

statement: Exception handling should follow an explicit processing strategy instead of treating every exception event in isolation.
condition: when exceptions are frequent enough to require team workflow management

statement: Unique exceptions should be acknowledged, handled, and eliminated as they appear under an exception-inbox-zero policy.
condition: when applying inbox-zero practice to exception management

statement: Companies that apply exception-inbox-zero are claimed to gain clearer log files, better application understanding, and more developer focus on important new work.
condition: when exception-inbox-zero is consistently implemented

statement: Third-party tools and integrations are important for scaling alerting workflows and delivering critical runtime details to the right team member.
condition: when alert volume or system scale makes manual alert handling impractical

statement: Integrating error analysis with deployment automation can help teams detect unforeseen error conditions introduced by new releases.
condition: when application servers are instrumented and releases are deployed regularly

statement: Exceptions should be monitored as first-class production signals because new and recurring exceptions both indicate conditions that may require attention.
condition: when operating a production application

statement: Misused or frequent exceptions can create memory, CPU, and logging overhead that degrades application performance.
condition: when exceptions occur at high frequency

statement: An exception whose frequency exceeds a low operational threshold should trigger root-cause investigation rather than being left as background noise.
condition: when exception occurrence rate is materially above the method-call baseline discussed by the source

statement: Exceptions can serve as runtime outputs that reveal otherwise hidden application state, especially when debugging unfamiliar or legacy code.
condition: when exception data is captured with enough context to support diagnosis

statement: Teams should promote observability by using tools and techniques that turn exception events into insight about what is happening inside the application.
condition: when operating or debugging production applications

statement: Logs often contain large amounts of low-value information, making unexpected failures hard to diagnose by manual log search alone.
condition: when log streams are noisy or broad

statement: Exceptions should be reserved for exceptional scenarios that require attention such as acknowledgement, a ticket, or a fix.
condition: when deciding how application code should use exceptions

statement: Better exception handling requires teams to inspect existing exceptions and address each one as part of an exception-inbox-zero practice.
condition: when a team wants to reduce recurring exception noise

statement: Growing exception volume makes it harder to distinguish important exceptions from background noise, increasing the risk that urgent issues are missed or dismissed.
condition: when exception counts are increasing without triage

statement: Keeping exception levels under control can make unresolved performance problems easier to isolate.
condition: when performance problems are connected to exception overhead or exception noise

statement: Teams should measure exception rates rather than relying on raw exception counts alone.
condition: when assessing whether exceptions are operationally acceptable

statement: Root-cause tooling should show how often each exception happens and the failure rate relative to relevant execution volume.
condition: when calculating operational priority for exceptions

statement: Because exceptions disrupt normal control flow, using them as routine application flow is an undesirable design and operations practice.
condition: when exceptions are being used for normal application behavior rather than abnormal conditions

statement: Each exception should be actionable and lead toward code or configuration changes that eliminate the underlying condition.
condition: when applying exception-inbox-zero or production reliability discipline

statement: Reducing manual debugging work can improve developer experience because being stuck on issues is identified as a leading source of developer unhappiness.
condition: when debugging work repeatedly blocks developer progress

statement: Manual production debugging wastes time when engineers must reconstruct the variable state that originally caused an error.
condition: when the runtime state was not captured at failure time

statement: Log files are insufficient for many debugging tasks because the needed data may be absent even when an error is logged.
condition: when diagnostic logging does not capture full runtime state

statement: Some developer unhappiness can be reduced by better tooling, while causes tied to management, planning, or team dynamics are harder to solve with tools alone.
condition: when evaluating which developer pain points a debugging platform can address

statement: High-scale, frequently released applications need rapid detection of every new error or exception that could affect performance or users.
condition: when a service runs at large user/device scale and releases frequently

statement: Inconsistent personal log-query practices cause teams to inspect different signals and can undermine shared alert effectiveness.
condition: when monitoring depends on individual predefined queries rather than shared detection logic

statement: Noisy alerts become less effective at scale and may be disregarded even when some of them represent real problems.
condition: when alert streams are too broad or noisy for teams to prioritize

statement: At large scale, manually pinpointing or reproducing a single production error can consume too much team time and resources.
condition: when millions of devices or users exercise the application

statement: Integrating root-cause analysis with deployment automation and server instrumentation helps detect unknown error conditions introduced by releases.
condition: when teams deploy new versions regularly

statement: Automated analysis can reduce log-sifting work by surfacing issues as soon as they appear.
condition: when runtime instrumentation is deployed with monitoring

statement: A focused exception burn-down effort can reduce application noise and uncover problems that previously escaped investigation.
condition: when automated detection has identified accumulated exceptions and logged errors

statement: Operational dashboards should expose trends and aggregated metrics so teams can find highly problematic areas before user experience is harmed.
condition: when teams monitor application behavior over time

statement: Root-cause tools should group errors by dimensions such as service, server, application, and deployment to support triage at the right operational scope.
condition: when a system has multiple services, servers, apps, or release versions

statement: Teams should create custom alert views that focus on the errors they actually care about rather than treating all captured events equally.
condition: when alert volume exceeds a team’s capacity to review every event

statement: Critical-error notifications should integrate with the team’s existing communication and incident tools so response happens in the normal workflow.
condition: when teams already coordinate through chat, paging, ticketing, or email systems

statement: Capturing code and variable state for production debugging requires controls such as redaction and encryption when sensitive data may be present.
condition: when diagnostic tooling collects source code, variable values, or other sensitive runtime data

statement: Production diagnostic tooling should have low enough overhead to run continuously in staging and production environments.
condition: when the diagnostic tool is intended for always-on runtime monitoring

statement: Regularly shipping quality software is commonly painful, but that pain is avoidable.
The goal of continuous delivery and DevOps is to ship quality software regularly without the pain.
Aim to deliver what the customer wants just before they need it.
condition: releasing too early risks building solutions the customer later abandons, and releasing too late risks losing the customer to a competitor

statement: Small software houses naturally exhibit CD/DevOps-friendly traits because there are minimal barriers between development and operations, who are often the same people.
Giving developers access to the production environment lets them closely monitor their own software.
exception: unrestricted access also enables risky ad-hoc infrastructure changes

statement: Aligning the whole business on getting software into production quickly and delighting customers is characteristic of effective delivery.
When software breaks, having the whole team swarm to fix the problem speeds recovery.
Evolving software in small incremental chunks with frequently added features is a healthy delivery practice.
Cutting corners to hit deadlines compromises software design and elegance.
Under deadline pressure, engineering best practices get compromised.
When time is short, testing is deprioritized and working test-first becomes impractical.
Not using source and version control religiously is a delivery weakness.
Unrestricted production access lets engineers make ad-hoc infrastructure tweaks that later cause outages.
Treating releasing as a mainly manual afterthought of system design is a weakness of immature delivery.
Allowing rough-and-ready prototypes to become production code without the opportunity to refactor is a delivery anti-pattern.
When management treats improvement investments such as source control, automated testing, and automated provisioning as unaffordable time sinks, delivery improvement stalls.
As an organization scales and adds corporate process, software delivery slows so that what once took days takes weeks or months.
Releases become more complex and risky as the platform grows and more integrated features are added.
When developers are removed from the production environment they become ignorant of how their software actually performs once live.
Applying last-minute changes and frantic bug fixes to fit release cycles degrades software quality.
Cutting scope at the last minute to fit a release cycle leaves redundant, dead code behind.
Diverting development resource to assist releases reduces capacity for building new features.
Deployments that cause planned or unplanned downtime erode stakeholder trust and reputation.
Delivery decay is dangerous because it accrues slowly over months and often goes unnoticed by people busy delivering.
Heavy change-ticket bureaucracy and email-only communication between R&D and Operations signal a damaging organizational disjoin.
Tooling alone cannot relieve delivery pain; the fundamental problem is the organization itself and its disjointed silos.
A dedicated continuous-delivery team should act as a catalyst for cultural and behavioral change, not merely as another development team.
Begin a delivery transformation by talking with as many people as possible across the end-to-end conception-to-consumer process, which both gathers information and builds a coalition.
Run in-depth sessions to map out the end-to-end product delivery process.
Refine and simplify delivery tooling continuously based on feedback from the people using it.
Explicitly address the complexity of managing dependencies and deployment ordering.
Engage independent external experts in continuous delivery to assess the progress being made.
Have R&D and Operations attend continuous-delivery and DevOps training together, because collaboration grows from shared, informal contact.
Reduce the number of handover and decision-making points throughout the software release process.
Remove barriers so developers can safely deploy their own software to the production platform.
Share delivery and progress information openly and transparently across all areas of the business.
Let developers closely monitor their own software in production rather than relying solely on complex pre-production performance testing.
A mature pipeline can build, fully test, and deploy a code change to production in under twenty minutes, many times a day, initiated and monitored by the developer who made the change.
A healthy delivery process is not the simplest possible one; it retains useful checks and balances but optimizes them to enhance rather than impede flow.
Reaping delivery rewards depends on letting developers solve problems through code, letting operators run stable platforms, and keeping software and hardware working in harmony.
The only way to fully understand delivery problems is to inspect and adapt, the fundamental premise of agile methods.
Teams often suffer elephant-in-the-room blindness: they recognize a major impediment yet accept or ignore it and invest effort in costly workarounds.
Before investigating a delivery process, define your approach and lay down ground rules.
A process investigation will surface uncomfortable facts, and people emotionally attached to the process they built may react defensively even while you still need them to help fix it.
exception: they may still have an emotional attachment even when they agree the process is broken

statement: Retrospection used incorrectly causes more harm than good, so understand what you are undertaking before you begin.
exception: if used incorrectly it backfires

statement: Avoid closed-session investigations run by management or outside consultants because they breed distrust, non-disclosure, and disengagement.
exception: closed sessions can suit situations needing to contain rumors or quickly gather information

statement: Gather problem information in an open, transparent environment that lacks secrets, without requiring every conversation to be public or every decision made by committee.
Secure management agreement to participate, not drive the agenda, allow subordinates to speak without fear of retribution, stay out of the way, and trust the facilitator.
For distributed teams use video conferencing rather than voice-only, and collocate people where budget permits, because the exercise is highly interpersonal.
condition: teams are not collocated

statement: Include in the investigation almost everyone who actively contributes across the business, prioritizing those who are engaged and want to contribute.
Do not dismiss people with an axe to grind outright, because they may bring valuable observations, but hold them to the ground rules.
Do not run a single interactive session with too many people; split into multiple sessions when oversubscribed, because excess voices add noise rather than information.
Cast the net wide across every role that defines, builds, tests, ships, and supports software to capture the most relevant information.
Open, interactive information-gathering sessions are more effective, engaging, and collaborative than closed sessions.
Use value stream mapping to break a delivery process into steps and handover points and reveal where bottlenecks and non-value-adding delays occur.
In value stream mapping, lead time (idea to revenue) is the key metric.
Every process step, delay, and mistake carries a cost, and real value is created only when the customer uses the software, so long lead times risk losing customers.
Build a value stream map with people from across the business who have hands-on understanding of each stage of the delivery lifecycle.
Start value stream mapping from a recent example project or release rather than the entire business process, which is too daunting at first.
Retrospectives are the inspect half of agile inspect-and-adapt, reviewing a period to highlight what was good and bad.
Run retrospectives as time-boxed, game-based exercises to keep focus and encourage engagement.
The end goal of any retrospective is a set of concrete action points that feed an improvement plan.
The timeline game has the team post notable events and tag their emotions, then discuss the most emotive events to agree stop/start/keep actions.
The StoStaKee exercise collects stop, start, and keep notes with dot-voting to produce a prioritized set of actions.
Engage a specialist to help select and tailor investigation techniques to your culture and environment.
Large, infrequent big-bang releases breed an environment for escaped defects and bugs.

Common delivery problems include too many handover and decision points, unnecessary wait time, big-bang releases, dreaded releases, low morale, changes distrusted until heavily tested, over-complex dependencies, and duplicated tasks.
Set a clear goal and vision and communicate it well, because poor communication loses business and senior-management buy-in.
Continuous delivery and DevOps benefits are hard for the uninitiated to grasp and partly intangible, such as increased collaboration and happiness.
Keep the goal simple (KISS): distill the issue list into one easily understood tagline, such as releasing working code to production ten times per day.
Canvas the opinion of people whose judgment you trust, including PR or marketing, on the proposed goal.
Break the vision into a prioritized backlog with the overall goal as the epic.
Present the goal and vision to as wide an audience as possible, not just management, to gain agreement.
Make all plans, data, and information internally public through wikis, blogs, intranets, and forums to ensure transparency and enable feedback.
Standardize vocabulary, because misinterpreted terms such as release can cause a project to fail when people deliver different things from the same word.
Maintain a shared glossary that defines what each term is and is not.
Once you standardize on terminology, use it consistently across all written and verbal communication so it becomes ingrained.
Treat continuous delivery and DevOps adoption as a full business-change project with the gravitas of any cross-business project, not a skunkworks effort.
Continuous delivery and DevOps impact is far-reaching beyond Development and Operations, so functions like marketing and program management must adapt to a faster cadence.
A reliable delivery capability builds trust that removes the need for backup plans B, C, and D.
You may start small to find your feet, but the business must accept the far-reaching impact before momentum builds, or barriers can stop the implementation.
exception: starting small is fine initially

statement: Assign a dedicated team to a CD/DevOps project, because unbacked skunkworks projects fade away as resourced projects take priority.
Staff the dedicated team with passionate, like-minded people seconded from across the business, not just developers and operations.
Do not recruit a brand-new external team for the implementation, because they lack the business domain knowledge and established connections; second key internal people for months instead.

A dedicated delivery team must comprise more than developers to have credibility, ideally including Development, QA, Operations, and Change Management plus a scrum master, product owner, and senior-manager sponsor.
Prefer collocation for the dedicated team, and where teams are geographically diverse place members on the ground.
condition: teams are geographically diverse

statement: To evangelize CD and DevOps convincingly, you and the team must believe in it completely, because others will not buy in if you do not.
Practice what you preach: build and deploy your own tools using the exact techniques and tools you are evangelizing.
Be patient when evangelizing and use the slowest adopters as a yardstick: when they start to understand, your message is probably right.
Tailor the message to the audience: developers want new technology, operators want stability and predictability, and managers want efficiency and risk reduction.
Do not waste effort on people who refuse to listen, and do not be discouraged by one or two laggards.
exception: win them round if you can

statement: Keep evangelism consistent with the standardized language, goal, and vision, and route new ideas to the backlog rather than promising things outside the agreed scope.
Adopting CD and DevOps requires courage and determination because some necessary decisions are irreversible, such as committing to end big-bang releases with no fallback plan.
Implementing CD and DevOps ultimately saves money through reduced release effort, faster time to market, higher quality, and lower cost of doing business, but it is not free.

Budget for CD/DevOps costs including a dedicated team, process and SOP documentation changes, virtualized hosting, lighter change-management, PR materials, external specialists, and an initial slowdown.
Make the business aware of the costs from the outset so they do not scupper the project later.
Expect indirect costs such as people who cannot accept the change leaving, and renegotiate contractual deadlines during the transition slowdown.
condition: you have contractual deadlines during the transition

statement: Reach out to the CD/DevOps community and experts before transforming the business rather than struggling alone.
CD rests on the premise that quality software can be developed, built, tested, and shipped quickly and repeatedly, ideally within hours or days.
In most projects, development, build, and test are already fast; it is shipping that consumes the time.
Finding software problems early is essential, because problems not caught early slow the project later, whereas software delivered with almost no bugs is easy to release.
Always use source control, for which there is no excuse given the many commercial and open-source options, gaining versioning, availability, security, and backup.
Store anything that can be represented as a text file in source control, including system configuration, startup scripts, and server and network configuration, not just application code.
Keep changes small and frequent, because small changes have small impact, reduced risk, and increased opportunities for change.
Small changes ease code merging and enable working from trunk all of the time.
Apply the small-frequent-change discipline to operations too, because an isolated server-configuration tweak is safer and its impact easier to attribute than sweeping changes.
Model platform dependencies as consumer/provider relationships governed by a predefined interface or service contract.
When a provider changes the data or contract it exposes, consumers that do not expect the change can error or crash.
Apply the never-break-your-consumer rule to operations as well, ensuring an OS change or upgrade does not break the platform that consumes it.
Treat breaking changes as the exception, and when one is unavoidable plan a strategy such as side-by-side versioning to run multiple versions at once.
exception: sometimes the interface spec must change to add functionality

statement: Provider teams are often unaware of all their consumers, so open and honest peer working practices reduce the risk of breaking them.
Share your code rather than treating it as precious, because everyone makes mistakes and hoarding code creates bugs and wastes time.
Include Operations in the peer-review group, not only developers, because they understand how the live platform behaves and ask pertinent questions.
Apply peer review to operations configuration changes too, because more eyes reviewing any platform change reduce risk.
A change that fails peer review never reaches production, which is failing fast rather than discovering the failure live.
Fail fast and often, because a bug caught after going live costs far more to fix and can damage reputation and revenue.
Use test-driven development to find faults early by writing tests before code, so failures impact only the engineer rather than customers.
Do not chastise people for bugs found early; instead find the problem, understand why it happened, fix it, learn, and move on.
When retrofitting tests onto a legacy platform not built for them is daunting, start small and build the suite up.
condition: the platform was not built around testing principles

statement: Automate build and test for speed, consistency, repeatability, and confidence, because manual processes are slow, inconsistent, and error-prone.
When a consistently passing automated process suddenly fails after a change, it is strong evidence the change broke something.
Start automated testing by covering the primary use cases (KISS) and refine or add tests over time, and have each test create and tear down its own data to avoid stale test data.
Continuous integration is a must for continuous delivery, because building and testing changes frequently is what lets you ship frequently.
CI also helps operations by running changes against an isolated test environment, where a previously green suite failing after a single config change pinpoints the cause.
A legacy monolith that must be released as one single bundle severely restricts CD and DevOps.
The real constraint on delivery is often the release process rather than the architecture, since even tightly coupled platforms are made of small components.
When re-engineering a platform, prefer loosely coupled, discrete modules such as web services or SOA so components can be developed and released separately.
A component-based architecture enables small, frequent releases and simplifies the platform infrastructure.
A component-based architecture still released as one big bang is more painful than releasing a legacy platform.
Use layers of abstraction, such as SQL views between code and database, to remove hard dependencies so you do not have to deploy tightly coupled assets together.
