Do not go overboard on environments, because too many environments are counterproductive and create noise and overhead.
The ideal minimum is two environments, development and production, which many small businesses run successfully.
exception: as a business grows, risk-aversion drives the need for more environments

statement: The hard part of having many environments is keeping them all in line on software versions, OS patch levels, and network configuration.
A sufficient lean environment set is development, CI, pre-production, and production.
Build a release binary once and use the self-same unchanged binary in every environment including production.
Hold environment-specific configuration in version-controlled startup scripts or config files loaded at runtime, so one binary serves all environments with per-environment configuration.
Version binaries and store them in a repository, just like source code.
Develop against a like-live environment that contains the live versions of code, so the production dependencies your software expects are validated.
Do not develop directly against production because of the high risk of inadvertently causing an outage; a like-live environment is the next best thing.
Do not develop against CI versions, because you cannot know which CI versions will go live before yours, especially when someone is testing a breaking change.
A like-live environment only needs to match production software and infrastructure versions, not necessarily live data, and should be deployed to only after a successful production deployment.
exception: populating it with live data is good but usually too costly

statement: Deployment-orchestration tooling is scarce and may not fit your ways of working, so consider building your own to future-proof the CD process.
CD tooling is relied upon daily, so it must be excellent, very easy to use, and ideally one click to deploy.
Treat in-house CD tooling as an internally open, shared product so the whole engineering team, not just the dedicated team, can extend it.

Evaluate CD tooling against deploying the same binary to multiple environments, repository access, remote install control, database changes, environment-specific config, release queuing, security, no-downtime deployment, automated provisioning, integrations, dashboards, CI orchestration, scalability, and simplicity.
CD tooling should record an audit of what was deployed, when, and by whom.
On virtual infrastructure, make automated provisioning a deployment step: provision the server, deploy the asset, install it, add it to the platform, and start using it.
condition: the platform can run on virtual infrastructure

statement: Automated provisioning at deployment time helps enable no-downtime deployments.
Taking the platform offline to release software is avoidable and unacceptable for a real-time service, because downtime breeds customer distrust and drives them to competitors.

Achieve no-downtime deployments by following never-break-your-consumer, keeping changes small and discrete, using automated provisioning, orchestrating servers in and out of a load-balanced pool, and rolling out unavoidable breaking changes gradually from the bottom of the stack up.
Treat every environment you depend on for development, testing, and CD with the same maximum-uptime expectation as production.
Monitor everything across all environments so the impact of any change is visible and there are no hidden surprises.
Make monitoring visible to everyone in the business, not just the Operations team.
Aggregate disparate monitoring tools, such as infrastructure monitoring and application metrics, into a single unified and coherent view.
Mark deployments on time-series monitoring graphs so you can visually confirm or rule out a change's impact, including proof that CD is not harming production.
Simple manual processes still have a place, because over-automation can rebuild barriers and remove the human interaction that DevOps depends on.

Use a deployment-transaction rule, agreeing that only one change goes to production at a time enforced by collaboration rather than tooling, which gives an implied safe ordering and avoids dependency hell.

Support the one-change-at-a-time rule with a physical production-change token, a whiteboard deployment queue agreed at a daily stand-up, real-time chat that announces deployments, an optional dedicated deployment station, and simple rollback by redeploying the previous version.
Ensure everyone in the delivery process can openly discuss ideas, issues, and concerns without fear of ridicule or retribution.
Openness and honesty are key to making CD and DevOps work, because without them you cannot break down the barriers.
Give every role a forum to share thoughts and actively encourage its use.
Do not heavy-handedly police or moderate collaboration tools, because it discourages openness and makes the tool redundant.
Maintain a quick feedback loop on what is and is not working, with walking around and asking people the simplest effective method, or lightweight surveys when that is impractical.
Provide a safe zone, amnesty, or anonymous channel for courageous dialogue so people can speak up without it counting against their record.
When several people independently raise the same point, treat it as a real issue that needs addressing.
Treating no news as good news is misguided, because absence of feedback hides impending failure.
Embedding CD and DevOps is hard, complex, time-consuming, and frustrating, but perseverance makes it work very effectively.

The physical environment affects open dialogue, so remove barriers by opening or removing doors, creating communal areas, holding a scrum of scrums, removing cubicles, and moving people closer together.
condition: the office is not open-plan and has physical barriers

statement: Stop relying on email for communication and encourage people to talk and agree in person, following up with email only if needed.
People naturally drift back into silos, especially during lulls in implementation activity, so keep collaborative working at the forefront as the default mode of operation.
Make collaborating the easy choice and do not force it, because people need to feel the new way of working is their own idea.
Watch and listen for early signs of teams slipping back into silos and use your network to detect it.
Foster grassroots innovation and build a culture that recognizes it as worthwhile rather than a risky way to advance a product.
Allow engineers room for investigation and experimentation while still delivering the product.
Innovation is not the exclusive right of architects; give everyone the opportunity to contribute ideas, for example through a regular innovation forum.
With the freedom to innovate comes responsibility, ownership, and accountability for what is produced, because new things increase risk.
A culture of blame quickly erodes openness, honesty, collaboration, innovation, and accountability.
When mistakes happen, encourage people to learn, prevent recurrence, share the lessons, and move on without a big song and dance.
Adopt a blame-slow, learn-quickly culture: do not blame people who quickly and openly fix issues, and instead focus on those who create issues but do not fix or own them.
As blame diminishes, learning grows, because people stop looking over their shoulders and sticking only to what they are told.
Trust is earned over time through people's actions, not granted by decree, so building it requires patience.
Distrust between Development and Operations is common and deeply ingrained, and the business must overcome it to deliver effectively.

Build Dev/Ops trust by mixing software and operations engineers at training and conferences with shared social time, keeping promises, discouraging us-and-them behavior, and organizing job swaps or secondments.

Do not reward failure: celebrating a release that missed scope or took the platform offline sends the wrong message, because failing to deliver what the business asked for or impacting customers is a failure.
Reward people for delivering what is needed when or before it is needed, and make the reward a group reward rather than targeting an individual.

Reserve special rewards for genuinely exceptional, above-and-beyond effort such as clearing technical debt, not for routine releases, and treat consistent long hours as a sign of mis-prioritized work.
As releases become continuous and individually unnoticeable, shift rewards toward business milestones such as a customer count or product launch.
condition: CD and DevOps are embedded so individual releases are no longer noticeable

statement: Recognize the structural conflict that Development teams are incentivized to deliver change while Operations teams are incentivized to ensure stability and uptime, so their incentives are at odds.
Realign incentives by sharing them across Dev and Ops, cross-including each side in the other's scheme, or ideally replacing the scheme with one that rewards good DevOps behaviors.
Whatever the incentive scheme, instill positivity around change while ensuring risk is reduced.
Any change to production increases risk, and since eliminating risk entirely by changing nothing is impractical, the goal is to manage, reduce, and accept risk.
CD and DevOps reduce change risk through small incremental changes, transparency, the building and supporting teams working together, and individual ownership and accountability.

Convince risk-averse functions that risk is controlled with a proof-of-the-pudding demonstration: take a small change, publicize it, invite observers, post regular blog updates with stats such as code coverage and test pass rate, capture metrics through to production, and present a post-release report.
Run a full proof-of-the-pudding demonstration only once or twice to build confidence, because doing it for every change is too costly.
exception: doing it for every change consumes too much time

statement: Small changes vastly reduce risk and repeating the process many times all but removes it, whereas infrequent releases containing large change carry large risk.
Being highly visible about what you are doing is key to breaking down barriers, because secrecy undermines an open, honest, trust-based culture.

Install big screens that display business-relevant CD information such as release counts versus prior periods, the release queue and who initiated it, production availability, and business metrics, not just technical stats.
Displaying improvement data visibly provides proof that things are getting better.
Expect hurdles including change-resistant individuals, the impatient, emotional reactions, lack of external visibility, corporate red tape, distributed teams, tooling problems, and recruitment.
A few loud dissenters can divert attention from the vision and goal, so do not let them.
Adopters fall into three types: a small number of innovators, a larger group of followers, and laggards; focus effort on the innovators and followers who form the majority.
Do not over-invest attention in laggards; they either shape up or ship out, even if they are senior managers.
When the majority have bought in based on their own input, they will not be easily distracted, so use your network to reduce dissenter noise and convert laggards into followers.
Address troublemakers with a calm, non-confrontational face-to-face conversation, escalating to their manager only as a last resort, and never resort to email tennis.
A lull in visible progress lets dissenting voices gain ground, so communicate progress regularly even when little is happening.
Recognize that identifying and removing a problem is itself a big change that affects individuals emotionally and should not be taken lightly.
People respond to change differently, welcoming, accepting, or hostile, and the same person can be all of these, so anticipate this before implementing change.
Use a transition or change curve to understand the stages an individual goes through as change is implemented.
People may traverse the change curve multiple times at their own unique speed, even quiet people are somewhere on it, and those stuck in the dip need more help, guidance, and leadership.
Leaders and the change agents themselves also move through the change curve, so be mindful that it applies to everyone including you.
The proportion of people actively involved depends on organization size, and in a corporate most people are outsiders to the implementation.
Outsiders ignorant of your work may unknowingly obstruct it, for example when a corporate strategy change is made without awareness of your effort.
Watch the wider organization, not just close to home, and extend communication and visibility beyond the immediate team, for example through internal comms and PR.
Good PR can attract senior-leadership recognition and even sway management dissenters to reconsider their position.
Regulatory or SLA obligations constrain how you implement CD and DevOps, so work with the rule-setters to find what wriggle room exists.
condition: you operate under commercial SLAs or regulatory guidelines

statement: Some corporate rules are overkill, kept because following the book was easier than tailoring them to the business.
Change-management and auditability rules provide a safety gate and a record of recent changes, so do not ignore or break them; instead work with their owners to adapt them.
Owners of processes flagged as waste may be defensive about change, so help them understand CD and DevOps and what they can safely change, using open, honest, and courageous dialogue.

For geographically diverse teams, use daily teleconferences, dial remote teams into the scrum of scrums, run an always-on video link as a virtual window, swap people between offices, and use chat and forums instead of email.
condition: teams are geographically diverse

statement: Time-zone and cultural differences complicate stand-ups and openness, so work with local HR or management and be mindful that not all cultures are equally open.
condition: teams span time zones and cultures

statement: Lead by example in how you react to change so others learn how to deal with it.
Use agile methods such as scrum or Kanban to drive the implementation so you can change direction quickly without impeding progress.
A one-change-at-a-time deployment transaction that worked at slow release speed can itself hinder CD once releases become fast, because an asset ready first must wait on its dependencies.
When a deployment-transaction rule blocks flow, move its boundary so full integration testing happens before assets go to production, and have teams work out the deploy order.
Keep reviewing and listening to people so you can spot potential hurdles before they fully block progress, using open, honest, and courageous dialogue.
Inconsistent, non-repeatable process results erode trust, because people will not use automation they cannot rely on.
Internal and labor-saving tooling must be production quality, not held to a lower standard merely because only internal staff use it.
You must be able to trust that the same actions produce the same results, so that differing results reliably signal something has gone wrong.
Consistent, repeatable results enable useful metrics, such as a stable deploy time whose increase flags an infrastructure issue or a bug in the CD tooling.
As output, efficiency, and reputation grow, recruitment becomes a priority, and you must hire people who will work the new way and exhibit the embedded behaviors.
Putting experience in CD and DevOps on a job spec will not work, because few people have it and recruiters rarely understand the term.
Repeatedly knowledge-share with your recruiters until they understand what you are looking for.
Use an emotionally framed interview question, such as how a candidate would feel if their code reached production thirty minutes after commit, to filter for cultural fit.
Take time to pick the right people, because you need innovators and followers more than laggards.
Measure as many aspects of the delivery process as possible so you can see how far you have come and how far you have to go.
Start measuring early, because you cannot compare now to then without baseline data representing then.
Do not cut corners on monitoring and reporting, because most of it is long-lived and becomes integral, and a poor solution quickly erodes trust.

Measure engineering best practice through code quality, complexity, unit-test coverage, comments-versus-code, and commit rates, while remembering these metrics can hide bad practice as well as highlight good, so agree first what constitutes good and bad.
Sell code-analysis tools to engineers as a positive benefit and involve dissenters in configuring thresholds, because engineers may otherwise feel the measurement questions their craftsmanship.
Encourage comments in source code for future readability and maintenance, while watching for engineers who game the metric with filler comments.
Overly complex code harms debugging and extension, so measure complexity using a metric such as cyclomatic complexity and understand the underlying principles before setting thresholds.
exception: some highly optimized or real-time code legitimately needs complexity

statement: Unit-test coverage is only meaningful when unit tests or TDD are in use, and the coverage percentage can be misread as risk, so set context, especially for new tests on an existing codebase.
exception: quality code can be produced without unit tests

statement: Encourage frequent commits to source control, because code left on workstations is risky and causes duplication or blocking, and holding off committing is the real risk rather than committing often.
Use commit-rate league tables cautiously, because they can invite the wrong behaviors.
exception: they can invite the wrong behaviors

statement: Remove redundant, unused code, because it wastes debugging time and can mislead root-cause analysis, using tools to find dead code and starting small to gain authority.
Detect duplicate code and refactor it into shared libraries, because duplication increases the effort to change the same logic in multiple places.
Analyze adherence to coding standards to highlight areas of potential risk, agreeing rule severities with the engineering teams.
Measuring code quality is worthwhile because it provides quality proof that builds trust, aids componentization, and frees engineers to focus on new features.
Add code-quality analysis as gates within CI so a component that fails the checks goes no further even if its build and tests pass.
Most code-analysis tools target mainstream languages, so consider building your own where your stack is not covered.
condition: your language stack is not covered by available tools

statement: Blaming a live problem on an environmental issue without proof is counterproductive and damages Dev/Ops relationships.
Resolve the software-versus-infrastructure blame impasse by proving conclusively which layer is healthy, or by agreeing to find the root cause collaboratively in a DevOps way.

Group automated tests and run them continuously against an environment with a simple pass/fail dashboard, so you can see environment health and pinpoint root cause from what changed since the last green run.

Continuous test suites carry caveats: they need good coverage, heterogeneous tests may conflict, tests with mocking or stubbing may not be bulletproof, some tests flap, and long sequential runs take hours.
Combine automated tests with continuous infrastructure monitoring of CPU, storage, memory, and network to judge whole-environment health and where problems originate.
Combining test and monitoring outputs into one dashboard takes effort to normalize the formats.
Automated tests plus monitoring prove only that the platform is up and tests pass, and are largely limited to non-production because you cannot freely run test data in production.
To truly understand behavior, gather data from deep within the software itself, not just external observation, just as a Formula One team relies on in-car sensor data.
Existing logs such as HTTP and error logs are a head start for deep metrics, but real-time log harvesting is difficult and storage-heavy.
Build health-check functionality into component APIs so a health-checker tool can query each component and report its health.
The pull-based health-checker approach is limited by API design and is itself a single point of failure that blinds you if it stops working.
Prefer having components push their own metrics to a platform such as Graphite, which avoids API changes and the single-point-of-failure of a central poller.
Post CD deployment markers onto metric graphs so you can spot release-related incidents immediately, for example a TPS drop just after a release indicating a likely bug.
Roll a change back by re-releasing the previous version of the component.
Agree collaboratively between Dev and Ops what deep metrics to capture, because the richest picture comes from combining in-depth software metrics, automated tests, and system monitoring.
Provide return-on-investment and business-level metrics, because CD and DevOps are costly and managers want summary information rather than low-level technical counts.
The key CD and DevOps measures are improvements in efficiency and throughput, because they translate directly into faster time to market and value realization.

Build CD metrics into the tooling, capturing deployment count, time to take a release candidate to production, commit-to-production time, release-candidate count, components released, and unique components in the pipeline.
Summarize CD metrics simply, display them on office screens, and use them to open discussions about progress and where optimization is still needed.
Include financial data such as cost per release to inform managers and help engineers understand what activities cost.
Do not restrict access to metrics; keep them highly visible so everyone can see progress against the original goal.
Share all collected metrics including bad news for transparency, because refusing to air dirty laundry is just an excuse.
Never forget the original goal and vision, because you will be sidetracked and must refine direction while sticking to the overall aim.
As you near the goal, the original major issues are replaced by new, smaller problems that now matter, because the release process has become effortless background noise.
Surfacing of new problems is positive, because teams freed from big-release constraints can now address improvements previously dismissed as low priority.
Reaching the goal is not a failure when new issues appear; tweak and refine the goal by inspecting and adapting rather than starting over.
Plan an exit strategy so the business, now equipped with the tools, knowledge, and confidence, owns the new issues rather than the CD team.
Shift the dedicated team's focus from delivering to assisting delivery, pushing others to take responsibility for their own problems.
Once the business can identify and remove new impediments quickly, guard against complacency.
Consider extending CD and DevOps to the pre and post stages of product creation to unlock greater business value.
condition: it fits the business needs and the biggest pain points

statement: After a successful implementation the dedicated team becomes the subject-matter experts, while most of the business is now where the team started.
The CD and DevOps landscape constantly changes with new tools and ideas, so stay engaged with the community to share findings and bring knowledge back.

Decide deliberately whether to retain a dedicated team to advance tooling, train people, evangelize, and prevent regression, or to disband and embed its members back into engineering at the grassroots.
Avoid creating elitists who become disconnected from day-to-day work.
A vast amount of CD and DevOps success is built on behaviors, culture, and environment, not just technical choices and tools.
Teams who successfully implement CD and DevOps seldom regret it or are tempted to return to the era when releases meant working late nights and weekends.

You need not implement CD and DevOps at the same time, but each complements the other, because Dev and Ops cannot collaborate well without fast releases and fast releases require Dev and Ops to collaborate.
For technical choices such as tooling, seek advice and do not settle for something that is only pretty close and then bend your ways of working to fit the tool.
Build bespoke in-house tools when they fit better, and consider open-sourcing them to help others starting out.
Reach out to the global CD and DevOps community for help, assistance, and advice.
Do not adopt CD or DevOps merely because it is the new thing; have a good reason, or you will neither reap the benefits nor truly believe in it.
Do not implement everything you read about; take the parts that work for your situation, as you would with any agile methodology.
Embed inspect-and-adapt deeply in everyone's mindset and bring it to bear whenever you hit hurdles.
Share both failures and successes so that you learn and others can learn from you.
Persevere and do not give up, because the journey is hard but the rewards are worth it.
SRE principles and practices are intended to apply at any scale, not only at Google's scale or within Google's culture.
The core SRE operating rule is to set the service level as a measurable target and, when the service is below that target, prioritize reliability work over shipping new features.
condition: when the service is below its SLO target

statement: DevOps is a loose, generic set of principles while SRE is an opinionated, explicit implementation of them ('class SRE implements interface DevOps'); the two are complementary, not in conflict.

SRE is deliberately highly opinionated; the authors state it is not the only way, nor necessarily the universally best way, to build and operate highly reliable systems — only the way most successful for them.
Adopting SRE should mean making definitive behavior changes focused on outcomes and reliability, not merely relabeling existing operations roles or job titles.
When adopting SRE, also revisit adjacent concerns such as architecture, security, governance, and compliance and convert the people responsible for them into allies, or expect internal resistance.

DevOps is a loose set of practices and culture for breaking down silos across development, operations, networking, and security, summarized by the acronym CALMS: Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, and Sharing.
Break down silos: separate operations and development teams, siloization of knowledge, and incentives for purely local optimization have in many cases been actively bad for business.
Accidents are normal: failures result from missing safeguards for when things inevitably go wrong rather than from the isolated actions of a single individual.
It is more profitable to focus on speeding recovery than on preventing accidents, because punishing the mistake-maker only creates incentives to confuse issues, hide the truth, and blame others.
Make changes small and frequent: split changes into smaller subcomponents where possible and build a steady pipeline of low-risk change rather than batching large changes for periodic review.
exception: higher-risk changes, or those not validatable by automated means, should still be vetted by humans

statement: Couple small, frequent changes with automatic testing of those changes and reliable rollback of bad changes, which leads to continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment.
DevOps proponents emphasize organizational culture over tooling as the key to success: a good culture can work around broken tooling, but the opposite rarely holds true.
Use objective measurement to establish the reality of what is happening, verify that changes have the expected effect, and create an objective foundation that different functions can agree upon.
The basic tenet of SRE is that doing operations well is a software problem, so SRE should use software-engineering approaches to solve it.

Do not attempt to give a service 100% availability — that is the wrong target; instead the product and SRE teams jointly select an appropriate availability SLO for the service and its user base and manage the service to that objective.
Treat SLO violations as blameless triggers that bring stakeholder teams back to the drawing board, since the SLO was a collaborative decision among stakeholders.

Minimize toil: if a machine can perform a desired operation, then a machine often should, because any time spent on operational tasks is time not spent on project work that makes services more reliable and scalable.
exception: under operational underload, push new features and changes more often so engineers stay familiar with the service

statement: Operational tasks provide 'the wisdom of production' — real-time feedback on how a system actually behaves — that should inform better system design rather than a whiteboarded view isolated from the facts on the ground.
Cap the time an SRE team member spends on toil at 50%, and treat this limit as a guarantee of engineering time for an engineering-based approach rather than merely as a ceiling.

A main benefit of SRE engagement is improved product-development velocity, not just increased reliability, because a reduced mean time to repair (MTTR) for common faults frees developers from cleaning up after issues; the later in the product lifecycle a problem is discovered, the more expensive it is to fix.

Share ownership across product-development and SRE teams: both should have a holistic view of the whole stack and no team should jealously own single components, since blurring the lines spreads the knowledge and authority to make changes.
An SRE's core competencies are the availability, latency, performance, efficiency, change management, monitoring, emergency response, and capacity planning of the services they look after.

Product-development teams own their services by default; SRE is a shared ownership model that is neither available nor warranted for the bulk of services, though SRE principles still inform how all services are managed.

Teams minding a service should use the same tools regardless of role or job title, because divergent tooling between SREs and product developers can behave differently in different situations and reduces the benefit of every tooling improvement.
Do not over-focus on a specific toolset: API orientation for system management is a more important philosophy that will outlast any particular tool implementation.

Do not structure incentives to be narrowly tied to launch-related or reliability-related outcomes: any single numeric measure will be gamed (Goodhart's law), so allow people the freedom to find the right tradeoffs.
Engage SRE early, ideally at design time, because a system with early SRE engagement typically works better in production after deployment regardless of who later manages the service.

Remove incentives to pass blame between groups: actively encourage engineers to change code and configuration when required, support blameless postmortems, and allow support to be withdrawn from irredeemably operationally difficult products.
exception: support-withdrawal leverage assumes a sufficiently large organization; it makes little sense for a very small single-product startup

statement: Strive for parity of esteem: hold DevOps/SRE roles in the same esteem as their product-development counterparts by rating them with roughly the same methods and giving them the same financial incentives.

Implementing DevOps or SRE is a journey, not a quick fix: it requires management support and buy-in from the people doing the work, and the practice of 'rename-and-shame' (retitling a team without changing its practices) yields no benefit.
The basic foundations of SRE are SLOs, monitoring, alerting, toil reduction, and simplicity.
A well-thought-out and adopted SLO is the key tool for making data-informed decisions about the opportunity cost of reliability work and for prioritizing that work.
SREs' day-to-day tasks are driven by SLOs — defending them in the short term and keeping them maintainable in the medium to long term; without SLOs there is no need for SREs.
Prioritize between competing reliability projects by calculating each project's estimated impact on the error budget to determine which is most beneficial to users.

Adopting an error-budget-based approach requires four preconditions: SLOs approved by all stakeholders, agreement that the SLO is achievable under normal circumstances, an organizational commitment (formalized in an error budget policy) to use the budget for decision-making, and a process for refining the SLO; otherwise SLO compliance is merely another KPI rather than a decision-making tool.

An SLO sets a target level of reliability for the service's customers: above the threshold almost all users are happy, below it users start to complain or stop using the service; ultimately user happiness is what matters.

Each additional nine of reliability comes at increased cost while its marginal utility to customers steadily approaches zero, partly because the long, complex chain of systems between you and your customers means they never experience your internal 100%.

Change — pushing new features, applying security patches, deploying new hardware, and scaling up — is the number one source of outages, so a service kept 100% reliable can never be updated or improved.

An SLO below 100% must be owned by someone empowered to make tradeoffs between feature velocity and reliability — typically the CTO in a small organization or the product owner/manager in a larger one.

A service level agreement (SLA) is distinct from an SLO: an SLA is a business contract that comes into effect — typically requiring compensation — when users are so unhappy that they must be compensated.
Express each SLI as the ratio of good events to total events on a scale from 0% to 100%, and define the error budget as 100% minus the SLO.
Make all SLIs follow a consistent numerator/denominator/threshold style so that alerting logic, SLO analysis tools, error-budget calculation, and reports can all expect the same inputs.

Separate the SLI specification (the user-relevant outcome, independent of how it is measured) from the SLI implementation (the specification plus a way to measure it); a single specification can have multiple implementations differing in quality, coverage, and cost.
Your first SLI and SLO do not have to be correct; the most important goal is to get something measured and to set up a feedback loop so you can improve.

Avoid setting an SLO purely from current performance, which can commit you to unnecessarily strict targets; current performance is acceptable only as a starting point when paired with a good iteration process, and should not limit later refinement.
condition: acceptable as a starting point only when a good iteration process is in place

statement: Choose a small number of SLI types — five or fewer — that represent the most critical functionality to your customers.

To start defining SLIs, pick aspects that are relevant but easy to measure: choose one application, decide clearly who the users are, consider common user interactions, and draw a high-level architecture diagram showing key components, request flow, data flow, and critical dependencies.

Abstract a system into a few common component types — request-driven, pipeline, and storage — and choose SLI types relevant to each: availability, latency, and quality for request-driven; freshness, correctness, and coverage for pipelines; and durability for storage.

Use multiple grades (thresholds) of SLO for an SLI to capture both the typical user experience and the long tail — for example, 90% of requests faster than 100 ms and 99% of requests faster than 400 ms.

For your first SLI implementation, choose the option that requires the minimum engineering work — for example, use already-available web server logs rather than spending weeks setting up probes or months instrumenting JavaScript.

When an option is already available, prefer SLI implementations that more closely capture the actual user experience — for example, load-balancer monitoring gives SLIs closer to the user than application-server logs.
If a correctness SLI is based on manually curated test data, ensure that curated data is representative of real-world data, or the SLI will not be representative of the actual user experience.

Choose the SLO time window deliberately: rolling windows align more closely with user experience while calendar windows align with business planning; define a rolling window as an integral number of weeks so it always contains the same number of weekends; use shorter windows for quick course-corrections and longer windows for strategic project decisions.
A four-week rolling window is a good general-purpose SLO interval, complemented by weekly summaries for task prioritization and quarterly summarized reports for project planning.

Get explicit stakeholder agreement before relying on an SLO: product managers accept the threshold as good enough for users, developers commit to reducing risk when the error budget is exhausted, and the production team agrees the SLO is defensible without Herculean effort, excessive toil, or burnout.
Defend an SLO by setting up monitoring and alerting so that engineers receive timely notifications of threats to the error budget before those threats become deficits.
Once you have an SLO, derive an error budget from it, and create a policy outlining what to do when the service runs out of budget.

Getting the error budget policy approved by all key stakeholders — product manager, development team, and SREs — is a good test of whether the SLOs are fit for purpose; if all three parties do not agree to enforce it, iterate on the SLIs and SLOs until they do.

Lowering an SLO also lowers the number of situations to which SREs will respond, and the product manager must understand this tradeoff when reliability objectives are relaxed to protect feature velocity.
Enforcing an error budget means that once you exhaust it (or come close), you take written, pre-agreed actions to restore stability; the policy must specify the actions and who will take them.

Common error-budget-exhaustion actions are: the development team gives top priority to reliability bugs, the development team focuses exclusively on reliability until the system is within SLO (with approval to push back on external feature requests), and a production freeze halts risky changes until budget is restored.

Document the SLO prominently with its authors, reviewers, and approvers, approval and next-review dates, a service description, the objectives and SLI implementations, how the error budget is calculated and consumed, and the rationale for the numbers — recording even that an SLO is ad hoc so future engineers do not make bad decisions based on it.
Review the SLO document at a cadence matched to the maturity of your SLO culture: frequently (perhaps monthly) when starting out, and quarterly or less often once the SLO is established.

The documented error budget policy must include a clear escalation path to follow when there is disagreement on the error-budget calculation or on whether the agreed actions are appropriate in the circumstances.

Maintain reports and dashboards that show in-time SLO compliance and SLI trends, so you can communicate status to other teams and detect when you are consuming error budget at a higher-than-usual rate.

Use error budget consumption to quantify and rank incidents — for example 'this outage consumed 30% of the quarterly error budget' — and identify the most critical incidents that merit closer investigation.

To improve SLO targets you need a source of information about user satisfaction (manually discovered outages, forum posts, support tickets, social sentiment, in-code happiness sampling, or surveys); start with a measurement that is cheap to collect and iterate from there.

Validate an SLO by checking that periods of known outages or support-ticket spikes correlate with drops in the error budget (for example using Spearman's rank correlation), and investigate outliers where they do not.

If outages or ticket spikes are not captured by any SLI/SLO, or SLI dips and SLO misses do not map to user-facing issues, the SLO lacks coverage; treat this as normal and refine SLIs and SLOs over time as the service changes.

When tightening an SLO to improve recall (the fraction of user-impacting events captured), do not lower precision so far that the team must constantly respond to unimportant events; balance recall against precision.
Improve an SLI implementation in one of two ways: move the measurement closer to the user to improve metric quality, or improve coverage so it captures a higher percentage of user interactions.

When you need a tighter SLO but improving the product to meet it will take time, declare an aspirational SLO that is measured and tracked alongside the current SLO but explicitly marked in the error budget policy as not requiring action, so you can track progress without a perpetual state of emergency.
condition: when a tighter SLO is needed but the product cannot yet meet it

statement: When iterating on SLOs, pick the option most likely to give the highest return on investment, and especially in the first few iterations err on the side of quicker and cheaper metrics to reduce uncertainty before investing in expensive ones.

Drive SLO-based action from three dimensions — performance against the SLO, the amount of toil required to operate the service, and the level of customer satisfaction — for example tightening the SLO when it is met but satisfaction is low, or offloading toil and fixing the product when the SLO is missed with high toil and low satisfaction.
If a service runs flawlessly and needs little oversight, move it to a less hands-on tier of support and refocus SRE effort on systems that need more support.
condition: when the service is running flawlessly and needs little oversight

statement: Write SLOs in terms of user-centric actions, and use critical user journeys — sequences of core tasks essential to a user's experience — to capture customer experience; modeling critical user journeys improves recall without affecting precision.

Grade interaction importance because not all requests are equal: use bucketing — add labels to SLIs and apply different SLOs per label, for example by customer tier (premium 99.99% vs free 99.9%) or by expected responsiveness.

A critical dependency's reliability guarantee should be at least as high as the reliability guarantee of the action that depends on it, and the team that runs that component must own and manage its SLO like the overarching product SLO.

If a component has inherent reliability limitations below what a dependent user journey needs, engineer around the limitation — use a different component or add defenses such as caching, offline store-and-forward processing, or graceful degradation.

Do not naively compute reliability gains from redundancy: deploying a service in two zones does not multiply independent failure probabilities because instances share dependencies, failure domains, shared fate, and global control planes, so such calculations are deceptive unless every shared dependency and failure pattern is enumerated and accounted for.

When a missed SLO is caused by another team's dependency, enacting a change freeze regardless of the cause makes users happier than continuing to release; decide what is practical for your service and record the decision in the documented error budget policy.
exception: freezing changes may not be practical depending on the nature of the outage and dependency

statement: Experiment with deliberately relaxing reliability (for example adding latency) to measure its impact on user behavior only when you are confident you have error budget to burn; cross this Rubicon thoughtfully and beware misinterpreting the data, since no measured conversion loss may simply mean users currently lack an alternative.
condition: only when confident there is error budget to burn

statement: An error-budget/SLO approach removes subjectivity from reliability conversations so that operations and development teams make similar decisions when presented with the same facts; the SRE model embraces the differences between ops and dev rather than transforming one discipline into the other.

Start the SLO conversation from the customer's point of view — what promises you are trying to uphold — and make your first SLO the single most important, common customer need (for example service availability), keeping the first pass simple.

Measure availability with a status endpoint that exercises most of the stack and returns 200 when healthy, polled by an external prober independent of your environment so it tests all components including load balancing; require a second, geographically separate prober to confirm a failure before marking a node down, to avoid false positives from random internet issues.
Treat planned maintenance windows as downtime in SLO calculations, because uninformed users experience them as generic, unexplained downtime.

Perfect is the enemy of good: an imperfect SLO that covers most (but not all) user interactions is good enough to guide improvement over time, and is preferable to spending months chasing a perfect SLO that measures every interaction and edge case.
When defining and revising SLOs, balance what you would like to measure against what is actually possible to measure.

Adopt a periodic SLO review cycle that strikes a balance between changing SLOs too often and letting them become stale — for example a six-month review cycle complemented by a monthly SLO performance review.

Do not build a wall between yourself and your cloud provider: share your SLO and real-time performance against it so both teams work from the same dashboards, which yields notifications specific to your environment and a shared framework for major-incident response.

A cloud provider's global SLO can show as green while your own slice is much worse, because your footprint is a small percentage of the provider's global total and outages isolated to your region can be lost in the global rollup.

Agree with partners that when shared-SLO impact is high enough, both parties escalate the issue to P1 with special handling (such as a shared conference bridge), even when the normal ticket model would rank it lower.

A full-stack 'freedom and responsibility' ownership model lets developers push code when they want but makes them jointly responsible for operating their service; for this joint ownership to work, operations and development must share a common language — service level objectives.

Services that depend on each other should publish, via SLOs, how reliable they are (how many nines), whether there is planned downtime, expected upper-bound latency, how they handle request volume and overload, and whether they have met their SLOs over time — giving dependent teams clear visibility, trust, and accountability.

Build a culture of SLOs with a strategy spanning people, process, and technology across four areas: a common vernacular, evangelism (training, early adopters, a catchy acronym), automation that auto-collects SLIs for any deployed service, and incentives such as annual goals for managers to set and measure SLOs.

Base an SLO framework on the small, consistent set of signals that services already monitor — traffic volume, latency, errors, and utilization (closely matching Google SRE's Four Golden Signals) plus availability — and standardize their naming and measurement across services.

Summarize the SLO framework in a memorable acronym to accelerate adoption: VALET — Volume (business volume the service can handle), Availability (is it up when needed), Latency (does it respond fast), Errors (does it throw errors), and Tickets (does it require manual intervention).

Do not set SLOs on infrastructure utilization: users do not care about utilization as long as traffic is handled and the service is up, fast, error-free, and not in danger of running out of capacity; continue to monitor utilization and do capacity planning, but keep it out of the SLO framework.
exception: you must still monitor utilization and perform capacity planning outside the SLO framework

statement: Use percentiles rather than arithmetic averages for latency SLOs (at minimum a 90th-percentile target, with user-facing services preferring 95th and/or 99th), and supplement white-box performance monitoring with black-box monitoring to catch issues in the network, caches, or proxies outside the service.

Standardize error semantics for web services: never signal an error in the body of a 2xx response; throw a 5xx for errors caused by the service and a 4xx for errors caused by the client; track both but set SLOs only on 5xx errors, keeping the definition generic so batch services can map errors to failed records.

Each microservice should publish availability and latency SLOs for the API calls that other microservices make on it, so callers can consult those SLOs to determine whether the dependency can meet their reliability requirements.

Automating SLI/SLO data collection accelerates adoption, but it is not a prerequisite: organizations that cannot build complex automation should still adopt SLOs, because there are real benefits to just writing SLOs in the first place.

Treat SLOs as a trending tool tracked at daily, weekly, and monthly granularity, and run regular (weekly or monthly) SLO reviews that produce action items either to return a service to its SLO or to adjust an unrealistic SLO.

A volume/availability/latency/errors/tickets framework extends to batch applications (volume = records processed, availability = how often the job finishes by a deadline, latency = run time, errors = failed records, tickets = manual fixes) and can record the impact of destructive (chaos) testing on those metrics.

The business owner of a service (often the product manager) should set its SLO based on the service's criticality to the business; cast the SLO levels in business terms with example metrics and emphasize the investment required to move between levels, to reduce misaligned reliability expectations between product and development.

Introducing an SLO culture to a large company takes a good strategy, executive buy-in, strong evangelism, easy adoption patterns, and above all patience; it may take years to become firmly established, and can be implemented piece by piece.

SLO culture is an ongoing process, not a one-time fix, and SLO implementation need not be Google-specific: each organization should tailor SLIs, SLOs, and implementation details to its own environment.

Monitoring exists to alert on conditions requiring attention, investigate and diagnose issues, display system information visually, give insight into resource and health trends for long-term planning, and compare system behavior before and after a change or between experiment groups; the relative importance of these uses drives monitoring-system tradeoffs.
Metrics and structured logging are the two data sources best suited to SRE's fundamental monitoring needs.

Monitoring data more than four to five minutes stale can significantly impair incident response, because slow data leads you to act on incorrect data or deduce false correlations between cause and effect; determine your data-freshness and retrieval-speed requirements ahead of time.

Retain monitoring data over a multi-month time frame so you can analyze long-term trends such as system growth; summary (aggregated) data suffices for growth planning, while retaining all detailed metrics helps answer 'has this happened before?' but may be expensive to store or retrieve.

Record event and resource metrics as monotonically incrementing counters so the monitoring system can compute windowed functions such as request rate per second, which are the building blocks for SLO burn-based alerting.

Choose a monitoring system that can compute percentiles (50th, 95th, 99th) when recording latency, because the arithmetic mean masks bad behavior and cannot tell you whether 50%, 5%, or 1% of requests are too slow.
Tailor dashboards to their audience — high-level management needs different views than SREs — and display the same types of data consistently across each set of dashboards so they aid communication.

Classify alerts into multiple categories and severity levels so responses can be proportional — for example, file a ticket for a low error rate lasting over an hour, but treat a 100% error rate as an emergency demanding immediate response.

Use alert suppression to avoid distracting on-call engineers with redundant noise — for example alert once on the global error rate instead of per node, and suppress your service's alert when a dependency it relies on is already alerting — but ensure alerts are no longer suppressed once the event is over.

Use metrics — near real-time but less granular — for alerts and dashboards so engineers are notified rapidly, and use logs — more granular but delayed and usually more accurate — to find root cause and to generate detailed non-time-sensitive reports.

Prefer metrics-based alerting even when you must be notified of a single exceptional event: increment a counter metric when the event happens and alert on that metric's value, which keeps all alert configuration in one place and easier to manage.

Move important signals from logs into metrics by exporting a low-cardinality attribute (such as the HTTP status code) as a metric label, which enables per-category graphing and more accurate per-category alerting thresholds without impractically increasing metric volume.

Tie alerts directly to SLOs using a uniform control surface that decides at request time whether an error is user-impacting and writes that decision to both logs and metrics, which makes alerts more clearly actionable and significantly lowers the false-positive rate.

Do not use a high-cardinality value (one that can take millions of values, such as an entity ID) as a metric label; instead keep it in logs and document — or automate — the one-off log query in the alert so responders can run it quickly.
Treat your monitoring system as a production service that is as important as any other you run, and give it the appropriate level of care and attention.

Treat monitoring configuration as code stored in revision control — gaining change history, easier rollbacks, linting checks, and enforced code review — and prefer a monitoring system that supports intent-based configuration over one offering only web UIs or CRUD-style APIs.

Encourage monitoring consistency by converging on a single, centrally-run framework (helping engineers ramp up across teams and easing collaborative debugging) and make basic monitoring coverage effortless by having all services export a consistent set of basic metrics so any new component automatically gets monitoring.

Keep the components of your monitoring system loosely coupled, with separate components for collecting, storing, alerting, and visualizing and stable interfaces between them, so you can swap any component for a better alternative as your services evolve.
Make SLI metrics the first metrics to check when SLO-based alerts trigger by placing them prominently on the service's dashboard, ideally on its landing page.

Because SLO dashboards show that you are violating an SLO but not why, add monitoring of intended changes — the binary version, command-line flags, and dynamic configuration version (or last build/package timestamp if unversioned) — and surface it in dashboards linked from your alerts to correlate outages with rollouts.

Monitor the responses coming from your direct dependencies — exporting request and response size, latency, and response codes, keeping the four golden signals in mind — and instrument the lower-level RPC client library once rather than each client, for consistency and to monitor new dependencies for free.

Monitor the saturation of every resource the service relies upon — hard-limit resources such as RAM, disk, and CPU quota and soft ones such as file descriptors, thread-pool threads, queue waiting times, and log volume, plus language-specific resources like the Java heap or Go goroutines — and alert when a resource approaches a hard limit or a degradation threshold; track all resources for capacity planning.

Add metrics or labels that break down served traffic by status code: for HTTP traffic monitor all response codes even those that do not provide enough signal for alerting (since some are triggered by incorrect client behavior), and monitor aggregate counts of requests denied due to quota or rate limits.
Each exposed metric should serve a purpose: resist exporting a handful of metrics just because they are easy to generate, and instead design metrics around how they will be used.

Design metrics used for alerting so their values change dramatically only when the system enters a problem state and stay steady during normal operation, whereas debugging metrics have different requirements and should point at the aspect of the system potentially causing the issue.
When writing a postmortem, identify which additional metrics would have allowed you to diagnose the issue faster, and add them.

Subject monitoring and alerting code to the same testing standards as production code — using synthetic time series and assertions on derived series and alert firing across three tiers (binary metric reporting, rule evaluation, and alert routing) — because alerting rules may not fire for months or years and you need confidence they will work when a threshold is crossed.

SREs must be intimately familiar with their service's monitoring system, combine some mix of metrics and logging (the exact mix is context-dependent), and collect only metrics that serve a particular purpose — capacity planning, debugging, or direct notification.

The goal of SLO-based alerting is to be notified of a significant event — one that consumes a large fraction of the error budget — where the error budget is the number of allowed bad events and the error rate is the ratio of bad to total events, applied to all SLIs not just those named 'error'.

Evaluate any SLO alerting strategy on four parameters simultaneously: precision (the proportion of detected events that were significant), recall (the proportion of significant events detected), detection time (how long to notify), and reset time (how long alerts keep firing after the issue resolves).

Alerting whenever the immediate error rate over a short window exceeds the SLO threshold gives good detection time and recall but poor precision: it fires on many events that do not threaten the SLO, so you could receive up to 144 alerts per day and still meet the SLO.

Increasing the alert window improves precision by requiring a sustained error rate before firing, but it worsens reset time (an alert can keep firing for the full window after recovery) and calculating rates over longer windows is expensive in memory and I/O.

Do not use a duration parameter ('for' clause) as part of SLO-based alerting criteria: the duration does not scale with incident severity (a 100% outage alerts no faster than a 0.2% one) and the timer resets if the metric momentarily returns within SLO, so a fluctuating SLI may never alert.
exception: duration clauses can occasionally help filter out ephemeral noise over very short durations

statement: Alert on burn rate — how fast, relative to the SLO, the service consumes its error budget (a burn rate of 1 exactly exhausts the budget at the end of the window) — to achieve good detection time and high precision with a smaller, cheaper alerting window at a constant budget spend.

Use multiple burn-rate alerts with different time windows so you catch both fast, high error rates and lower-but-sustained error rates that would otherwise go unnoticed while still exhausting the budget.

As reasonable starting numbers for SLO alerting, page on 2% error-budget consumption in one hour and 5% in six hours, and raise a ticket on 10% consumption in three days; the appropriate numbers depend on the service and its baseline page load.

Send an active page for issues that will exhaust the error budget within hours or a few days, and a ticket for slower issues to be addressed the next working day; pages and tickets are the only valid ways to get a human to take action.

Prefer multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerting: require a shorter window (a good guideline is about one-twelfth the duration of the long window) to also be over threshold, so the alert fires only while you are still actively burning budget, which reduces false positives and gives a much better reset time.

When several burn-rate conditions can be true at once (for example a fast budget spend also satisfies the slower thresholds), implement alert suppression so the monitoring system does not fire multiple notifications for the same incident.

Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerting can over-page low-traffic services because a single failed request is a large fraction of the error rate — at ten requests per hour, one failure is a 10% error rate and a 1,000x burn rate against a 99.9% SLO — so low-traffic services need a modified approach.

Handle a low-traffic service by generating artificial traffic to compensate for the lack of signal, combining smaller related services into a larger monitoring group, or modifying the product so it takes more requests to qualify a single incident as a failure or the impact of a single failure is lower.

Generating artificial traffic lets you reuse existing monitoring logic and SLO values, but you can synthesize only a portion of user request types (worse for stateful services), and if an issue affects real users but not the synthetic traffic, the successful artificial requests hide the real-user signal.

Combine multiple low-traffic services for monitoring only when they are related (microservices of the same product or request types handled by the same binary); choose services with a shared failure domain such as a common backend database so a failure affects the group, and keep longer-period alerts to eventually catch individual 100% failures.
condition: only when the services are related and ideally share a failure domain

statement: Reduce the user impact of a single failed request by modifying the client to retry with exponential backoff and jitter and by setting up fallback paths that capture the request for eventual execution; this helps high-traffic systems and especially low-traffic ones by allowing more failed events in the budget, more monitoring signal, and more time to respond.

If a small number of errors loses error budget but would not noticeably impact users, consider lowering the SLO or increasing the alert window so engineers are paged only on a larger sustained outage; remember that lowering the SLO is a product decision affecting behavioral expectations and the error budget policy.

For a service with a very low availability target (for example 90%), a 100% outage may consume too little of the budget in the alert window to ever fire a percentage-of-budget alert, so you must tune the alerting parameters when error budgets are set over long periods.

For an extremely high availability goal a 100% outage exhausts the budget faster than an alert can be generated (a 99.999% monthly target burns out in about 26 seconds), so the only way to defend that level is to design the system so a 100% outage is extremely unlikely — for example by rolling a change out to only 1% of users so you burn budget at 1% of the rate.
condition: applies to services with extremely high availability goals

statement: Keep alerting scalable: do not specify the alert window and burn-rate parameters independently for each service, because that accumulates toil and cognitive load; decide on the parameters once and apply them to all services.
exception: temporary changes to alerting parameters are acceptable while fixing an ongoing outage

statement: Manage a large number of SLOs by grouping request types into a few buckets of similar availability requirements (such as CRITICAL, HIGH_FAST, HIGH_SLOW, LOW, and NO_SLO) rather than assigning unique availability and latency objectives to every request type, which gives sufficient fidelity with far less toil.

Toil is the repetitive, predictable, constant stream of tasks of maintaining a service, falling on a spectrum characterized as manual, repetitive, automatable, nontactical/reactive, lacking enduring value, and growing at least as fast as its source; also weigh a task's effect on team morale, since toil deflates morale and causes burnout and turnover.

Reward root-cause fixes over fixes that merely mask a problem: a workaround that hides the severity of an issue wastes time by not fixing the actual problem and removes the incentive for the responsible team to fix the root cause.
Use an objective cost/benefit figure (such as the dollar cost per hour of a recurring problem) to convince the owning team to fix the root cause rather than the symptom.

Measure toil objectively rather than by experience and intuition, which are not repeatable, objective, or transferable; an objective measure lets a team evaluate the severity of toil and prioritize remediation for maximum return on engineering investment over projects that may span quarters or years.

Before a toil-reduction project, analyze cost versus benefit and confirm the time saved will be at least proportional to the time invested in developing and maintaining the automation; but projects that look unprofitable on hours-saved-versus-invested alone may still be worth it for indirect benefits such as morale, fewer human-error outages, improved security, and career growth.

Measure toil in three steps: identify it (ideally with the stakeholders who perform the work), select an objective, consistent, well-understood unit of human effort (minutes/hours, or an applied patch, completed ticket, manual change — accounting for context-switching cost), and track these measurements continuously before, during, and after reduction efforts, streamlining the measurement so it does not itself create toil.

Common sources of toil to look for are business processes (especially ticket-driven ones), production interrupts, release shepherding, technology migrations, cost engineering and capacity planning, and troubleshooting opaque distributed architectures.

Ticket-driven business processes hide toil because they usually accomplish their goal and spread the toil evenly across the team; even when you are not yet planning to automate, simplify and streamline the process so it is easier to automate later and easier to manage in the meantime.

A large-scale migration approached manually likely involves toil even though it is tempting to view it as one-time 'project work', because much migration work is repetitive refactoring that delivers the same business value as before.

Focus troubleshooting energy on novel failure modes rather than the same brittle-architecture failure every week, and remember that each new critical dependency of availability P reduces overall availability by 1 minus P — a four-nines service that adds nine critical four-nines dependencies becomes a three-nines service.
Eliminating toil at its source is the optimal solution; only if that is not possible should you handle the toil by other means.

If a team is experiencing toil overload, treat toil reduction as its own project and adopt a data-driven approach — Google SRE teams track toil in bugs ranked by the cost to fix and the time saved — so remediation can be prioritized objectively.

Before investing effort in managing the toil from existing systems, examine whether you can engineer the toil out by changing the system: an SRE team's hands-on operating experience should feed product development to build operationally friendly software that is less toilsome and also more scalable, secure, and resilient.

Consider rejecting a toil-intensive task as the first option: analyze the cost of responding to the toil versus not doing so, and intentionally delay or batch toil so tasks accumulate for parallelized processing, which reduces interrupts and reveals patterns of toil you can then target for elimination.

Use SLOs to reduce toil: a well-defined SLO lets you safely ignore operational tasks that do not consume or exceed the error budget, and an SLO focused on overall service health rather than individual devices is more flexible and sustainable as the service grows.

For a complex problem with many edge cases, start with a human-backed interface ('engineer behind the curtain'): accept structured data via a defined API but let engineers still handle some operations, and reduce free-form requests over time so you can incrementally move toward full automation without overengineering a big-bang solution before the domain is understood.

Once a service offering is defined via a typed interface, provide self-service methods (a web form, script, API, or documented pull-request process) and let them gracefully degrade to a ticket for specialized requests or failures; moving 80–90% of requests to self-service is a huge reduction in workload even though some one-off cases remain.

Secure management and colleague support for toil reduction: although it reduces short-term capacity for feature work, it makes the team healthier and more productive long-term, and manager support backed by objective toil metrics is crucial for defending staff from new demands.

Meaningful SLOs that are understood and represented in metrics let you configure alerting to notify an on-caller only when there are actionable, specific threats to the error budget, and in most cases the multiwindow, multi-burn-rate technique is the most appropriate approach to defending an application's SLOs.

To build a strong business case for toil reduction, couple it with another desirable feature or business goal such as security, scalability, or reliability, so customers willingly give up their toil-generating systems and reducing toil becomes a side effect of helping them.

Do not try to design the perfect system that eliminates all toil at once; automate a few high-priority items first, reinvest the time gained to improve the solution, and pick a clear metric such as Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) to measure success.

Increase uniformity because a diverse production environment becomes exponentially harder to manage at scale: adopt a 'pets versus cattle' approach giving many devices the same interface so they are interchangeable and require less maintenance, accepting a high initial cost for lower maintenance, disaster-recovery, and utilization cost over the medium to long term.
Align incentives so that teams remain free to choose their own tools but must own the toil generated by unsupported tools or legacy systems they keep.

When automation wields admin-level powers, defensive software is crucial: assess every action for safety before execution (including changes that reduce serving capacity or redundancy), validate input carefully even from upstream systems, build in safeguards equivalent to the alerts a human operator would receive (timeouts, metric and outage-count checks), and default to a human operator whenever automation hits an unsafe condition.

When automating toil, do not literally transcribe the human workflow into a machine workflow and do not let automation eliminate human understanding of what is going wrong; instead break the documented manual work into separately implementable, composable software components that other automation can reuse.

Use or extend open source and third-party tools to reduce toil rather than building bespoke tooling, especially for one-off efforts like migrations where you are probably not the first organization to tread the path.

Actively seek feedback from the people who use your tools and automation — the less familiar they are with the underlying systems, the more important this is — using surveys and UX studies, and measure automation effectiveness with metrics like latency, error rate, rework rate, and human time saved compared before and after.

The journey away from a legacy system usually follows four stages: avoidance (accepting technical debt), encapsulation/augmentation (wrapping it in abstracted APIs, automation, configuration management, monitoring, and testing), replacement/refactoring (done incrementally), and retirement/custodial ownership where remaining stragglers own the remnants.

Encapsulating a legacy system behind abstracted APIs, automation, monitoring, and testing is like refinancing high-interest technical debt into low-interest technical debt: the system stays brittle, but you can reliably detect misbehavior and roll back, making it a stopgap to prepare for incremental replacement.

When replacing a legacy system whose specification is defined only by its historical usage, put a common interface in front of it to migrate users incrementally with canarying or blue-green deployments, and build production-sized datasets of historical expected inputs and outputs to confirm the new system is not diverging unexpectedly.

Operational automation UIs should not introduce overhead or complexity: ensure the system is safe and ready for repair before the operator arrives, give the operator feedback on progress, and keep the UI state reliably synced with the actual state of the system to avoid acting on a wrong assumption.

Do not rely on human expertise to compensate for gaps in automation, and test the automation with new, inexperienced users: experienced operators take shortcuts the software did not anticipate — in one case a technician initiated concurrent drains on every line card and caused user-visible packet loss.

Build complex automation workflows from separable, well-defined, reusable components rather than monolithic designs, so each component can be reused or adapted across successive generations of the system and new features are easier to add.

Do not overthink the problem: do not let a quest for precise diagnosis block a simple, good-enough repair policy — Google spent three unnecessary years collecting data to classify memory errors before realizing that acting on any detected error with a drain/reboot/reinstall (and escalating to replacement on recurrence) was sufficient, since most failures were transient.

Sometimes imperfect automation is good enough: where a check is unavailable but the risk is low (for example links that carry no customer traffic), allow the automation to skip that check and add the functionality later if it turns out to matter.
condition: when the bypassed check covers low-risk, non-customer-facing operations

statement: Repair automation is not fire-and-forget: automation can have a very long lifetime, so plan for project continuity as people leave and join, train new engineers on legacy systems so they can fix bugs, and design automation to evolve flexibly — policy-based automation that separates intent from a generic implementation engine evolves more transparently than inflexible automation.

Build risk assessment and defense in depth into automation: add a secondary check that sets upper limits on the number of impacted links and devices and automatically opens a tracking bug when a threshold is exceeded, tuning the limits over time to reduce false positives; such a check also catches atypical repair rates from power outages and software bugs.

Establish an error budget and secure manager support for anti-toil automation, because repair automation can fail especially when first introduced; explain to stakeholders that automation is essential despite the risk of failures because it enables continuous improvement in reliability and efficiency.

Before automating a workflow, reexamine whether you can simplify the system or workflow first; pay attention to all aspects of the workflow rather than just your own toil, test with the people who do the work, and ensure the automation does not create new toil (such as opening unnecessary tickets) because creating problems for other teams increases resistance to future automation.

Before deprecating a service, gather usage data — daily and monthly active users, which job families use it, and what they access — combined with user surveys, to validate that the business needs it serves could be better met by lower-cost alternatives.

When no single alternative can replace a generalized legacy system, break the problem into smaller addressable components: in aggregate a handful of specialized alternatives can cover all use cases, each giving a better user experience than the generalized solution, trading flexibility for improved scalability, latency tolerance, and security.

The first step to retiring a legacy system is to stop, slow, or discourage new adoption, because it is much more painful to take something away from users than to never offer it; migrate the lightest users first and grow the scope as confidence in the alternatives and tooling builds.

Make a large migration or decommissioning effort as low-touch as possible with a self-service portal — a landing page, continually updated FAQ, per-user status, and options to request, archive, migrate, or extend — rather than an untenable manual ticket-based process.

When communicating with users during a migration, identify the right users for the right communications: both false positives (erroneously reporting action required) and false negatives (failing to notify a user you are taking something away) are unacceptable, costing lost credibility and customer-service work.

Tickets can serve as a quick-and-dirty GUI for automation: they keep a log of work, update stakeholders, and provide a simple human fallback mechanism that routes a request to a manual queue when the automation cannot process it.

Melt snowflakes: because automation craves conformity, either retool the automation to handle edge cases specifically or delete and modify nonconforming entities to match the tooling's expectations, so you can approach zero-touch automation.

Employ organizational nudges to move users toward better, less toil-intensive alternatives — for example require escalations for new requests of the old service and recognize users who retire their usage — and provide good documentation such as codelabs or cookbooks so most onboarding does not require help from the team that owns the service.

A low-and-slow iterative approach that builds tooling on an as-needed basis in response to each phase's requirements and user feedback keeps the team lean, reduces user disruption, and avoids wasted engineering effort, at the tradeoff of a long-lived project during which the team must endure the existing operational toil.

Eliminating toil is not always the best solution: once you identify toil, determine when reduction makes sense using metrics, return-on-investment analysis, risk assessment, and iterative development, and be relentless because the benefits usually exceed the costs even if you can only start with a small proof of concept.
Simplicity strongly correlates with reliability: simple software breaks less often and is easier and faster to fix when it does break, and simple systems are easier to understand, maintain, and test.
