Treat simplicity as an end-to-end goal that extends beyond the code itself to the system architecture and the tools and processes used to manage the software lifecycle.

Code complexity can be measured fairly objectively (for example cyclomatic complexity, the number of distinct code paths through a set of statements), but tools are less able to tell whether the measured complexity is necessary or accidental, how one method's complexity influences the larger system, and which refactoring approaches are best.

Because formal system-level complexity metrics are rare, use practical proxies for systems complexity: training time for a new member to go on-call, explanation time for a high-level view of the service, administrative diversity (how many ways similar settings can be configured), diversity of deployed configurations, and age (per Hyrum's Law, users eventually depend on every aspect of an API's implementation).
Complexity will increase in living software systems unless there is a countervailing effort, and providing that effort is a worthwhile thing to do.

Complexity is an externality — its cost typically falls not on the individual or team that introduces it but on those who later work in and around it — so a system needs a champion for end-to-end simplicity, and SREs are a natural fit because their work requires them to treat the system as a whole.

Before an engineer goes on-call for the first time, have them draw and redraw the system architecture diagrams and keep a canonical set in documentation; and ensure an SRE reviews all major design docs so that, if a design adds complexity, the SRE can suggest simplifying alternatives.

Prefer structured data types such as Protocol Buffers or Apache Thrift over abstract general-purpose alternatives like a generic key/value bag: although they seem more complex, they produce simpler end-to-end solutions because they force upfront design decisions and documentation, whereas abstract APIs push a documentation and compatibility penalty onto every client.

When considering a rewrite, account for the full project lifecycle — development toward a moving target, a full migration plan, and the cost of supporting both systems during a migration that may take years — and remember that wide APIs with many users are very hard to migrate.

Do not compare an expected rewrite to your current system; instead compare it to what your current system would look like if you invested the same effort in improving it, and do not underestimate the rewrite's costs.

Most simplification work consists of removing elements from a system — sometimes directly (removing a dependency on unused data) and sometimes through redesign (fetching shared remote data once and forwarding the result rather than fetching it twice).

Leadership must ensure simplification efforts are celebrated and explicitly prioritized, treating successful simplification projects like useful feature launches and measuring and celebrating code addition and removal equally, since lines of code are 'spent', not merely 'produced'.

Treat simplification as a feature: prioritize and staff simplification projects and reserve SRE time for them (for example a separate bucket of 10% of engineering project time), because if developers and SREs do not see simplification as beneficial to their careers they will not undertake it.

Splitting SRE teams as a system grows focuses each new team on a smaller part but can lessen their motivation or ability to drive larger simplification projects; consider designating a small rotating group of SREs who maintain working knowledge of the entire stack and can push for conformity and simplification across it.

Diagram the system to identify deeper design problems such as amplification (a retried call multiplying the total number of RPCs across several levels) and cyclic dependencies (a component depending on itself, which can make a cold start of the whole system impossible).

Integrate an already-running system into your own infrastructure incrementally; treat redundant lookups within a single request as a 'system smell' analogous to a code smell; and create well-defined standards with buy-in from both SREs and developers to give managers a clear blueprint for removing complexity that they are more likely to endorse and reward.

Converge bespoke per-team production stacks onto a single managed microservices platform that bundles best-practice reliability and debugging features, but keep services 'managed, not hosted' — empower teams to manage their own services with provided workflow tools (UI, API, and CLI) rather than removing their control and responsibility.

A high-quality shared platform lets developer teams run hundreds of services without deep SRE engagement and enables tiered SRE engagement — a spectrum from light consulting and design reviews to deep engagement where SREs share on-call duties.

Standardizing onto a shared platform is a long-term investment, so aim for incremental productivity wins unlocked at each stage rather than trying to convince people to perform a huge refactor that pays off only at the very end.

Be careful about your service's dependencies: use an explicit whitelist of services allowed to call a component to prevent accidental dependency additions, and actively watch for circular dependencies that compromise system integrity.

Involve SREs early in design discussions so their end-to-end understanding can weigh the costs and benefits of alternatives with an eye toward simplicity, and let them proactively develop standards to homogenize production; because systems inevitably creep toward complexity, the fight for simplicity requires continuous attention and commitment.
SRE operational work breaks down into four interconnected categories: on-call work, customer requests (most commonly tickets), incident response, and postmortems.

Healthy documentation procedures embed themselves into all of your work rather than being a separate activity — documenting code, playbooks, service features, and complete tickets is simply another facet of project and operational tasks.

SREs should spend at least 50% of their time on project work — anything less makes for unsustainable engineering and burned-out teams — with roughly one-third of time on operational tasks and two-thirds on project work, a ratio that also informs an ideal on-call rotation size where engineers are on-call only about one-third of the time.

Conduct periodic reviews against a clearly defined rubric to track whether a team is striking the appropriate balance between operational, project, and overhead work, and to generate team-health metrics you can track over time.

Guard against operational underload — too little operational time risks engineers forgetting crucial aspects of the service — by taking more risks and moving faster (shorter release cycles, more features per release, more disaster-recovery testing), and if a team is perpetually underloaded, onboard related services or hand a service that no longer needs SRE support back to the development team.
condition: when a team is spending too little time on operational tasks

statement: Let operational issues feed project work: SRE project work should be strategic, time-bounded initiatives that make the system more efficient, scalable, and reliable and reduce operational load and toil, forming a continuous feedback loop between the sources of operational load and the project work that systematically improves production.

Being on-call means being available during a set period and ready to respond to production incidents with appropriate urgency — diagnosing, mitigating, fixing, or escalating as needed — alongside nonurgent production duties.

The overall goal of on-call is to provide coverage for critical services while never achieving reliability at the expense of an on-call engineer's health, so teams must strive for a healthy balance of on-call and project work and staff adequately to ensure time for project work.

Target a maximum of two incidents per on-call shift (counting one problem as one incident regardless of how many alerts fired) to ensure adequate time for follow-up, and take corrective action whenever pager load gets too high.

Psychological safety is vital for effective on-call rotations: because being on-call is daunting and stressful, on-call engineers should be fully supported by a series of procedures and escalation paths that make their lives easier.

Compensate out-of-hours on-call work (for example time-off-in-lieu or cash capped at some proportion of salary), which both incentivizes participation in on-call and ensures engineers do not take on too many on-call shifts for economic reasons.
Reorganizing or renaming a DevOps team into SRE is often a red flag for an organization that is not actually practicing DevOps, because a name change will not fix more structural problems.

Build an on-call training roadmap as a checklist of hands-on focus areas to practice before going on-call — such as administering production jobs, draining traffic away from a cluster, rolling back a bad software push, rate-limiting unwanted traffic, bringing up additional capacity, using the monitoring systems, and describing the architecture and dependencies of the services.

Coach new on-call engineers to explore a service from first principles rather than requiring years of expertise, and be open about the limits of your own knowledge so engineers learn when to ask for help.

Practice being on-call through 'Wheel of Misfortune' exercises that role-play recent incidents to rehearse debugging production problems, continue them after ramp-up by rotating the session leader, and record the sessions for future reference.

Establish precise on-call responsibilities: at the start of each shift read the handoff from the previous shift, minimize user impact first and then ensure issues are fully addressed, send a handoff email at the end of the shift, and define when to escalate and how to write postmortems for large incidents.

Maintain on-call playbooks with high-level instructions for each automated alert — its severity and impact, debugging suggestions, and possible mitigation actions — and create a corresponding playbook entry whenever an alert is created, because playbooks reduce stress, mean time to repair, and the risk of human error.

Because playbook content is contentious (general and slow-changing versus step-by-step to reduce variability), at least agree with your team on the minimal structured details every playbook must contain, and if a playbook is a deterministic list of commands run every time an alert fires, implement automation instead.

Onboard engineers to on-call in stages: first shadow the outgoing on-call team, then become primary on-call with experienced engineers as backup to escalate to, and have newer members shadow local SREs before joining the rotation.

For ongoing one-person-at-a-time turnover, formalize on-call training into a series of exercises that can be completed semi-independently with minimal mentor involvement, supported by maintained service architecture diagrams.

In a dynamic cloud environment of live migrations and network latency, monitor at a higher level using user-facing indicators such as API responsiveness rather than low-level infrastructure signals, and reframe paging events in terms of explicit first-principle SLOs to trim the fat from monitoring and avoid chasing transient problems.

Classify monitoring events into tiers to keep the signal-to-noise ratio low: P1 deal-with-immediately events page the on-call and are SLO-impacting, P2 events are handled the next business day via email and event-stream notification, and P3 events are informational only; attach an incident ticket to every P1 and P2 event.

Explicitly free the on-call engineer from any expectation of project work so they can take immediate follow-up action and identify major gaps in tooling or process after the post-incident review, creating a constant cycle of improvement that aims to make every on-call shift better than the last.

Track on-call burden over time as a barometer of team health by holding a recurring open service review of the previous period's SLO performance, and discuss remediation actions whenever you exceed your pager budget.

Expressing objectives as SLOs provides a basis for engaging your cloud provider's reliability engineers — for example having them paged alongside your own engineers for SLO-impacting events — which helps triage root causes hidden behind cloud abstraction and reduces mean time to repair.

Set response-time expectations by severity rather than requiring an immediate response to everything: a revenue-impacting outage may need a five-minute response, a stuck batch system thirty minutes, and a failing pre-launch backup only a ticket during work hours; longer allowed response times give the on-call engineer more freedom.

Audit whether you should actually be paged for everything that currently pages: issues better served by automated repair or by a ticket should not page a human, since it is generally better for a computer to fix a problem than to require a person to.
Pager load is influenced by three main factors — bugs in production, alerting, and human processes — so reducing pager load requires addressing all three.

Because there will always be preexisting bugs in production, find and prevent them before they page by keeping systems only as complicated as necessary, regularly updating dependencies for bug fixes, performing regular destructive testing or fuzzing, and performing regular load testing in addition to integration and unit testing.

Reduce the number and lifetime of new bugs reaching production by improving testing over time — for each production bug ask 'how could we have detected this preproduction?' — not neglecting load testing, running staging with production-like synthetic traffic, canarying in production, and keeping a low tolerance to new bugs with a 'detect, roll back, fix, and roll forward' strategy.
A roll-back-first strategy requires predictable and frequent releases so that the cost of rolling back any one release is small.

Expand your testing regimen to cover behaviors that do not occur every day, since some bugs manifest only under particular load (such as Black Friday or seasonal peaks), with a particular mix of requests, or when users exercise the system in unexpected ways.

Prioritize fixing existing production bugs above delivering new features, because minimizing the number of bugs in production not only reduces pager load but also makes it easier to identify and classify any new bug when a page fires.

Make all changes to production systems via automation informed by human-developed intent configuration, because humans are error-prone (human error was the second most common cause of new production bugs in one team) and automation can perform safety testing that humans cannot before a change enters production.
Adopt a strict policy that every outage must have a tracking bug, so the team can examine the root causes of new bugs in aggregate and identify the dominant causes of pager load.

Reduce the delay in identifying a page's root cause — which otherwise lets the problem recur — by linking pages to relevant monitoring consoles and correlating black-box and white-box alerts, practicing emergency response, performing small frequent releases (so bugs correlate with the change that introduced them, and canarying signals new-release bugs), and logging changes into a searchable timeline.
The on-call engineer is never alone: encourage the team to feel safe asking for help during incidents.

Reduce mitigation delay by promptly rolling back a recent code or configuration rollout that introduced a bug, since even a 'quick fix' must still be tested, built, and rolled out; generally prefer 'roll back, fix, and roll forward' over 'roll forward, fix, and roll forward again'.
exception: a rollback alone is necessary but not sufficient if the bug caused data corruption

statement: Rolling back usually impacts users far less than rolling forward, because the build step of rolling forward can take longer than a tight error budget allows — a 99.99% availability target affords only about 15 minutes of error budget per quarter.
If at all possible, avoid changes that cannot be rolled back, such as API-incompatible changes and lockstep releases.

Use feature isolation: design the system so that if one feature goes wrong you can disable it via a feature flag without affecting other features, which also improves release velocity and makes the decision to disable that feature much simpler.

Drain requests away from the elements of your system exhibiting a bug — for example the part of a gradual rollout that received a bad update — to mitigate customer impact in seconds rather than the minutes or longer a rollback may take.

All paging alerts should be immediately actionable — expecting a human to take an action the system cannot take itself — with a high signal-to-noise ratio and few false positives, because a low signal-to-noise ratio causes on-call alert fatigue.
For a team fully committed to SLO-based and symptom-based alerting, relaxing alert thresholds is rarely an appropriate response to being paged.

Review new alerts as thoroughly as new code, give each alert a corresponding playbook entry, introduce new paging alerts only when truly needed (since pages have a negative psychological impact), and test a new alert in production by emailing its author for long enough to experience typical periodic conditions (about a week) before upgrading it to a paging alert, using its trigger rate to predict pager-budget consumption and approving it as a team.

Aim to identify the root cause of every page — root causes extend out of the machine into team processes, so a bug a unit test would have caught is really a process bug — and rarely conclude that a page was 'cause unknown', because explaining a page away as transient or self-fixed invites it to recur and trouble the next on-call engineer.

Do not merely point-fix a bug: use the paging alert as an opportunity to surface engineering work that obviates an entire class of future bugs, filing a project bug and justifying its priority with break-even data — comparing the project's implementation cost against the number of pages it would remove times the average cost per page.

Choose among three levels of fix for a recurring problem: a point fix (correct this instance), a systemic fix (automate so the whole class of similar cases is prevented and self-corrects), and a monitoring/prevention fix (alert preemptively before the condition becomes service-impacting, ideally as a ticket rather than a page).

Reserve a fraction of both SRE and developer team time for responding to production bugs as they arise, routinely prioritize production bugs above other project work, and escalate to developer decision-makers when bugs are not being dealt with promptly.

File a placeholder bug in your bug tracker for each paging alert and link the alert to the bug it is symptomatic of, building structured data that reveals which bugs and which components cause the most pages so you can prioritize fixes by page count rather than anecdote.

Because the quality of the data you collect determines the quality of the decisions humans or automation can make, define and document your team's policy on data collection for pages and set up non-paging alerts that highlight when pages were not handled according to those expectations.

Stay vigilant against operational overload accumulating 'by a thousand cuts' by regularly reviewing pager-load trends (a 21-day trailing average is useful), setting ticket alerts to tech leads or managers when pager load crosses an agreed warning threshold, and holding regular SRE-developer meetings on outstanding production bugs.

Limit on-call shifts to 12 hours, because long shifts risk exhaustion and tired people make mistakes; a 12-hour shift system does not require a globally distributed team, since even a single site can split the day and overnight shifts between two engineers rather than running unsustainable 24-hour shifts.

Embrace flexibility as a principle for on-call rotations rather than a fixed set of rules, because team members' needs change over time and a healthy, fair, equitable balance of on-call and personal life requires accommodating diverse needs.

Automate on-call scheduling with a tool that rearranges and rebalances shifts as team members' needs change, factors in personal preferences and recent on-call load to ensure fairness (which does not mean a perfectly uniform distribution), and never changes an already-generated schedule so engineers can plan around it.

Plan for short-term on-call swaps with a documented swap policy and peer review of schedule changes (a good tradeoff between safety and flexibility), and account for commute coverage when you have a strict pager-response SLO so someone can respond while an engineer is in transit.

Size on-call teams to allow a temporary staff reduction without overloading the rest: a sustainable 24/7 rotation needs a bare minimum of five engineers per site in a multisite configuration or eight in a single-site one, plus one extra engineer per site as protection, giving six per site (multisite) or nine per site (single-site).

Part-time work is compatible with on-call if you adjust scheduling: for engineers working fewer full days, configure the scheduler not to put them on-call on non-working days; for engineers working reduced daily hours, split the on-call shift with another engineer; and give reduced-hours engineers a proportionately smaller amount of on-call.

Empower operations engineers by making it clear that SREs own site operation — defining a shared reliability roadmap, driving full resolution of issues, and maintaining monitoring rules — with feature developers as necessary collaborators rather than owners; a change of name to SRE can communicate this shift in responsibilities but is not by itself a panacea.

Invest in on-call team relationships — through offsite activities, having all members of the rotation sit and eat together regardless of job title — because stronger bonds create a 'I protect my colleagues' mentality that makes engineers more likely to fix bugs, finish action items, and avoid carelessly paging teammates.

Distinguish resolving an incident (mitigating the impact and restoring the service) from managing an incident (coordinating the responding teams efficiently and ensuring communication flows both among responders and to interested stakeholders).

Respond to incidents in a structured way agreed on beforehand: formulating rules for how to communicate and coordinate before disaster strikes lets the team concentrate on resolving the incident rather than on process when it occurs.

The basic principles of incident response are: maintain a clear line of command, designate clearly defined roles, keep a working record of debugging and mitigation as you go, and declare incidents early and often.

Incident response frameworks share three common goals — the three Cs: Coordinate the response effort, Communicate between responders and to the organization and outside world, and maintain Control over the response; failures of incident response usually trace to one of these three areas.

Organize incident response into three main roles: the Incident Commander (who leads and coordinates the response and assumes any role not yet delegated), the Operations Lead (who applies operational tools to mitigate and resolve the incident), and the Communications Lead (the public face who gives periodic updates to stakeholders); the person who declares the incident typically becomes the Incident Commander.
Perform rollouts only during business days and hours so developers are available in case something goes wrong, rather than rolling out on weekends when developers are not readily reachable.

Successful incident management should not rely on heroic efforts of individuals tapped during their free time — if they had been unreachable the response would have failed — so provide coverage through an on-call rotation with paid out-of-hours coverage instead.

First stop the impact of an incident, then find the root cause (unless it happens to be identified early); after a mitigation succeeds, postpone any risky rollout until the root cause is fully determined rather than continuing and risking a larger disruption.

Declare an incident early and often, because managed incidents are resolved faster: early declaration prevents miscommunication between teams, brings root-cause identification and resolution sooner, and loops in relevant teams earlier for faster external communication.

Use centralized communication during an incident: gather all responders in one place — a physical or virtual 'war room' such as a conference room, IRC channel, or video call — to communicate in real time and coordinate the response.

When three or more people work on an incident, start a collaborative document that lists working theories, eliminated causes, and useful debugging information such as error logs and suspect graphs, so this information is preserved rather than lost in the conversation.

Put a formal incident response structure in place early, because without it a handful of first responders pursue their own uncoordinated investigations; the Incident Commander should proactively coordinate information and make decisions rather than just relaying messages.

Develop generic mitigations — actions first responders can take to alleviate user pain before the root cause is fully understood, such as rolling back a recent release correlated with the outage or reconfiguring load balancers to avoid an affected region; they are blunt instruments that may cause other disruptions but can be applied quickly to stop the bleeding.

To mitigate an incident you do not need to fully understand its details — you only need to know the location of the root cause — and the ability to mitigate an outage before its cause is fully understood is crucial for running robust, highly available services.

Create general-purpose mitigation tools (such as rollback tooling) before an incident occurs, not while responding to an emergency, and browse past postmortems to discover mitigations and tools that would have been useful in retrospect and build them into your services.

First responders must prioritize mitigation above all else or time to resolution suffers, because customers do not care whether you fully understand what caused an outage — they simply want to stop receiving errors.

Address an active incident in order: assess the impact, mitigate the impact, perform a root-cause analysis, and after the incident is over fix what caused it and write a postmortem; then run incident-response drills to exercise the system's vulnerabilities.

Early in an incident, quickly verify that the issue is affecting actual customers and use an incident management system prepared beforehand to bring in a communications person who informs customers of the outage.

Hand over incident command — including across a shift boundary — to the more experienced or available commander when coordination and communication are becoming a challenge, rather than waiting for the normal handover time.

Assign the Incident Commander role to the team with the best visibility into customer impact, delegate well-understood problems (like restoring power and rebooting servers) to the Operations Lead, and keep the response focused on the most important aspect — addressing the needs of impacted customers as quickly as possible.

When a problem is vague and not covered by existing procedures, the Incident Commander should assign a dedicated owner to coordinate it, monitor progress closely, and organize more engineers when the work requires new tools to be written quickly.

The Communications Lead is responsible for reporting accurate information tailored to each audience — company leaders need the extent and assurance of progress, dependent teams need recovery timelines, external customers need proactive notification, and ticket-filers need workarounds and timelines.
Treat incident-response processes as purposefully non-static: review them periodically (for example every few months) and update them to reflect changing business needs as the organization grows.

Practice teamwork for incidents with regular failure-injection exercises that use the same processes and vernacular as a real incident (with a trainee acting as Incident Commander), supplemented by time-bound simulation games that capture the urgency real drills cannot.
During a long-running incident, rotate the on-call engineers and the Incident Commander periodically (for example every four hours) to encourage rest and bring fresh ideas into the response team.

Equip incident response with the right tools: store on-call information, service ownership, postmortems, and incident metadata in one system to assemble the right team fast; use a dedicated chat channel as the scribe's information ledger of actions, owners, and timestamps; make coordination decisions on a conference call with outcomes recorded in chat; and record calls so any timeline can be reconstructed.
The time to start thinking about an incident-management process is before an incident occurs, not when a pager alerts you to a problem.

Train responders to organize an incident so they have a pattern, a common language, and shared expectations that reduce miscommunication; you need not adopt the full Incident Command System but can select the parts important to you (letting on-calls delegate and escalate, encouraging a mitigation-first response, and defining IC, Communications Lead, and Operations Lead roles), and make the training hands-on by analyzing past incidents.

Decide and agree on a single incident communication channel beforehand and practice using it, preferably one the team is already familiar with, so the Incident Commander never has to make that decision during an incident.

Keep your audience informed with regular status updates throughout an incident, because unless you acknowledge it is being actively addressed people assume nothing is being done, and if you forget to call off the response after resolution people assume the incident is ongoing.

Prepare two or three ready-to-use templates for sharing information publicly and make sure the on-call knows how to send them, so no one has to write announcements under extreme stress with no guidelines, and think ahead about how public posts will be drafted, reviewed, approved, and released.

Prepare a list of contacts to email or page beforehand, since having prepared distribution lists saves critical time and ensures you do not miss anyone when you need to make an 'all hands on deck' call.
Establish an explicit list of criteria for determining whether an issue is truly an incident, derived from looking at past outages and known high-risk areas, so it is clear when to declare one.

Practice incident management with regular drills — controlled emergencies that do not impact customers (such as company-wide disaster-recovery testing), Wheel of Misfortune role-plays, or deliberately treating a minor problem as a major one — using real tools as much as possible, and follow each drill with a report of what went well, what went poorly, and how to improve.

Establish incident procedures ahead of time when the world is not on fire and practice them regularly to build the muscle memory needed to stay calm and follow the structure during a real emergency, securing leadership support for dedicated practice time.

A truly blameless postmortem culture results in more reliable systems; introducing postmortems is as much a cultural change as a technical one, so start small with a very basic postmortem procedure and then reflect and tune it to suit your organization, since there is no one size that fits all.
When written well, acted upon, and widely shared, postmortems are a very effective tool for driving positive organizational change and preventing repeat outages.

Postmortem action items pay off measurably: at Google, the action items implemented from one outage's postmortem dramatically reduced the blast radius and rate of a similar incident that occurred three years later.

Make destructive automation idempotent and protect it with sanity checks and rate limits, because a bug that treated an empty filter list as 'no filter' (act on all) rather than 'act on none', combined with insufficient rate limits, sent every machine globally to be disk-erased.

A blameless postmortem must attribute failure to systemic and process causes — for example that nothing stopped a human from running unsafe automation multiple times and no documentation warned of the gotcha — rather than blaming an individual's 'careless ignorance', which is the hallmark of a bad postmortem.

Provide context in a postmortem by explaining domain-specific terms in Background and Glossary sections (linking to longer documents if needed), because the audience extends beyond the immediate team and an uncontextualized postmortem may be misunderstood or ignored.

Present numbers to give a consistent representation of an outage's impact; even when there is no concrete data, a well-informed estimate is better than none, because if you cannot measure the impact you cannot know it is fixed.
Identify the root causes and trigger of an incident down to the lower-level details, since doing so is one of the most important reasons to write a postmortem.

Document the recovery efforts so the postmortem records what happened, how the issue was mitigated, and how users were impacted, giving the reader a complete view of the outage and something new to learn.

Include preventative action items, not just mitigative ones, and prefer fixing automated systems and processes over trying to change human behavior, because changing humans is less reliable — plan for a future where people are as fallible as they are today.
Assign priorities to postmortem action items rather than tagging them all equally, so it is clear which action to tackle first.

Write action items in precise, measurable language with a verifiable end state, avoiding vague phrases like 'improve' or 'make better' that are open to interpretation and make success criteria hard to measure.
Assign every action item a tracking bug, because without a formal tracking process postmortem action items are often forgotten, resulting in repeat outages.

Every postmortem following a user-affecting outage must have at least one high-priority (P0/P1) bug associated with it, because to users a postmortem without subsequent action is indistinguishable from no postmortem at all.

Avoid finger-pointing and blaming individuals or teams in a postmortem, because blame leads team members to become risk-averse for fear of public shaming and motivates them to cover up facts critical to understanding and preventing recurrence.

Keep postmortem language factual and free of personal judgments, superfluous or animated wording, and dramatic descriptions, since such language distracts from the key message and erodes psychological safety; justify the severity of any statement with verifiable data instead.

Give a postmortem a single owner who is the point of contact responsible for the document, follow-up, and completion, with multiple collaborators, and ensure every action item has a clear owner, because action items without clear owners are less likely to be resolved.

Share postmortems as widely as possible — by default to everyone in the company and perhaps even with customers — because the value of a postmortem is proportional to the learning it creates, wider learning reduces repeat incidents, and a thoughtful, honest postmortem helps restore shaken trust.

Publish the postmortem promptly — within days rather than months — while information is fresh in contributors' minds, because a delayed postmortem loses key details and the people affected by the outage fill the gap with their imagination, which seldom works in your favor.

For a large incident with many action items, group the action items by theme (such as prevention, emergency response, monitoring, provisioning, and cleanup) to make it easier to assign owners and priorities.

Blamelessness means focusing on the gaps in system design that permitted the failure: the root-cause section should focus on what went wrong rather than who caused it, and the action items should aim at improving the system instead of improving people.

Give a postmortem depth: rather than only investigating the proximate area of failure, explore the impact and system flaws across multiple teams and perspectives, and base every conclusion on facts and data that are linked from the document.
Balance verbosity and readability in a postmortem by abstracting lengthy data sources such as chat transcripts and system logs in the main document and linking the unedited versions.

Senior leadership should support and encourage effective postmortems and consistently exemplify and enforce blameless behavior in every aspect of postmortem discussion, because a healthy postmortem culture depends on leadership modeling it.

Defend destructive operations with layered safety patterns drawn from postmortem action items: require a separate safety-check or approval service to authorize destructive work, reject operations that omit an expected-present constraint, disallow any single operation from affecting servers spanning namespace or class boundaries, cap the number of nodes one operation can affect, add an emergency-stop 'big red button', rate-limit the workflow, and alert when more than a set percentage of machines are removed.

Use blameless, non-leading language in postmortem discussions, because blameful or leading questions instantly put recipients on the defensive and stifle collaboration; reframe toward systemic and process improvements instead.
Include all incident participants in authoring the postmortem, because writing it in isolation or by a single team makes it easy to overlook key contributing factors to the outage.

Reward closing postmortem action items, not just writing the postmortem: rewarding the writeup alone risks an unvirtuous cycle of unclosed postmortems, so balance incentives between writing the document and successfully implementing its action plan.

Incentivize a healthy postmortem culture by rewarding the positive organizational change postmortems drive (peer bonuses, performance reviews, promotion), holding up postmortem owners as recognized experts, and gamifying action-item closure with scoreboards, burndowns, or periodic FixIt weeks.

Share postmortems openly through organization-wide announcements, cross-team reviews and reading clubs where one team walks through their incident while others learn, Wheel-of-Misfortune reenactments for training, and weekly outage reports shared with the widest possible audience.

Counter signs that postmortem culture is failing: review high-visibility postmortems for blameful prose to prevent people avoiding association, redirect blameful language (even from senior leaders) into generic questions like 'were there warning signs we could have heeded, and why did we dismiss them?', and investigate the source of misleading information rather than assign blame, since people act in good faith on the best information available.

Treat postmortems as letters to future team members and keep a consistent quality bar, because overloaded teams write subpar postmortems with incomplete action items that make recurrence far more likely; prioritize postmortem work, track its completion and review, and give teams adequate time to implement the action plan.

When incidents repeat, dig deeper by asking whether action items are taking too long to close, whether feature velocity is trumping reliability fixes, whether the right action items are being captured, whether the service is overdue for a refactor, or whether people are applying Band-Aids to a more serious problem — then bring the collaborators from each similar incident together to prevent repeats.

Bootstrap a postmortem culture with a standard template and tooling: a consistent format makes postmortems accessible to readers outside the domain, and tooling that prepopulates incident metadata, stores postmortems in a searchable repository, files action items as tracked bugs whose closure is monitored, and analyzes trends (mean duration, time to detect, time to resolve, blast radius) keeps action items from slipping through the cracks.

Ongoing investment in cultivating a postmortem culture pays dividends in fewer outages, a better user experience, more trust from dependents, better system design, less downtime, happier engineers, and faster recovery with more data when an incident does recur.

No service is 100% available 100% of the time, and there is no single solution for equalizing and stabilizing network load; instead use a combination of tools, technologies, and strategies working in harmony to keep services reliable.
Most companies should use a larger public cloud provider's global load-balancing service rather than developing and maintaining their own global load-balancing solution.

DNS-based load balancing is the simplest and most effective way to balance load before a user's connection even starts, but it has an endemic weakness: it relies on client cooperation to properly expire and refetch DNS records.

Anycast routes clients to the topologically nearest frontend using a single virtual IP, providing low latency and allowing a higher DNS TTL, but watch for two issues: too many nearby users can overwhelm a frontend site, and BGP route flaps reset in-progress TCP streams unless you stabilize them at a connection-level load balancer.

Model load-balancer redundancy as N+1 by spreading packets evenly across a pool of balancer machines (so you scale by simply adding servers) rather than relying on active/passive pairs that give only 1+1 redundancy, which enhances availability and reliability.

Terminate TCP and SSL sessions in a reverse-proxy front end as close to the user as possible, then forward requests to backend services deeper in the network over long-lived encrypted connections, to minimize end-user latency (especially the two round trips an HTTPS handshake requires).

Health-check your backends and use a 'lame duck' mode — a backend that fails health checks while continuing to respond to in-flight requests — so you can gracefully remove or update a backend without disrupting any user requests.

Have the front end maintain persistent, pre-warmed connections to its recently active backends so a connection is ready to use as soon as a request arrives, which reduces user latency particularly when the connection is secured with SSL.

Use canarying and gradual rollouts to maintain high availability: deploy a new version to a very small number of servers, gradually increase traffic while observing for regressions, let the load balancer route around any instance that fails health checks, and administratively remove a regressed instance group without touching the main version of the application.

Load-test for a wide safety margin but recognize that even generous testing can be exceeded: Niantic load-tested Pokémon GO to five times their most optimistic traffic estimate, yet the actual launch request rate was nearly fifty times that estimate.

A high-level (Layer 7) proxy operating on a large edge network handles SSL termination, HTTP request buffering, and low-level network attacks such as SYN floods better than a packet-level, IP-layer load balancer, which cannot effectively ameliorate such attacks.

Terminating SSL and buffering HTTP requests at backend proxies costs two client round trips and can exhaust proxy-tier resources when clients send bytes slowly, so push that work to a high-level edge proxy instead.

Measure load as close to the client as possible, because connections refused at the frontend are not surfaced in inbound-request monitoring, so the backends never see them and true client demand is underestimated.

A traffic surge beyond capacity causes a classic cascading failure: overloaded backends become extremely slow rather than refusing requests, requests time out to the load balancer, the load balancer retries them, the retries add still more load, and the combination collapses frontend capacity.

Avoid a synchronized 'thundering herd' of client retries — which a single-immediate-retry-then-constant-backoff strategy produces when a shared backend returns a burst of quick errors — by giving clients jitter and truncated exponential backoff.

Treat your frontend or load-balancer backends as a potentially significant source of load, and institute qualification and load-testing practices to detect frontend performance degradation caused by slow or otherwise misbehaving backends.

To contain one overloading service without harming others sharing the infrastructure, isolate its frontends into a separate pool, enlarge that pool until it can handle peak traffic, and apply administrative rate limits to contain client demand while the service reestablishes normal operation.

Autoscaling — whether vertical (more resources per machine) or horizontal (more machines in the pool) — enhances service availability and utilization when used correctly, but can negatively impact the service if misconfigured or misused.

Prevent unhealthy, non-serving instances (slow-to-warm or zombie instances) from skewing the autoscaler's utilization average by autoscaling on a capacity metric observed by the load balancer, waiting for new instances to stabilize (a cool-down period) before collecting metrics, and combining autoscaling with autohealing that restarts unhealthy instances.

For stateful systems that pin a user session to one backend, adding instances (horizontal scaling) does not relieve overburdened pathways — use intelligent task-level routing such as consistent hashing to spread load — while vertical autoscaling can absorb short-term hotspots but should be used cautiously because its uniform growth can make low-traffic instances unnecessarily large.

Configure autoscaling conservatively: scaling up is more important and less risky than scaling down because a failure to scale up results in overload and dropped traffic, so add capacity quickly but reduce it cautiously, keep the service far from key bottlenecks such as CPU, and reserve spare capacity for both overload protection and redundancy.

Set minimum and maximum bounds on the autoscaler (and ensure you have quota to reach the maximum), because a bug that burns CPU without doing work, or a failing dependency that wedges requests, can otherwise make the autoscaler scale out of control — wasting all quota and even preventing the failing dependency from recovering.

Include a kill switch and manual override for autoscaling that on-call engineers know how to use to disable autoscaling and scale manually; this functionality should be easy, obvious, fast, and well documented.

Perform a detailed dependency analysis on backend services before deploying an autoscaler, ensuring backends have spare capacity, degrade gracefully when overloaded, and that one microservice scaling up will not exhaust quota shared with others — implementing limited scaling or separate per-microservice quotas where needed.

Avoid traffic imbalance by having autoscalers rebalance instances across zones within a region, which evens out zone sizes and per-zone quota usage and, by autoscaling across regions, provides more diversity of failure domains.

As a system grows complex, combine multiple load-management techniques — load balancing, load-based autoscaling, and load shedding — since they all serve the same goal of equalizing and stabilizing system load and are not entirely independent.

Load-management tools configured in isolation can form catastrophic feedback loops: in one case a utilization-aware load balancer read each load-shed (dropped) request as cheaper per-request CPU, concluded the failing region was more efficient, and sent it even more traffic, because the load-shedding and load-balancing systems were not communicating.

Be deliberate about how load-management tools interact: when adopting a new tool, carefully examine and instrument its intersection with the tools already in use, add monitoring to detect feedback loops, and coordinate emergency shutdown triggers across all load-management systems.

Because autoscaling and load balancing together can form a positive feedback loop that concentrates all serving capacity in the location closest to demand, set a minimum number of instances per location so spare capacity remains for failover if that location goes down.
Set load-shedding thresholds so the system autoscales before load shedding kicks in, otherwise the system may start shedding traffic it could have served had it scaled up first.

Set deliberate deadlines on RPC requests, because in the absence of a deadline a process holds resources for every in-flight request up to a very large default, raising latency and risking resource exhaustion and crashes; servers should terminate requests that take too long and clients should cancel requests that are no longer useful to them.

There are no perfect traffic-management configurations: traffic management works best from a holistic view of how the systems interact, and no amount of load shedding, autoscaling, or throttling will save services when they all fail in sync, so plan ahead to fail gracefully with measures like flags, changed defaults, expensive logging, or exposing the parameters the system uses for decisions.

Reliability is the most critical feature of any production system, and deferring reliability issues during design is akin to accepting fewer features at higher costs; an iterative style of system design and implementation arrives at robust, scalable designs with low operational costs.

Non-Abstract Large System Design (NALSD) is the skill of assessing, designing, and evaluating large systems by combining capacity planning, component isolation, and graceful system degradation — starting from a basic whiteboard diagram, thinking through the scaling and failure domains, and focusing the design into a concrete proposal for resources.

Keep system design 'non-abstract' by turning the whiteboard design into concrete estimates of resources at multiple steps, because all systems eventually run on real computers, networks, and datacenters; this up-front rigor leads to fewer last-minute design changes for physical constraints, and sound reasoning with reasonable assumptions matters more than perfect final numbers.

Drive large-system design through two iterative NALSD phases — basic design (Is it possible? Can we do better?) and scaling (Is it feasible? Is it resilient? Can we do better?) — bouncing between the questions, restarting when a design flounders, and expressing the requirements as SLOs so each iteration can be compared against a goal and error budget.

Start a system design from the simplest possible point — a single machine — and evaluate it, because even an infeasible single-machine design yields valuable information about how to reason about the system's constraints and requirements.

Build an appropriate indexed data structure as data arrives so lookups remain fast as the system handles ever-larger volumes, rather than scanning the raw logs to answer each query, which becomes very inefficient beyond a few records.
Estimate resource requirements with deliberately rounded-up assumptions and scientific notation, to avoid prematurely hitting a limit and to limit errors caused by arithmetic on inconsistent units.

Identify the binding constraint rather than only the total capacity: a single machine might hold 100 TB of disk yet be limited by its IOPS (a common HDD sustains only about 200 IOPS), so choose storage media that meets the IO requirement, not just the size requirement.

Test a design by asking what happens when each component fails: a single machine has a long list of single points of failure (CPU, memory, storage, power, network, cooling) and cannot support meaningful SLOs, since even a simple power cycle would significantly impact users.

MapReduce-style batch processing scales horizontally — adding machines always lets it complete without running out of disk or RAM — but it cannot meet a low data-freshness SLO, and its arbitrary, non-overlapping batches cannot join records that span batches (a query in one batch and its click in the next will never be joined).

When joining two data sets of very different sizes, scale the larger one: build an on-demand lookup store keyed for the bigger input and loop only over the smaller stream, pulling in the specific large-side records it references.
When joining streams where one side may lag, set aside a record that has no match yet and retry up to a time limit, then discard it if no match is found by that limit.

Shard the inputs and outputs across multiple instances by hashing a key (and taking it modulo the shard count) to get past a single machine's IO limits, sharding each component by the key it is read and written by so the same hashing approach gives every component a consistent view of the data.
Prefer scaling horizontally — adding more instances, each receiving only an evenly distributed trickle of the load — over scaling vertically with more CPU and RAM per machine.

Make a sharded design resilient to instance failure by replicating each unit of work to a duplicate shard so the system keeps running at full speed when one instance fails, distributing the workload so no two duplicate shards land on the same machine, and covering the residual risk of concurrent double-failure with the error budget and log reprocessing.

Treat a single datacenter as a single point of failure: duplicate data across geographically separate datacenters so that if one datacenter suffers a multi-day power or network outage, the system can fail over to another.

Replicating state across datacenters without multiplying compute is the consensus problem: make three or five replicas that use a consensus algorithm such as Paxos to reliably store state through a datacenter-sized failure, accepting that each write needs at least one inter-node network round trip — which bounds sequential throughput — while parallelizing writes where possible.

Separate software components based on how you expect the system to grow, so different parts can scale independently and no part depends on a single piece of hardware or a single software instance, producing a more reliable system.

Evaluate every design iteration with the four NALSD questions — Is it possible (can we build it without 'magic')? Can we do better (is it as simple as we can reasonably make it)? Is it feasible (does it fit budget and time)? Is it resilient (will it survive inevitable disruptions)? — and treat NALSD as a learned skill that needs regular practice.
Data processing is often business-critical, so delayed or incorrect data in a pipeline can manifest as user-facing issues that are expensive, labor-intensive, and time-consuming to fix.
Involve SREs in data-processing-pipeline work from its early stages, consulting on the design so the pipeline can be easily released, modified, and run without causing issues for customers.

Use the Extract-Transform-Load (ETL) model — extract data from one or more sources, transform it (reformatting fields, aggregating across sources, or applying an index), and load it into a specialized format — to prepare data for further analysis or serving and increase system efficiency.

Define and measure service level objectives for a data pipeline so you automatically detect when it is unhealthy or failing to meet customer needs, and receive notifications when you are in danger of exceeding the error budget, while balancing reliability against feature launches.
Most pipeline data-freshness SLOs take one of three forms: X% of data processed within Y time, the oldest data is no older than Y time, or the pipeline job has completed successfully within Y time.

Create data-correctness SLOs to be alerted about data errors (such as a billing pipeline over- or under-charging); when there is no predefined correct output, generate 'golden data' using test accounts to compute the expected output, then monitor and alert on discrepancies between expected and actual output as test data flows through production.

When you promise a tighter SLO on high-priority data, ensure that data is processed before lower-priority data if resources become constrained — implemented as separate priority queues or jobs, with work that fails on lower-provisioned workers retried on higher-provisioned ones.

Measure pipeline SLOs end-to-end rather than per-stage, because per-stage SLOs do not capture the customer's experience and can miss end-to-end data-corruption bugs where each stage reports success but a field one stage adds is dropped by a downstream stage that does not expect it.

Plan for dependency failure: confirm you are not over-depending on other products' SLOs/SLAs, design for at least the largest failure accounted for in a dependency's advertised SLA, and if a dependency's guarantee is below what your SLO requires, replicate data across regions for higher availability or accept and offer a looser SLA to your own customers.

Stage planned outages (such as disaster-recovery testing that simulates a regional outage) to encourage building pipelines that fail over automatically, and regularly practice disaster-recovery scenarios so your systems are resilient to common and uncommon failures, because even the best products will eventually fail.

Maintain three categories of pipeline documentation: system diagrams showing each component and the transformation at each step with quick links to live and historical monitoring, process documentation for common and uncommon tasks (automating manual work and generating docs from source to stay in sync), and a playbook entry for each alert condition linked in the alert message.

Follow a pipeline development lifecycle: prototype and unit-test the business logic, run a 1% dry run on real production data in a non-production environment and scale up gradually while tracking performance, stage on production-like data with A/B comparison against known-good output, then canary, partially deploy, and deploy to production.

Canary the entire pipeline rather than a single process: process the same real production data as the live pipeline but skip writes to production storage (for example using two-phase mutation), then compare the canary's results with the live pipeline's to check for data differences; for replicated or multihomed pipelines that cannot canary per region, roll out a small percentage of data first or in dry-run mode.

Perform a partial deployment for a major feature or performance change by gating it behind a flag or config that accepts a subset of data and ramping gradually (for example one or two accounts, then ~1%, ~10%, ~50%, and finally 100%), to avoid promoting a corrupt set of data to low-latency frontends and to catch issues before they reach users.

When a pipeline deployment goes wrong, be able to quickly restore from a known good state (such as rolling back the binaries) and mark any potentially broken data as bad — replacing it with a previous backup version, ensuring no jobs read the affected data, and reprocessing it if necessary.

Combat hotspotting — where a resource is overloaded by excessive access (task overload, single-machine CPU exhaustion, row-level lock contention, disk-head contention, or an oversized work unit) — by blocking fine-grained data such as individual records so the rest of the pipeline progresses, letting the framework dynamically rebalance by breaking work into smaller pieces, and building an emergency shutdown that can skip input matching a problematic pattern or user.

Reduce hotspotting structurally by restructuring your data or access patterns to spread load evenly, reducing the load through static allocation of some or all data, and reducing lock granularity to avoid data-lock contention.

Use autoscaling for variable and streaming pipelines so you do not have to provision for peak load 100% of the time — autoscaling turns down idle workers so you do not pay for unused resources — while noting that batch pipelines will consume as many resources as are available.

Plan pipeline resources against an estimate of future growth, weighing the cost of resources against the engineering effort to make the pipeline more efficient and accounting for hidden costs such as data storage, cross-region replication, and expensive data stores; periodically examine the data set and prune unused content to drive down costs.

Although a series of pipeline stages should be measured for effectiveness by its end-to-end SLO, measure pipeline efficiency and resource usage at each individual stage so you can quickly determine which job is responsible for a cost increase and focus engineering effort there.

Enforce least-privilege access control and security for persisted pipeline data: avoid storing personally identifiable information in temporary storage (and encrypt it if you must), grant each pipeline stage only the minimal access it needs to read the previous stage's output, and put time-to-live limits on logs and PII.

Design a pipeline to be resilient enough that a machine or zonal outage never triggers an SLO-violation page, because by the time you are paged all automated measures have been exhausted and you must intervene manually; with well-defined SLOs and reliable alert detection you are alerted before customers notice, and when an SLO is violated you should respond quickly and send proactive communication to customers.

Spend significant time in the design phase assessing which pipeline technology best fits, comparing and contrasting the options against user needs, product requirements, and system constraints, since some platforms are fully managed while others give more flexibility but require more hands-on management.

When machine-learning decisions, classifications, or recommendations are missing, stale, or incorrect, diagnose by asking whether data is stuck coming into the pipeline before preprocessing, whether the model is poor (a software bug, too much spam, or poorly chosen features), and whether a stale model version is running in production instead of a freshly generated one.
Maintain a set of tools to monitor and detect pipeline issues before customers experience any problems, so that when an outage does occur you can quickly repair or roll back the offending code.

Optimize a data pipeline for the features it actually needs and skip features it does not — for example you do not need 'exactly once' semantics if your work units are idempotent and can be performed more than once with the same result.

Use the idempotent-mutation design pattern — a mutation that can be applied multiple times with the same result — so that separate executions of a pipeline on the same input always produce the same result and reprocessing after a failure does not store duplicate or incorrect data.

Use the two-phase-mutation design pattern to test or canary a pipeline safely: store the proposed mutations in a temporary location, run a separate verification step or pipeline to validate them for correctness, and apply the mutations only after they pass validation.

Use checkpointing so a long-running pipeline periodically saves partial state to storage and can resume after early termination, preemption, or rescheduling without re-executing the whole pipeline — detecting which work units are already processed and skipping potentially expensive reads or computations.

Implement reusable code libraries across pipelines so you can add a monitoring metric in one place and share it across multiple pipelines or stages, gaining insight across all pipelines in a standard way and alerting on the same metric (such as a generic data-freshness alert) for many jobs.

Apply the microservice approach to pipelines: instead of one monolithic pipeline application, build smaller pipelines that each perform a single task well, share the same core libraries, vary only in business logic, and can be released and monitored separately.

Use a pipeline maturity matrix to score key characteristics — failure tolerance, scalability, monitoring and debugging, transparency and ease of implementation, and unit and integration testing — on a 1-to-5 scale from 'Chaotic' (unplanned, ad hoc, manual) to 'Continuous improvement', to get a clear picture of where the system needs improvement.

When improving a pipeline's weak areas, first look for existing products or open source tools that fit your needs and reuse out-of-the-box pipeline support, rather than creating your own, because the more tools and processes you can reuse the better.

Track mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to repair (MTTR) for pipeline outages and SLO violations to measure how effective you are at detecting and repairing issues, and analyze each outage's cause in a postmortem to elicit patterns and address sources of operational toil.

Stale data is almost always better than incorrect data: design a pipeline so that when input is delayed it stalls, waits for the data, and resumes once it becomes available — keeping data high quality — rather than processing incomplete or corrupt data and propagating errors downstream, and create data dependencies respected by all stages.

Streaming systems are more flexible than batch systems for handling delayed data: with event-time processing a downstream stage can start a portion of work as soon as the corresponding upstream portion completes, whereas in batch processing each stage must wait for its predecessor to finish entirely.

Guard against corrupt data with tests that identify it and logic that alerts on potential corruption, and implement blocking policies and abuse/spam detection to automatically or manually filter out bad sources of data before they cause user-facing issues.

Fix corrupt data in two steps — first mitigate by preventing further corrupt data from entering the system, then restore from a known good version or reprocess to repair — draining or rolling back the offending region or binary, and reduce reprocessing cost with selective reprocessing of only the impacted users or accounts or by using persisted intermediate checkpoints.

Plan for the eventuality that even with the best testing, development, and release practices a software or configuration bug will introduce data corruption, by ensuring you can quickly reprocess and restore data, since recovering from data corruption is labor-intensive and difficult to automate.

Investigate a pipeline's dependencies — storage, network systems, or other services — when diagnosing an outage, because they may be throttling requests or refusing new data when out of resources; some such issues will not self-resolve, so file a ticket, allow time to add resources, and mitigate by load balancing and dropping low-priority data.

Application or configuration errors are the most common cause of pipeline outages; respond by rolling back the binary or config, cherry-picking a fix, repairing permissions, or restructuring the problem data, and prevent them by ensuring new binaries and configurations perform well in a non-production environment before full deployment.

When a pipeline fails from unexpected resource growth, autoscale the application jobs to meet the new load but be aware that increased pipeline load also strains downstream dependencies (plan for more storage and network), become familiar with requesting emergency resources because acquisition can be slow, and prepare interim solutions such as prioritizing different classes of data.

A region-level outage is especially dangerous for singly-homed pipelines, which stop until the region returns, whereas a multihomed pipeline with automatic failover can simply drain processing or serving from the affected region; a down region can strand or delay data and compromise the correctness of dependent jobs.

Decouple data collection from data delivery using an intermediate globally distributed persistent queue, so the two act as independent failure domains that limit the impact of production issues and produce a more resilient system.

Give each ETL or pipeline component a single responsibility, which makes the components easier to develop, test, and operate, and isolate independent data streams (such as different event types) so they cannot impact one another.

Define and measure a pipeline's SLO at the interface its consumers actually use (for example delivered hourly buckets per event type rather than internal stages), and let customers dynamically enable or disable work via simple configuration while autoscaling acquires and releases the resources needed.

Clear SLOs help a system in three ways: during design and development they give goals that drive pragmatic choices and optimization for simplicity, in production they identify which parts of the system are underperforming and where to focus, and they guide operation.

Use SLOs to manage customer expectations and avoid unnecessary support requests, because when the limits of your system are clear to customers they are empowered to design, build, and operate their own systems that depend on your data.
Measure your SLOs using independent external systems to stay objective and to avoid bloating the service with measurement features that have nothing to do with its core function.
Split a delivery or timeliness SLO into priority tiers (such as high, normal, and low) that customers configure per data type, so you can prioritize the most important data during an incident.

Define strong correctness SLOs only where they are needed — for finance-bearing data — and expose no such SLO for data where best-effort delivery is good enough, letting customer configuration declare which data requires the stronger guarantee.

Timestamp events by when they were received at your servers, not when they were produced on the client, because clients may buffer events offline for many days and users can modify their device's system time, producing inaccurately timestamped events.

Do not provide quality or accuracy SLOs for data whose quality depends on customer-owned business logic; keep the system focused exclusively on delivery — behaving like a postal service that delivers mail on time, intact, and unopened — and leave quality SLOs to the teams that own and understand the content.

Provide a complex system to its consumers as a fully managed service that hides the system's complexity behind a well-defined, easy-to-understand API, and support only a limited set of functionality to keep the API simple while still covering the majority of use cases.

Require each data type or stream to be explicitly enabled with explicit ownership defined, because holding producing teams accountable for what they produce results in higher data quality and gives a clear channel of communication during incidents.

Treat documentation like any other software product, classifying every support request as either an issue with the documentation or an issue with the actual product, with the goal of minimizing the number of support requests as the customer base grows.

Because monitoring on SLO violations only alerts you after customers are affected, add sufficient operational monitoring of the system — starting with basic metrics such as CPU usage and building to more complex ones — so you can resolve or mitigate issues before an SLO is broken.

Gather only the right amount of logging data: logging every request of a high-volume component drowns useful logs, fills disk faster, and degrades performance, so rate-limit logged requests or log only interesting ones such as those that result in unhandled exceptions, and treat reading application logs in production as a last resort.

Provision each component for about 50% CPU usage at peak as a safety margin for unexpected traffic bursts, use autoscaling for stateless components to avoid the waste of static allocation, but continue to capacity-plan by ensuring enough quota and setting the maximum instance count high enough to serve peaks yet low enough to limit runaway autoscaling.

CPU-based autoscaling depends on a strong correlation between CPU usage and work done; if that correlation breaks (a CPU-hungry daemon, or instances burning CPU without doing work), the autoscaler scales indefinitely until it exhausts all quota, so limit the maximum instances, restrict daemon CPU, and aggressively throttle a component's CPU as soon as you detect no useful work is being done.

Use CI/CD with a testing-pyramid philosophy — many unit tests on internals, fewer integration tests on each component's public API, and a system-wide black-box end-to-end test — gating merges on peer review and all tests passing; for a critical system, deploy each change in stages (staging with mirrored production traffic, then a canary subset, then full production) requiring manual approval between stages.

During an incident, prioritize mitigating damage and returning the system to a stable previous state and refrain from deploying major changes — the exception being to immediately roll back to a previous working version when recently deployed code is the cause.
exception: deploy a rollback when the incident was caused by recently deployed code

statement: Having a single team responsible for the development and operation of a system throughout its entire lifecycle lets the team apply the experience it gains from maintaining the system to continually improve it.

Configuration is a human-computer interface for modifying system behavior with low overhead, used instead of a code change when behavior must change quickly without an expensive rebuild and redeploy; a system can be reasoned about as three components — the software, the data set it works with, and the configuration — which are often not cleanly separated.
A good configuration interface allows quick, confident, and testable configuration changes, whereas a poor one makes mistakes more likely and increases users' cognitive load and learning curve.

The quality of a configuration interface impacts an organization's ability to run a system reliably, much as code quality impacts maintainability, but configuration differs from code because a single configuration change can dramatically alter functionality (one bad firewall rule can lock you out), configuration often lives in an untested or untestable environment, and changes are frequently made under incident pressure.

Separate configuration philosophy (how to structure configuration, the correct level of abstraction, and how to support diverging use cases — all independent of implementation) from configuration mechanics (language design, deployment strategies, and system interactions), and reason about them separately, since even the simplest inputs cause problems in a cumbersome interface and the best language fails if it demands huge, hard-to-understand input.

Treat 'no configuration at all' as the ideal — a system that recognizes the correct configuration from its deployment, workload, or existing config — and aim away from a large number of tunables toward simplicity, because fewer knobs decrease both the surface area for error and the operator's cognitive load, and training operators on complex controls is no longer feasible for most of the industry.

Since configuration ultimately boils down to an interface that asks users questions about how the system should operate, favor the user-centric view — the fewer knobs the better, because answering configuration questions is a chore — over the infrastructure-centric view that adds as many knobs as possible.

A user-centric configuration approach requires designing the software around a particular set of use cases for your key audience (which requires user research), and counterintuitively, limited configuration options can lead to better adoption than highly versatile software because onboarding effort is substantially lower and the software mostly works out of the box.
A system that begins from an infrastructure-centric view can move toward a more user-centric focus as it matures by progressively removing configuration knobs.

Ask configuration questions close to the user's goals — letting users describe their needs in their own high-level terms rather than specifying exactly how the system should implement them — because when users describe high-level goals the system can evolve over time and improve how it implements them.

Distinguish mandatory configuration questions (which must be answered for any functionality) from optional ones (which only improve quality), and minimize the number of mandatory questions, because the life of an engineer is an endless chain of small steps and principled reduction of those steps dramatically improves productivity.

Reduce mandatory configuration questions by converting them to optional ones — providing default answers that apply safely and effectively to most or all users, such as defaulting an execution to dry-run.

Make defaults dynamic where appropriate — determined from system properties rather than a single static value, such as deploying as many threads as the container has cores or sizing a JVM heap to the container's available memory — to further simplify configuration, while allowing the dynamic default to be overridden when you need to restrict resource usage.

If a significant portion of users report problems with a dynamic default, your decision logic no longer matches the user base, so improve the dynamic defaults broadly rather than adding configuration knobs; if only a small fraction are unhappy, let them set options manually rather than adding complexity and cognitive load for everyone.

Choose default answers carefully, because experience shows most users will use the default — so it is both a chance to nudge people in the right direction and a responsibility, since the wrong default does a great deal of harm (as the dramatic difference between opt-in and opt-out organ-donor defaults illustrates).

Add a configuration knob only when motivated by a real need, remove optional questions that have no clear use case (since a large number of optional questions confuses users), and — if your configuration language supports inheritance — allow reverting to the default value for any optional question in leaf configurations.

Accommodate power users through optional overrides of high-level default behavior — letting a user configure the high-level goal and then fine-tune a low-level aspect — rather than lowering everyone to the lowest common denominator of complexity that even the simplest use cases must then reason about.

Optimize configuration for the total hours spent configuring across the whole organization — including decision paralysis from too many options, time to correct a wrong turn, and a slower rate of change due to lower confidence — so an option that accomplishes a complex configuration in fewer but harder steps may be preferable if it makes the most common use cases significantly easier.

If more than a small subset of your users need a complex configuration, you have probably incorrectly identified the common use cases, so revisit the initial product assumptions and conduct additional user research.
