Make configuration both code and data but keep the two separate: have the system infrastructure operate on plain static data (such as Protocol Buffers, YAML, or JSON) while users interact with a higher-level interface — a DSL, Lua, Jsonnet, or a web UI — that generates that data.

Separating the configuration interface from its static data representation gives the system deployment flexibility — it can be adapted to diverse organizational norms, support multiple languages, and externalize configuration to end users — and the separation can be invisible to the user, who edits the configuration language while it is automatically compiled into raw data behind the scenes.

Store metadata about how each configuration was ingested (such as the original source path before it was compiled into data) so you can track down configuration authors, and use the static configuration data for analysis — for example loading JSON into a database to query which configuration parameters are used and by whom, which helps you remove unused features or measure a buggy option's impact.

Provide semantic validation of configuration, not just syntax validation: even a syntactically valid configuration may reference a nonexistent directory or request a thousand times more RAM than available due to wrong units, so validate that the configuration is semantically meaningful at the moment the user commits it, rather than after the change is submitted, to prevent outages and reduce operational cost.

Equip a configuration system with tooling — syntax highlighting in editors, a linter to catch common inconsistencies, and an automatic syntax formatter — because standardized formatting minimizes unimportant formatting debates, decreases cognitive load as contributors switch projects, enables automatic editing, and prevents dangerous incorrect indentation in whitespace-oriented configs.

Give each configuration snippet a clear single owner (for example one owning group per directory) so it is easy to track who makes changes, and version all configuration — including configuration ingested by web UI or remote API — so you can go back to see what it looked like at any point in time.

Log both changes to the configuration and the resulting application of those changes to the system, because committing a new version of a configuration does not always mean it is directly applied; during incident response this lets you quickly determine the full set of configuration edits, enabling confident rollbacks and notification of impacted parties.

For a configuration change to be safe it must have three properties: the ability to be deployed gradually (avoiding an all-or-nothing change), the ability to be rolled back if it proves dangerous, and automatic rollback (or at minimum the ability to stop progress) if the change leads to loss of operator control.

Push a new configuration out gradually (for example with a rolling update) rather than a global all-at-once push, so you can detect issues and abort a problematic push before causing a 100% outage, and prefer rolling back the offending configuration over patching it with a lower-confidence temporary fix to shorten the incident.

Make configuration hermetic so it can be rolled forward and back reliably, because configuration that requires external resources able to change outside its hermetic environment — such as version-controlled configuration that references data on a network filesystem — is very hard to roll back.

Take special care with changes that might cause sudden loss of operator control — like firewalling yourself out of a system or an incorrect monitor setting that prevents reverting — by using a confirm-or-revert mechanism such as a countdown that resets if the user does not confirm; these principles apply equally to upgrading binaries and pushing new data sets.

Configuration starts lightweight (a few data-only files) but grows complex and verbose as the number of applications, servers, and variations increases, producing 'replication toil' — the mundane task of managing configuration duplicated across a system — which is especially common in microservice architectures with many independently configured components.

Building a configuration language or framework to remove replication toil does not eliminate configuration toil but introduces 'complexity toil' — the frustrating task of dealing with the emergent and sometimes undesirable behaviors of complex automation — which materializes in larger organizations and compounds with growth, so tackle it as early as possible since configuration size and complexity only grow over time.

Treat configuration as a programming-language problem: if you do not intentionally design the language, the format you end up with creeps from data-only toward an esoteric complex programming language (a 'count' attribute that needs an evaluator, or string interpolation that hides code) that is unsuited to tooling; an efficient configuration system must provide tooling for config health, hermetic evaluation for rollbacks and replayability, and separation of config and data.

Do not add ad hoc programming-language features to a simple config format over time, because ad hoc languages are more complex and usually less expressive than formally designed equivalents and develop gotchas and idiosyncrasies since their authors could not consider feature interactions ahead of time; consider the need for simple programming constructs at the initial design phase instead.

Building too much domain-specific optimization into a custom configuration solution is costly: a smaller user base means you wait longer to justify building tooling, engineers are unwilling to learn a language with little applicability outside the domain, and learning resources are less likely to exist.

Do not interleave configuration evaluation with side effects — making changes to external systems or consulting out-of-band data sources like DNS, VM IDs, or build versions during a config run — because that violates hermeticity and prevents separating config from data; instead evaluate the config first, make the resulting data available to inspect, and only then allow side effects.

Using an existing general-purpose scripting language such as Python, Ruby, or Lua for configuration is heavyweight and needs intrusive sandboxing to ensure hermeticity and security (since such languages can access the local system), and you cannot assume maintainers know the language; prefer a purpose-built configuration DSL.

Use an existing domain-specific configuration language rather than inventing one — even if a DSL seems too powerful for your needs, you may need the additional functionality at some point and can always restrict the language with an in-house style guide.

Generate configuration in each application's required format from a single source so you can drive several applications from one config — unifying, synchronizing, and eliminating repetition across the whole config corpus, for example defining a port only once and outputting both a web-server config and a firewall config.

Abstract commonalities across configurations to promote separation of concerns with the same benefits as modularity in programming languages — useful when one team maintains almost-identical variants across environments, architectures, or geographies, and when an infrastructure team maintains reusable component templates that application teams instantiate.

When integrating a custom application with a configuration language, let the config language handle the language aspect of the problem and the application handle all other functionality, and have the application consume a single pure-data file that the config language splits via imports.

Represent a collection of named entities as an object whose field is the entity name and value is the rest of the entity, rather than an array of objects each with a name field, because this makes the collection easier to extend and lets you reference entities by name (animals.cat) instead of by brittle indexes (animals[0]).

Structure configuration data so that logically related configuration is grouped in the same subtree rather than grouping entities by type at the top level, so that abstraction at the config-language level can follow functional boundaries.

Keep the configuration data representation simple: do not embed language features in the data representation (they are underpowered and force users to choose where to abstract), do not worry about overly verbose data (manage verbosity in the config language), and avoid interpreting custom string-interpolation syntax in the application, letting the config language do as much language-level work as possible.
If you can remove configuration altogether, doing so is always your best option.

Do not rely on the configuration language to fix inconsistent naming, plurals, or mistakes in the underlying model — fix them in the model itself; if you cannot fix the model's inconsistencies, it is better to live with them at the language level than to introduce even more inconsistency.

Because configuration changes tend to dominate outage root causes over time, validate the generated config data immediately after configuration execution, going beyond syntactic validation (which finds few bugs) to check domain-specific properties such as whether required fields are present, referenced filenames exist, and provided values are within allowed ranges.
Do not ignore unrecognized field names when validating configuration, because they may indicate a typo at the configuration-language level, and perform the same validation in a precommit hook.

Apply ordinary software-engineering discipline to 'configuration as code': version shared template libraries so consumers can migrate independently (with deprecated-version users incurring technical debt), keep configuration in source control for history, easy rollback, and code review, enforce a consistent style with linters via editor and precommit hooks, and write unit tests for upstream template and utility libraries.

Make a configuration language hermetic — generating the same config data regardless of where or when it executes — so the high-level configuration is always interchangeable with the expanded data it represents and can be generated at any time.

Choose when to evaluate configuration — before check-in, at build time, or at runtime when the application needs the data — according to your use case's tradeoffs, noting that storing configuration in version control gives the earliest opportunity to validate it before check-in.

Checking the generated data into version control alongside its source lets reviewers sanity-check concrete changes (a refactor should not change the output) and avoids running the config tool at runtime, but the generated data may be unreadable, too large, contain secrets, or cause merge conflicts when concurrent edits converge.

Evaluating configuration at build time and embedding the generated data into the release artifact controls runtime complexity, binary size, and risk exposure without rebuilding per pull request, and eliminates the risk of desynchronization between the originating source and the resulting data.

For a breaking change to a shared configuration library used by many teams, either commit a global update that refactors all client code (which may not be organizationally possible) or version the library so different consumers can use different versions and migrate independently.

Implement unit tests for upstream configuration template libraries and utility functions, verifying that they generate the expected concrete configuration when instantiated in various ways, so the libraries can be maintained with confidence.

Configuration execution should terminate quickly, but bugs or deliberate attacks can make it consume arbitrary CPU time or memory, and restricting the language to be non-Turing-complete does not prevent overconsumption because you can write practically nonterminating programs even in simple formats like XML and YAML.

The risk of abusive configuration depends on trust: trusted config run by a command-line tool can mitigate an accidental nontermination with Ctrl-C, but a service that evaluates arbitrary end-user config in a request handler must guard against denial-of-service by sandboxing the execution — for example in a separate process under a resource limit (forking to an executable rather than linking the library) so over-limit programs fail safely and inform the user.

The critical properties of a configuration language are good tooling, hermetic configurations, and separation of configuration and data; transition to a domain-specific configuration language only when your complexity increases, not before.

Release engineering covers all the processes and artifacts for getting code from a repository into a running production system, and automating releases avoids the traditional pitfalls of repetitive manual toil, the inconsistency of a nonautomated process, not knowing the exact state of a rollout, and the difficulty of rolling back.

The basic principles of release engineering are reproducible builds (the same inputs always produce the same artifacts), automated builds, automated tests, automated deployments performed by computers rather than humans, and small self-contained deployments.

Automating releases lets you release more often, which for software with a nontrivial rate of change means fewer changes are bundled in each release artifact, making any given release cheaper and easier to roll back when a bug appears and getting bug fixes to users faster.

Monitor the release pipeline to measure and continuously improve it, answering questions like how long a release takes to reach production, how often releases succeed (made available with no severe defects or SLO violations), what changes catch defects earliest, and which steps can be parallelized or optimized.

Release velocity and reliability are not strictly opposing goals: aim to ship as quickly as possible while meeting the specific reliability targets your users expect, recognizing that a majority of incidents are triggered by binary or configuration pushes.

Rather than advocating against change — since bug fixes, security patches, and new features are necessary for the business to succeed — use SLOs and error budgets to measure the impact of releases on your reliability.

Separate components that change at different rates (binaries, runtime environment, libraries, service config, feature config, and user config) and use feature-flag or experiment frameworks to separate feature launches from binary releases, so you can enable features one at a time and selectively disable a misbehaving feature without waiting for the next build and release cycle.

Canarying is a partial, time-limited deployment of a change together with an evaluation that decides whether to proceed with the rollout; the part of the service that receives the change is the 'canary' and the remainder is the 'control', making canarying effectively an A/B testing process.

Even a fully automated release pipeline cannot detect all release-related defects until real traffic hits the service, because test environments are not 100% identical to production and tests do not cover 100% of scenarios; canarying initially exposes only some production traffic to a new release to detect defects as quickly as possible with as little impact as possible.

A canary process requires a method to deploy the change to a subset of the service population, an evaluation process to decide whether the change is good or bad, and integration of those evaluations into the release process; it demonstrates value when it detects bad release candidates with high confidence and identifies good releases without false positives.

Deploy a release candidate to a small labeled segment of production and send it only a small portion of traffic so defects are spotted before all of production is affected; traffic can be split using application versions, load-balancer backend weights, proxy configurations, or round-robin DNS.

Track the canary's key metric broken down per version rather than only in aggregate, because the canary serves a small subset of traffic so its errors are masked in the overall trend, and automate the deployment to pause and roll back (or page a human) when the canary metric is too far from the control metric.

Canarying minimizes risk to the SLO and error budget because the impact on the budget is directly proportional to the amount of traffic exposed to defects — a 5% canary of a candidate that fails 20% of requests yields only a 1% overall error rate versus 20% for a global deployment — so you learn about the new version at much lower cost.

Use the simplest canary risk model that meets your technical and business objectives, because focusing on making the model as technically correct as possible often leads to overinvestment and, for complex services, incessant model tuning for no real benefit — all models are wrong, but some are useful.

Choose canary duration factoring in development velocity (a daily release cannot run a week-long canary; continuous deployment requires much shorter canaries), and run only one canary deployment at a time, since simultaneous canaries add significant mental effort to track system state and risk signal contamination if they overlap.

Make a canary sizeable and long enough to be representative of the overall deployment — the higher the processing rate, the less time is needed for a representative sample — and deploy during heavy load rather than off-peak, since performance defects typically manifest only under load.
Once you have gathered metrics from past canaries, choose your canary parameters based on the system's typical canary-evaluation failure rates rather than on hypothetical worst-case scenarios.

Select canary metrics that indicate actual user-perceivable problems, starting from your SLIs because good SLIs have strong attribution to service health and reuse work already done for SLO compliance, and avoid metrics like CPU usage whose increase does not necessarily impact users, since a flaky or noisy canary process tends to get disabled or ignored by operators — defeating its purpose.

Define the notion of acceptable behavior for each canary metric carefully: too strict a definition yields false positives that flag a good canary as bad, too loose a definition lets a bad canary go undetected, and you must reevaluate these expectations regularly as the service and its behavior evolve.

Stack-rank candidate canary metrics by how well they indicate user-perceivable problems and select only the top few (no more than about a dozen), because too many metrics bring diminishing returns and a maintenance cost that, if unmet, erodes trust in the release process.

Handle ambiguous canary metrics such as an HTTP 404 — which can come from a user requesting a wrong URL or from the server incorrectly dropping a resource — by excluding the ambiguous codes from the canary evaluation and adding black-box monitoring (for example probing for the presence of a specific URL) to isolate the canary process from odd user behaviors.

Choose canary metrics whose changes are clearly attributable to the change being canaried and not influenced by external factors, because in a large population outliers — oversubscribed machines, machines on different kernels, or an overloaded network segment — mean a canary-versus-control difference reflects the infrastructure difference as much as the deployed change.

Isolate canary metrics from confounding sources: prefer the CPU time the process spent serving the request (ideally over the window the process was actually scheduled on a CPU) over whole-system CPU, since other processes like database load or log rotation can drive whole-system increases that are not caused by the canaried change and should not be flagged as a canary failure.
Canary metrics must be attributable — tied to SLIs — because a metric that can change wildly with no impact to the service is unlikely to make a good canary metric.

Before/after canary evaluation — fully replacing the old system and comparing behavior before and after the change over time — is risky because time is one of the biggest sources of change in observed metrics, so a degradation may have occurred in the control too, and over a longer period you may be comparing dissimilar periods such as a business day against a weekend, introducing large noise.

Use a gradual, multi-stage canary so that metrics which do not meet the ideal properties can still add value: in the first small stage, where you have no confidence in the release, prefer the clearest indicators of a problem such as application crashes and request failures to minimize negative impact, and increase the canary population in later stages to gain confidence.

Because the canary and control share backends, frontends, networks, and data stores and may interact in nonobvious ways, imperfect isolation means a canary result that says to stop does not necessarily mean the canary is at fault and a bad canary can hurt the control — so also use absolute measures such as defined SLOs to confirm the system is operating correctly.

For noninteractive systems such as asynchronous processing pipelines, make the canary duration at minimum span the processing time of a single work unit, ensure each work unit's stages are always handled by the same pool (canary or control) so signals do not mix, and select metrics like end-to-end processing time and application-specific processing quality.

Structure the monitoring system so you can perform fine-grained breakdowns that differentiate metrics between the canary and control populations, because monitoring that reasons about the whole service is insufficient to analyze a canary — a 5% canary running at a 20% error rate shows only a 1% overall error rate that may be indistinguishable from other error sources.

When using metrics to evaluate canary success, make the aggregation interval of the metric the same as or less than the canary duration, because using an hourly-computed metric to evaluate a 30-minute canary produces a muddied signal contaminated by unrelated earlier events.

Blue/green deployment keeps one instance serving traffic (green) and another ready to serve (blue), cutting over without downtime and rolling back by a trivial reversal of the router change, at the cost of using twice the resources; it is effectively a before/after canary, but can be run as an A/B canary by slowly splitting traffic between the green control and the blue canary.

Testing with synthetic load maximizes code coverage but not state coverage, is hard to simulate in mutable systems with caches, cookies, or request affinity, may not model organic traffic shifts, and can be dangerous on mutable systems — generating artificial load on a billing system could send callouts that actually charge customers.

Traffic teeing copies real traffic to both the production system (which serves users) and the test system (which serves the copy and discards the responses), giving representative traffic but being more complex to set up and poor at identifying risk in stateful systems, since for example a shared cache would artificially inflate the canary's hit rate and invalidate its performance measurements.

No single testing methodology is a panacea: canarying is a simple, robust way to supplement testing that catches defects early with minimal user impact and gives confidence for frequent releases, and like testing it must evolve alongside the system's requirements and design.

As workload increases, team members work longer hours on tickets and pages and spend less time on engineering, and the resulting stress causes more mistakes that impact reliability and ultimately end users, so the team loses its ability to regulate its daily work and manage the service.

Operational load is the ongoing maintenance that keeps systems running and comes in three types — pages, tickets, and ongoing operational responsibilities — where pages and urgent tickets are 'interrupts' because they preempt SREs from engineering project work.

A team is in operational overload when urgent issues continually preempt project work so it cannot progress on key priorities; cap operational work (Google caps it at 50% of an engineer's time) so the team can complete the engineering projects that reduce the operational load of the services they manage.

Distinguish actual overload — an objective reality where the number of tasks cannot be completed within their deadlines — from perceived overload, a more subjective state where individuals feel they have too much work, which usually arises when several organizational or work changes occur over a short period with little opportunity to communicate with leadership; perceived overload has the same effects but starts as a misperception.

When workload is hard to predict, cognitive biases make you misjudge it — a ticket queue can feel too large to finish even when it is not — and starting the day with the preconception that there is too much work reduces your progress, whereas diving in without that preconception lets you accomplish more.

If work is not properly prioritized, every task seems equally urgent, leading to both actual and perceived overload; reprioritizing decreases the amount of urgent work and creates space for the team to tackle the sources of overload through project work.

Do not assume the workload itself needs to change: first quantify the work your team faces (for example the number of tickets and pages) and how it has changed over time, collect a one-time snapshot by asking every member to list all their tasks, and review the psychological stress factors, so you have a stable basis for deciding whether to change the workload.

Identifying and scoping overload is the first step toward fixing it: get the whole team in a room and reevaluate the entire backlog of project, operational, and ticket work — viewing every task even if the list barely fits on a whiteboard — to identify and redefine actual priorities and find work to minimize, hand off, or eliminate.

Beware the sunk-cost fallacy when reducing overload: dropping in-progress work feels like wasted effort, but most backlog turns out to be obsolete, redundant, or not as urgent as claimed, so when in doubt drop a task but mark it for a second triage phase — at which point almost none prove important enough to resume.

Reduce a backlog-driven overload by deploying low-effort automation that significantly cuts operational load, documenting common problems to enable customer self-service, closing stale, obsolete, or nonactionable tickets (fixing the monitoring artifacts behind nonactionable ones), and documenting progress on issues you set aside so you do not lose context.

Prevent overload from recurring with periodic interrupt triage (for example every two weeks) and a per-member open-ticket cap (for example ten or fewer), and when the cap is exceeded have the lead remind the team to close stale tickets, offload tickets from overloaded members, run a one-day team ticket fix-it, or assign work to fix the sources of tickets.

Perceived overload is in fact overload and has as much impact on a team as work overload from other causes: it can be triggered by losing members, increased cognitive load, ticket noise, and a tight new ticket SLO even when the number of pages has not changed, and the perceived overload of a few team members can quickly become overload for the whole team.

Because long-term stress from overwork or feeling unsafe decreases productivity and harms health, the most important short-term action against overload is to provide stress relief and rebuild trust and psychological safety, so team members can think clearly and help drive the whole team forward.

A manager who is not part of the on-call rotation does not directly feel the team's stress, and a team that is not heard feels distant from management; assigning a dedicated manager who is not shared across multiple teams and uses a participatory management style helps rebuild psychological safety.

Choose a load metric that captures the real burden: the number of pages was insufficient, so the team adopted a better metric measuring how much time an on-caller needed to resolve a ticket after their shift had ended.

Relieve alert-driven overload by auditing and removing alerts that do not represent user-facing problems and silencing alerts generously — silencing each only for a limited period (typically a day, up to a week) so it does not mask outages, and assigning any alert that cannot be fixed within a few minutes to a tracking ticket — rather than trying to find the source of every single alert at once.

As medium-term overload relief, limit operational work to on-call time so the team can concentrate on permanent fixes and project work, return responsibility for a service back to its development team, and have team members train each other, since disseminating knowledge speeds future troubleshooting and builds the confidence that comes from realizing how much they already know.

As long-term overload relief, make services more uniform — uniformity decreases SRE cognitive load and makes automation reusable across services — align each service's SLOs with the SLOs of its backends, and update long-standing services to current production standards.

Attend to a team's stress levels so members trust each other enough to work together, because otherwise the team enters a vicious cycle in which overload causes stress that in turn prevents the team from tackling the overload.

Recognize the symptoms of overload: decreased team morale (rants and negative surveys, surfaced through regular active listening without judgment), members working long hours or while sick (which leaders should counter by modeling contractual hours and staying home when ill), more frequent illness, an unhealthy task queue (where even failing to perform the regular backlog review signals accumulating interrupts), and imbalanced metrics like long times to close an issue, a high proportion of time on toil, and many days to close on-call-originated issues.

There is no one-size-fits-all measure of overload, so the team should decide together which measures to use, and a manager should not impose a measure without understanding each individual's workload and work habits, since for example time-to-fix differs between someone who fixes an issue in one full day and someone who distributes the work across several days.

Giving team members more control and power reduces perceived overload, so resist the temptation to micromanage under stress and instead keep the team in the loop and work on prioritization together to increase performance and job satisfaction.

To fix a dysfunctional team, members must first regain psychological safety because a team can function only as well as its individual members; identify and alleviate the psychosocial stressors you actually control — you cannot control a member's major illness, but you can control the backlog size or silence pages.
Communicate to your partner product-developer teams that your team is overloaded, because they may be able to lend a hand, provide compassion, or even take over entire projects.

Once team members achieve enough psychological safety to take interpersonal risks, give individuals more responsibility — uncovering areas of expertise and assigning point people and technical leads to specific technologies to build their self-confidence — and keep decision-making transparent and democratic so each member feels a sense of control.

Prioritize and triage issues within a quarter, schedule interrupt-free time with no on-call so engineers can work on qualitatively difficult tasks like developing automation and investigating the root causes of interrupts, and if absolutely necessary drop work — for example by returning on-call support for a service to its development team.

Protect against future overload by establishing workload metrics and regularly reviewing whether they measure the right things, maintaining a lightweight triage process to detect a growing backlog, and — when the team is overloaded — prioritizing project work that pays down repetitive toil even more than you otherwise would, because it pays off in the future.

Excessive interrupts can easily slip a team from a normal workload into overload, and overload creates psychosocial stressors that impact work further in a self-reinforcing cycle, so constantly monitor for overload (perceived or not) and show respect to yourself and your team to keep the workload in balance.

SRE principles aim to maximize the engineering velocity of developer teams while keeping products reliable, but the SRE model is less effective when the domain is too large and complex (a problem the microservices movement makes more acute), so given a production landscape too large to cover, an SRE team must collaborate with product development to decide where to focus for the best results.

SRE engagement entails much more than the services themselves — it focuses on understanding the aims of the developer and product teams and finding the right way to support them — so regardless of team size, proactively define the role of SRE and manage communication and collaboration with product development.

An SRE team's contributions to service reliability happen throughout all phases of the service lifecycle, and applying production knowledge and experience can substantially improve a service's reliability well before any SRE picks up the pager for it, though engagement can begin at any stage of the lifecycle.

In the architecture and design phase, SRE can influence a system by creating best practices such as resilience to single points of failure, documenting the dos and don'ts of infrastructure systems from prior experience, providing early-engagement consulting, and codesigning the service — and because fixing architectural mistakes becomes more difficult later, early engagement avoids costly redesigns that become necessary when systems meet real users and must scale.

Define SLOs before a service reaches general availability so the service teams have an objective measure of how reliable it is and the product team can still withdraw a product that cannot meet its target reliability, and share incident and operational work between the developer and SRE teams during limited availability so both gain experience with the service's failure modes.

After general availability, even though SRE performs the majority of operational work, the developer team should continue to handle a small part of all operational and incident-response work — for example permanently including one developer in the on-call rotation — so they do not lose perspective on the operational aspects of the service under real load.

When deprecating a service in favor of a better replacement, close the existing system to new users and focus engineering on transitioning users to the new one; because SRE then effectively supports two full systems during the transition, headcount and staffing should be adjusted accordingly.

Align developer and SRE goals by having each team keep its individual focus while explicitly supporting the other's: SRE commits to supporting the developers' release velocity 'as quickly as is safe' (generally meaning within error budget), and developers commit a reasonable percentage of engineering time to fixing and preventing reliability problems, paying down technical debt, and including SREs early in design conversations.

Frame the SRE function's core mission as empowering product-development teams with tools and processes to maximize reliability rather than doing their operational work for them, using a shared-goals model that balances reducing the SRE automation backlog against engaging with other teams — partly prioritizing a help request by whether a joint engagement also reduces the SRE backlog.

For a full-time SRE engagement, prefer embedding an SRE within the product-development team to provide focus and give both sides maximum time to learn from each other as developers ramp up on SRE skills, reserving part-time engagement for fairly brief, constrained projects, and gauge the team's or application's maturity relative to SRE practices when scoping.

Set clear shared expectations: the application owners, not the SREs, are directly responsible for making changes to an application; SRE engagement should improve company-wide common tools rather than produce one-off scripts; SREs are not traditional operations engineers and do not support manual work like running a deployment job; and SRE should give the developer team a heads-up about any new processes the engagement introduces, such as load testing.

Write shared goals jointly with the development team, divide them into milestones, define the scope of the engagement, and call out an explicit end-result success story — for example, that after the engagement the product team can handle its own service outages without escalation.

Measure the impact of an SRE engagement and the partner team's maturity to confirm SREs are doing high-value work and to tailor the collaboration — for example, conduct a point-in-time assessment that walks a maturity matrix and agrees on scores for areas like observability, capacity planning, change management, and incident response before the engagement, and repeat it afterward to measure the value SRE added.

Every SRE team should pursue a short-term goal of providing an operationally stable, available, scalable, and maintainable system that fulfills the product's business needs, and a long-term goal of optimizing operations until ongoing human work is no longer needed so the team can move on to the next high-value engagement.

Agree on principles of cooperation up front: a definition of and hard limit on operational work, a measured SLO used to prioritize engineering work for both teams, a quarterly error budget that determines release velocity and safety parameters, and developer involvement in daily operations so ongoing issues stay visible — establishing the SLO from the start of the relationship rather than backtracking to it later.

Plan at two connected levels: with developer leadership, set product and service priorities and publish yearly roadmaps, then review and update them regularly and derive quarterly goals that line up with the roadmap; in a stable environment, the absence of a roadmap may signal that the SRE team can merge with another team, hand work back to developers, expand scope, or dissolve.

Invest time in working better together: have SREs meet regularly with their developer counterparts and periodically with other SRE teams whose services send them traffic or provide shared infrastructure, so that during outages or disagreements the teams can escalate quickly and confidently because they already know each other and have set expectations for how escalations are managed.

Maintain an open line of communication beyond day-to-day contact: have SREs give a quarterly 'state of production' talk to development leadership explaining where to invest and how SRE is helping, and have developers give a periodic 'state of the product' talk to the SRE team covering what they accomplished and where the product is going.

Hold regular service reviews where the SRE and developer leads responsible for a service meet face-to-face at least once a year to share 12-to-18-month roadmaps and discuss projects, and facilitate a stop-doing / keep-doing / start-doing retrospective with full-team participation, which is often the most useful session because it yields details that drive significant service changes.

When agreed-upon ground rules begin to regress, both teams should change priorities proportionally to the urgency — identifying specific engineers to drop lower-priority tasks, calling a reliability hackathon, declaring a feature freeze, or mounting an 'all hands on deck' response when the product's reliability is at acute risk.

Use the SLO and error budget to set priorities: if a service is in danger of missing its SLO or has exhausted its error budget, both teams work with high priority to restore safety through tactical measures (such as overprovisioning) and strategic fixes (such as optimizations, caching, and graceful degradation); if a service is well within SLO with ample budget, use the spare budget to increase feature velocity rather than over-investing in service improvements.

Handle interpersonal mistakes blamelessly by focusing on system behavior: do not conduct follow-up conversations when tired or emotions are high (people remember how words made them feel, so use video chat to convey tone), meet in person to resolve issues rather than letting code-review or document-only interactions drag out, thank people for positive behaviors, and understand each team's differing communication norms.

Because SREs have specialized skills and are a scarce resource (Google generally keeps the SRE-to-developer ratio below 10%), one SRE team commonly supports multiple developer teams, and when SREs are scarce relative to the services that merit support, the team should focus its efforts on one service or a few services from a small number of developer teams.

Limited SRE resources scale to many services when those services are part of a single product (giving end-to-end ownership of the user experience), built on similar tech stacks (minimizing cognitive load and enabling reuse of skills), and built by the same or a small number of related developer teams (minimizing relationships and easing priority alignment).

When grouping multiple SRE teams, group them either within a product (so they coordinate with fewer developer teams) or within a technology stack such as storage or networking, and prefer organizing SRE teams by technology rather than by the developer reporting structure to prevent churn in SRE teams during developer reorganizations.

Adapt SRE team structures by creating, sharding, merging, and dissolving teams based on service needs and engineering and operational load, giving each team a clear charter; when a single team has too many services, prefer sharding the existing team into multiple teams (to transfer culture and grow leadership) over building new teams from scratch, and restructure only when necessary because it is disruptive.

For global 24/7 coverage, distribute SRE teams around the globe and colocate them by adjacency and by similarity of services and shared technology; singleton teams are generally less effective and more vulnerable to outside reorganizations, so create them only for a clearly defined business need, and maintain at least a two-location arrangement even when split only across buildings.

When balancing responsibilities that not everyone should own (such as test restores from backups) across a distributed team's sites, assign each responsibility to a single location but rotate it regularly (for example yearly) or share it between locations with balanced involvement, and do not lock a responsibility to one location for multiple years, because doing so fosters an 'us versus them' mentality, hinders knowledge distribution, and risks business continuity.

End an SRE engagement when it is no longer impactful — when the value proposition has gone away or the majority of the work is operations rather than engineering — and hand a service back to its developers if SRE no longer provides business value worth the cost, such as when the service has been optimized enough, its importance has diminished, or it is reaching end of life.

The easiest way to launch a new service when you are already running large distributed services is to minimize the additional cognitive load it imposes by making systems as homogeneous as possible — so a collection of services can share the same release structure, capacity planning, and storage-access subservices — and by building an abstraction layer so developers do not have to worry about lower-level production details like monitoring, logging, and storage.

Building production-and-domain experts inside the developer team (rather than keeping all production knowledge in the SRE team) lets the SRE team stop vetting every new feature integration, which reduces time to production for new features and increases developer velocity, while the SRE team can refocus on the underlying infrastructure without compromising reliability.

When the cost of maintaining an SRE support relationship is higher than the value it provides, it can make sense to end it by disbanding the SRE team and combining the SRE and product-development functions into a single team, which lets the team balance operational needs and velocity and resolves the continual tension over where to invest engineering effort.

Keeping an existing system operational while its replacement is designed and built is challenging, especially when the old-system and new-system teams are organizationally separate, so regular, open, and cooperative communication is vital throughout the cycle to preserve the working relationship — and a gap in that communication can break the relationship down.

Realigning ownership of an old system with the people who have greater knowledge of its internals can result in more effective troubleshooting and quicker issue resolution despite extra operational load and a learning curve, and the departing SRE team's final job is to make the knowledge transfer as smooth as possible.

For an effective relationship between SRE and product development, a shared sense of purpose and goals with regular and open communication is key, and for sustaining long-term success, investing in aligning team goals and understanding each other's objectives is as important as defending SLOs.

Reliability is the most important feature of any system: if a system is not reliable users will not trust it, if they do not trust it they will not use it when given a choice, and because all software systems are governed by network effects a system with no users is worth nothing — so choose your metrics carefully because you are what you measure.

Your users, not your monitoring, decide your reliability: the only measure that matters is how your users experience reliability, so telling a user 'our monitoring looks fine, the problem must be on your end' does not help — they experience your system as unstable and remember that — and your monitoring, logs, and alerting are valuable only insofar as they help you notice problems before your customers do.

Once your system exposes an API consumed by other machines you are running a platform, and the reliability your users experience becomes a partnership not limited to your choices — a user who achieves only 99% availability on your 99.999% platform has a best-case experience of about 98.999%, and they will hold you accountable for whatever they experience even when it is not your fault.
condition: applies once your system is consumed by other machines via an API

statement: Everything important eventually becomes a platform: as a system's value grows with its users, other software will integrate via APIs, and even if you never build a machine-consumable API others will wrap your UI into one and consume it — so APIs, official or unofficial, will be part of your future and you only choose whether you control the outcome.

When your customers have a hard time, their frustration becomes friction and triage work for you — even via Stack Overflow or social media — and that energy is energy you cannot invest in advancing your system, so teams consumed by break/fix toil end up with an ever-diminishing innovation budget; this applies doubly to internal platform teams, whose customers are the consumers within the company.

If you want your customers — including internal customers — to design and operate reliable systems on your platform, you have to teach them how, undertaking most of the work that normally leads up to pager handoff (meaning the system has met minimum viable reliability requirements) with at least a representative sample of your users.

Get your customers to measure SLIs and alert on SLOs and share those measurements with you, because in the absence of a stated SLO a customer will inevitably invent one and not tell you until you fail to meet it; sit down with them to explain SLOs, SLIs, and error budgets and help them describe their critical applications in those terms.

Audit a customer's monitoring and turn off the alerting that has zero impact on their SLOs (often up to half of what they measure), assemble the remaining useful measurements into their SLOs, help them cover the uncovered SLO dimensions, and build shared SLO dashboards so that neither side has to swap extra information when an SLO is threatened.

After measuring against new SLOs for a month or two, expect a customer to discover that the application they thought was operating at five nines is really achieving only 99.5 to 99.9 percent; if their users are happy and there is no evidence that improving performance or availability would increase adoption, retention, or usage, then you are done — and periodically re-ask this question to confirm budgets and priorities are still correct.

Conduct design reviews and risk analysis on a customer's application as you would for your own — looking for hidden single points of failure and manual rollouts or rollbacks — rank the issues found by how much of their error budget each consumes, and observe which ones the customer chooses to fix to earn back the nines they want, which sets realistic reliability expectations that shape their perceptions and trust.

Build operational rigor with a customer by practicing simulated problems (Wheel of Misfortune exercises, disaster and recovery testing, paper game days) to develop muscle memory for crisis communication, lower MTTR, and surface edge cases, and conduct joint postmortems with them rather than merely sharing your own.

Because you cannot run a deep SRE engagement with more than a small percentage of your customers, make a principled selection — by revenue coverage, by feature coverage, or by sampling one or two customers from each workload cohort — and stick to it, because mixing and matching approaches confuses stakeholders and overwhelms your team.
You can adopt SRE practices without having a single SRE, by using SLOs, which are the foundation of SRE practices.
SRE Principle #1 is that SRE needs SLOs with consequences: the performance of your service relative to its SLOs should guide your business decisions.

Even without SRE staff, implement the crucial first steps of SRE: acknowledge you do not want 100% reliability, set a reasonable SLO measuring the reliability most important to your users, agree an error budget policy that guides both tactical outage mitigation and longer-term reliability work, and measure the SLO and commit (with company-leadership agreement) to following the policy — because an implicit 100% SLO means the team can only ever be reactive.

Your first SRE may not have explicit SRE experience, so interview for the areas relevant to the role — operations (production insight), software engineering (understanding and improving the software), monitoring systems (measurable SLOs), production automation (scaling operations), and system architecture (scaling the application) — and expect them to occupy an ambiguous position between velocity and reliability that demands resilience and flexibility.

Place your first SRE — in a product-development team, an operations team, or a horizontal consulting role — based on your own sphere of influence, your immediate challenges, the challenges you expect over the next 12 months, your plan for changing the organization (avoid embedding in product if you plan to centralize, since they are hard to remove later), and the individual's skills; experiment to find the model, but commit to one stable, coherent model long-term because instability undermines the effectiveness of SRE.

Your first SRE's initial mission is to get up to speed on the service — understanding its current problems, its required toil, and the engineering needed to keep it within SLOs — and if the organization does not yet have SLOs and error budgets, that first SRE must do the engineering to design and implement them.

Defer large, complex, or risky features on an existing system in favor of its planned replacement once that effort coalesces, applying the informal rule that if a project's complexity or the risk of modifying the existing system is sufficiently high it is better invested in the new system — while recognizing that as resources shift, even conservative changes to the old system become harder even as its usage keeps growing.

In a healthy relationship, when an old system needs stabilizing the SRE team can hand production work back to the developers for a short period and then reassume responsibility once the system is restabilized and hardened for expected growth, so SRE and development teams must be willing to address tensions head-on and identify points that need resetting.

SRE Principle #2 is that SREs must have time to make tomorrow better than today, because without it toil only increases as service usage grows and the system becomes larger and more complex; a healthy balance between operational responsibilities and project work is essential, or talented engineers will flee the team.

Watch for signs that SRE work is not going well: the SRE's mix of work is indistinguishable from other engineering work, an SRE on a product team is doing more than their fair share of operational work or is the only person making service-configuration changes, or the SLOs are not being taken seriously and the SRE is not progressing in measuring and defending the customer experience.

If your organization does not have a discrete SRE team, construct a community for distributed SREs that advocates the SRE's distinctive role and drives consistent reliability-focused changes across teams, so individual SREs do not feel isolated.
SRE Principle #3 is that SRE teams have the ability to regulate their own workload.

Assemble an SRE team with combined experience in changing application software to improve reliability and performance, writing software to detect and mitigate problems and automate manual processes, using strong software practices for long-term maintainability, taking a methodical and careful approach to operational changes (being able to explain why practices are reliable), and understanding distributed-system architecture; seed the team with internal transfers to reduce ramp-up time.

When converting an existing team into an SRE team, be careful to avoid renaming a team from 'Operations' to 'SRE' without first applying SRE practices and principles, because if the rebranding effort fails your organization may be poisoned against the entire concept of SRE in the future.

Build team cohesion by providing a regular forum to learn and discuss SRE practices and reflect on how the team is performing — such as a recurring lunch showing an SREcon video or a book club discussing relevant content — and encourage new SREs to speak out about SRE practices that do not fit your organization.

A new SRE team formed for a major project risks spreading itself too thin across too many services (constant firefighting leaves no time to address risk permanently), becoming over-introspective about SRE principles (for example perfecting an SLO definition while neglecting the service), abandoning SRE practices to hit product milestones, or lacking the breadth of skills (such as programming) needed to instrument the product and deliver the improvements.

Mitigate the risks of a new project SRE team by engaging on a single important service as early as possible (ideally at the design stage) with input focused on defining SLOs and analyzing reliability risks, not expecting the SRE team to hold operational responsibility on day one (which initially sits with the product or project team), agreeing clear conditions a service must meet to be onboarded, and keeping new hires to less than a third of the team so training does not overwhelm existing members.

A horizontal SRE team risks being perceived as a gating organization that adds no value; mitigate this by seeding it with respected engineers who have relevant subject-matter expertise, delivering tools (monitoring, alerting, rollouts, checklists) with short-term beneficial impact on at least two other teams, communicating and celebrating its successes, and having the team see themselves as enablers rather than gatekeepers, focusing on solutions rather than just problems.

A team converted in place to SRE may fear the conversion is a path to job losses and may lack slack capacity, software-engineering skills, or interest; mitigate by securing senior-leadership support, renegotiating responsibilities to create slack, managing communication carefully, dealing with the job-loss concern head-on (automation eliminates portions of work and frees time for more valuable work), providing training, changing how the team and individuals are evaluated (team metrics aligned with SLOs and individual metrics with evidence of SRE skills), and adding an experienced SRE or developer.

A team reaches SRE maturity (norming) when SLOs and error budgets are in place and the error budget policy is exercised after significant incidents, on-call rotations are established, sustainable, and compensated with sufficient tooling and documentation, toil is documented, bounded, and managed so SREs complete impactful projects, postmortem culture is established, the team runs regular training exercises and captures lessons to prevent repeat problems, the product team stays in the on-call rotation, and the team produces regular stakeholder reports.

A team driven by tickets and production issues in a continuous reactive mode has no time to improve or innovate and would have to grow linearly with the products it supports; invert the responsibility model to remove SRE from the critical path and empower product-development teams with self-service so they push their own changes, which speeds delivery and frees SREs to make real system-wide improvements.

Schedule regular office hours to make time-consuming review interrupts more manageable by batching questions and discussions predictably, which also provides a venue for sharing knowledge with teams undergoing onboarding.

In the performing stage, an SRE team should partner on all architecture design and change — defining from the initial design phase onward the patterns for how software is built and structured for reliability — and have complete workload self-determination, applying Principle #3 with a view to the holistic health of the system.

Early SRE input into the design of a new service architecture reduces the likelihood of high-cost reengineering later, and the product-development and SRE teams should acknowledge their differing perspectives on architectural decisions to arrive at a good design process that improves reliability, scalability, and operability and reuses existing patterns.

An SRE team's ability to regulate its own workload requires strong team leadership and clear upfront commitment from senior management, and it secures the team's position as an engineering team that works on the organization's most important services, equal to its product-development peers.

With a partner product-development team, an SRE team chooses if and when to onboard a service, can reduce toil under operational overload by lowering the SLO or transferring operational work to another team, and can hand a service back if it cannot be operated at SLO within agreed toil constraints; an SRE team without a partner dev team (one that develops or packages what it runs) cannot transfer work back, so it should stop feature-related project work for reliability work and reduce its SLOs unless management provides more capacity.

SRE engagement is not perpetual — it feeds itself by solving problems at scale and improving service reliability — so once an SRE team has solved a service's problems you must intentionally find new reliability challenges for it to tackle or make an intentional decision to hand the service back, or the team risks attrition as SREs move to more interesting work, and that slow bleed can put production at risk.

When creating an additional SRE team (for service complexity, broader SRE rollout, or a geographic split), read the postmortems written after earlier teams were established to repeat what worked and fix what did not, seed the new team with your best and highest-potential SREs from an existing team (since qualified candidates are hard to find and growing quickly with new hires is unrealistic), standardize the framework for establishing teams, and change on-call responsibilities slowly — keeping members on-call for their previous systems through a transitional period and waiting three to six months to split the rotations.

Split a service that is too complex for a single team by architecture (compute/storage/network or frontend/backend), by language (if your SREs are deeply involved in the source), or by location, and when a team splits, designate one team as responsible for everything not covered by the other's charter or appoint a senior SRE as an overarching technical lead across both teams so no component is orphaned.

When rolling out SRE to more services, prioritize services where reliability has high financial or reputational impact and define the minimal viable set of services the product needs to function (ensuring others degrade gracefully); a service should not become a priority for SRE simply because it is unreliable, since SRE should be applied tactically where most relevant and developers should not be allowed to ignore reliability until SREs engage.

Staff sister SRE teams on different continents for service reliability (one team can continue if a disaster stops the other), reduced on-call stress (12-hour shifts), broader recruiting (shifts that overlap the normal working day), and improved production maturity (the need for documentation, training, and standardization grows); colocate each SRE team with its development team where possible, because separation makes it harder for SREs to understand how services evolve and for developers to value infrastructure improvements.

When choosing where to locate two sister SRE teams, balance the mutually exclusive objectives of minimizing out-of-normal-hours on-call work and maximizing the overlap when both teams are online; staffing teams six to eight time zones apart works well and avoids midnight-to-6 a.m. on-call shifts, and the first team in a new office sets the norms, so seed it with one or more SREs willing to relocate and a high-value project that requires interaction with the sister team.

When one of two sister SRE teams is colocated with the product-development team, be vigilant that the non-colocated office does not become a 'night shift' that has little contact with developers, takes more than its fair share of toil, or is assigned only the less interesting or impactful projects.

Maintain parity between two SRE offices by balancing on-call load (giving more tickets to the office that fields fewer pages), associating development areas with a specific office's SRE team so developers do not just lean on the colocated office, assigning more internal-improvement projects to the non-colocated office, spreading the most interesting projects fairly, keeping similar team size and seniority across offices, deliberately splitting projects across sites to spread knowledge and build trust, and letting engineers travel between offices regularly.

Avoid splitting SRE teams across three sites, because it becomes impossible to hold a production meeting all SREs can attend, it is harder to ensure parity of knowledge and operational response across three offices, and if all on-call happens only during office hours there is less incentive to automate low-value toil, since the personal cost of off-hours pages is what sharpens the motivation to eliminate them.

Create opportunities for high-quality face-to-face interaction between geographically split teams despite effective video conferencing — for example having every SRE, manager, and tech lead visit the other site at least annually, leadership visit at least twice a year, and all SREs convene at least once a year — and have the decision-makers in each office meet regularly to debate solutions, resolve differences, advocate for each other's team to prevent an 'us versus them' mentality, and support each other's team health.

Embed product-development engineers in an SRE team for a fixed period (such as six months, in a different area from their expertise) to train them in production systems and have them go on-call, because some stay in SRE while others return with a much better appreciation of the production environment, and the SRE team gains engineering resources and insight into gaps and inaccuracies in its training material and documentation.

Run an exchange program where an SRE spends a week working alongside a different SRE team to observe how they work and share useful practices from their home team, ending with a trip report of observations and recommendations for both teams — particularly valuable when SRE teams are highly specialized.

Establish a standard training curriculum for all SREs — such as an immersive course introducing the key concepts, tooling, and platforms almost all SREs work with — to provide a baseline level of knowledge that simplifies team-specific and service-specific training, and recognize the SREs who facilitate this training in your performance-management process.

Because SRE teams tightly aligned with their services tend to build proprietary monitoring, rollout, and configuration tools — causing significant duplication of effort — allow some solutions to compete for adoption but eventually converge on a standard solution that meets most teams' requirements and provides a stable, scalable platform for the next layer of innovation, built and run by a horizontal team that partners with others to ensure smooth adoption.

Let SREs transfer freely between SRE teams with open headcount (and to product-development teams if they pass the software-engineer bar), which is healthy because engineers can occupy roles of interest, move to less demanding on-call if personal circumstances change, broaden the teams they join, maintain cultural consistency across offices, and are not compelled to work on unhealthy services or for unsupportive managers — which also keeps SRE managers focused on healthy, happy services and teams.

Use a Launch Coordination Engineering team to apply SRE principles to product teams whose services do not merit full SRE engagement, developing standard tooling and frameworks that enable product teams to design, build, and launch their service in production, and like any SRE team it should actively automate its own daily operations.

As the number of SRE teams grows, run a regular service review in which senior SRE leaders assess every team on standard measures such as pager load, error budget usage, project completion, and bug closure rates, applauding outstanding performance and supporting underperforming teams — using experienced reviewers who can distinguish, for example, a project-completion drop caused by a team merger or split from a genuine performance issue.

Fund SRE from the same source as product-development funding because reliability is a core pillar of product development like testing or security, and keep the supply of SREs smaller than demand — having fewer SREs than the organization would like, only enough for their specialized work — so you regularly review and prioritize which services receive SRE support; SRE-to-developer ratios range from about 1:5 for low-level infrastructure to about 1:50 for standard-framework consumer apps, often around 1:10.

An organization of any size can implement SRE practices by applying three principles: SRE needs SLOs with consequences, SREs must have time to make tomorrow better than today, and SRE teams have the ability to regulate their workload.

SRE teams are characterized by rapid innovation and a large acceptance of change, with organizational change management as a core responsibility: SREs sit in the middle of a rapidly shifting landscape, responsible for balancing the risks inherent in change against product reliability and availability, with error budgets as a primary mechanism for achieving that balance.

Lewin's three-stage 'unfreeze–change–freeze' model manages organizational change by first persuading a group that change is necessary, then executing the change, then institutionalizing the new patterns of behavior, treating the group as the primary dynamic instrument, which makes it most useful for planning organizational change at the macro level.

Kotter's eight-step change process is particularly relevant to SRE teams, with the exception that SRE teams supporting fast-growing products rarely need to create a sense of urgency because they already face urgent scaling, reliability, and operational challenges, and SRE is uniquely motivated to lead change because it is on the front line when problems occur.

The Prosci ADKAR model (awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, reinforcement) is a people-centric framework whose applicability to SRE is limited because operational responsibilities impose time constraints that make its iterative pacing hard, though it has been used successfully for introducing high-level changes while preserving local autonomy for implementation details.

The Deming Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle suits cyclic continuous improvement of existing processes (such as adopting CI/CD) but is not suited to organizational change management because it does not cover the human side of change, and for large organizational changes iteration is counterproductive since frequent, wrenching org-chart changes sap employee confidence and harm company culture.

No change-management model is universally applicable to every situation, so do not standardize exclusively on one; SRE managers in particular benefit from familiarity with emotion-based models like the Bridges Transition Model and the Kübler-Ross Change Curve to support employees through organizational change, since unhappy people are rarely productive.

Highlighting the severity of an operational crisis — such as an SRE team firefighting around the clock and restarting components hourly while feature velocity suffers — can convince leadership to reevaluate priorities and dedicate engineering time to reliability work, after which a small guiding coalition can form a strategic vision of a future where the toil is no longer necessary.

To replace a critical overloaded system while keeping it running, first buy operational breathing room — enlist the dependent teams to trim unnecessary load (for example cutting message volume and adding a compression layer) and offload the heaviest component — to open a window in which to build and test a prototype of the replacement.

Migrate from an old system to a new one safely by rebuilding the client libraries so they can publish and receive on either or both systems via a centralized control surface to switch traffic, migrating low-traffic but high-importance flows first with dual-writes as a backup path, automating the traffic migration so the rate accelerates, and only declaring the old system deprecated once enough momentum has built behind the new one.

When spinning up two sister teams, choose among models — both halves starting at the same time, setting up the developer-colocated site first so SREs engage earlier in the product lifecycle, or setting up the non-colocated site first (or sharing the pager) for a service already in production — according to where the right people are at the right time.

Early backup paths can deliver the short-term wins that justify a large migration's investment: writing low-traffic, high-importance flows to both the old and new messaging systems produced a couple of near misses where the backup path kept core services running while the old system faltered, demonstrating value before the full migration.

Meaningful change is a cycle: eliminating one bottleneck in a system often highlights another, and each completed change cycle's improvements, standardization, and automation free up engineering time that lets teams examine their systems, identify more pain points, and trigger the next cycle of change.

Manual, SRE-owned releases hinder development velocity, and large, costly, infrequent releases make each release a large delta that increases the chance a major defect forces a rollback; slimming components down (for example with a microservices framework) so each can iterate and release rapidly addresses this.

Win adoption of a superior new deployment process by demonstrating its value rather than mandating it: build a centralized dashboard showing release status and standard metrics so teams can link their releases to metric changes and gain confidence, work closely with a few volunteer teams first, and let those early wins spark a chain reaction of accelerating adoption in which engineers begin to pressure the laggards.

Grassroots-instigated change requires close collaboration between SRE and development plus support from executive leadership, and creating a small, focused group with members from SRE, development, and management is key to success — such ad hoc groups can and should evolve over time into more formal cooperation where SREs are automatically involved in design discussions.

Incremental change is much easier to manage than jumping straight to the 'perfect' solution, which is too large a step (and likely infeasible if your system is about to collapse, and the notion of 'perfect' will evolve as you learn): an iterative approach demonstrates early wins that build organizational buy-in and justify further investment, and wastes less if you must abandon the change — but still keep a master plan that describes the goals broadly, stays flexible, and ensures each iteration moves toward them.

Sometimes your current solutions cannot support your strategic vision's requirements, and building something new — despite its large engineering cost — is worthwhile if it pushes you out of a local maximum and enables long-term growth; as a thought experiment, find where bottlenecks will arise as you grow and consider redesigning or replacing any element that does not scale horizontally or that grows superlinearly with a core business metric.

Adoption of the same solution by a critical mass of users and developers creates a virtuous cycle that reduces reinvention of wheels and lets teams who otherwise would not interact share practices and policies automated using the same software.

Multiple independent tools for approximately the same problem arise when tool builders are dissociated from their users and the rapidly changing production landscape and when consumers have varied or orthogonal needs (such as 'this rollout must be fast, approximate is fine' versus 'this rollout must be 100% correct, slow is okay'), so those waiting for a perfect future solution build their own niche tools while those with small specific needs refuse to adopt a broader, less-tailored one.

If the initial configuration of a common product captures a wide representation of approaches to most functional needs, a well-informed general solution becomes inevitable over time, as the critical mass of engineers outgrows whatever solution they were using and self-selects to migrate to the common, well-supported set of tools, abandoning their custom-built tools and the associated maintenance costs.

A virtual team that splits members' time roughly 80/20 between building shared software and on-call duties is hard to coordinate — on-call breaks focus across time zones, there is much state to swap between running a service and building software, and consensus-gathering and code reviews suffer without a central location and common time — and its headcount must initially come from existing teams, creating tension between supporting the system as is and building future infrastructure.

Build shared SRE software with small, agile, mostly co-located groups of senior engineers who have plenty of on-call experience but are now heads-down focused on building software (not split between project work and on-call), since small-group development of six to ten people is more efficient in one room, while still collecting requirements across the whole engineering organization via videoconference, email, and travel.

After a common framework unites teams on a shared platform, reduce remaining duplicated effort by building an opinionated zero-config layer on top that provides standard comprehensive displays based on the assumption that a service is organized in one of a handful of popular styles, so most services migrate to the standard while very large or unique services can still deploy custom views.

Migrating interdependent systems is often harder than a blank-sheet design: the hardest engineering work by far is evolving many small, constrained systems into fewer, more general systems without disturbing the already-running services many customers depend on, so resist the intellectual attraction of starting anew with a big design.

Designing horizontal software for broad adoption is much like the role of a product manager — it requires a lot of listening to prospective end users and absorbing and prioritizing their needs — so add product-management and user-experience talent to the teams building shared tooling.

For a common solution to be adopted, the cost of migrating to it from older, fragmented solutions must be small relative to the net benefits — otherwise the migration itself becomes a barrier to adoption — so migration costs need to be nearly zero (for example 'just recompile and you pick up the new thing') and the benefits clear (for example 'now you're protected from this vulnerability') to the team, individuals, and company.

No matter how good new software is, the cost of migrating away from something already working is always perceived as very high, because individual engineers feel they are merely swapping one working piece for another rather than improving the system; this knowledge-to-ability gap means recognizing and embracing change requires giving people time, coaching, and training, while implementing the change technically requires understanding adoption costs and including work to minimize them in the launch.

Building tools on a 'best effort' basis — fitting development into the cracks between primary services, capacity planning, and outages — yields unreliable, unpredictable execution and low consumer trust, so horizontal software projects gain real traction only when staffed by production-experienced engineers who are 100% dedicated to building software, with schedules and support identical to the rest of the organization's software development.
