Build common software transparently and like clockwork with great communication ('we'll have X done by Y date'), because people trust a new system when they can observe how it was developed from an early stage — perceptions of how the sausage is made matter more than expected, and the belief that 'if you build something great people will naturally flock to it' does not hold; instead a project must be clearly defined, advertised in advance, evaluated against many use cases (targeting the grumpiest adopters first), leaps and bounds better than existing options, and adoptable with little to no effort.

Adoption of common software or processes is analogous to reliability as a feature — you may build the best thing in the world, but if people do not adopt it (or cannot use it because it is unreliable) it is useless — so having a plan for adoption (champions, beta testers, executive sponsors, and dedicated engineers who minimize barriers to adoption) is both the end goal and the starting point, and the first measure of success should be adoption.

Adoption drives a network effect: as the scale and reach of common tools grow, incremental improvements become more valuable to the organization, which justifies more development effort (some of it toward further reducing migration costs and incentivizing more adoption) and staffing full teams to support the tools long-term; such tools should be characterized by rapid development, feature stability, common control surfaces, and automatable APIs.

Incentivize adoption of a new framework by bundling all the steps needed to get started (for example creating a new microservice) into the framework itself, and start with quick-and-dirty prototype tooling whose value becomes apparent to the wider organization before investing further.

No single formal model of change management applies neatly to the spectrum of changes an organization tackles, but frameworks like Kotter's eight-step process and the Prosci ADKAR model provide useful insights, and one commonality across change in a dynamic environment is constant reevaluation and iteration, with most grassroots changes benefiting from structured coordination and planning as they mature.

You do not have to adopt all of SRE at once: smaller firms successfully adopt SRE practices regardless of whether they can staff a full globally distributed SRE team, because although the substance and sequence of the practices matter, people do not have to eat the whole SRE meal in one sitting.

SRE principles and practices are increasingly being applied to other disciplines — particularly security, reflected in the emergence of the term DevSecOps recognizing that development, security, and operations are interdependent — making 'how would SRE apply to this other discipline?' a promising and unexplored direction.

Structure an SLO document with metadata (status, author, reviewers, approvers, approval date, and revisit date), a service overview, a precise definition of each SLI including its exact measurement formula and its SLO target, a rationale, and a clarifications-and-caveats section.

Even when the numbers in an SLO are not strongly evidence-based, document that fact so future readers understand it and can make their decisions appropriately, including deciding whether it is worth the investment to collect more evidence.
Give each SLO objective a separate error budget defined as 100% minus that objective's goal, and enact the error budget policy when any one objective has exhausted its error budget.

Document the measurement caveats of an SLO — for example that request metrics measured at the load balancer may fail to capture requests that never reached the load balancer, and that only HTTP 5XX statuses are counted as errors while everything else is treated as success.

The goals of an error budget policy are to protect customers from repeated SLO misses and to incentivize balancing reliability with other features; it is explicitly not intended as a punishment for missing SLOs, but rather gives teams permission to focus exclusively on reliability when the data indicates reliability is more important than other product features.

Under a typical SLO-miss policy, if the service is at or above its SLO releases proceed according to the release policy, but if the service has exceeded its error budget over the preceding window, halt all changes and releases other than the highest-priority issues or security fixes until the service is back within its SLO.

An error budget policy should distinguish when a team must work on reliability — a code bug or procedural error caused the miss, a postmortem reveals an opportunity to soften a hard dependency, or miscategorized errors hid budget consumption that would have caused a miss — from when the team may continue feature work, such as when the outage was a company-wide networking problem, was caused by another team that has itself frozen releases, or the budget was consumed by users out of scope for the SLO like load tests or penetration testers.

Set an outage policy that requires a postmortem with at least one highest-priority action item addressing the root cause whenever a single incident consumes more than 20% of the four-week error budget, and a highest-priority item on the quarterly planning document whenever a single class of outage consumes more than 20% of the budget over a quarter.

Define an escalation policy for the error budget: when parties disagree about the calculation of the error budget or the specific actions it requires, the issue is escalated to a designated decision-maker (such as the CTO) to make the call.

Error budgets are the tool SRE uses to balance service reliability with the pace of innovation: because changes are a major source of instability (representing roughly 70% of outages) and feature development competes with stability work, the error budget forms a control mechanism for diverting attention to stability as needed.

Use a standard postmortem template that consistently captures the incident root cause and trigger, because doing so enables trend analysis that helps target improvements against systemic root-cause types such as faulty software interface design or immature change deployment planning.

In an analysis of thousands of Google postmortems over 2010-2017, the top outage triggers were binary pushes (37%) and configuration pushes (31%) — together about 68% — followed by user-behavior change (9%), processing pipeline (6%), service-provider change (5%), performance decay (5%), capacity management (5%), and hardware (2%).

In the same analysis of Google postmortems, the top contributing root-cause categories for outages were software (about 41%), development-process failure (about 20%), complex system behaviors (about 17%), deployment planning (about 7%), and network failure (about 3%).
SRE has grown into a global community of practitioners that now extends far beyond Google, of which Google is just one member, and DevOps and SRE are complementary rather than at odds.
A monolithic application packages all functionality in a single artifact deployed as a single process on one server.
Monolithic architectures slow development velocity because modules are tightly coupled and often undocumented, making new features slow, expensive, and lengthening release cycles to months or years.
Tight coupling in a monolith makes its modules hard to maintain and test.
A monolith is locked to the single framework and language it was built in, preventing polyglot programming and technology upgrades.
A monolith can only be scaled as a whole unit, so achieving partial horizontal scaling forces inefficient scaling of the entire application.

Microservices architecture structures an application as a suite of small, independently deployable services, each running in its own process and communicating with lightweight mechanisms, typically an HTTP API.
Microservices should be built around business capabilities and organized using a divide-and-conquer split into independent, composable services.
Microservices use a bare minimum of centralized management and each service may be written in a different language and use different data storage technologies.
Microservices communicate over HTTP or HTTP/2 (for example gRPC, RESTful APIs, Protocol Buffers, or Thrift) or through message brokers such as ActiveMQ or Kafka.

Cloud-native architecture offloads infrastructure ownership to cloud providers and uses tools like Kubernetes and Docker for horizontal scaling, reducing operational overhead and increasing development velocity.
To build, test, and safely deploy cloud-native applications, continuous integration and continuous deployment/delivery must be implemented in a cloud-native manner.

Configuring builds, tests, and deployments manually through a GUI and chaining individual jobs makes troubleshooting and reverting to a last-known-good configuration painful; pipeline-as-code stores that configuration as trackable code in a central Git repository to alleviate those pains.

Microservices differ from SOA by using single-purpose services, minimizing sharing through bounded context with minimal dependencies, communicating over lightweight HTTP/REST, and deploying in containers rather than on application servers and VMs.
Microservices can be scaled independently per component without service interruption, and stateless microservices on Docker or Kubernetes can scale horizontally within seconds.
condition: the microservice is stateless

statement: Because microservice components are loosely coupled, a failing microservice does not stop the others and can be replaced without affecting the whole system, allowing incremental modernization where a monolith would risk outages.

Microservices enable polyglot programming and let autonomous teams develop and deploy services independently without colliding in each other's code, increasing team productivity and reducing technology lock-in.
Microservices architecture combined with Agile development enables continuous delivery, shrinking the release cycle so many features can be released per day through CI/CD pipelines.
Microservices increase complexity over a monolith due to the number of services, requiring substantial automation to handle interservice communication, monitoring, testing, and deployment.

Deploying microservices carries operational overhead because each service must be isolated with its own runtime and resources, so traditional virtualization must be replaced with containerization solutions like Docker.
Adopting microservices requires organizational cultural change, and Agile and DevOps practices are mandatory to coordinate multiple teams working on different services.

The CNCF defines cloud-native technologies (containers, service meshes, microservices, immutable infrastructure, declarative APIs) as enabling loosely coupled systems that are resilient, manageable, and observable, allowing frequent high-impact changes with minimal toil.
Cloud-native architecture provides resiliency by isolating services and offering availability patterns such as Circuit Breaker, Throttling, and Retry.

Serverless computing deploys customer code to fully managed, ephemeral, time-boxed containers that live only during function invocation, so businesses can grow without managing horizontal scaling or complex infrastructure.
Serverless does not mean no-ops: you still handle monitoring, deployment, and security, having only outsourced sysadmin work.

Serverless benefits include reduced operational overhead, horizontal autoscaling with the function as the unit of scale, cost optimization through paying only for consumed compute, and polyglot runtimes.
A major concern when going serverless is vendor lock-in, so the vendor should be chosen based on the specific use case.
Continuous integration is the practice of routing all changes through a pipeline before integrating them into a shared central code repository.

A classic CI pipeline triggers a build on every commit, runs unit and pre-integration (quality and security) tests, builds the artifact, then runs acceptance tests and pushes the result to an artifact-management repository.
Automated testing is integral to CI/CD pipelines; without automated tests a pipeline lacks the quality checks needed to release the application.

CI pipelines can include unit tests, quality/static-analysis tests, security tests, UI tests across browsers and platforms, and integration tests covering component interactions such as with a database.
Continuous deployment automatically releases every change that passes the CI pipeline to staging/preproduction, but a pure continuous deployment approach is not appropriate for everyone.
exception: clients prefer a predictable release cycle or commercial and marketing considerations dictate release timing

statement: Continuous delivery is like continuous deployment but requires human intervention or a business decision before deploying the release to production.

When adopting CI/CD, automate source-code compilation first and prioritize functional testing before UI testing, because UI tests change often and force frequent pipeline changes; break the CI/CD steps into smaller segments automated in patches.
Adopting CI/CD should be a whole-organization decision rather than one made alone by the DevOps team, because it demands discipline, dedication to quality, and a new-skills learning curve.

CI tools fall into three categories: cloud-managed solutions (AWS CodePipeline, Google Cloud Build, Azure Pipelines), open source solutions (Jenkins, Spinnaker, GoCD), and SaaS solutions (Travis CI, CircleCI, TeamCity).
Choose a CI tool based on team experience and skills, target platform and operating system, programming language and architecture, and the deployment solution.

Jenkins is a Java-based cross-platform CI tool with over 1,400 community plugins that supports distributed builds via master-worker architecture with built-in parallelism, integrates with major SCM systems, and defines pipelines as code in Groovy.

Self-hosting a CI tool like Jenkins gives more control over data security and job pipelines, whereas hosted SaaS platforms offload maintenance and updates for extra cost; Jenkins must run on a server and needs frequent updates and maintenance.
Choosing the right CI/CD tool is critical to long-term success and should be based on platform complexity, integration, learning curve, pricing, and work-time efficiency.
Pipeline configuration should be managed as code and rolled out automatically so the same standards that apply to application code apply to the pipeline itself.

Pipeline as code lets users define pipelined job processes in code stored and versioned in a source repository, eliminating manual job creation and letting Jenkins discover, manage, and run jobs across multiple repositories and branches.

Pipeline as code yields speed, consistency that standardizes setup and reduces human error, risk management because version control lets every change be tracked and reverted to a working version, and efficiency.

To use pipeline as code with Jenkins, the repository top-level folder must contain a Jenkinsfile, which lives alongside the source code and can be pulled, edited, pushed, and code-reviewed like any other file.
A Jenkinsfile uses a Groovy-based DSL, and pipeline phases are expressed with the stage keyword, where a stage is a block grouping a series of steps.

A typical CI/CD pipeline defines stages for Checkout, Quality/static-analysis tests, Unit tests with coverage, Security dependency-vulnerability tests, Build, Push, Deploy, and Acceptance/smoke tests.

If any pipeline stage throws an exception the build status is set to fail; this default can be overridden with try-catch blocks, and a finally block can clean up the workspace or run post-steps such as Slack notifications.
Code coverage indicates how much application code is executed during tests and gives some indication of how well a team applies practices like test-driven or behavior-driven development.

The security-test stage should identify project dependencies and check them against known publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, producing a report grouped by severity; OWASP Dependency-Check is a well-known plugin for this.
The Pipeline Stage View plugin visualizes pipeline stages as a matrix with one row per build and one column per stage, which helps track progress of complex pipelines.
Blue Ocean is a modern Jenkins user experience for graphically creating, visualizing, and diagnosing pipelines, requires Jenkins 2.7 or later, and is reached by appending /blue to the server URL.
The Blue Ocean visual pipeline editor is useful for prototyping and debugging stages before generating a working Jenkinsfile, and any visually created pipeline can be edited in a text editor.
Blue Ocean does not support all Jenkins features such as administration, node management, or credential settings, so you must switch back to the classic UI for those.
exception: tasks requiring administration, node management, or credential settings

statement: Jenkins 2 supports two pipeline styles: scripted and declarative.
A scripted pipeline wraps steps in a node block (a node is a Jenkins agent) mapped to the cluster by a label, and may contain any valid Groovy code with stricter Groovy syntax.

A declarative pipeline (Pipeline 2.5+) is easier to read and write, restricts the author to predefined sections such as agent, environment, post, stages, and steps, and does not allow arbitrary Groovy like variables, loops, or conditions.
The general practice is to create pipeline stages that mimic the separate pieces of a traditional pipeline, though how much logic goes into a stage is up to the developer.
The agent section defines where the pipeline runs, must be defined at the top level or overridden at the stage level, and can be a Jenkins node, a Docker container/Dockerfile, or a Kubernetes pod.

In a GitFlow-style workflow a feature branch is created from develop, its pull request triggers Jenkins pre-integration tests, and after review it merges to develop and deploys to the sandbox environment.
Promotion flows from develop to a preprod branch (deploying to staging) and then to master (deploying to production after user approval), giving each environment a dedicated branch.
When a production issue is detected, create a hotfix branch from master and, once complete, merge it back into both develop and master.
condition: a production issue is detected

statement: GitFlow offers a logical branch structure and easy parallel development for big teams, but it can be overkill for smaller projects and teams, which can use just master, preprod, and develop branches.
exception: smaller projects and teams, for which GitFlow is overkill

statement: Editing a Jenkinsfile externally makes it harder to discover problems up front; mitigate this by developing the pipeline as a project on the Jenkins server first, using Blue Ocean as a playground, or running a declarative pipeline linter against the Jenkinsfile outside Jenkins.

The Jenkins Replay button lets you edit a Jenkinsfile and rerun the job live without changing the pipeline configuration or creating a new commit, which is ideal for rapid iteration and avoids filling Git history with junk debugging commits.

Jenkinsfile syntax can be validated before committing via the Jenkins REST linter API, the CLI declarative-linter over SSH, or an IDE extension that posts to the pipeline linter endpoint, saving development time and catching errors early.
When calling the Jenkins linter API on a server with CSRF protection enabled, you must request a crumb from the crumbIssuer endpoint and include it in the request's Authorization header.
condition: CSRF protection is enabled on the Jenkins server

statement: Supplying a real password to the Jenkins API is supported but not recommended because of the risk of revealing it and the human tendency to reuse passwords; use an API token instead.

Infrastructure as code manages infrastructure through configuration files, which decreases cost and risk, speeds deployment, and makes infrastructure testable, repeatable, self-healing, idempotent, and self-documenting.

IaC tools split into cloud-specific tools (AWS CloudFormation, Azure Resource Manager, OpenStack Heat, Google Cloud Deployment Manager) and cloud-agnostic tools (Terraform, Vagrant, Chef Provisioning, Pulumi).
Terraform is open source, platform-agnostic, and supports multiple IaaS providers such as AWS, Azure, GCP, and DigitalOcean with a simple unified syntax.

Configuration-management tools like Ansible and Puppet install and manage configuration on existing servers, whereas Terraform focuses on bootstrapping and provisioning servers and other infrastructure resources.

Terraform uses a push approach: the engineer describes the desired infrastructure in a template and Terraform interacts directly with the cloud provider's API through a provider plugin that uses the provider's official SDK.
Terraform stores the managed infrastructure state in a terraform.tfstate JSON file and uses diffing to detect changes before any operation, letting teams change infrastructure safely and predictably.
Storing Terraform state locally is not ideal for team collaboration and may expose sensitive information, so use a remote backend such as Amazon S3 to store the state.
exception: a single-user setup where team collaboration and SCM versioning of state are not concerns

statement: Deploy the Jenkins cluster inside a purpose-built VPC with private subnets rather than the default VPC, to fully control the network topology and isolate Jenkins from application workloads.
Use a bastion host to SSH into private Jenkins instances without exposing them to the public internet.
Terraform describes resources in HCL within .tf files, and a modular approach that splits deployment into multiple files per component is preferable to one large template file.

The Terraform AWS provider supports static inline credentials, environment variables, a shared credentials file, and an EC2 IAM instance profile, the last of which is preferred when running on EC2 because it avoids hardcoding credentials.
condition: running Terraform from an EC2 instance for the IAM instance profile method

statement: Use Terraform variables instead of hardcoded values so resources are reusable and portable and can be overridden at runtime.
A typical VPC is divided into public and private subnets with separate public and private route tables to give fine-grained traffic control.
A public route table sends all traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to an internet gateway and must be associated with the public subnets for their traffic to reach the internet.
A private route table forwards outbound traffic to a NAT gateway placed in a public subnet, letting instances in private subnets reach the internet without being publicly exposed.
Generate a Terraform execution plan with terraform plan before applying, to avoid surprises when Terraform manipulates infrastructure.
Spread VPC subnets across multiple availability zones so the cluster can tolerate the failure of a single zone.
An Elastic IP attached to a NAT gateway is a static public IPv4 address that can be rapidly remapped to another NAT gateway to mask a NAT gateway failure.
A bastion host (jump box) deployed in a public subnet provides secure access to private-subnet instances through a single controlled point of entry using SSH or RDP.
SSH access to newly created EC2 instances is disabled by default and must be enabled by attaching a security group that allows inbound traffic on port 22.
Restrict the SSH ingress CIDR source to your own public IP address /32 or network address rather than 0.0.0.0/0 to enhance security and prevent breaches.
For an extra layer of security, bake the bastion host's own machine image with HashiCorp Packer instead of using a stock image.
Deploy the bastion host in an Auto Scaling group with min and max set to 1 to ensure one is always available, and use Spot instances instead of on-demand for cost optimization.
Deploy the Jenkins master in a private subnet so it has no public IP and is not directly reachable from the internet, accessing it through the bastion host via an SSH tunnel.

Size the Jenkins master's EBS volume to the number and size of projects built, because Jenkins settings and build logs are stored on the master by default, and set delete_on_termination to false to preserve that data.
A proper tagging policy for Jenkins instances is pivotal for cloud cost optimization because tags enable filtering AWS bills and enforce cost tracking and allocation.
Terraform loads every file ending in .tf in the directory, so files can be named freely; naming them after the AWS resource they declare aids identification.
A bastion host can be skipped if you instead set up remote VPN access such as OpenVPN Access Server to reach private instances.
condition: a remote-access VPN is set up instead

statement: Setting up a Jenkins master-worker cluster requires a bidirectional connection, so the worker security group should allow inbound SSH from the Jenkins master security group, and allowing SSH from the bastion host aids debugging.

A user-data boot script can make each Jenkins worker auto-join the cluster by reading its private IP and hostname from EC2 instance metadata and calling the Jenkins API to register itself as an agent.
Configure the number of executors per worker to control parallel builds, and set the Jenkins master's executor count to 0 so builds run only on worker machines.
condition: you want the master used only as a job scheduler

statement: The worker workspace directory holds nothing mission-critical because everything important is transferred back to the master after a build, so it usually does not need to be backed up.
Assign a label such as workers to worker nodes so they join the cluster under that label and build jobs can be restricted to run only on worker machines.
Jenkins worker costs can be reduced by up to 90% by using Amazon EC2 Spot instances or by subscribing to Amazon Savings Plans.
Deploy Jenkins workers in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum and maximum size spread across multiple private subnets for resiliency.
An AWS launch configuration is immutable, so changing the worker instance type or base AMI requires destroying and recreating it, which is why the create_before_destroy lifecycle setting is used.
Use Terraform depends_on so the Jenkins master instance is running before the workers deploy, because the workers need the master IP to join the cluster successfully.

Define CloudWatch CPU-based autoscaling policies to scale out when average CPU utilization is at or above 80 percent for two minutes and scale in when it is at or below 20 percent, giving extra build capacity without paying for excess idle workers.
The most useful metrics for deciding when to scale Jenkins workers up or down are CPU utilization, memory utilization, and network utilization.
Set an Auto Scaling group cooldown period (for example 300 seconds) so it does not launch or terminate additional workers before the previous scaling activity takes effect.
CloudWatch basic monitoring refreshes every five minutes, so load tests must run long enough for an autoscaling metric to be met for its required consecutive minutes before policies trigger.
Run terraform destroy to remove created cloud resources when finished experimenting so the provider does not keep charging for them.

Running all builds on a single standalone Jenkins server creates a single point of failure and cannot handle the load of larger, heavier projects, which is why a distributed master-worker cluster is preferred.
In Jenkins master-worker architecture the master schedules and dispatches build jobs, monitors worker state, and aggregates results in the dashboard, and can also execute builds directly.

A Jenkins worker (agent) is a Java executable on a remote machine that listens for master requests and executes build jobs; you can run 100+ workers and add or remove them on the fly so the workload is distributed off the master.
The slave terminology was deprecated in Jenkins 2.0 and replaced by agent.
Labels are virtual group names assigned to worker nodes and can restrict a build job to run on a node with a specific label, for example a CPU-optimized instance.

Host the Jenkins master on an instance with enough CPU and network bandwidth for concurrent users, make workers immutable and disposable so they can be added with minimal manual interaction via Auto Scaling groups, and spread workers across multiple availability zones for high availability and fault tolerance.
Jenkins can be installed from a marketplace AMI, via a package manager such as APT or Yum on Linux, Windows, or macOS, or run as a playground from the official Jenkins Docker image.

After installing Jenkins on an EC2 instance, configure the attached security group to allow inbound traffic on port 8080 where the dashboard is exposed, and optionally allow inbound SSH from your own public address for maintenance.
A security group acts as a firewall at the instance level while a network ACL acts as a firewall at the subnet level, so combining them adds an additional layer of security.
Vertically scaling the Jenkins master can absorb load spikes but has a hard limit, so larger and more complex projects need distributed builds across multiple workers.
Configure an Auto Scaling group alarm on aggregated average metrics across all worker instances so the group does not add capacity just because a single worker is busy.

The default ASG termination policy selects the instance closest to the next billing hour, the oldest instance, or the one with the oldest launch configuration; Amazon EC2 termination protection can protect a worker from accidental termination.

Memory utilization is not available by default in CloudWatch because AWS only records hypervisor-level metrics such as CPU and network; install a metrics-collector agent on the instances to capture memory utilization.

Jenkins workers can be scaled on custom metrics such as the number of jobs waiting in the build queue by exporting cluster metrics with Prometheus and using a Lambda function to trigger scale-out or scale-in via the AWS API.

An internet gateway provides internet connectivity to instances and maps a private IP to an associated public or Elastic IP, while a NAT gateway in a public subnet forwards outbound traffic from private subnets without allowing inbound internet traffic.

Place a public-facing Elastic Load Balancer in front of the Jenkins instance, listening on HTTP 80 and HTTPS 443 and forwarding to instance port 8080, so the Jenkins instance is not directly exposed to the internet.

When configuring an HTTPS listener, attach an SSL certificate (free via AWS Certificate Manager or imported) so the load balancer terminates TLS and decrypts client requests before forwarding to Jenkins.
condition: an HTTPS listener is specified

statement: Jenkins core does not support multiple masters by default, but you can run multiple masters behind a reverse proxy such as HAProxy or NGINX with an active master and a passive backup that takes over if the active goes down.

Use Amazon EFS (a shared NFS-style filesystem with strong consistency and file locking) to persist the $JENKINS_HOME directory so multiple Jenkins masters or containerized Jenkins on Kubernetes, ECS, or Fargate can share and preserve state across failover.
The AWS CLI is built on the AWS API, so anything achievable in the AWS Management Console can be scripted with the CLI to automate and control infrastructure.

AWS CLI credentials can be supplied via environment variables, a shared credentials file, or IAM roles, the last of which is preferred on an EC2 instance because it removes the need to manage credential files in production.
condition: using IAM roles requires running on an EC2 instance

statement: Do not use the AWS root account for any task except billing, because it has ultimate authority; instead create an IAM user granted only the permissions it needs.
Follow the principle of least privilege by granting a user only the minimum permissions needed for the task, starting with a minimal set and adding more only if necessary.
Save IAM access keys in a safe location when they are generated, because AWS will not display them again.
It is highly recommended to launch the Jenkins deployment within a private subnet in a VPC for security.
Jenkins is a crucial component of the DevOps chain whose downtime adversely affects the whole environment, so it needs a high-availability setup.

Packer machine images speed deployment by launching pre-provisioned machines, scale well because one image can spawn any number of identical instances without extra configuration, and support multiple cloud providers such as AWS, GCP, and Azure.
A drawback of Packer is that you must manage baked images yourself with tags or versions and delete old unused ones, because cloud providers charge for the storage of each machine image.

Packer bakes an image by booting a temporary instance from a base image, provisioning it into the desired state with a configuration tool or script, creating a new image, and then shutting the temporary instance down.
Booting servers from a baked image yields identical, repeatable configuration, which smooths deployment, speeds scaling, and lets you recreate identical servers when things go wrong.

A Packer template (JSON or YAML) has three components: user variables that parameterize it and keep secrets out for portability, builders that create an instance and map to a single image, and optional provisioners that install and configure software.
Keep secret and environment-specific values out of the Packer template and pass them at runtime via the -var flag, environment variables, or HashiCorp Vault.
Use a source_ami_filter with the most_recent attribute to automatically select the newest base AMI instead of hardcoding an AMI ID that changes over time and across regions.
Make each baked AMI name unique, for example by prefixing it with the installed software version or appending a {{timestamp}}.
Validate Packer template syntax with packer validate, which returns a zero exit status when the template is valid, before running packer build.

Install the Jenkins LTS release rather than the weekly release for production: LTS lags in features but is more stable and receives only important bug fixes, while weekly releases deliver fixes and features rapidly.
exception: users who need the newest features and bug fixes quickly may prefer the weekly line

statement: Configure Jenkins to start automatically on boot (for example with chkconfig) so it comes back up after a machine restart.
Grant Packer's IAM user only the minimal set of EC2 permissions necessary to build images rather than full access, following the principle of least privilege.
Running packer build deploys an instance from the template, runs the provisioners on it, and outputs the resulting build artifacts, typically the new AMI ID.

A single Packer template can build machine images for multiple providers by adding additional builders (for example GCP and Azure) from the same specification, avoiding repetitive per-provider coding.
Packer provisioning supports configuration-management tools such as Ansible, Chef, and Puppet as well as plain Bash scripts to bring the instance to its desired state.

Groovy init scripts placed in init.groovy.d run on every Jenkins restart to apply configuration and enforce the desired state automatically, so settings do not have to be reapplied manually after each restart.
Writing Groovy init scripts to customize Jenkins requires knowledge of Jenkins internals and its API.
Automate Jenkins plugin installation with a script that reads a plugins list file and resolves dependencies, rather than installing many plugins manually through the dashboard.
Before installing a Jenkins plugin, review its changelog on the description page because not all plugins are safe to use, and always pick the latest stable version.

Commonly essential Jenkins plugins include blueocean, git, ssh-agent, ssh-credentials, slack, credentials-binding, github-pullrequest, job-dsl, jira, htmlpublisher, email-ext, sonar, and embeddable-build-status.
When Jenkins configuration is fully automated, disable the initial setup wizard with a Groovy init script that marks the install state as completed.
condition: the server is already configured and seeded as code

statement: The credentials-binding plugin binds credentials to environment variables so a job's secret files and passwords can be packaged and accessed during the build.

In a Packer build, use the file provisioner to copy scripts and config to the temporary instance and a shell provisioner to move them into place and run setup, because Packer can upload only to locations the provisioning user can access (such as /tmp).
When generating an SSH key with ssh-keygen, entering a passphrase is recommended from a security perspective.
Jenkins captures launch configuration parameters in /etc/sysconfig/jenkins, which is where Java arguments should be added.
The only requirement for an instance to act as a Jenkins worker or build agent is a JDK, and modern Jenkins versions require at least a Java 8 runtime.
Install on the Jenkins worker image whatever tools the builds require, such as Git and Docker, and add the build user to the docker group so it can run Docker.
Defining the Jenkins configuration as code in a baked image lets you spawn the same configured instance many times on different machines with identical results and no manual GUI setup.
Remove unused AMIs because they are stored in S3 and incur ongoing storage charges.

To upgrade Jenkins or add plugins under an immutable-infrastructure approach, automate the Packer baking workflow with a Jenkins pipeline triggered by a GitHub push that validates the template, bakes a new AMI, and creates an instance, rather than provisioning manually.

For Packer to build images on GCP, create a dedicated service account authorized for the needed APIs, granting at least Compute Engine Instance Admin and Service Account User roles rather than full Project Owner.

A GCP service account is associated with a JSON or P12 key used for service-to-service authentication; download it, store it in a secure folder, and ensure the Compute Engine API is enabled on the project.

The service account JSON key file is not required when running Packer or Terraform from a GCE instance with a properly configured service account, because the tool fetches credentials from the metadata server.
condition: running from a GCE instance with a configured service account

statement: The same Packer template can build identical Jenkins virtual machine images for AWS, GCP, or Azure by changing only the builder section, which is the core strength of template-driven image baking.
A cloud provider's credentials can be supplied implicitly through environment variables such as GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS rather than hardcoding the key path in the template.
Run terraform init to download the provider plugin first, then terraform plan to preview changes, then terraform apply to provision the infrastructure.
When a deployment has many variables, store their values in a variable-definitions file ending in .tfvars or .tfvars.json and pass it with the -var-file flag rather than many individual -var flags.
Create public and private subnets in different availability zones for resiliency.
A GCP VPC network uses regional routing mode by default; switch it to global routing mode if you plan to deploy instances across multiple regions.
condition: deploying across multiple GCP regions

statement: Restrict the bastion host's SSH firewall ingress to only the specific IP address you want to allow rather than opening it to 0.0.0.0/0.
Deploy the Jenkins master VM in a private subnet and expose it through a public load balancer on port 8080 to reach the web dashboard without exposing the instance directly.
Deploying a vendor's prebuilt Jenkins marketplace template is quick, but building a Jenkins cluster from scratch gives full control to customize it and scale workers on demand.

An Azure service principal represents an application accessing Azure resources, is identified by a client (application) ID, authenticates with a password or certificate, and must be granted an appropriate role such as Contributor to provision resources.
Cloud credentials such as Azure subscription, client, secret, and tenant IDs can be sourced from environment variables (for example the ARM_ variables) rather than hardcoded in the configuration.
When running Packer inside a cloud virtual machine you can assign it a managed identity so no credential properties need to be configured.
condition: Packer runs inside a cloud VM with a managed identity

statement: Choosing a base OS that shares the same package manager across clouds (for example CentOS on Azure and Amazon Linux on AWS, both using Yum) lets the same provisioning scripts produce consistent, identical Jenkins images on every provider.

Azure Bastion is a managed jump-box service that provides RDP and SSH access to VMs without having to manage or patch a hardened bastion instance, removing that operational overhead, and is deployed into a dedicated AzureBastionSubnet.
Tag cloud resources with key-value pairs to support cost optimization and tracking.
Harden the Jenkins virtual machine by disabling password authentication and using SSH key authentication only.
Provision enough disk for the Jenkins VM (for example 30 GB) because Jenkins needs space to perform builds and keep archives and build logs.
Select the VM family or instance type based on the project's build needs; a burstable family such as Azure B-series balances compute and network bandwidth.
Deploy the Jenkins master in a private subnet with a private IP so it is reachable only through the bastion host.
Use Terraform output variables to expose useful provisioned values such as the bastion host's public IP address.

Cloud-native autoscale settings (such as an Azure monitor autoscale setting on a VM scale set) can scale Jenkins workers out when average CPU exceeds 80 percent and in when it falls below 20 percent over a time window, mirroring the AWS CloudWatch approach across providers.
In security-group and firewall rules it is recommended to restrict SSH ingress to your own network CIDR block rather than allowing it from anywhere.

DigitalOcean offers simple, affordable virtual machines (Droplets) with a friendly interface and few services, making it a cost-efficient starting point for beginner businesses and startups compared with the feature-rich AWS, GCP, and Azure.

The same Packer template can build identical Jenkins images across AWS, GCP, Azure, and DigitalOcean by changing only the builder, snapshotting a provisioned image to serve as the foundation for new workers.
Choose a larger instance or Droplet size for heavier workloads, larger projects, and many concurrent users connecting to the Jenkins web dashboard.
condition: heavier workloads, larger projects, or many concurrent dashboard users

statement: Upload your SSH public key to the cloud provider account and attach it to instances at creation time so you can log into the Jenkins master passwordlessly while remaining secure.

Pass the worker autojoin script through the instance's user_data so it runs the first time the instance boots, fetching the instance IP and hostname from the provider metadata server to register the node as a Jenkins agent.
Take a multi-cloud Jenkins architecture further by placing a load balancer in front of the master that forwards to port 8080 and creating a DNS record pointing to the load balancer's FQDN.
Run terraform destroy with the variable file when finished to tear down the cluster and avoid incurring further costs.

Provider choice can be driven by needs: GCP has seamless native Kubernetes support, Azure is a viable alternative especially with enterprise agreements, and DigitalOcean is cost-efficient for startups.
A Multibranch Pipeline job automatically creates a nested pipeline for each Git branch that contains a Jenkinsfile.

Jenkins job types include Freestyle (UI-configured), Inheritance (shared properties across jobs), Pipeline (single repo and branch, suited to trunk-based workflow), Folder (grouping), Multibranch pipeline (per-branch Jenkinsfile), and Organization (org-wide for GitHub or Bitbucket).
The availability of a given Jenkins job type depends on having the requisite plugins installed.
Use a dedicated Jenkins service account rather than a personal GitHub account to let Jenkins access Git repositories.

Authenticate Jenkins to GitHub with a personal access token instead of the account password, selecting the repo scope for private repositories, and copy the token immediately because it cannot be viewed again.
condition: the repo scope is required for private repositories

statement: Because the Jenkinsfile is versioned in GitHub alongside the source, it can be peer-reviewed, commented on, and approved before being merged into main branches.

Jenkins scans a repository for branches containing a Jenkinsfile at the root and by default auto-triggers builds for newly discovered branches; a branch without a Jenkinsfile gets no scheduled pipeline.

In a pipeline node block, a label like workers restricts execution to worker machines; if no label is provided Jenkins runs the pipeline on the first available executor on any machine, master or worker.
The Git client must be installed on the worker where a build that checks out source code is executed.
The Jenkins Stage view works only with Pipeline and Multibranch pipeline jobs.
Copy an existing job's configuration to quickly create similar jobs for other services, then update the repository URL, name, and description.
Jenkins has built-in Subversion support in addition to Git, accepting an SVN URL over the HTTP, SVN, or File protocols with an optional username/password credential.
A Jenkins job can be created or cloned by exporting its config.xml and issuing an HTTP POST of that XML to the createItem API, which lets job creation be automated.
Generate a Jenkins API token from the user's profile page for API authentication, and when CSRF protection is enabled use an API token rather than a crumb.
condition: CSRF protection is enabled

statement: Use Jenkins folders to organize and group related jobs, accessed via a JENKINS_DNS/job/<folder>/job URL path.
The Jenkins CLI for importing and exporting jobs is deprecated and not recommended because of security vulnerabilities in Jenkins 2.53 and older versions.
A webhook is a mechanism that automatically triggers the build of a Jenkins project when a commit is pushed to a remote Git repository.
To let Git webhooks reach a Jenkins server behind a firewall, forward them through a reverse proxy or an API Gateway plus Lambda forwarder that posts to the Jenkins webhook endpoint.
condition: the Jenkins server is private or behind a firewall

statement: Add an extra security layer to webhooks by requiring a request secret and validating the incoming request signature on the receiving side.
If Jenkins is running locally or privately, use a poll-SCM build trigger to periodically check the repository and start a build when something changes.
condition: Jenkins cannot receive inbound webhooks

statement: Polling SCM is less intuitive than webhooks but is useful when Git commits are frequent and builds take a long time, where building on every push would cause overload.
The development branching workflow should be chosen carefully within the team because it affects the CI process and defines how code is developed.
Choosing a mono-repo or multi-repo strategy determines the complexity of the CI/CD pipeline as the number of applications grows in an organization.

When the Jenkinsfile and application source live together in the same Git repository, the pipeline can go through the standard code-development process of code review, pull requests, and automated testing.

Test automation is a cornerstone of Agile delivery: releasing fast with reasonable quality requires automated testing, and although you cannot always automate every test, the goal is to automate whatever testing is possible since it matures over time.
Unit testing is the frontline effort to identify issues as early as possible, and unit tests should be small and quick to execute to be efficient.
Run unit tests inside a Docker container so Docker is the consistent execution environment across all Jenkins workers, avoiding installing each service's language runtime on every worker.
Use a Dockerfile.test naming convention for the test image to avoid conflicting with the Dockerfile used to build the main application image.
Use the docker run --rm flag so the container and its filesystem are automatically cleaned up when the container exits.
On a Windows worker use the pipeline powershell step, which has the same options as the sh instruction.
condition: the build runs on a Windows worker

statement: Prefer the Jenkins Docker DSL (such as docker.build and the inside block) over running raw Docker commands through the shell, because the DSL provides high-level encapsulation and ease of use.
Use the JUnit report plugin to consume a test-result XML file (for example produced by xmlrunner) and present test results graphically in Jenkins.
Modern CI pipelines include continuous inspection that continuously checks code quality, not just continuously integrating code.

Linting checks source code for programmatic, syntactic, and stylistic errors and enforces a uniform format; several linters exist (JSLint, JSHint, ESLint), with ESLint preferred for TypeScript and Node.js.

A linter that returns a nonzero exit code breaks the pipeline, so configure the linter's rules (for example enabling the test-framework environment) to clear false errors rather than ignoring lint failures.
Code must not be tested only in isolation; integration and end-to-end tests give extra confidence because in a large system units of code rarely work separately even when each works on its own.
Integration and end-to-end tests need the database in a clean, predictable state, which requires setup and teardown code that runs at the beginning and end of every test case or suite.
Using a real database for testing is relatively slow, complex, and increases operational overhead, so prefer an in-memory database such as H2 with DbUnit for Java or mongo-unit for Node.js.
When tests depend on other services, use Docker Compose to simplify starting and connecting all the services the application depends on.
condition: the tests depend on other services

statement: Code coverage reports commonly report statements, branches, functions, and lines metrics.
Publish HTML coverage reports in Jenkins using the HTML Publisher or Cobertura plugin, mapping a volume to the folder where the coverage tool writes its reports.
Set the publishHTML allowMissing parameter to false so that a missing coverage report causes the pipeline to throw an error rather than passing silently.
Coverage tools are language-specific, for example Istanbul/nyc for JavaScript, SimpleCov for Ruby, Coverage.py for Python, and JaCoCo for Java.
Run independent test stages in parallel using a parallel block to reduce the total waiting time of the test phase.
Integrate SonarQube static analysis by injecting its config with withSonarQubeEnv and running sonar-scanner, which posts the analysis report to the SonarQube server.
SonarQube evaluates code against Quality Profiles and a quality gate: code that crosses the error threshold is dropped and fails the pipeline, while code under the threshold may advance.
Attach the Jenkins build number to each SonarQube analysis (for example with the -Dsonar.projectVersion override flag) so analyses are traceable to builds.
Use the waitForQualityGate step together with a SonarQube webhook to pause the pipeline until analysis completes and abort the build if the quality gate fails.
Place the quality-gate wait outside the node block so the pipeline does not occupy a Jenkins worker while waiting for the SonarQube notification.
Promoting traditional security practices such as external dependency scanning into the CI/CD workflow adds a security layer that helps avoid breaches and vulnerabilities.
Headless Chrome runs UI tests in a headless environment without the full browser UI.

A complete CI pipeline checks out source on a push event, runs pre-integration tests (unit, security, quality, UI) inside Docker with coverage and static analysis, compiles and builds a Docker image, then tags and stores it in a private registry, reporting success or failure at every stage.
Because a Docker image is built on top of a base image, a broken or outdated base image can cause production outages and security breaches, so use an up-to-date, well-maintained base image.
Prefer official base images from DockerHub because they tend to be better controlled than community-created images.
Pin a specific base-image version rather than a floating tag such as latest or lts, so anyone rebuilding the image on another machine gets the same version and avoids accidental upgrades.
Pin all application dependencies with their transitive versions (for example in a requirements.txt) to keep image builds consistent.
Order Dockerfile instructions so that rarely-changing steps like dependency installation come before frequently-changing source copies, so Docker layer caching speeds up rebuilds.

Use Docker multistage builds to leave build tools and SDKs out of the final image, dramatically reducing image size (for example from about 300 MB to 8 MB); this feature requires Docker engine 17.05 or higher.
Name Docker multistage build stages with AS rather than referring to them by integer index, for clarity.

Store built Docker images in a private registry, choosing either a self-hosted option such as Nexus Repository OSS or a managed service such as Amazon ECR, Azure Container Registry, or Google Container Registry.
A hosted Docker repository is exposed over HTTPS by default; if you expose it over plain HTTP you must configure the Docker daemon to allow insecure connections with the --insecure-registry flag.
condition: the registry is exposed only on a plain HTTP endpoint

statement: Authenticate to a Docker registry with docker login before pushing or pulling, using the provider's login command such as aws ecr get-login-password for ECR.
Use a scoped RBAC token with least privilege (for example a push-only scope) for CI rather than the registry admin account, which is intended for a single user and mainly for testing.
Store registry credentials in Jenkins as a Username with Password credential; a generated registry password cannot be retrieved after the dialog closes but a new one can be generated.
Use the Docker DSL withRegistry block to authenticate against the registry and push the image, persisting the auth token to ~/.docker/config.json.
Tag Docker images meaningfully; the Git commit ID is a better, more traceable identifier than the Jenkins build number.
Also tag images by branch name (such as latest for production, preprod for staging, and develop for sandbox) so each image maps to its target environment for continuous deployment.
Give Jenkins workers permission to push to a cloud registry by assigning an IAM instance profile with the container-registry push policy rather than embedding static credentials.
condition: pushing to a cloud-managed registry such as Amazon ECR

statement: Read the current branch in a pipeline from the BRANCH_NAME environment variable.
Create a helper function (or a shared library) that fetches the Git commit ID via the Git CLI for image tagging, to avoid duplicating that logic across Jenkinsfiles.
Run CI checks at every check-in and pull request so only passing code is merged, catching bugs early and automatically to reduce the number of problems reaching production.
Post the Jenkins build status back to GitHub so each commit shows a green, yellow, or red check reflecting the build state.

Add a GitHub branch protection rule that requires the Jenkins status check to pass before merging, preventing direct pushes and merges without a successful build, and apply it to the develop, preprod, and master branches.
Optimize Docker images for production using layer caching, multistage builds, and lightweight base images such as Alpine.
Tag Docker images with the commit ID and build ID for versioning and to enable rollback to a working version if an application deployment fails.
Anchore Engine is an open source tool that scans Docker images for security vulnerabilities during the CI workflow.
Binary repository tools like Nexus and Artifactory manage and store build artifacts for later use.
Isolate workload environments in separate VPCs for auditing and security compliance; while not mandatory, it is strongly recommended as a best practice.
exception: deploying everything in one VPC is acceptable but not recommended

statement: Add the build user (such as ec2-user) to the docker group so it can run Docker commands without sudo.
Docker Swarm has been bundled into Docker Engine since Docker 1.12 (2016) for orchestrating container deployment across a cluster of machines.

Automate Swarm cluster joining by distributing the join token through a shared store such as an S3 bucket, AWS SSM Parameter Store, or a consistent key-value store like etcd, Consul, or ZooKeeper, so nodes autojoin on launch.
Use an odd number of Swarm managers in production because a majority vote is needed for consensus and an odd count provides a tie-breaker.
condition: running Swarm in production

statement: Use Terraform depends_on to create Swarm managers before workers so the cluster is initialized and the join token is available in the shared store before workers start.
Deploy Swarm managers and workers in separate Auto Scaling groups spread across multiple availability zones in private subnets for resiliency.
For Jenkins to deploy over SSH, create an SSH Username with Private Key credential; Jenkins needs access only to the Swarm manager because the manager controls the other nodes.
Wrap all SSH and SCP commands in a pipeline inside the sshagent block (Credentials Binding) so the SSH credentials are injected for those commands.
Deploy a Docker stack to Swarm by running docker stack deploy with the --with-registry-auth flag over SSH against the Swarm manager.

Swarm mesh routing makes every node aware of each container's location via the gossip network, so a request hitting a node not running the target service is routed to one that is, letting any node run any service and be load-balanced equally to reduce complexity.
To restrict deployment of a service to worker nodes rather than managers, use Docker placement constraints with labels.
condition: you want a service to run only on worker nodes

statement: Trigger the deployment job at the end of a successful CI pipeline using the build job step so continuous deployment runs automatically after each successful build.

Inject environment-specific configuration such as an API URL at image build time using per-environment files (for example Angular environment files selected with ng build -c sandbox), so the same source builds an environment-specific image.
Send Slack notifications from the pipeline with slackSend, configured through the Jenkins Slack integration plugin and an integration token, to broadcast build and deployment status to the team.
Use StrictHostKeyChecking=no for non-interactive SSH and SCP commands run from a pipeline against freshly provisioned hosts.
Jenkins posts the build status on a pull request, and merging the PR after validation triggers a new build that runs the deployment.
Tag images by branch so each branch maps to its target environment, for example pushing the develop tag from develop, preprod from preprod, and latest from master.
Require manual validation before deploying to production using the Input Step plugin to pause the pipeline, simulating business or QA approval of the release.
Set a timeout on the production-approval input step so the pipeline is aborted if no one approves within the allotted window.
Move a Deploy stage that waits for manual input outside the node block to avoid tying up a Jenkins worker while waiting, and send a Slack reminder when input is pending.
Promote code through environments by merging feature into develop (sandbox), then develop into preprod (staging), then preprod into master (production with approval).
Limit the deployment job's branch discovery with a regular expression to the main environment branches so Jenkins is triggered only when those branches change.
Adding Slack notifications to CI/CD pipelines speeds delivery because the sooner team members learn of a build, integration, or deployment failure, the quicker they can act.
If the deployment target is a single host, a Swarm cluster is not needed and the same docker-compose.yml and procedure suffice for single-host continuous deployment.
condition: the deployment target is a single host

statement: Docker Swarm is a good solution for beginners and smaller workloads, but for large deployments and at scale you should consider shifting to Kubernetes.
Managed Kubernetes services are available from the major clouds: Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, and Google GKE.
Amazon EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane across multiple availability zones to eliminate a single point of failure and requires subnets in at least two availability zones.
Tag the EKS cluster's VPC subnets with kubernetes.io/cluster/<cluster-name> so EKS can discover the subnets and manage network resources.
A Kubernetes node is an EC2 instance that runs Kubernetes objects (pods, deployments, services), and the master scheduler places work according to each node's available resources.
Grant the EKS control plane and worker nodes only the needed managed IAM policies (such as the cluster policy for the control plane and worker-node, CNI, and ECR read-only policies for workers).
kubectl is the command-line tool for communicating with the cluster API server; grant it access by generating a kubeconfig file, for example with the aws eks update-kubeconfig command.
Expose a Kubernetes service externally with a Service of type LoadBalancer, using annotations to set the backend protocol and an ACM SSL certificate so the load balancer terminates TLS on port 443.
The metrics-server must be running in the cluster (collecting resource metrics from Kubelet) for metrics and graphs to appear in the Kubernetes dashboard.

Access the Kubernetes dashboard securely by creating a dedicated service account and ClusterRoleBinding, then logging in via kubectl proxy with the service account's token rather than exposing the dashboard openly.
Kompose converts a docker-compose.yml file into Kubernetes deployment and service manifests based on the compose settings and network topology.

Writing and maintaining raw Kubernetes YAML manifests is tedious and full of duplicated hardcoded values (even simple deployments need several manifests), which is why a tool like Helm packages them into a single advertisable unit.
Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes; Helm 3 removed the server-side Tiller component, leaving a client-only architecture.
Helm's core concepts are the Chart (a package of preconfigured Kubernetes resources), the Release (a deployed instance of a chart), and the Repository (a group of published charts).
Helm is assumed compatible with n-3 versions of Kubernetes, so check the Helm version support policy against your cluster version.
A Helm chart is structured with values.yaml for injectable values, Chart.yaml for chart version and metadata, .helmignore for excluded files, and a templates/ folder holding the actual manifests.
Move variables out of Helm templates into values.yaml as overridable defaults so the chart is a portable package that can be customized by overriding values at install time.
Store sensitive data such as database credentials in Kubernetes Secrets (base64-encoded) rather than in plain manifests, and put non-sensitive configuration in ConfigMaps.
Inject the Jenkins build ID and Git commit ID as deployment annotations so running Kubernetes deployments can be traced back to their build for debugging and troubleshooting.
Reuse a stable, official Helm chart (such as the MongoDB chart) declared as a chart dependency instead of writing your own manifests for that component.
Run post-deployment smoke tests and health checks after deploying, because a deployed service is not necessarily configured correctly or performing all its expected jobs.

A simple health check issues an HTTP GET to the service URL and verifies a 200 response, using a timeout (such as curl -m) to give the cluster enough time to pull the new image and deploy before checking.
Compute the target service URL from the current branch (for example via a function) so the health check hits the correct environment.

A responding service does not prove the new version deployed, so have the service expose its version and assert it matches the expected value (for example the injected Jenkins build ID) during the health-check stage.
Use the Jenkins HTTP Request plugin (httpRequest with JsonSlurper) to issue advanced HTTP requests and assert on parsed response content rather than only checking the status code.
Jenkins X is a CI/CD solution for Kubernetes that simplifies configuration with ready-to-go templates and bundled open source tools such as Helm, ChartMuseum, Nexus, and a Docker Registry.

Jenkins X uses GitOps: each environment has its own Git repository of Helm charts and configuration, making Git the single source of truth for both infrastructure and application code so changes are auditable and easy to revert.
In Jenkins X promotions are performed via Git pull requests: a merge to master auto-promotes to staging, while production must be promoted manually with the jx promote command.
jx import detects the project language, selects a build pack, generates a Jenkinsfile, Dockerfile, and Helm chart, and creates the remote repository with a registered webhook.
Jenkins X uses semantic versioning to tag application releases.
Jenkins X can run Jenkins in serverless mode so Jenkins runs only when needed instead of a continuously running dashboard that consumes CPU and memory.
Jenkins X automatically spins up a preview environment for each pull request so users can evaluate features, bug fixes, or hotfixes and get fast feedback before changes are merged.

Serverless functions can be organized either as a mono-repo where cohesive functions serving a business feature are grouped together, or as one repository per function each with its own CI/CD pipeline.
Build a Lambda deployment package as a zip archive containing the function code and its dependencies, then push it to an S3 bucket for versioning.
Name each deployment package with the Git commit ID to give releases meaningful unique names and enable rollback to a specific commit if something goes wrong.
Delete the generated build artifact at the end of the pipeline to save disk space on the worker.
Wrap pipeline stages in try/catch/finally so an error sets currentBuild.result to FAILED and a Slack notification is sent on start and on completion regardless of outcome.
Keep proper unit tests in place for a Lambda function to safeguard against breakage from subsequent code updates.
For a compiled-language Lambda such as Go, use a Docker multistage build, copy the built binary out of the container, and zip it as the deployment package.
Cold start is a drawback of dynamically provisioned functions: a function that has not been used for a while takes longer to start up and to handle its first request.
The deployment package size affects function cold start, so keep it small by installing only runtime/production dependencies (for example npm install --prod=only).
Use the Serverless framework to create a zip per function that excludes unused dependencies and files.
Run the build and push stages in parallel when they take a large share of execution time, to keep the pipeline turnaround short.
Publish a new Lambda version on each deploy and point a per-environment alias (such as sandbox, staging, production) to the published version based on the current branch.
Use API Gateway stage variables to select the Lambda alias at runtime per deployment stage instead of hardcoding a Lambda function version.
Create a separate API Gateway deployment stage per environment, each setting the environment stage variable so requests route to the matching Lambda alias.
Deploy a static website to multiple environments by injecting the environment name as a build argument and pushing the built static files to per-environment folders or buckets in S3.
Require developer authorization with the Jenkins Input Step plugin before actually deploying serverless functions to production.
Slack can be used not only for build notifications but also to take actions from the chat window, such as confirming a production deployment or triggering a Jenkins job.
Configure Jenkins email notifications with the Email Extension plugin by setting up an SMTP server and a recipient list.
Send email or other heavy notifications only for builds on the production (master) branch to avoid spamming developers.
Invoke notification functions in the finally block of a scripted pipeline or the post block of a declarative pipeline so they run regardless of build outcome.
Declarative Jenkinsfiles provide a post section (with conditions such as always, success, and failure) for placing post-execution steps like notifications.
Attach the job's build logs to a notification email by enabling the attachLog attribute.

Expose Jenkins metrics with the Prometheus Metrics plugin (default /prometheus endpoint) so a Prometheus server, an open source monitoring system with a dimensional data model, query language, time-series database, and alerting, can scrape them.
Configure the Prometheus scrape_configs with a job targeting the Jenkins metrics path to collect Jenkins metrics on a scrape interval.
Collected metrics are not useful unless visualized, so connect Prometheus to Grafana as a data source and build dashboards on the metrics.

A comprehensive Jenkins monitoring dashboard should cover application-level metrics (queued, pending, and stuck jobs), internal JVM operation metrics, and system-level metrics such as disk I/O, network, and memory.
The Monitoring (JavaMelody) plugin is an alternative that produces HTML reports on CPU and system load, average response time, and memory usage served from the Jenkins dashboard.
Persist Jenkins logs in a centralized logging platform for auditing and troubleshooting, because log rotation and discard-old-build policies mean old job logs can otherwise be lost.
Jenkins logs are at /var/log/jenkins/jenkins.log and viewable from the dashboard System Log page, where a custom log recorder can capture logs for a specific plugin's Java package.
Ship Jenkins logs with Filebeat (a lightweight agent on the Jenkins master) to Logstash for processing, store them in Elasticsearch, and visualize them in Kibana, forming the ELK stack workflow.
Configure Filebeat multiline settings to correctly group multiline log messages such as Java stack traces into a single event.
condition: logs contain multiline messages like stack traces

statement: Annotate each shipped log event with host, cloud, Docker, and Kubernetes metadata so events can be correlated by source.
Create a Kibana index pattern (such as jenkins-*) mapping to the Elasticsearch indices to explore the logs, using @timestamp as the time field.

Parse raw log lines into named fields with Grok expressions (%{PATTERN:IDENTIFIER}) at the Logstash filter level before storing them in Elasticsearch; Grok ships with a pattern dictionary and supports custom patterns.
Use the Kibana Grok Debugger to develop and iteratively test a Grok expression against sample log data until it matches the expected event.
Matrix-based authorization gives granular per-user permissions, but assigning them to many users is tedious, so define reusable roles instead.

The Role-Based Authorization Strategy plugin lets you define roles such as Admin, Developer, and QA with appropriate permissions and assign them to users, scaling access control in a large organization.
In an organization, use an OAuth2 authentication service such as GitHub, GitLab, Google, or OpenID for Jenkins instead of manually managing users and passwords.

To enable GitHub OAuth for Jenkins, register a GitHub application with the callback URL JENKINS_URL/securityRealm/finishLogin and configure its client ID, secret, and OAuth scopes in the Jenkins security realm.

The GitHub Committer Authorization strategy derives Jenkins project permissions from GitHub repository permissions: for a public repo all authenticated users get read-only and collaborators can manage the job, while for a private repo only collaborators can manage it.

Keep an audit trail of who did what to the Jenkins configuration, which many organizations require for security compliance, using the Audit Trail plugin to record key actions and the user in rolling log files.
Stream Jenkins audit logs to a centralized ELK platform and set up alerts on unauthorized user activities.
Centralize duplicated pipeline helper functions in a Jenkins shared library so the same code can be referenced across all pipelines instead of being copied into each Jenkinsfile.

A Jenkins shared library is a collection of Groovy scripts stored in a Git repository, so it can be versioned and tagged; per-function scripts in a vars folder each implement a call method, or functions can be defined in classes under src/.
Define a shared library globally under Manage Jenkins Global Pipeline Libraries so all pipelines can use its functionality.
Import a shared library with the @Library annotation in a scripted pipeline or a libraries block in a declarative pipeline, and pin a specific version with the id@version format.
Back up Jenkins by capturing the $JENKINS_HOME directory, which holds all settings, build logs, and artifacts, using a plugin like ThinBackup or a scheduled cron job that uploads to an S3 bucket.
Store Jenkins backups on a remote server or external storage rather than only locally.
Regular backups let you restore Jenkins to an earlier point in time in case of data corruption or a human-caused event.
Trusted shared-library code can use third-party Java libraries from Maven Central via the @Grab annotation.

The Docker plugin runs dynamic Jenkins agents inside Docker containers that are provisioned on demand and stopped after each build, giving a clean build environment every time and efficient use of the underlying host.

Use jenkins/ssh-agent (which has SSHD installed) as a base image for Docker-based Jenkins workers, or build a custom agent image containing all the dependencies and packages your projects need to build.
Jenkins itself can be run locally inside a Docker container for development or testing.
If you prefer not to use a backup plugin, schedule regular Jenkins backups with a cron job that copies $JENKINS_HOME to a remote repository such as an S3 bucket.
Pipeline as code is still an emerging practice but awareness is growing rapidly, and adoption lets organizations release faster and shorten the feedback loop.

Reliability engineering should account for the full lifecycle of a service, including design, deployment, operation, refinement, and decommissioning, because a large share of system cost occurs after initial release.

SRE work applies computer science and software engineering to large distributed systems, including service code, reusable operational infrastructure, and adaptation of existing solutions to new reliability problems.
Reliability should be treated as a fundamental product property because a service that users cannot use delivers little value.
Teams should invest in reliability improvements only until the service is reliable enough, then shift effort toward features or new products.
condition: when the service has reached an explicitly sufficient reliability level

statement: Web-service SRE lessons can be reused outside Google when practitioners adapt the lessons to their own environment instead of copying Google-specific implementation details wholesale.
condition: when applying Google-specific SRE practices in another organization

statement: Small organizations should put lightweight reliability support in place early because expanding an existing reliability structure is less costly than introducing one after it is absent.
condition: when an organization is small but expects its services to keep evolving

statement: An organization can begin improving reliability by identifying people already doing SRE-like work, formally recognizing that work, and rewarding it.
condition: when reliability work already exists informally inside the organization

statement: Operational tools should be understood as parts of broader processes that also include software chains, people, and data.
Scaling a service is more than enlarging system architecture; reliability work must also scale the business and operational processes around the service.
Critical systems should be designed with awareness of human error, preparation, and documentation because a thorough understanding of operations alone does not prevent mistakes.
condition: when operating systems where human mistakes can produce severe consequences

statement: For critical human-triggered failure modes, built-in error detection and recovery safeguards are preferable to relying solely on operator perfection or procedural warnings.
condition: when a foreseeable operator action can put the system into an unrecoverable or hazardous state

statement: If a software safeguard is not implemented, explicit operational documentation about the failure mode can still materially help responders recover under time pressure.
condition: when a known failure mode cannot yet be prevented in software
exception: documentation should not be treated as a substitute for prevention when prevention is feasible

statement: Site Reliability Engineering staffs operations work with software engineers who design automation to replace manual operational labour, rather than with traditional sysadmins.
A traditional ops-focused team scales roughly linearly with service size because manual change-management and event-handling work grows with traffic.
The number of SREs needed to run a system scales sublinearly with the size of the system, because SREs automate away repetitive work.
Google caps aggregate operational ('ops') work for SREs at 50% of their time (tickets, on-call, manual tasks).
The 50% ops cap is an upper bound; the remaining time should be spent on development and project work, and over time ops load should fall well below the cap.

Measure how SRE time is spent, and when a team consistently spends less than 50% of its time on development, shift operational load back to the product-development team or add staff without new ops responsibilities.
The goal of SRE automation is systems that are automatic (self-running and self-repairing), not merely automated.
Without constant engineering investment, operational load increases and the team must keep hiring just to keep pace with workload growth.
An on-call SRE should receive on average a maximum of about two paging events per 8-to-12-hour on-call shift, so each event can be handled, cleaned up, and followed by a postmortem.
condition: when focused on operations work during an on-call shift
