statement: Receiving more than two paging events per on-call shift regularly prevents thorough investigation and causes pager fatigue that does not improve with scale.
Consistently receiving fewer than one event per on-call shift makes keeping an engineer on point a waste of their time.
Write a postmortem for every significant incident, regardless of whether it triggered a page.
Postmortems for incidents that did not trigger a page are especially valuable because they typically reveal monitoring gaps.
Operate a blameless postmortem culture whose goal is to expose faults and apply engineering fixes rather than to blame or punish individuals.
100% is the wrong reliability target for essentially every service, because users cannot distinguish full availability from very high availability given other unreliable systems in the request path.
exception: life-critical systems such as pacemakers and anti-lock brakes

statement: The right reliability target for a service is a product/business decision, not a technical one, and must account for user expectations, available alternatives, and how usage changes with availability.
A service's error budget equals one minus its availability target (e.g. a 99.99%-available service has a 0.01% error budget).
Spend the error budget to maximize feature velocity using risk-tolerant tactics such as phased rollouts and 1% experiments.
Adopting an error budget reframes outages as an expected, managed part of innovation and replaces a 'zero outages' goal with maximizing feature velocity within the budget.
When the error budget is depleted, halt new releases for the remainder of the period until the budget recovers.
condition: once the error budget for the period is exhausted

statement: Monitoring should never require a human to interpret the alerting domain; software should do the interpretation and notify a human only when action is required.
Alerting that requires a human to read an email and decide whether to act is fundamentally ineffective.
There are three valid monitoring outputs: alerts (a human must act immediately), tickets (a human must act but not immediately), and logging (recorded for diagnostics, normally unread).
Reliability is a function of mean time to failure (MTTF) and mean time to repair (MTTR), and MTTR is the most relevant metric for evaluating emergency response.
A system that avoids emergencies requiring human intervention achieves higher availability than one needing hands-on intervention, even if it has more underlying failures, because humans add latency.
Maintaining recorded on-call playbooks produces roughly a 3x improvement in MTTR compared with improvising a response.
Roughly 70% of outages are caused by changes to a live system.
Reduce the impact of bad changes by automating progressive rollouts, fast and accurate problem detection, and safe rollback.
Removing humans from the release loop increases both release velocity and safety by avoiding fatigue, complacency, and inattention to repetitive tasks.
Capacity planning must account for both organic growth (natural product adoption) and inorganic growth (feature launches, marketing, business events).

Mandatory capacity-planning steps are an accurate organic demand forecast extending beyond capacity lead time, incorporation of inorganic demand, and regular load testing that correlates raw capacity to service capacity.
Because capacity drives availability, the SRE team should own capacity planning and therefore also own provisioning.
Provisioning must be performed quickly, only when necessary (capacity is expensive), and correctly, and should be treated with more caution than load shifting because it is riskier.
Run a job as multiple identical tasks (replicas) rather than a single process, both for reliability and because one process usually cannot handle all of a service's traffic.
A cluster scheduler should continually monitor tasks and automatically kill and restart any malfunctioning task, possibly on a different machine.

Bin-pack tasks across machines in a way that respects failure domains — for example, never place all of a job's tasks on one rack, since that makes the top-of-rack switch a single point of failure for the job.
If a task tries to exceed its requested resources, kill and restart it, because a slowly crash-looping task is preferable to one that is never restarted.
Refer to fluidly-scheduled tasks through a naming/indirection service rather than by IP address and port, because tasks are reallocated across machines.
Use a consensus-based (Paxos) lock service for distributed locks and master election so that, when only one replica of a redundant job may act, exactly one is selected.
Direct users to the closest datacenter that has available capacity to minimize latency for globally distributed services.
Require code review for every change: all software is reviewed before it is submitted to the mainline.

Run continuous testing so that each submitted change triggers tests on all directly or indirectly dependent software and notifies the change owner if it likely broke something; some teams auto-deploy on green.
Provision a serving job with N+2 redundancy so it can lose one task to a rolling update and one task to a machine failure simultaneously and still serve peak load.
Replicate data stores per region to lower cross-region data-access latency and to provide resilience if a storage server fails.
condition: acceptable when eventual consistency is tolerable and data is updated infrequently

statement: Redundancy may be reduced from N+2 to N+1 in a region to save hardware cost, accepting a small risk of higher latency when traffic is redirected to other regions.
condition: when the cost saving outweighs a small latency risk and other regions can absorb redirected load

statement: Past a certain point, increasing a service's reliability harms it: it limits feature-development speed, slows delivery, and dramatically increases cost, reducing the features a team can afford to offer.
The cost of reliability does not increase linearly; an incremental improvement in reliability can cost roughly 100x more than the previous increment.
Reliability cost has two dimensions: the cost of redundant compute/storage resources and the opportunity cost of engineering effort diverted from user-visible features.
Explicitly align the risk a service takes with the risk the business is willing to bear, making the service reliable enough but no more reliable than it needs to be.

Treat the availability target as both a minimum and a maximum — aim to exceed it but not by much, since substantially over-shooting wastes opportunities to add features, repay technical debt, or cut operational cost.
Toil is mundane, repetitive operational work that provides no enduring value and scales linearly with service growth; eliminating toil is one of SRE's most important tasks.
To make service risk tractable and consistent across systems, reduce it to a single objective metric: unplanned downtime.
Express a service's risk tolerance as an acceptable level of unplanned downtime, stated in 'nines' of availability where each additional nine is an order-of-magnitude improvement.

For globally distributed services, define availability as a request success rate (yield) over a rolling window rather than as time-based uptime, because such services are almost always partially up somewhere.
condition: for globally distributed, fault-isolated services

statement: The request-success-rate availability metric also applies to non-serving systems (batch, pipeline, storage, transactional) by defining successful versus unsuccessful units of work.
Set quarterly availability targets for a service and track performance weekly or daily so meaningful deviations can be found and fixed as they arise.
Not all requests are equal — failing a new-user sign-up matters more than failing a background poll — so weight request importance when assessing availability.
Identify a service's risk tolerance by working with product owners to translate business goals into explicit reliability objectives that engineers can target.
If you cannot monitor a service you cannot know what is happening to it, and if you are blind to its state you cannot make it reliable.
Simplicity, once lost, can be extraordinarily difficult to recapture, so preserve simplicity as a first-class engineering quality.

A service's target availability should depend on its function and market position — user expectations, whether it ties to revenue, paid versus free, competitor service levels, and consumer versus enterprise audience.
Back an external/contractual availability target with a stronger internal target so there is margin before contractual penalties are triggered.
Set a lower availability target for products where rapid feature development matters more, such as early-lifecycle consumer products, than for mature enterprise products.
condition: when rapid feature development is more valuable than maximal availability

statement: The shape of failure matters as much as the error count: a constant low failure rate and an occasional full outage can produce the same total errors but very different business impact.
When a failure risks exposing private data, taking the entire service down during debugging and cleanup is the appropriate response, because eroded user trust is worse than the outage.
condition: when the failure mode can leak private data

statement: Regular outages during predictable maintenance windows can be counted as planned downtime rather than unplanned downtime.
condition: when the work occurs during predictable, low-traffic hours and is scheduled

statement: Set the availability target with an explicit cost/benefit analysis: estimate the incremental revenue from one more nine of availability and compare it against the cost of achieving that nine.

When reliability cannot be translated into revenue, target driving the service's measured error rate below the Internet background error rate so failures fall within the noise of users' own connections.
condition: when failures are measured from the end-user perspective

statement: The typical background error rate for ISPs falls between roughly 0.01% and 1%.
Examine a service's risk tolerance on metrics beyond availability, such as latency, to find degrees of freedom for taking thoughtful risks.
A looser latency requirement enables provisioning trade-offs — for example consolidating serving into fewer geographic locations — that substantially reduce cost.
Infrastructure components inherently serve multiple clients whose needs vary and can be antithetical, such as low-latency clients versus throughput-oriented clients.

Engineering all infrastructure to be ultra-reliable is usually far too expensive; instead partition infrastructure into explicitly delineated service levels (e.g., separate low-latency and throughput clusters).
Low-latency users want request queues to be almost always empty (inefficient queuing causes high tail latency), whereas throughput users want queues never empty so the system never idles.
Provision low-latency clusters with slack capacity for reduced contention and increased redundancy, and provision throughput clusters to run hot with less redundancy.
Expose the cost difference between service levels to clients so they are motivated to choose the lowest-cost service level that still meets their needs.

You can run multiple classes of service on identical hardware and software by adjusting resource quantities, redundancy, geographic provisioning constraints, and infrastructure software configuration.

Engineer edge and frontend infrastructure (reverse proxies, load balancers terminating user connections) for extremely high reliability, because a request that never reaches the application is simply lost.
condition: for systems at the edge that terminate end-user connections

statement: Define a quarterly error budget from the service's SLO so both SRE and product development share an objective metric for how unreliable the service may be, removing politics from risk negotiation.
Measure actual uptime with a neutral monitoring system, and permit new releases to be pushed as long as measured uptime stays above the SLO (i.e., error budget remains).
When the error budget is exhausted, temporarily halt releases and invest in testing and resilience; a subtler approach is to slow or roll back releases as the budget nears depletion.
condition: once SLO violations have consumed the error budget

statement: Error budgets make the product-development team self-policing about release risk, but only if the SRE team has the authority to actually stop launches when the SLO is broken.
condition: only when SRE can enforce launch stops on SLO breach

statement: Infrastructure failures such as network or datacenter outages also consume the error budget and can reduce the number of permitted pushes for the rest of the period.
A team that is struggling to launch features may deliberately loosen the SLO to enlarge the error budget and increase innovation.

Distinguish three terms precisely: an SLI is a quantitative measure of a service level, an SLO is a target value or range for an SLI, and an SLA is a contract with explicit consequences for meeting or missing SLOs.
Common SLIs include request latency, error rate, throughput, availability (yield), and — for storage systems — durability.
Prefer measuring the SLI that directly reflects the user experience (e.g., client-side latency), but accept a server-side proxy metric when the direct measure is unavailable.
Choosing and publishing SLOs sets user expectations and reduces both over-reliance (users assuming more availability than exists) and under-reliance on the service.
When a service consistently exceeds its SLO, deliberately inject controlled outages to flush out hidden, unreasonable dependencies before they cause real harm.
condition: when true failures have not already dropped availability to the SLO target

statement: Tell an SLO from an SLA by asking what happens if it is missed: if there is no explicit consequence, it is an SLO, not an SLA.
Choose only a handful of representative SLIs — too many dilute attention from the indicators that matter, and too few leave significant system behaviors unexamined.

Relevant SLIs differ by system type: serving systems care about availability, latency, and throughput; storage systems about latency, availability, and durability; big-data pipelines about throughput and end-to-end latency; and all systems should care about correctness.
Collect some service-level indicators on the client side, not only the server side, because server-side metrics can miss problems that degrade the user experience (for example, slow page JavaScript).
Treat most metrics as distributions rather than averages, because a simple average obscures long-tail behavior such as a slow tail of requests.

Use percentiles for indicators — a high-order percentile (99th or 99.9th) shows a plausible worst case while the 50th percentile (median) shows the typical case — so you can reason about the shape of the distribution.
Users typically prefer a slightly slower system to one with high variance in response time, so optimizing high-percentile latency tends to also protect the typical experience.

Prefer percentiles over the arithmetic mean and do not assume data is normally distributed without verifying, because computing-system latency data is skewed (e.g., bounded below by 0 and above by timeouts).

Standardize SLI definitions into reusable templates that fix aggregation interval and region, measurement frequency, which requests are included, and how data is acquired, so SLIs need not be reasoned about from first principles each time.
Define SLOs by working backward from what users care about to specific indicators, rather than starting from whatever is easy to measure.
An SLO should specify how it is measured and the conditions under which it is valid.
When the shape of the performance curve matters, specify multiple SLO targets at different percentiles and thresholds rather than a single target.
Define separate SLOs for heterogeneous workload classes — for example a throughput-oriented bulk pipeline versus a latency-sensitive interactive client.
condition: when distinct workload classes have different needs

statement: Do not require SLOs to be met 100% of the time; instead allow an error budget — a permitted rate of SLO misses — and track it on a daily or weekly basis.
Track the SLO violation rate as an indicator of user-perceived health: daily or weekly to spot trends early, and monthly or quarterly for management assessment.

Do not choose an SLO target based on current performance, because adopting current values without reflection can lock you into a system that requires heroic effort to sustain and cannot improve without redesign.
Keep SLIs simple, because complicated aggregations obscure changes in system performance and are hard to reason about.
Avoid absolute SLO targets such as 'infinitely scalable' or 'always available', because such requirements are unrealistic and expensive and usually exceed what users would be happy with.
Have as few SLOs as possible and defend each one: if quoting a particular SLO can never win a conversation about priorities, that SLO is probably not worth having.
Start with a loose SLO target that you tighten over time rather than choosing an overly strict target that must later be relaxed when found unattainable.
SLOs should be a major driver in prioritizing work for both SREs and product developers because they reflect what users care about.
Manage systems with an SLI/SLO control loop: monitor the SLIs, compare them to the SLOs, decide whether action is needed, and take the action.
Keep a tighter internal SLO than the one advertised to users, to create a safety margin for responding to chronic problems before they become externally visible.

Avoid overachieving your SLO, because users build on your actual performance; deliberately reduce over-delivery via planned outages, request throttling, or not being faster under light load to prevent hidden over-dependence.
Be conservative in the SLAs you advertise, because the broader the user constituency the harder it is to change or remove an SLA that proves unwise.
Toil is work tied to running a production service that tends to be manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of enduring value, and scaling linearly (O(n)) with service growth.
Distinguish toil from overhead (administrative work not tied to running the service) and from grungy work that produces a lasting improvement, which is not toil.
Cap operational toil below 50% of each SRE's time and spend at least the other 50% on engineering project work that reduces future toil or adds service features.
Toil tends to expand if left unchecked and can quickly fill 100% of everyone's time.
On-call duty puts a floor on toil: a 6-person rotation implies at least 33% (2/6) of an SRE's time on on-call interrupt handling, and an 8-person rotation at least 25%.
When an individual SRE reports excessive toil, managers should rebalance the toil load more evenly across the team and steer that engineer toward engineering projects.
condition: when a team member's toil is well above the team norm

statement: Excessive toil is harmful: it stalls career progress, lowers morale and causes burnout, slows feature velocity, sets a precedent for Devs to offload more operational work, and promotes attrition.
A single incident may have multiple independent root causes, and each one should be repaired.
Distinguish white-box monitoring (metrics exposed by the system's internals) from black-box monitoring (testing externally visible behavior as a user would experience it).
Never trigger an alert simply because something seems a bit weird; alert only on real, urgent, actionable conditions.
exception: narrowly scoped security auditing may warrant anomaly alerts

statement: Paging a human is an expensive use of their time, and too-frequent pages cause engineers to skim or ignore alerts and can prolong outages, so effective alerting must have high signal and very low noise.
Prefer simpler, faster monitoring systems paired with good post-hoc analysis tools, and avoid 'magic' systems that try to learn thresholds or automatically detect causality.
Keep the rules that page humans simple and robust, and avoid complex alerting dependency hierarchies.
A monitoring system should answer two questions — what is broken (the symptom) and why (the cause) — and clearly distinguishing 'what' from 'why' is key to high-signal, low-noise monitoring.

Black-box monitoring is symptom-oriented and represents problems happening right now, while white-box monitoring inspects system internals and can detect imminent problems and failures masked by retries.

White-box monitoring is essential for debugging, because localizing a fault often requires both the caller's and the callee's view of a dependency (e.g., how slow the web server perceives the database versus how slow the database believes itself to be).

Prefer black-box monitoring for paging because it forces the discipline of paging only on problems that are both ongoing and producing real user-visible symptoms; black-box monitoring is useless for not-yet-occurring imminent problems.
The four golden signals for a user-facing system are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation; if you can measure only four metrics, measure these.

Distinguish the latency of successful requests from the latency of failed requests and track error latency explicitly, because a slow error is worse than a fast error and lumping errors into overall latency is misleading.

Track errors that are explicit (e.g., HTTP 500s), implicit (a 200 response with wrong content), and policy-defined (exceeding a committed response time), using end-to-end tests to catch wrong-content failures that response codes cannot express.

Measure saturation against the most-constrained resource and set a utilization target below 100%, because many systems degrade in performance before reaching full utilization; rising latency is often a leading indicator of saturation.
Do not base monitoring on means; collect request counts bucketed by latency (a histogram), with boundaries spaced roughly exponentially, so the slow tail is visible.
In a fan-out system the 99th-percentile latency of a single backend can easily become the median response time of a frontend that depends on several such backends.

Measure different aspects of a system at appropriate granularities, and where high resolution is needed without low latency, sample internally on the server and aggregate externally to avoid the cost of frequent collection.
Design monitoring for simplicity and remove rules, collection, and signals that are rarely exercised or are not used by any dashboard or alert.

Keep monitoring as distinct, loosely coupled components rather than blending it with profiling, single-process debugging, load testing, or log analysis, because over-combination yields complex, fragile systems.

Before adding an alert rule, confirm it detects an otherwise-undetected condition that is urgent, actionable, and actively or imminently user-visible, and that you cannot safely ignore or automate it.
Every page must be actionable and require human intelligence; a page that merits only a rote, robotic response should not be a page.
Spend much more effort catching symptoms than causes, and when monitoring causes worry only about very definite, very imminent ones.

Treat pages that have rote, algorithmic responses as a red flag, and automate them; unwillingness to automate such pages signals the team lacks confidence to clean up its technical debt and is worth escalating.

Accept a controlled, short-term decrease in availability when it buys long-term stability — for example, temporarily relaxing an SLO target and disabling noisy email alerts so engineers can fix the underlying root causes.
Email alerts are of very limited value and easily become noise; instead favor a dashboard that surfaces ongoing subcritical problems, optionally paired with a log for historical correlation.
Treat zero-redundancy (N+0) situations and nearly-full resources as imminent conditions that warrant alerting.
Review page frequency (incidents per shift) in quarterly reports with management so decision-makers can track pager load and overall team health.

Treat automation as a force multiplier rather than a panacea, since thoughtless automation can create as many problems as it solves; the ideal is a higher-level autonomous design that needs neither manual nor automated intervention.

A primary value of automation is consistency: humans cannot perform a well-scoped procedure identically hundreds of times, and the resulting inconsistency causes mistakes, data-quality issues, and reliability problems.

Well-designed automation provides an extensible platform that centralizes mistakes — a bug fixed in the code is fixed once and everywhere — and can export metrics that reveal otherwise-hidden details of a process.
Automation that runs regularly and successfully to resolve common faults reduces their mean time to repair and frees engineers, increasing overall developer velocity.

The later in the product lifecycle a problem is discovered the more expensive it is to fix, and production problems are the most expensive, so automated detection at onset can lower total system cost for sufficiently large systems.

For well-defined operations such as failover or traffic switching, automate the action rather than requiring a human to approve continuation, but scope automatic procedures to well-defined domains because they can otherwise worsen a bad situation.
condition: when the operation is well-defined and bounded

statement: Encapsulating a task in automation decouples operator from operation, so the time savings apply to everyone who could plausibly use the automation, not just its author.

Prefer building and owning APIs and platforms — even writing your own when a vendor provides none — over short-term cheaper manual or purchased solutions, because owning the stack yields greater long-term control and reusability.
Do not attempt to automate every component of every system; some essential systems began as quick prototypes not designed to interface with automation.

Higher-level automation abstractions are easier to manage and reason about, but they fail systemically and inconsistently when an abstraction leaks, whereas lower-level tooling is more powerful but harder to use.

Operations that look atomic, such as pushing a new binary to a cluster, are not truly atomic in the real world (network, machine, or control-plane failures leave inconsistent states), so well-built automation should halt and call for intervention when it cannot model the outcome.

Automation maturity follows a hierarchy: no automation; externally-maintained system-specific automation; externally-maintained generic automation; internally-maintained automation that ships with the system; and finally systems that need no automation because they self-heal.
The ideal is a system designed to need no external glue logic, by handling first-order operations such as turn-up and account creation directly within the application itself.
Externally-maintained automation suffers 'bit rot' because it is maintained separately from the core system and fails to change when the underlying system changes.
Infrequently-executed automation, such as a cluster failover that runs only every few months, is particularly fragile and hard to test because of its extended feedback cycle.
Embrace failure as inevitable and optimize to recover quickly through automation, rather than optimizing the system to avoid failover.
Automating database master failover requires adding more failure-handling logic to all client applications, because you can no longer assume the database is the most stable component in the stack.
Go the extra mile to deliver a reusable platform rather than merely replacing manual procedures, because the time it frees cascades into automating further work.
Automation must not rely on implicit 'safety' signals: at Google an assumption that an unused first disk meant a machine had no storage caused automation to wipe a multi-petabyte Bigtable cluster.
Free-form SSH scripts used to configure systems become brittle technical debt that does not scale to many contributors or to the growing number of configuration permutations.

Validate service readiness with real-world unit tests that confirm all dependencies are available and correctly configured, that configurations are consistent with other deployments, and that every configuration exception is intended, aborting dependent tests when one fails.
When one team is delayed by another team's misconfiguration, extend the production test suite so that the same class of problem is detected earlier in the future.
Pair each failing production test with an idempotent fix so the fix can be re-run repeatedly without damaging configuration and so dependencies resolve automatically once they become available.
Test-fix-retest loops with latency between steps can produce flaky results, and a non-idempotent fix run after a flaky test can leave the system in an inconsistent state.
Automation processes vary along three axes: competence (accuracy), latency (how quickly steps execute), and relevance (the proportion of the real-world process they cover).

Separating automation ownership from the team that runs the service erodes the automation's relevance and competence and creates perverse incentives, since a turnup-only team has no incentive to reduce the service team's later technical debt.
The most functional tools are usually written by the people who use them, which is one reason product-development teams benefit from retaining operational awareness of their systems in production.
Automation code, like test code, decays unless the maintaining team obsessively keeps it in sync with the codebase it covers, because the surrounding world keeps changing.

Replace SSH-based administrative access with an authenticated, ACL-driven, RPC-based admin daemon that enforces least privilege, gates changes on code review, and logs the requestor, parameters, and results of every request for auditability and security.

Make lifecycle and turnup automation owned by the team that owns the service, exposed as a service (e.g., an Admin Server with fine-grained ACLs) behind a stable API contract, so the implementation can change without breaking callers.
Beyond a certain scale a system must be self-repairing, because a large number of component failures is statistically guaranteed to occur every second.
Moving a system up the hierarchy from manually triggered to automatically triggered to autonomous requires some capacity for self-introspection in order to survive.

Highly effective automation erodes operators' direct contact with the system and degrades their skills and mental models, so when the automation eventually fails they can no longer operate the system; mitigate by exposing internal state to humans and running regular practice drills.
In nonautonomous systems the manual fallback actions that automation replaced silently become impossible over time, because the functionality that permitted them no longer exists.
Reliability is the fundamental feature of a system, and autonomous, resilient behavior is one effective way to achieve it.

The highest-leverage point for building autonomy is the design phase, since autonomy is hard to retrofit to large systems; apply standard good practices such as decoupled subsystems, APIs, and minimized side effects.

Never treat an empty set as a special 'all' value in destructive automation, and protect destructive workflows with sanity checks, rate limiting, and idempotency, because misinterpreting empty-as-everything once wiped an entire CDN's disks.
Reliable services require reliable, reproducible, automated release processes so that releases are repeatable rather than unique snowflakes.
Every change to any aspect of the release process should be intentional rather than accidental.
Adopt a self-service release model that gives product teams the tools to run their own releases, automated enough that engineers are involved only when problems arise.
Release frequently, because frequent releases mean fewer changes between versions, which makes testing and troubleshooting easier.
Use a 'Push on Green' model that deploys builds which pass all tests, or select the deploy candidate from a pool of frequent builds based on test results and contained features.

Use hermetic builds that are insensitive to whatever software is installed on the build machine and depend only on known versions of build tools and dependencies, so the same source revision produces identical results on any machine.

Version the build tools themselves by source revision so that rebuilding an old release uses that release's compiler and tools rather than the current versions, which may contain incompatible changes.

Gate release operations — approving source changes, defining release actions, creating a release, approving integrations and cherry-picks, deploying, and changing build configuration — behind layered security and access control.
Require code review for almost all changes to the codebase.
Produce an automated report of all changes contained in a release and archive it with the build artifacts, so SREs can understand a release's contents and troubleshoot it faster.

Branch from mainline at a specific revision and never merge the branch back; submit bug fixes to mainline and cherry-pick them into the release branch, so the exact contents of every release are known.

Run continuous unit tests on the mainline on every change, make the continuous-build test targets the same targets that gate the release, and cut releases at the last revision that passed all continuous-build tests.
Re-run the unit tests against the release branch during the release to create an audit trail, because cherry-picks can produce branch code that exists nowhere on the mainline.

Name packages, version them with a unique hash, and sign them to ensure authenticity, and use movable labels such as dev, canary, and production to reference the current version at each stage of the release.
Use role-based access control lists to determine who may perform each action in the release and deployment pipeline.

Fit the deployment process to the service's risk profile: auto-push hourly builds in development, expand exponentially across clusters for large user-facing services, and extend rollouts over several days interleaved across geographic regions for sensitive infrastructure.
Use canary deployment — starting a few jobs in production after system tests pass — before performing a full rollout.
Store all system and service configuration in the primary source code repository and enforce a strict code-review requirement on configuration changes.

Apply the hermetic principle to configuration by snapshotting and releasing configuration alongside its binaries keyed by build ID, packaged separately from the binary so configuration and binary can be changed and cherry-picked independently.
Decoupling configuration from binary releases tends to cause skew between the checked-in configuration and the running configuration, because jobs must be updated to pick up the changes.
For configuration that must change frequently or dynamically while the binary runs, read it from an external store at runtime rather than baking it into the package.
condition: when configuration must change at runtime

statement: Budget for release engineering from the beginning of the product development cycle, because it is cheaper to put good release practices in place early than to retrofit them later.
Developers, SREs, and release engineers should collaborate on how code is built and deployed; developers should not build and throw the result over the fence to be released by someone else.
Software systems are inherently unstable because every change risks introducing bugs, so the core SRE job is to keep agility and stability in balance.
Reliable processes tend to increase developer agility, because rapid, reliable rollouts make production changes easier to see and bugs faster to find and fix.
Predictable, 'boring' software is a virtue, because surprises in production are the enemy of reliability.

Distinguish essential complexity (inherent in the problem) from accidental complexity (removable with engineering effort), push back when accidental complexity is introduced, and continually eliminate it in systems you onboard.

Delete dead code using source control rather than commenting it out or hiding it behind a permanently-disabled flag, because commented-out or flag-gated dead code is a time bomb (as in the Knight Capital incident).
Treat every line of code as a liability: scrutinize that code serves an essential business purpose, routinely remove dead code, and build bloat detection into all levels of testing.
A smaller project is easier to understand, easier to test, and tends to have fewer defects, so be reluctant to add new features.
Write clear, minimal APIs, because fewer methods and arguments are easier for consumers to understand and let you invest more effort in making each one excellent.
Favor loose coupling between binaries and between binaries and their configuration, so a bug in one component can be fixed and pushed to production independently of the rest of the system.
Version APIs so that consumers can keep using the version they depend on and upgrade on their own cadence, rather than being forced to rebuild the entire system on every API change.
Give each component a clear, well-scoped purpose and avoid 'util' or 'misc' grab-bag binaries, just as grab-bag classes are poor object-oriented design.
Design data and wire formats to be backward and forward compatible.
Prefer simple releases of small batches over large simultaneous batches, because the impact of a single change is far easier to measure and attribute than that of many changes released at once.
Software simplicity is a prerequisite for reliability.

Service reliability builds as a hierarchy, with monitoring as the foundation, then incident response, postmortem and root-cause analysis, testing, capacity planning, development, and finally the product itself.
Without a thoughtfully designed monitoring infrastructure you are flying blind, so build monitoring that makes you aware of problems before your users notice them.

Respond to an incident first by stopping the bleeding — reducing precision, disabling features for graceful degradation, or redirecting traffic to a healthy instance — before pursuing a permanent fix.
Aim to be alerted on and manually solve only new problems, not the same issue repeatedly; reserving human attention for novel problems is a key differentiator of SRE from traditional operations.

At scale, alerting on single-machine failures is unacceptably noisy, so build systems robust to dependency failures and design monitoring to aggregate signals and prune outliers while retaining the granularity to inspect individual components.

Make time-series collection a first-class role of the monitoring system, paired with a rich language for turning those series into charts and alerts, rather than relying on isolated check-and-alert scripts.

Use a common data-exposition format with white-box monitoring — scraping metrics that applications export — instead of custom check scripts, to enable low-overhead mass collection and to reuse the same data for both charts and alerts.
Use service discovery to maintain the monitoring target list, because the target list is dynamic and discovery reduces maintenance cost and lets monitoring scale.
Spread metric collection across the scrape interval so that targets are not collected in lockstep with one another.

Record synthetic per-target variables (whether the name resolved, whether the target responded to collection, whether it passed a health check, and when collection finished) so that rules can detect unavailable tasks and so collection failure itself becomes an alerting signal.

Keep the barrier to adding instrumentation low (ideally a single declaration in code), but pair it with tooling to validate and generate monitoring rules, because decoupling a metric's definition from its use requires careful change management.
Store metrics as named time-series identified by a set of label key=value pairs, which enables flexible, multidimensional querying and slicing of the data.
Keep recent time-series in a fixed-size in-memory arena that garbage-collects the oldest entries for fast queries, and archive older data to a cheaper, larger time-series database.
Build the monitoring hierarchy to follow the service topology, aggregating and summarizing at each level (e.g., per-cluster collectors feeding global aggregators) and strategically discarding detail.
Adopt a naming convention that suffixes a derived time-series with the operation that produced it (for example, a rate or a ratio of rates), so derived series are self-describing.
Alert on a computed ratio such as error rate divided by request rate combined with an absolute floor on the count, so that tiny absolute numbers of errors do not trigger a page.
Require an alerting condition to remain true for a minimum duration of at least two rule-evaluation cycles before firing, to prevent flapping and avoid false alerts caused by missed collections.

Route alerts through a central alert manager that deduplicates alerts with identical labelsets from multiple sources, inhibits certain alerts while related ones are active, and fans alerts in or out based on their labels.
Send page-worthy alerts to the on-call rotation, important-but-subcritical alerts to ticket queues, and retain all other alerts as informational data for status dashboards.

Avoid collecting from all of a service's tasks in one global place, because it becomes a scaling bottleneck and a single point of failure; instead shard collection into scraping and aggregation layers, run two or more global replicas across failure zones, and let upper tiers filter which series they stream.

Complement white-box monitoring with black-box probing that runs protocol checks as a user would, because white-box monitoring only sees the queries that arrive and lets you alert only on failures you expected (DNS errors and crashed queries are invisible to it).

Validate the response payload in black-box probes (e.g., that the HTML contents are as expected) and export response-time histograms by operation type and payload size to measure user-visible performance.

Probe both at the public frontend domain and behind the load balancer, so you can both confirm traffic is still served when one datacenter fails and isolate where in the traffic path a failure occurred.
Separate monitoring rule definitions from the targets they monitor, so the same rule set can apply to many targets without rewriting nearly identical configuration.
Build reusable rule templates and libraries for monitoring configuration to reduce repetition and the likelihood of configuration bugs.

Unit- and regression-test monitoring rules using synthetic time-series, run through a continuous-integration service that packages and ships the configuration, which production validates before accepting.
Ensure that the cost of maintaining monitoring and other sustaining operations work scales sublinearly with the size of the service, which is key to keeping operations maintainable at scale.

Set paging response times according to required availability — on the order of 5 minutes for user-facing or time-critical services (a 99.99% target allows only ~13 minutes of downtime per quarter) and tens of minutes for systems with relaxed SLOs.
Treat a paging event as taking priority over almost every other task, including project work, while non-paging events such as lower-priority alerts and releases are handled during business hours.

Use primary and secondary on-call rotations, with the secondary acting as a fall-through for missed pages or handling non-urgent production work; two related teams can serve as each other's secondary.
Manage on-call along two axes — quantity (the percentage of time spent on-call) and quality (the number of incidents per shift) — and hold managers responsible for keeping both sustainable.

Cap on-call at no more than 25% of an SRE's time (alongside at least 50% engineering), which implies a single-site 24/7 rotation needs at least eight engineers, or about six per site for a dual-site team.
Prefer a multi-site 'follow the sun' rotation to avoid unhealthy night shifts, but weigh it against the added communication and coordination overhead.
condition: when the workload justifies growing beyond a single-site team

statement: Limit incidents to at most two per 12-hour on-call shift, because handling one incident end to end (root-cause analysis, remediation, and writing the postmortem) averages about six hours; aim for a flat page distribution with a median of zero per day.
When the incident-per-shift limit is exceeded for a period, put concrete corrective measures into quarterly planning to return operational load to a sustainable level.
condition: when paging load exceeds the sustainable limit

statement: Cap on-call compensation at some proportion of salary, which in practice limits the on-call any individual takes on, curbing burnout while still incentivizing participation.
Incidents in complex systems are handled better with deliberate, rational thinking than with intuitive, automatic reaction, so reduce on-call stress to keep engineers in the deliberate mindset.
Stress hormones impair cognition and push responders toward unreflective heuristics such as confirmation bias, so provide resources that make on-call less stressful.
Equip on-call engineers with clear escalation paths, well-defined incident-management procedures, and a blameless postmortem culture so the experience is less daunting and safer.
Escalate outages that have significant unknown dimensions, and adopt a formal incident-management protocol when an incident involves multiple teams or has no estimable upper bound on its duration.
condition: when an incident spans multiple teams or its duration cannot be bounded

statement: Use tooling to automate the overhead of incident management — role handoffs, status recording, and communication — so responders can focus their cognitive effort on the incident itself.
Make the symptoms of operational overload measurable (for example, daily tickets under 5 and paging events per shift under 2) so corrective goals can be quantified.
Treat misconfigured monitoring as a common cause of operational overload: align paging alerts with the symptoms that threaten the service's SLOs and ensure every paging alert is actionable.

Regulate alert fan-out by grouping related alerts, silencing duplicate or uninformative ones during an incident, and tuning noisy alerts toward a 1:1 alert-to-incident ratio so the on-call engineer can focus on the incident.

When developers introduce changes that make a system noisier or less reliable, set common improvement goals with them, and in extreme cases temporarily reroute paging to the developer on-call or 'give back the pager' until the system meets the SRE team's standards.

Operational underload is also harmful: a too-quiet on-call leads to confidence and knowledge gaps, so size teams so each engineer is on-call at least once or twice a quarter and use practice drills such as the Wheel of Misfortune and disaster-recovery training.
Troubleshooting is a learnable, teachable skill rather than an innate talent, and it depends on both a generic troubleshooting process and solid knowledge of the specific system.

Treat troubleshooting as the hypothetico-deductive method: examine telemetry and logs, hypothesize causes from how the system should work and its failure modes, test each hypothesis by comparing evidence or making controlled changes, iterate to a root cause, then fix it and write a postmortem.
Fixing the proximate cause of an incident need not wait for full root-cause analysis or postmortem writing.

Avoid common troubleshooting pitfalls: examining irrelevant or misunderstood metrics, not knowing how to safely test hypotheses, latching onto improbable or past causes, and chasing spurious correlations.

Prefer simpler and more probable explanations when diagnosing ('when you hear hoofbeats, think horses not zebras'), while remembering that several common low-grade problems may jointly explain the symptoms better than one rare cause.
Remember that correlation is not causation: correlated events may share a common cause or be coincidental, and coincidental correlations become inevitable as the number of monitored metrics grows.
A good problem report states the expected behavior, the actual behavior, and, if possible, how to reproduce it, and is stored in a consistent, searchable form such as a bug tracker.

Open a bug for every issue, even those received by email or chat, and discourage reporting problems directly to a person, because direct reports are lower quality, invisible to the team, and concentrate load on a few individuals rather than the on-call engineer.

In a major outage, resist the instinct to root-cause first; instead make the system work as well as it can under the circumstances — diverting traffic, shedding load, or disabling subsystems — while preserving evidence such as logs for later analysis.
Treat stability like a pilot's first duty to 'fly the airplane': prioritize keeping the system safe — for example freezing it to prevent unrecoverable data corruption — over immediate diagnosis.
Examine a system using its recorded metrics, logs, and end-to-end distributed request tracing to understand component behavior and find where problems began.

Provide multiple log verbosity levels that can be raised on the fly without restarting the process, use statistical sampling for high-traffic services, and add a selection language to filter operations of interest.

Expose current internal state through server endpoints — recent RPCs sent and received, per-RPC error-rate and latency histograms, and current configuration — so a server's behavior can be understood without referring to an architecture diagram.

Simplify and reduce during diagnosis: examine components across their well-defined interfaces, inject known test data at each step, and build a solid reproducible test case that can be run in a non-production environment where riskier techniques are available.

Use divide-and-conquer to localize faults: work systematically from one end of the stack to the other, or, in very large systems, bisect by examining the communication paths between halves until the faulty component is isolated.
Diagnose by asking what a malfunctioning system is actually doing, then why it is doing that and where its resources are being consumed or its output is going.

Start troubleshooting from recent changes, because a working system tends to stay working until acted on by an external force such as a configuration change or load shift; log all version deployments and configuration changes at every layer and annotate dashboards with them.
Build diagnostic tools specific to your services, but look for commonalities across services and teams to avoid duplicating effort.

Test hypotheses experimentally: prefer tests whose outcomes are mutually exclusive, run them in decreasing order of likelihood while weighing risk to the system, beware confounding factors and test side effects, and accept that some tests (e.g., for race conditions) are only suggestive.

Take clear, timestamped notes of your ideas, the tests you ran, and the results — ideally in a shared document or chat — and make active changes systematically so the system can be returned to its pre-test state.
Do not ignore or discount negative results: an experiment that disproves an effect is conclusive about production or the design space and helps others avoid dead ends.
Tools and methods built for an experiment, such as benchmarks and load generators, often outlive the experiment and inform future work.
Publish your results, including negative ones, to reduce bias in metrics and accelerate collective learning, and be skeptical of any design document or review that never mentions failure.

Definitively proving a single root cause in production is often impossible because systems are complex with multiple jointly-causing factors and path dependence and cannot always be safely reproduced, so you frequently can only identify probable causal factors; a non-production environment can help.
After identifying the causes of a problem, write a postmortem recording what went wrong, how you tracked it down, how you fixed it, and how to prevent recurrence.

Build observability — white-box metrics and structured logs — into every component from the ground up, and design well-understood, observable interfaces between components, to make troubleshooting faster.
Propagate a unique request identifier across all the RPCs a request generates so log entries on upstream and downstream components can be correlated, reducing time to diagnosis and recovery.

It is sometimes correct to apply a good-enough mitigation (such as allocating more resources) so work can proceed, for example a scheduled launch, and investigate the root cause later, because eliminating every known bug first is often impractical.

A common performance antipattern is per-request work whose cost scales with the amount of in-memory cached or configuration data (e.g., a linear scan over cached objects), which can inflate latency and resource usage without generating any extra RPC calls.
A sudden increase in latency and resource usage usually indicates one of three causes: an increase in traffic, a change in configuration, or a change in the type of work the system is doing.
Effective emergency response requires preparation and periodic, hands-on, pertinent training, which in turn requires the support of management and the board.
Do not panic during an emergency; if you feel overwhelmed pull in more people — even paging the whole company if necessary — and follow the established incident-response process.
Proactively break your own systems through disaster and emergency testing to surface weaknesses and hidden dependencies before real failures expose them.
Test rollback procedures in a test environment before running large-scale tests, because untested rollback procedures are often flawed and lengthen outages.
Scope and review tests carefully, but accept that reality can reveal an insufficient understanding of system interactions even in a test that was thoroughly reviewed and thought to be well-scoped.

Canary every change regardless of its perceived risk, because a change that looks low-risk can exercise a rare configuration keyword and feature combination that a less stringent canary never tested and that crash-loops the fleet.

Maintain highly reliable, low-overhead, out-of-band backup communication systems and alternative command-line access methods, and exercise them regularly so engineers stay familiar with them for use when primary systems are down.
Rate-limit how quickly a system provides full updates to new clients, because doing so can throttle a crash-loop and keep jobs alive long enough to prevent a complete outage.

Watch real-time communication channels immediately after pushing a change, because noticing a surge of complaints right after a push enables a near-immediate rollback that prevents a much longer, harder-to-debug outage.
Add sanity checks to any automation that issues destructive commands, and never let an empty filter or empty set be interpreted as 'all'.
When automation begins causing cascading damage, immediately disable and freeze all team automation and production maintenance to prevent further harm.
Mitigate an outage by draining traffic from broken locations to healthy ones that are sized to absorb full load, and prioritize relieving any congested network links that result.
The person who triggered an incident often holds the most state about it, so involve them in the resolution.
Assume a solution always exists during an emergency; if you cannot find one, widen your net and involve more teammates, because the highest priority is to resolve the issue quickly.
After an emergency is mitigated, set aside time to clean up and write up the incident.
Keep a documented history of outages and publish and organize postmortems so the whole company can learn, and hold people accountable for following up on the specific actions to prevent recurrence.
Ask big, even improbable, 'what if' questions — building power failure, datacenter going dark, a compromised server — to test whether your disaster plans and systems would actually cope.
Until a system has actually failed you do not truly know how it, its dependent systems, or your users will react, so do not rely on untested assumptions about failure behavior.
Base incident management on a recognized, scalable structure such as the Incident Command System, known for its clarity and scalability.

Separate incident-response responsibilities into distinct roles and have each person stay within their role, because a clear separation of responsibilities paradoxically gives responders more autonomy by removing the need to second-guess colleagues.
Assign an Incident Commander who holds the high-level state of the incident, structures the response, assigns responsibilities, and by default holds every role they have not delegated.
During an incident, the operations lead and team should be the only group modifying the system.
Assign a dedicated Communications role to issue periodic updates to the response team and stakeholders and keep the incident document current.
Assign a Planning role to handle longer-term incident tasks such as filing bugs, arranging handoffs, and tracking how the system has diverged from normal so it can be reverted afterward.
Establish a recognized command post — a physical war room or a virtual channel — so all interested parties know where to interact with the incident commander.
Keep a living incident-state document that several people can edit concurrently, and do not host it on the very system you are trying to fix.
Hand off the incident-commander role explicitly, obtaining firm acknowledgment of the handoff and communicating it to everyone working the incident so it is always clear who is leading.

Declare an incident early and close it out if the fix turns out to be simple, rather than spinning up the framework hours into a growing problem, and set clear declaration conditions such as needing a second team, customer-visible impact, or being unsolved after an hour of focused analysis.

Unmanaged incidents spiral out of control through three common hazards: over-focusing on the technical problem at the expense of the bigger picture, poor communication, and uncoordinated freelancing changes.
Do not make uncoordinated production changes during an incident; coordinate every action with the person in charge of troubleshooting.

Use the incident-management framework routinely — for cross-team change management, disaster-recovery testing, and role-play of past incidents — because incident-management proficiency atrophies quickly when not exercised.

Follow incident-management best practices: prioritize stopping the bleeding and restoring service while preserving evidence, prepare and document procedures in advance, trust each role with full autonomy, monitor your own emotional state and ask for help when overwhelmed, periodically reconsider alternatives, practice routinely, and rotate roles across people.
Postmortems are essential because, without a formal process to learn from incidents, the same incidents recur indefinitely and can compound or cascade.
A postmortem is a written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, the contributing root causes, and the follow-up actions to prevent recurrence.

Define objective postmortem triggers before incidents occur — such as user-visible downtime beyond a threshold, any data loss, on-call intervention, excessive resolution time, or a monitoring failure — and allow any stakeholder to request a postmortem.

Write postmortems blamelessly: focus on the contributing causes without indicting any individual or team, assuming everyone acted in good faith with the information they had, because a culture of blame drives people to hide issues.
You cannot fix people, but you can fix systems and processes to better support people in making the right choices.
A blameless postmortem should still constructively call out where and how services can be improved, not merely avoid assigning blame.

Leave no postmortem unreviewed: have senior engineers assess each draft for completeness — data captured, impact assessed, root cause deep enough, action plan appropriately prioritized, and outcome shared — and store reviewed postmortems in a searchable repository.
Share postmortems with the widest audience that would benefit, but never include user-identifying information in them.

Cultivate a postmortem culture through senior-management participation and social reinforcement such as a postmortem of the month, reading clubs, and Wheel-of-Misfortune role-play, easing the practice into the workflow.
Visibly reward people for doing the right thing — a fast rollback or a well-written postmortem — and do not stigmatize individuals or teams who produce postmortems frequently.
Regularly survey teams on whether the postmortem process supports their goals and whether it imposes too much toil, and use the feedback to keep improving it.

Improving reliability over time requires starting from a known baseline and tracking progress, so passively collect all alerts in an outage-tracking tool that lets you annotate, group, and analyze them.

Postmortems only cover high-impact incidents, so also aggregate alert data systematically to catch frequent low-impact issues and find fixes whose benefit is small per case but large across many events.
Automatically escalate an alert that goes unacknowledged after a configured interval to the next destination, such as from primary on-call to secondary.
Group multiple alerts triggered by the same event into a single incident, so you can analyze incidents per day separately from alerts per day and avoid duplicated debugging or panic.
Multiple alerts per event are unavoidable given the trade-off between false positives and false negatives, so grouping alerts into incidents is the scalable way to handle the duplication.

Use free-form tagging with hierarchical namespaces (such as cause: and action: prefixes) to attach metadata to notifications, which gives teams an overview of a service's pain points even without formal analysis.

Analyze outage data in layers: basic counts and aggregates, comparison across teams and over time to reveal trends, and then semantic analysis to find systemic issues such as which component causes the most incidents.

Treat 'most incidents caused' as only a starting point, because it can be an artifact of over-sensitive monitoring or misbehaving clients, and incident count alone indicates nothing about fix difficulty or severity of impact.
Use cross-team incident visibility to mitigate faster: if your service is disrupted by an apparent dependency incident but the owning team has not been alerted, manually alert them.

Quantify confidence in a system by adapting classical testing at scale: past reliability comes from monitoring history, and future reliability from predictions that require either an unchanged site or a complete description of all changes.

Each test that passes both before and after a change reduces the uncertainty a change introduces, so higher test coverage lets you make more changes before reliability falls below an acceptable level.
When too many changes accumulate too quickly and predicted reliability approaches the acceptability limit, pause changes while new monitoring data accumulates to validate the revised execution paths.
condition: when change velocity pushes predicted reliability near the acceptable limit

statement: Passing tests do not prove reliability, but failing tests generally prove the absence of reliability.

Prefer tests that catch a bug with zero mean-time-to-repair by blocking the push so the bug never reaches production, because the more zero-MTTR bugs you catch, the higher the mean time between failures your users experience.
Better testing raises mean time between failures, which lets developers release features faster, and the new bugs that result then slow release velocity again — a self-correcting feedback loop.

Use the traditional test hierarchy: unit tests (the smallest, cheapest tests, which also serve as a specification), integration tests (using dependency injection to mock complex dependencies), and system tests (end-to-end on an assembled system).

Include smoke tests (simple critical behavior that short-circuits costlier testing), performance tests (to guard against gradual degradation in latency or resource use), and regression tests (to keep previously-fixed bugs from returning) among your system tests.

Remember that tests have real time and computational costs — unit tests are very cheap while standing up a full server with dependencies can take minutes to hours — and weigh those costs for developer productivity.
Run production (black-box) tests against the live system, not only hermetic tests, because production tests are essential to operating a reliable service.

Recognize that production is intentionally not hermetic — staged rollouts mean the live environment does not match any single source-control version — which can make tests run against live yield hermetically valid but operationally invalid results.

Use configuration tests that compare a binary's actual production configuration against the checked-in configuration file and report discrepancies, because the pass/fail pattern across production reveals unsafe configuration paths and how far production lags ongoing engineering work.
Use stress tests to find the limits of a system and its components, because many components do not degrade gracefully beyond a point but instead fail catastrophically.

Conduct a canary test by upgrading a subset of servers to the new version, incubating ('baking') them for a period, and progressively rolling out only if no unexpected variances occur, reverting the modified servers quickly if anything goes wrong.
A canary is structured user acceptance rather than a true test: it exposes code to unpredictable live production traffic and therefore does not always catch newly introduced faults.
A standard exponential canary rollout starts at about 0.1% of user traffic and scales by an order of magnitude roughly every 24 hours while varying the geographic location of the upgraded servers.

Most bugs are order-one and scale linearly with user traffic, and can be turned into regression tests from logs of unusual responses, but higher-order bugs that corrupt data seen by later requests must be caught during release because they escalate operational load very quickly.

When test coverage is low, begin where testing delivers the most impact for the least effort: prioritize mission-critical or business-critical code (such as billing) and the APIs other teams integrate against.
Never ship obviously broken software; creating a cheap set of smoke tests to run on every release is a low-effort, high-impact first step.
Convert every reported bug into a test case that initially fails, so that fixing the bugs builds up a comprehensive regression suite and a strong testing culture.
Build testing infrastructure on a versioned source-control system plus a continuous build that compiles and runs tests on every submission and notifies engineers the moment a change breaks the build.

When the build breaks, engineers should drop other work and prioritize the fix, because breakage is harder to fix once more changes land, it slows the whole team, and it undermines release cadences and emergency-release capability.
A predictably solid and reliable build drives agility, because stability lets developers iterate faster.
Use a build system that rebuilds and re-tests only the code affected by a change via dependency graphs, giving cheaper, faster, reproducible builds.

Approach creating well-tested code as an engineering project with explicit goals and deadlines rather than a vague call for 'more tests', and apply higher coverage to life-critical or revenue-critical systems than to short-lived scripts.
Treat SRE tools and automation tools as software that needs testing, recognizing that their risk footprint is out-of-band for a different service layer, which makes their testing needs more subtle.

Protect a live service from risky software that bypasses the tested API with a barrier: place a barrier so a replica fails its health check and is not served to users, restrict the risky tool to act only on barriered replicas, and remove the barrier with the same health-validation tool used for black-box monitoring.

Design disaster-recovery tools to operate offline — computing a checkpoint equivalent to a clean stop, making it loadable by existing validation tools, and supporting the release barrier and clean-start procedure — because keeping these constraints makes the tools easy to test with excellent coverage.

Statistical and chaos tests such as fuzzing, Chaos Monkey, and Jepsen are not repeatable, so log the random-number seed, refactor a failing run into a release test, and use the replay non-failure rate to gauge how hard it will be to later assert the fault is fixed.

A test's pass or fail result can vary across seemingly identical runs (flakiness), and estimating each test's true pass rate at every version is computationally infeasible, so form hypotheses about scenarios of interest and run targeted repeats.

Deliver test results to an engineer before they context-switch: treat quick hermetic tests as interactive feedback and slow orchestrated tests as batch tests that signal 'not ready for review' to the reviewer.
To incorrectly reject only about one in a hundred good patches across tens of thousands of tests, individual tests must pass over 99.9999% of the time, so test flakiness must be kept extremely low.
Recognize that some test failures indicate a larger impact risk than others, so apply a higher level of paranoia and coverage to high-risk areas such as irreversible architecture migrations.

Do not segregate testing infrastructure from production configuration; unify versioning and testing so the model of production can be related to the model of application behavior, which reduces migration risk and unblocks architectural change.

Shorten the feedback cycle by testing intermediate versions, which raises release quality by letting you map problems to their underlying causes, accepting that letting users try more versions lowers MTBF but reveals where more test coverage is needed.
Segment the reliability budget by functionality or by team so each team has its own uncertainty limit and therefore its own upper bound on release rate.

Categorize each configuration file by its release cadence — low-MTTR files edited only on failure versus files that change more than once per application release — and test and monitor the frequently-changing ones as rigorously as application releases, providing a deliberately noisy break-glass mechanism to push before testing completes.

When a break-glass mechanism is used to skip release testing, still run the tests in the background and back-annotate the push with any failures, ideally boosting those tests' priority, so a flawed manual push can be quickly followed by a corrected one.

Integration-test configuration files, treating their contents as potentially hostile input to the interpreter, and if the configuration is written in an interpreted language pair it with deadline checks because loading it executes a program with no inherent runtime bound.

Prefer a configuration format with an upfront, automatically-checked schema and a bounded load time (such as protocol buffers) over a custom syntax or an interpreted-language configuration, to reduce toil and latent failures.
Apply defense in depth across tools so that for each anticipated form of misbehavior some test or another tool's validated input check reports the problem before it becomes a catastrophic outage.
A tool that detects a problem should report it rather than attempt risky self-remediation — for example, noticing a partially-parsed user list but not deleting user data on its own.

Combine testing (which checks known data) with monitoring (which checks unknown data), but also use production probes to catch a third risk: frontend/backend release combinations that were never tested together because components have independent release cadences.
Maintain a bank of known-good and known-bad requests that can be reused as integration tests, release tests, and monitoring probes.

Gradually replace monitoring probes alongside the application so that all old-and-new probe-versus-application combinations are continuously exercised, and if the readiness check inspects the probes a bad new version safely receives no user traffic.
Give engineers test feedback as early as possible and automate the delivery of warnings so that it scales.

Make monitoring aware of all release versions on both sides of a service interface, run cross-version compatibility tests whenever either side cuts a release, and have rollout automation block a rollout until problematic version combinations are no longer possible.
Testing is one of the most profitable investments for reliability and is a continuous activity rather than a one-time event, because you can only understand a problem by measuring it.
Treat SRE-developed tools as full software-engineering projects with a product mindset — internal customers and a roadmap — rather than one-off hacks.

SREs are well-positioned to build internal production tooling because they have firsthand production knowledge, understand the tool's requirements, and get frank, high-signal feedback from their fellow-SRE users.
Team size should not scale directly with service growth; achieving sublinear team growth against exponential service growth requires perpetual automation and tool streamlining.

Software-development projects within SRE provide career growth, balance against on-call and interrupt work, and help attract and retain a diverse mix of software- and systems-engineering skills that prevents blind spots.

Traditional capacity planning is a never-ending cycle — forecast demand, devise build and allocation plans, review and sign off, then deploy — in which any change ripples through the plans of all subsequent periods.

Traditional capacity plans are brittle: a seemingly minor change such as an efficiency drop, a demand increase, a delivery slip, or a product-goal change forces cross-checking or re-creating the entire allocation plan.

Manual capacity planning is laborious and imprecise because bin packing is NP-hard, inflexible 'X cores in cluster Y' requests discard the underlying degrees of freedom, and spreadsheet tools do not scale and lack error-checking.

Use intent-based capacity planning: programmatically encode a service's true requirements and flexibility (its intent) and autogenerate the allocation plan, so that when demand, supply, or requirements change you simply regenerate the optimal plan.

Express capacity needs as the highest-level intent that is feasible — such as 'run at five nines' or 'meet demand per region with N+2 redundancy' — rather than as concrete resource requests, to gain flexibility and make the consequences of unmet requirements clear.

Capturing a service's intent requires three precursors: its dependencies (including nested dependencies and latency constraints), performance metrics that convert higher-level demand into lower-level resource needs via load testing and monitoring, and explicit prioritization.
Intent-based planning forces resource-constraint trade-offs to be made transparently, openly, and consistently, rather than ad hoc and opaque to service owners.

Keep the team that builds an internal tool grounded by making them both its developers and its consumers, so they are directly impacted by failures and feed firsthand experience into feature requests, which also lends the product credibility.
Do not chase perfection when the bounds of the problem are not well understood; launch and iterate, starting with a simplified heuristic implementation that proves the vision is achievable.
When using approximation to speed development, abstract it behind an interface so the simplified implementation can be swapped for a better one later.

Use fuzzy requirements as an incentive to design software that is general and modular, abstracting uncertain dependencies behind interfaces so a higher-level strategy change does not force a costly rewrite.

Design internal tools to be agnostic and general — 'come as you are; we'll work with what you've got' — so customers need not commit to a specific upstream tool, which lowers the barrier to entry and broadens adoption.
Stay grounded by giving every general solution a concrete real-world implementation that demonstrates the design's utility.
Do not underestimate the effort to drive adoption of internal software: it requires a consistent, coherent approach, active user advocacy, and the sponsorship of senior engineers and management.
Provide documentation even for internal tools aimed at technical users, because busy engineers will write their own solution if yours is too difficult or confusing.

Differentiate a product's aspirational goals from its minimum success criteria (minimum viable product), because over-promising loses credibility while under-promising fails to overcome adoption inertia; demonstrate steady incremental progress through small releases.
Pair a long-term roadmap with short-term fixes so that onboarding effort yields immediate benefit while the same configuration carries forward to deliver broader long-term value.

Target early adopters who have no existing solution and must invest configuration effort anyway, because their early successes turn them into advocates and quantified before/after case studies incentivize other teams.

Provide white-glove support to early adopters and directly address emotional concerns that automation will replace jobs, reframing the change so the team owns the configurations, processes, and results rather than the manual toil.
Avoid defining success as 100% adoption across the organization, because there are diminishing returns on closing the last mile for every long-tail use case.

Staff a software seed team with generalists who ramp up quickly and bring breadth, and add specialists only once the project is off the ground and demonstrably successful enough to benefit from their expertise.

A one-off tool is a good candidate to become a real software project when engineers with firsthand domain experience want to work on it, the user base is highly technical, it provides noticeable benefit such as reducing toil, and it fits the organization's objectives.

Poor candidate projects are those that touch many moving parts at once, require an all-or-nothing approach that prevents iterative development, are too narrowly specific to benefit few teams, or are so overly generic that they fit no concrete use case well.
