SREs doing software development should keep working as SREs rather than becoming full-time embedded developers, so they retain the production perspective of being both creator and customer of the product.
Aggressively defend dedicated, uninterrupted project time, because it is nearly impossible to write impactful code while thrashing between several tasks within an hour.

Introducing organized software development into an SRE organization is as much an organizational change as a technical one, because the ad hoc instinct to 'just write some code' does not scale and produces narrow, unshared, duplicated tools.

Do not lower standards for internally-developed SRE software: apply the same code review, integration and end-to-end testing, and production-readiness review you would require to onboard any other team's service.

Build credibility for a software-development effort by launching first on straightforward, uncontroversial targets and delivering value in a reasonable time, because credibility takes a long time to build and only a short time to lose.
Never rely on a single point of failure for large-scale systems; balance load across multiple machines and datacenters.

The optimal distribution of traffic load has no single answer; it depends on the hierarchical level (global versus local), the technical level (hardware versus software), and the nature of the traffic.
Route latency-sensitive traffic to the nearest datacenter by round-trip time, and route throughput-sensitive traffic to an underutilized path even at the cost of latency.
Inside a datacenter, optimize load distribution for resource utilization and for protecting individual servers from overloading, since all machines are roughly equidistant from the user.

Use DNS as the first layer of load balancing, but treat it as insufficient on its own because it gives weak control over client behavior and the recursive-resolver middleman means the authoritative server sees the resolver's address, not the user's.
Use anycast nameservers and the EDNS0 client-subnet extension so the authoritative DNS server can return a response that is optimal from the user's perspective rather than the resolver's.

Account for resolver caching in DNS load balancing by keeping TTLs low (which bounds how fast changes propagate), tracking the size and geographic distribution of the user base behind each resolver, and confirming the chosen datacenter has capacity and is healthy.
Keep every DNS reply within the 512-byte RFC limit so users do not have to open a TCP connection just to obtain IP addresses, which also bounds how many server addresses a single reply can contain.
Follow DNS load balancing with a virtual-IP layer in which a network load balancer forwards packets to backends behind a shared VIP, hiding the number of machines and easing maintenance and scaling.

Do not select a backend with a stateless modulo hash (id mod N), because removing a single backend remaps almost every connection and forces resets; use consistent hashing to minimize disruption when the backend pool changes.
Use simple connection tracking under normal conditions but fall back to consistent hashing when the system is under pressure, such as during a denial-of-service attack.

Use Direct Server Response when requests are small and replies are large, so only a fraction of traffic traverses the load balancer and no per-connection state is kept, but note that layer-2 DSR requires all machines to share one broadcast domain.

Use packet encapsulation (IP plus GRE) so the load balancer and its backends need not share a broadcast domain and can even be on separate continents, accepting the cost of inflated packet size and possible fragmentation.

Run a service as enough homogeneous, interchangeable backend tasks that losing a single machine does not cost too much capacity — at least three backends, since fewer means losing one machine costs 50% or more of capacity.

In the ideal case load is spread so every backend consumes the same CPU; because you can only send traffic until the most-loaded task reaches capacity, a large load spread wastes the reserved-but-unused capacity of every other task.
Poor in-datacenter load balancing artificially limits resource availability, so that a service reserving 1,000 CPUs may be unable to actually use more than about 700.

Use simple flow control — clients stop sending to a backend once their active-request count to it hits a limit such as 100 — as basic overload protection and crude load spreading, while recognizing it only catches extreme overload and can misfire on backends that are merely slow.

Give backends an explicit lame-duck state in which a task still serves but asks clients to stop sending new requests, and propagate that state to both active and (via periodic UDP health checks) inactive clients.

Implement clean shutdown via the lame-duck state: on SIGTERM the backend enters lame duck and redirects new requests, lets in-flight requests finish, drains active requests to zero, then exits after a service-dependent interval (a rule of thumb is 10 to 150 seconds).

Use subsetting to limit how many backend tasks each client connects to (typically a subset of 20 to 100), because every connection costs memory and CPU and unbounded fan-in or fan-out wastes a large amount of resources for little gain.
Choose a larger subset size when clients are far fewer than backends or when clients send bursty, high-fan-out requests, so that load stays spread evenly across the available backends.
condition: when clients are few relative to backends or send bursty high-fan-out requests

statement: Design the subset-selection algorithm to assign backends uniformly — since overloading one backend by 10% forces over-provisioning the whole set by 10% — and to minimize connection churn across restarts, failures, and resizes without knowing the client and backend counts in advance.

Random subsetting spreads connection load poorly at scale — needing impractically large subsets (~75%) to be even — so prefer deterministic subsetting that assigns each backend to one client per round using a per-round shuffle, which yields a near-uniform distribution.

Use a different shuffle seed for each round of deterministic subsetting, so that when a backend fails its load is spread across all remaining backends rather than only the others in its subset, where the effect would compound as more subset members fail.

Simple Round Robin distributes load poorly — up to a 2x CPU spread from least- to most-loaded task — because of small subsetting, varying query costs, machine diversity, and unpredictable performance factors.

Query costs can vary by a factor of 1000 or more and be unpredictable, so when discrepancies are large, cap the work per request through interface design such as pagination, accepting the added client-code and consistency complexity.

Handle machine diversity by normalizing CPU reservations to a virtual compute unit mapped from each processor architecture's performance, so the scheduler can account for resource equivalence without requiring a homogeneous fleet.

Recognize that unpredictable performance factors — antagonistic neighbors competing for shared resources (differences up to ~20%) and resource spikes after task restarts — mean a load-balancing policy that cannot adapt will yield a suboptimal distribution at scale.

Keep restarted servers in lame-duck state and prewarm them until performance normalizes, because freshly restarted tasks (especially on platforms that optimize code dynamically, like Java) need significantly more resources for a few minutes.
Least-Loaded Round Robin routes new requests among the backends in a subset that currently have the fewest active requests, naturally taking load away from slower or more loaded tasks.

Guard against sinkholing in least-loaded balancing: an unhealthy backend that returns fast errors appears least loaded and attracts traffic, so count recent errors as if they were active requests so the policy diverts load away from it.

The count of active requests is a poor proxy for a backend's capability, because I/O-bound requests block on the network rather than CPU and each client sees only its own requests, so Least-Loaded Round Robin still produces about a 2x load spread on large services.

Use Weighted Round Robin, in which backends report their query rate, error rate, and utilization in each response and clients maintain capability scores that weight request distribution and penalize failures, because it significantly reduces the spread between the most- and least-utilized tasks.

Avoiding overload is a goal of load balancing, but because some part of the system will eventually overload regardless, gracefully handling overload is fundamental to running a reliable serving system.
One way to handle overload is to serve degraded responses — less accurate or smaller responses that are cheaper to compute, such as searching only part of the corpus — rather than failing outright.

Use adaptive client-side throttling, in which each client probabilistically rejects requests locally based on the ratio of requests attempted to requests the backend accepts, so that even in heavy overload backends reject roughly one request per request processed, using only local information with no extra dependency or latency.

Tune the accepts multiplier in client-side throttling to trade resource waste against state-propagation speed: a 2x multiplier wastes more backend resources but propagates state changes to clients faster, while a lower multiplier throttles more aggressively.
Client-side throttling works poorly for clients that send requests only sporadically, because each such client has a drastically reduced view of the backend's state.
condition: when a client sends requests to a backend only sporadically

statement: Assign every request a criticality level (such as CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE_PLUS, and SHEDDABLE), provision enough capacity for all critical traffic, and shed lower-criticality requests first under overload.

Make criticality a first-class, automatically-propagated property of the RPC system so that outgoing sub-requests inherit their parent's criticality by default, set it as close to the client as possible (e.g., the HTTP frontend), and override it only where it specifically makes sense.
Criticality is orthogonal to latency and network quality-of-service requirements; for example, type-ahead search suggestions are highly sheddable yet latency-sensitive.

Base task-level overload protection on a utilization signal such as CPU rate or memory usage, and begin rejecting requests by criticality as utilization approaches configured thresholds, using higher thresholds for higher criticalities.

Use a smoothed executor load average — the count of active threads relative to available processors — as a generally useful utilization signal that tolerates brief fan-out spikes but rejects requests under sustained high load, while allowing other or combined signals to be plugged in.

Distinguish overload errors by scope: if a large subset of backends is overloaded, do not retry and let the error bubble up to the caller, but if only a small subset is overloaded, retry the request immediately on a likely-different backend.

Treat retries like new requests and rely on the probability they land on a different backend, so that retrying becomes a form of organic load balancing; a slightly-overloaded backend should reject new and retry requests equally and quickly so they can be retried elsewhere.

Limit retries with both a per-request retry budget (for example, three attempts) and a per-client retry budget that allows retries only while retries stay below about 10% of requests, which reduces retry-induced amplification from roughly 3x to about 1.1x.

Have clients include an attempt counter in request metadata and have backends keep histograms of attempts, so that when many retries are observed (indicating widespread overload) a backend returns an 'overloaded; don't retry' error instead of a retryable error.

Retry a rejected request only at the layer immediately above the rejecting layer, propagating an 'overloaded; don't retry' signal upward, to avoid a combinatorial retry explosion in deep dependency stacks.

Account for the load of connections themselves — the CPU and memory of maintaining and churning a large connection pool — not just request load, in large-scale RPC systems, and tune health-check frequency or create and destroy connections dynamically when many clients each send few requests.

Shield backends from bursts of new connections by routing batch jobs through a batch-proxy layer that acts as a fuse, absorbing the surge and reducing the number of connections against the real backends.

Protect individual tasks against overload so that a task provisioned for a given rate keeps serving at that rate without significant latency impact or crashing even under 2x to 10x excess traffic, while accepting that some breakdown point ultimately exists.
Take degradation conditions seriously, because ignored overload leads tasks to pile up work, thrash memory, crash, and trigger cascading failures across other components.
An overloaded backend should not simply turn down and stop accepting all traffic; it should keep accepting as much as it can process and reject the rest gracefully as capacity frees up.
There is no magic bullet for load balancing and overload protection; it requires a deep understanding of the system and the semantics of its requests.

A cascading failure grows over time through positive feedback: when one part of a system fails it raises load and failure probability on the rest, producing a domino effect that can take down all replicas.
The most common cause of cascading failure is server overload, where local overload crashes servers and shifts their load onto others, spreading the failure service-wide within minutes.

Resource exhaustion (CPU, memory, threads, file descriptors) is a desired pressure-relief effect of excess load, but it can also make servers less efficient or crash them, spreading the problem to others via the load balancer.

In a crash-loop snowball, restarted servers are immediately bombarded and fail again, so dropping load to just below the original healthy rate will not recover the service; you must drop load far lower, in proportion to the fraction of servers that can stay healthy.
Load-balancing policies that avoid servers which have served errors can worsen a cascade by removing those servers' capacity and snowballing load onto the rest.

The most important exercise for preventing server overload is to load-test the server's capacity limit and its overload failure mode in a realistic environment, because you otherwise cannot predict which resource will be exhausted or how.
Instrument servers to protect themselves by rejecting requests cheaply when overloaded — failing early and cheaply at the frontend or backend — rather than crashing.

Apply rate limiting at multiple layers (reverse proxies by IP for abuse, load balancers selectively on global overload, and individual tasks), while remembering that rate limiting ignores overall service health and cannot stop a failure already in progress.

Couple capacity planning with performance testing to find the load at which the service fails and provision for N+2, but recognize that capacity planning alone is not sufficient to prevent cascading failures.

For steady traffic, keep request queues small relative to the thread pool (for example 50% or less) so the server rejects excess requests early, because queued requests consume memory and add latency; bursty traffic may instead warrant a queue sized to threads in use and burst characteristics.

Use load shedding — dropping a proportion of traffic as the server approaches overload, such as returning HTTP 503 above a number of in-flight requests — to keep the server doing as much useful work as possible without melting down.

Replace FIFO queuing with LIFO or a controlled-delay algorithm such as CoDel to drop requests that are no longer worth processing because the user has likely given up, especially when combined with propagated RPC deadlines.
Use graceful degradation to reduce work by lowering response quality (for example, searching an in-memory cache subset or using a faster, less-accurate ranking) when overloaded.

Exercise rarely-used graceful-degradation code paths regularly by running a small subset of servers near overload, because the code path you never use is the one that does not work, and monitor and alert when servers enter degraded mode while providing a fast off-switch.

Recognize that naive retries can cascade: retries compound onto the offered load so that even reducing call rate below the original level may not recover the service if retries keep the backend overloaded or destabilized.
Always use randomized exponential backoff with jitter when scheduling retries, so that a small perturbation such as a network blip does not synchronize retry ripples that amplify themselves.

Limit retries per request and add a server-wide retry budget (for example, 60 retries per minute per process) that fails fast once exceeded, to contain a local capacity failure from escalating into a global cascading failure.
Avoid issuing retries at multiple levels of a stack, because the attempts multiply across layers — three retries at each of three layers can turn one user action into 64 attempts on the database.

Use clear response codes that separate retriable from non-retriable errors: never retry permanent errors or malformed requests, and return a distinct overloaded status so clients and upper layers back off.
Set an RPC deadline on every request, because no deadline or an excessively high one lets long-past problems keep consuming server resources until a restart.
Do not spend resources on a request whose deadline has already passed — there is no credit for late work — and check the remaining deadline before each stage of multi-stage request processing.

Use deadline propagation: set the deadline high in the stack and pass the remaining absolute deadline down the RPC tree so deep servers immediately abandon already-expired work, reducing it slightly for transit time and considering an upper bound.
Use cancellation propagation to avoid RPC leakage, in which an initial long-deadline request keeps consuming server resources after deeper short-deadline RPCs have already timed out.

Beware bimodal latency: a small fraction of never-completing requests with a long deadline can exhaust the thread pool and turn a 5% error rate into an 80% error rate, so examine latency distributions rather than just means, fail fast on unavailable backends, and avoid deadlines orders of magnitude above mean latency.

Limit in-flight requests per keyspace or per client — for example, allowing any single client to occupy at most 25% of threads — to keep one misbehaving client from exhausting a shared resource for everyone.
Expect processes to be slower right after startup (initialization and just-in-time warmup) and with cold caches, and provision the service to handle a cold cache or it is at greater risk of outages.

Distinguish a latency cache (the service can sustain expected load with an empty cache) from a capacity cache (it cannot), and be vigilant that caches added for performance do not silently become hard dependencies.
Warm caches by slowly increasing load when turning up or returning a cluster to service, and keep all clusters carrying nominal load so their caches stay warm.

Avoid intra-layer (peer-to-peer) communication cycles in the user request path, because they are susceptible to distributed deadlock and can switch from a low to a high intra-layer request mode under load, amplifying a cascade.
When a server receives a misrouted request, it should tell the client to retry on the correct backend rather than proxy the request itself, keeping the routing decision with the client.
A small event such as a Query of Death — an RPC whose contents crash the process — or a couple of task deaths can tip a service that is already near its capacity limit into a cascading failure.

Avoid updating too many tasks simultaneously: account for capacity overhead in the update infrastructure or push off-peak, and dynamically adjust the number of in-flight task updates based on request volume and available capacity.

During a cascading failure, check for and consider reverting recent changes — especially those affecting capacity or the request profile — and implement change logging so recent changes can be identified quickly.

Do not rely on overcommitted slack CPU as a safety net, because its availability depends on other jobs in the cluster and can vanish suddenly, and stay within committed resource limits when load testing.

Load-test each component separately until it breaks to learn its breaking point and overload behavior, because a well-designed component rejects a few requests and survives whereas a fragile one crashes or serves a high error rate.

Test both gradual and impulse load patterns, since caching effects make them behave differently, and also test recovery — whether the component self-exits degraded mode and how far load must drop for the system to stabilize.

Consider running failure tests on a small slice of real production traffic to find true breaking points that synthetic load misses, while keeping spare capacity available for manual failover if automatic protections fail.

Understand and test how your largest clients behave under failure — whether they queue work, use randomized exponential backoff, and are vulnerable to external triggers that create load spikes — and stage failures with the biggest internal clients.

Test that the unavailability of noncritical backends — including blackholing or never responding — does not degrade the critical path, because long deadlines on a noncritical backend can starve the frontend.

Distinguish process health checking (the cluster scheduler asking whether a binary responds at all) from service health checking (the load balancer asking whether it can serve this class of requests right now), and temporarily disable health-check-driven restarts when health-checking itself is making the service unhealthy.

Restart wedged servers (for example in a garbage-collection death spiral, deadlocked, or with deadline-less requests blocking threads), but first identify the cause, canary the change, and proceed slowly, because restarting can amplify a cold-cache cascade.

Use dropping traffic as a last resort to recover from a true cascading failure: first address the triggering condition, then reduce load aggressively (for example to 1%) until crashing stops, let servers become healthy, and gradually ramp load back up so caches and connections warm.
Do not return traffic to normal before fixing the root cause or triggering condition, because the cascading failure will simply re-trigger once load returns.

Recover from overload using levers such as adding resources (when idle capacity exists), entering degraded modes, eliminating batch and other non-critical load, and blocking bad traffic like queries of death.
Once a service passes its breaking point, it is better to allow some user-visible errors or lower-quality results than to try to fully serve every request.

Be careful that steady-state improvements — retries, shifting load off unhealthy servers, killing unhealthy servers, or adding caches — do not increase the risk of a large-scale failure, so that you do not trade one outage for another.

Wherever you have leader election, critical shared state, or distributed locking, use distributed consensus systems that have been formally proven and thoroughly tested, because informal approaches cause outages and subtle, hard-to-fix data-consistency problems.

Distributed consensus reaches agreement among a group of processes connected by an unreliable network and is the foundation for building reliable, highly-available systems that need a consistent view of state.

Solve master election, group membership, distributed locking/leasing, reliable queuing, and any consistently-viewed shared state only with formally-proven distributed consensus algorithms, because ad hoc approaches like heartbeats and gossip cause split-brain and data corruption under network partitions.
Prefer crash-recover consensus algorithms over crash-fail ones, because most real-system failures are transient (slow networks, restarts) and crashed nodes do return.

Solving asynchronous distributed consensus in bounded time is impossible (the FLP result), so in practice provide enough healthy replicas and connectivity to make progress most of the time and add randomized backoff to prevent retry cascades and dueling proposers.

Require a majority (quorum) to commit and have acceptors persist a journal whenever they accept a proposal, because overlapping majorities prevent two values being committed and persistence preserves the guarantees across restarts.

Treat consensus algorithms as low-level primitives that only agree on one value once, and build higher-level components — datastores, configuration stores, queues, locks, and leader election — on top, which reduces design complexity and lets the underlying algorithm be swapped.

Consume distributed consensus as a service (such as Zookeeper, Consul, etcd, or Chubby) rather than as a library, to free application maintainers from deploying and operating a highly-available consensus system themselves.

Implement a highly-available service as a replicated state machine, which executes the same operations in the same order on several processes, because any deterministic program can be made a highly-available service this way.

Do not rely on timestamps to bound data freshness in distributed systems, because clocks cannot be guaranteed synchronized across machines; model the worst-case clock uncertainty (as Spanner does) and slow down where necessary if you must.

Build a highly-available service by writing it as a simple program, replicating that process, and using leader election to ensure only one leader works at a time, where consensus is off the critical path so throughput is not the main concern.

Use renewable leases with timeouts rather than indefinite distributed locks so that a crashed process cannot hold a lock forever, and prefer a higher-level system that provides distributed transactions over raw distributed locking.

Implement reliable queues with a lease system rather than outright removal so that tasks claimed but not yet processed are not lost, and implement the queue itself as a replicated state machine so that losing the queue does not take down the whole system.

Distributed consensus algorithms are not inherently too slow for systems needing both high throughput and low latency; performance depends on the workload, the performance objectives, and the deployment, and there is no single best algorithm.
The availability benefits of distributed consensus require replicas to be placed in different, distant failure domains, which increases inter-replica latency — an inherent trade-off.

Use a strong, stable leader (as in Multi-Paxos) so that consensus needs only one round trip to a quorum, but carefully tune leader-election timeouts and backoff with randomness to balance unavailability against the dueling-proposers livelock.

Scale read-heavy workloads by serving reads from any replica when strong consistency is not required, since stale reads cause extra work rather than incorrect results; for strongly-consistent reads use a read consensus operation, the stable leader, or quorum leases.

Use quorum leases to grant a brief read lease to a quorum of replicas for strongly-consistent local reads at some cost to write performance, which is particularly useful when reads for a subset of data are concentrated in one geographic region.

Recognize that consensus performance is bounded by two physical constraints — network round-trip time and the time to write to persistent storage — and that round-trip time varies enormously with distance and congestion.

Use a pool of regional proxies that hold persistent connections to the consensus group to avoid per-client TCP setup overhead over long distances and to encapsulate sharding, load balancing, and cluster discovery when there are very many clients.

Do not assume Fast Paxos is always faster than Classic Paxos: when clients have a high round-trip time to acceptors, sending N parallel messages over slow links can be slower than one slow-link message plus N fast-link messages, because of the latency tail.

Note that a stable leader, while improving performance, makes the leader's outgoing bandwidth a bottleneck and ties whole-system throughput to the leader's machine, so rotating leadership or placing replicas near clients can lower client-perceived latency over a wide-area network.

Use batching to increase consensus throughput and pipelining (multiple in-flight proposals with a sliding window) to avoid leaving replicas idle, while preserving the global ordering required by a replicated state machine.
Acceptors must flush each consensus commitment to persistent storage before responding, or a crashed and restarted process may violate the protocol and produce inconsistent state.

Combine the consensus log and the replicated-state-machine transaction log into a single on-disk log to avoid alternating seeks between two locations, increasing the transactions per second the system can sustain; flush log writes directly to disk but write state changes to a memory cache flushed later in an efficient order.
Batch multiple client operations into a single consensus operation to amortize the fixed costs of disk logging and network latency and increase throughput.
A majority-quorum consensus system of 2f+1 replicas tolerates f failures (3f+1 for Byzantine fault tolerance), so the minimum useful deployment is three replicas, which tolerates a single failure.

Run five replicas rather than three for a critical consensus system, so that an unplanned failure during a planned-maintenance window still leaves a quorum, since most downtime comes from planned maintenance.

Recognize that a consensus system that loses its quorum is theoretically unrecoverable without risking data loss, so back up regular snapshots elsewhere even for robust consensus systems, because software bugs and human or administrator error are failure domains you can never escape.

Choose the number of replicas as a deliberate trade-off among reliability, frequency of planned maintenance, risk, performance, and cost, noting that allowing extra non-quorum replicas to lag can let a faster quorum run ahead.

Decide replica locations by trading off failure-domain coverage against latency, because spreading replicas farther apart tolerates larger failures but increases round-trip time and operation latency.
Do not expand the failure domain a consensus system survives beyond where its clients live, because surviving a regional outage gives no benefit if all the clients are down in that same region.

Measure consensus performance by client perception and minimize client-to-replica round-trip time; leaderless protocols such as Mencius or Egalitarian Paxos can have an edge over a wide-area network when reads can run on any replica.

Be aware that adding a replica to a majority-quorum system can reduce availability — six replicas need four for a quorum where five need only three — and that colocating multiple replicas in one datacenter can remove the system's remaining redundancy.
Do not blindly route all read requests to the nearest replica, because a regional load spike can overwhelm the nearest replica and then the next-closest, producing a cascading failure.

In highly-sharded consensus systems, balance leader processes evenly across datacenters so the system is not bottlenecked on one datacenter's outgoing bandwidth and a failure of the leader datacenter does not suddenly overload the links between the others.

Recognize that leader-placement heuristics — siting leaders near clients, on the fastest machines, or favoring longest-running processes — can unintentionally concentrate leaders in one location and cause extreme traffic shifts on failover, so balance placement against capacity distribution.

When replicas have very different round-trip times, a simple majority quorum is fragile because losing a linchpin replica drastically raises latency, so use a hierarchical quorum (a majority of groups, each needing a majority of its members) to reduce reliance on any one replica.

Monitor consensus systems specifically for the count and health of group members, persistently lagging replicas, whether a leader exists (no leader means total unavailability), the rate of leader changes (flapping signals network issues), an increasing transaction number (progress), proposals seen versus agreed, and throughput and latency.
Whenever you encounter leader election, critical shared state, or distributed locking, use distributed consensus, because any lesser ad hoc method such as heartbeats is a ticking bomb in your system.

A traditional cron's failure domain is a single machine, the only state that must persist across crond restarts is the crontab configuration itself, and cron launches are fire-and-forget with no tracking of whether they ran.
Use an anacron-style mechanism that relaunches jobs which would have run while the system was down (for jobs that run daily or less often), driven by a stored timestamp of each job's last launch.

Classify periodic (cron) jobs by whether they are idempotent and by whether a skipped launch or a double launch is acceptable, because a diverse scheduler has no single failure-mode answer that fits every job.
Prefer to fail closed in a scheduler — skipping launches rather than risking double launches — because recovering from a skipped launch is far more tenable than undoing a double launch.
Have periodic-job owners monitor their jobs, either by the scheduler exposing job state or by independently monitoring the jobs' effects, so they can react appropriately to a skipped launch.

Do not host a critical periodic-scheduling service on a single machine; decouple processes from machines via a reliable datacenter scheduler and place replicas in diverse locations so a single power-distribution failure cannot take out the whole service.

At datacenter scale, deploy scheduler components into isolation containers with resource requirements known up front, and track the full state of each launch from scheduled time to termination, because decoupling from specific machines exposes the system to partial-launch failures.
Keep base services such as cron with very few dependencies so they continue to function even when parts of the datacenter fail.

Store a scheduler's small but critical state within the service itself via consensus rather than on a distributed filesystem optimized for large files, because small writes on such filesystems are expensive and high-latency.
Run multiple replicas of a distributed scheduler with Paxos for consistent state, designating a single leader as the only replica that may modify shared state and launch jobs.

Synchronously inform a quorum of replicas at both the beginning and the end of each scheduled launch before proceeding, so that after a failover the new leader knows whether a launch already occurred and does not repeat it.
Require that a leader which loses its leadership immediately stops interacting with the datacenter scheduler, to guarantee mutual exclusion so the old and new leaders cannot take conflicting actions.
Make scheduler leader failover converge in under a minute, to avoid missing or unreasonably delaying job launches.

Resolve partial launch failures by requiring either that all external operations are idempotent or that their completion state can be looked up unambiguously — for example by precomputing job names, distributing them to all replicas, and having a new leader look up and launch only the missing ones.

Include the scheduled launch time in job identifiers and external job names, so that a slow failover does not cause a new leader to double-launch a frequently-run job whose prior launch already completed.

Compact a consensus state-change log with periodic snapshots to prevent unbounded growth, and treat snapshots as the most critical state, since losing logs only causes a bounded loss of recent state while losing snapshots loses everything.

Store consensus logs and snapshots on local disk across replicas and back up the critical snapshots to a distributed filesystem, but deliberately do not store the logs there, accepting a bounded log loss to avoid the performance penalty of frequent small writes.

Let a freshly started replica fetch the state snapshot and logs over the network from a running replica, so that startup is independent of local-machine state and rescheduling a replica to another machine is a non-issue for reliability.

Beware the thundering-herd problem in schedulers — many users picking the same launch time, such as midnight, can spike datacenter usage — and mitigate it by letting the scheduler choose the exact time, for example by hashing the job configuration over the allowed range to spread launches.

Treat the periodic-pipeline model as fragile: parameters carefully tuned at install time degrade as organic growth stresses the system, producing deadline overruns, resource exhaustion, and hanging processing chunks.

Recognize that a pipeline's depth (the number of chained processing phases) and the uniformity of throughput between jobs affect its stability, and that multiphase chaining is usually adopted for ease of reasoning rather than operational efficiency.
In a chunked Big Data pipeline, end-to-end runtime is capped by the largest indivisible chunk (such as the biggest customer), and which chunks are oversized is seldom obvious in advance.

The hanging-chunk problem blocks pipeline completion on the worst-case chunk, and the default response of killing and restarting the job wastes all prior work because pipelines usually lack checkpointing.

Periodic pipelines typically run as low-priority batch jobs subject to open-ended startup delay and preemption when cluster load is high, so running one well is a delicate balance between resource cost and preemption risk.

A periodic pipeline has an effective lower bound on latency equal to the minimum average scheduling delay; pushing the execution interval below it causes runs to stack up or the nearly-finished run to be killed, halting progress.
Secure dedicated production-priority capacity, distinct from shared batch resources, for pipelines that need reliable low-latency operation rather than relying on the batch scheduler.
Periodic pipelines that report metrics only upon completion provide no statistics when a job fails mid-run, whereas continuous pipelines expose real-time telemetry useful for operational support.

Large periodic pipelines cause thundering-herd spikes when thousands of workers start at once and overwhelm shared cluster and network services, and missing retry logic drops work while naive retry logic compounds the overload.

Beware Moiré load patterns, in which two or more pipelines whose runs occasionally overlap simultaneously consume a shared resource and produce damaging peak load, most visible in plots of shared-resource usage.

If a data-processing problem is continuous or will organically grow to be continuous, do not use a periodic pipeline; instead use a continuous model that provides strong, exactly-once correctness guarantees.

At the outset of designing a data-pipeline system, scope the expected growth trajectory, demand for design modifications, expected additional resources, and the latency requirements from the business.

Hold pipeline model state in memory for fast availability while synchronously journaling mutations to persistent disk (system prevalence), keep workers stateless and discardable, and store only pointers to work in the master with the actual data in a common filesystem.

Guarantee exactly-once processing with leases and unique output filenames: a worker may commit only work for which it holds a currently valid lease, and uniquely-named output files prevent an orphaned worker from destroying a valid worker's output.

Version tasks and require each worker to reference the configuration task ID it used, so that work performed under a now-stale configuration cannot be committed, ensuring consistency at the cost of discarding work held under old leases.

Embed a unique server token in each task's metadata and validate it on every client-server operation, to prevent a rogue or misconfigured master — such as a load balancer placed in front of independent masters — from corrupting the pipeline.

For pipeline business continuity, store the master's journal in a globally-consistent store with a distributed lock service electing the single writer, and run local instances plus global reference tasks with a heartbeat so a remote instance can seize in-progress work if the heartbeat times out.

Treat data integrity as whatever users perceive it to be, since data loss, data corruption, and extended unavailability are indistinguishable to users, so what ultimately matters is that data stays accessible.

Treat uptime and data integrity as independent requirements, because 99.99% good bytes in a 2 GB artifact would leave up to 200 KB garbled — catastrophic for executables and databases — unlike 99.99% uptime.

The secret to superior data integrity is proactive detection coupled with rapid repair and recovery, because detecting and fixing corruption before users are affected keeps effective integrity near 100%.
Recognize that detection-and-repair strategies trade uptime against data integrity, and choose among them based on your computing paradigm's mix of uptime, latency, scale, velocity, and privacy.
The real goal of backups is recovery (restore), which distinguishes a true backup from an archive: a backup can be loaded back into an application, whereas an archive cannot.
Archives safekeep data over long periods for auditing, discovery, and compliance with relaxed recovery times, while real backups must recover quickly, well within the service's uptime needs.
Choose backup frequency and method (daily, hourly, or continuous; full plus incremental) based on how quickly you must recover and how much recent data you can afford to lose.
From the user's point of view, data integrity without expected and regular data availability is effectively the same as having no data at all.
Define data-availability SLOs across a variety of failure modes and have teams practice and demonstrate meeting them, rather than merely 'practicing backups'.
Motivate backup work by focusing on the restore — the visible payoff of guaranteed data availability — rather than on the thankless ongoing tax of taking backups.
Data-loss failure modes vary along three factors — root cause, scope, and rate — yielding 24 combinations, and an effective restore plan must account for any of these combinations.

The most common and most challenging real-world data loss involves deletion or loss of referential integrity caused by software bugs, especially low-grade corruption discovered weeks or months later, which demands point-in-time recovery.
Adopt a tiered backup strategy and add point-in-time recovery where available rather than neither, trading them off as needed but using both when you can.
Replication and redundancy are not recoverability, because datastores that automatically sync replicas will push a corrupt row or an errant delete to all copies before you can isolate the problem.

Diversity is key to data protection: to guard against a failure at a given layer, store data on diverse components at that layer, using media isolation so that a bug or attack in one device driver cannot affect a different medium.

Data freshness competes with restore completeness, because the lower in the stack a snapshot is taken the longer it takes and the less frequently it can run, so a low-level restore loses more recent data and takes longer to load.

Plan retention carefully, because a gradual data loss may be noticed only days later and require restoring from much older snapshots and merging the result with current state, which significantly complicates recovery.
Assume your protection mechanisms can themselves fail at the worst time, and rely on multiple complementary, uncoupled practices each of which offers a high degree of protection on its own.

Because no single safeguard covers all data-loss failure-mode combinations, use defense in depth with layers covering progressively rarer scenarios — soft deletion, backups and recovery, and regular data validation — with replication only occasionally useful.

Use soft deletion as a primary defense against developer error and a secondary defense against user error: immediately mark deleted data unusable except to administrative code paths, then destroy it after a delay (commonly 15 to 60 days, since most issues surface within 60 days).
Provide a user-facing trash and undelete as the primary defense against accidental user deletion, which also mitigates deletions performed by account hijackers.

In developer-facing offerings, add lazy deletion — storage-controlled behind-the-scenes purging — as the primary defense against internal developer error, while noting it is costly for short-lived data and incompatible with guaranteed-destruction privacy requirements.

Build soft and lazy deletion and undeletion into the storage APIs and enable them by default, so developers unfamiliar with the code cannot bypass them, and apply the same soft or lazy deletion principles to revision history.

Let recovery drive backup decisions, not the reverse: the scenarios you must recover from should dictate which backup and recovery methods you use, how frequently you take full or incremental backups, where you store them, and how long you retain them.

Use a tiered backup strategy: frequent, quick-to-restore snapshots near the live data (hours to days) for software-bug and developer-error recovery; fewer site-local distributed-filesystem backups (days to weeks) for storage-technology mishaps; and nearline or offsite tiers retained longer for site-level disasters.

Replicate backups across sites that fail independently and choose a popular, continually-used redundancy scheme such as RAID, Reed-Solomon erasure codes, or GFS-style replication rather than an infrequently-tested one.

Backup and validation processes that work at terabyte scale do not scale to exabytes — a single sequential validation pass over hundreds of petabytes could take decades — so the strategy must be rethought at large scale.

Establish 'trust points' by verifying portions of data once they become immutable (usually through the passage of time), then take incremental backups of only changed data so backup time stays in line with mainline processing.
A long chain of incremental backups (for example a thousand daily increments since one full backup) makes a full restore slow and risky, so balance incrementals against periodic full backups.

Shard data so that N tasks run in parallel, each copying and verifying one Nth of the data, which requires schema and deployment design that balances data, ensures shard independence, and avoids contention, and can cut restore wall time by orders of magnitude.

Bad data propagates: references to corrupt or missing data fan out with every update and degrade the datastore over time, so the sooner you detect a data loss the easier and more complete your recovery will be.

Do not blindly trust a distributed-consistency storage API to keep application data correct, because real implementations have bugs, timeouts, and edge cases whose inconsistencies grow with scale — trust storage systems, but verify.

Use out-of-band data validation — checks within and between an application's datastores, often implemented as MapReduce or Hadoop jobs — to catch low-grade corruption before it becomes unrecoverable, which also accelerates development by giving engineers the courage to move faster.

Tune data-validation strictness carefully — too strict and engineers abandon it, too loose and user-affecting corruption slips through — by validating only the invariants whose violation would be devastating to users.

Have validators automatically fix detected inconsistencies where possible, turning what would be an all-hands data-loss emergency into a business-as-usual fix and improving engineering morale and predictability.

Mitigate the cost of out-of-band validators at scale — compute footprint and reduced cache hit rates — by rate-limiting them, refactoring to reduce disk contention, and sharding the largest validators across days, using a tiered strategy where daily validators catch the most disastrous scenarios and more rigorous validation runs less often.
Provide on-call engineers with playbooks, an investigation tool, and a dashboard to troubleshoot validation failures, because the causes of intermittent failures can vanish within minutes to days.

Structure teams so a central infrastructure team maintains a reusable out-of-band data-validation framework while product teams own the custom business-logic invariants, because small high-velocity teams cannot build and maintain all the supporting systems alone.

Recovery dependencies, especially backups, may be in a latent broken state you discover only when you try to recover, so continuously test the recovery process and set alerts that fire when a recovery fails to emit a success heartbeat.
The only recovery test that earns confidence is a full end-to-end test, automated and run continuously, because you only know you can recover your recent state if you actually do so.

Confirm many aspects of a recovery plan: that backups are valid and complete, that there are sufficient machine resources, that recovery completes in reasonable wall time, that progress is monitorable, and that there are no critical dependencies on resources outside your control such as a vault that is not available 24/7.
Treat failures as inevitable and use testing to force them to occur before a real catastrophe, so problems can be fixed before any harm comes to users.

Apply defense in depth to online systems by backing them up at multiple layers, including offline media such as tape, to guard against both a failure of the internal redundancy subsystems and a wide failure or zero-day in the storage medium's device driver or filesystem.

Coordinate a large recovery with a central choreographing plan built from regular dress rehearsals and dry runs, because smooth cooperation across many teams under pressure depends on prior disaster-recovery practice.

Fix a data-loss bug at its root before or while recovering, because re-enabling a buggy deletion pipeline to satisfy legitimate deletions would keep harming innocent users — a Catch-22 escapable only by fixing the root cause.
Regular disaster-recovery testing pays off in real incidents, because the tools built and the team knowledge gained during drills make a real large-scale recovery feasible and faster.

A data-deletion pipeline that makes simplifying assumptions about the age of its inputs can develop a probabilistic race condition that grows with data volume, nondeterministically deleting the wrong data, especially after performance optimizations erode the original safety margins.

Alert on the global aggregate data-deletion rate crossing an extreme threshold, such as 10x the observed 95th percentile, rather than on per-user deletion rates, to detect runaway-deletion bugs that affect users globally.
Adopt a beginner's mind: never assume you understand a complex system well enough to say it cannot fail in a certain way, and always trust but verify while applying defense in depth.

Trust but verify: any API you depend on will have defects regardless of engineering rigor, so check the correctness of your most critical data with out-of-band validators even when the API's semantics suggest you need not.
Hope is not a strategy: system components that are not continually exercised fail when you need them most, so prove data recovery works through regular, automated exercise.

Apply defense in depth, because even the most bulletproof system is susceptible to bugs and operator error and every strategy eventually fails in changing environments, so the best data-integrity strategies are multitiered with layers that fall back to one another.

Revisit and reexamine assumptions, because data that was safe yesterday is not guaranteed safe tomorrow: for example, data that was cheap to re-create becomes irreplaceable once a new feature adds user-generated content, which then requires real backups and restore testing.

Keep your eyes on the goal of data availability rather than the backup mechanisms, and prove your systems maintain data availability within a predicted maximum downtime, to avoid the trap where the operation succeeds but the system dies.
As you get better at recovering within some time N, drive that time toward zero with more rapid, finer-grained loss detection, then shift from planning recovery to planning prevention.
SRE's role in product launches is to enable a rapid pace of change without compromising the stability of the site.
Build kill switches into risky, high-traffic launches so that services can be protected if the launch threatens to overwhelm them.

Create a dedicated launch-coordination team to handle the technical side of launches — auditing products against reliability standards, acting as a liaison between teams, driving momentum, gatekeeping and signing off on safe launches, and educating developers.
A rapid launch rate both justifies and enables a streamlined launch process, whereas a company that launches rarely cannot accumulate enough experience to build a robust, mature launch process.

Staff launch coordination with engineers who hold strong communication and leadership skills and are incentivized to prioritize reliability, since a cross-product team provides breadth of experience, a holistic perspective, and objectivity as a non-partisan mediator.

Design a launch process to be lightweight, robust, thorough, scalable, and adaptable — criteria that conflict — and balance them with simplicity, a high-touch approach that customizes per launch, and fast common paths for recurring launch classes.
Continuously optimize the launch process to balance cost against benefit, because engineers will sidestep any process they consider too burdensome, especially when already in crunch mode.
Use a launch checklist, like aviation preflight and surgical checklists, to reduce failure and ensure consistency and completeness across launches.

Curb checklist growth by substantiating every question's importance (ideally with a past launch disaster), making every instruction concrete, practical, and reasonable, and periodically pruning obsolete items.

Use the launch checklist to drive convergence on common, hardened infrastructure for tasks like rate limiting, quotas, and releases, which cuts duplicate effort, transfers knowledge, and lets long checklist sections be replaced with a single 'use system X' instruction.

For an unusual or new type of launch, return to the abstract first principles of a safe launch and then respecialize the checklist, keeping each question's intent in mind rather than mechanically applying items irrelevant to the new product.

Conduct an architecture and dependency review at launch to confirm correct use of shared infrastructure, identify infrastructure owners as launch stakeholders, and feed the dependency list into capacity planning, while isolating user-facing from non-user-facing requests and validating that one page view can become many requests.
Minimize single points of failure including humans, and document every remaining manual process before launch so that any team member can execute it in an emergency.

Check all code and configuration files into version control — gaining history, change attribution, and review for configuration too — do most development on the mainline, and cut each release on its own branch with fixes cherry-picked.

Identify external dependencies — third-party code, data, services, and dependent partners — before a launch and plan mitigations such as filtering proxies, transcoding pipelines, and caches for vendor outages, bugs, security issues, or scalability limits, as well as for missed deadlines.

Plan a staged rollout with ordered configuration changes, interspersed verification steps, and contingency measures, because in large distributed systems few events are instantaneous and a configuration that works in a test instance does not guarantee a clean rollout to the live instance.

Never change a running system without minimizing risk: roll out gradually with canaries that observe the new software under real user traffic and automatically roll back any change that fails its validation period.

Apply gradual rollout even to client software — for example offering a new app version to a growing percentage of installs — so you can observe the backend impact and detect problems early, and use rate-limited or invite-based signups as another gradual-rollout mechanism.

Use feature-flag frameworks that roll changes out from 0% to 100% of users, run many changes in parallel each to a few users or servers, automatically handle failure of new code paths without affecting users, allow each change to be reverted independently and immediately, and measure each change's effect on the user experience.
Harden the feature-flag framework itself as much as possible so that most of its applications require no special launch review.

Control client behavior from the server side — using configuration the client periodically fetches to enable or disable features and set sync and retry rates — and ship dormant client code activated server-side, to reduce launch risk and avoid maintaining a combinatorial explosion of parallel client versions.

Guard against abusive client behavior, since a misjudged sync rate can multiply load tenfold, by having clients use exponential backoff and retry only appropriate errors (a network error usually warrants a retry; a 4xx client error usually does not).
Prevent synchronized client request storms (thundering herds) by having each client choose the time of periodic requests randomly and jitter its retry delays by a random amount.

Recognize that a service's CPU usage does not scale linearly with load: services are often slower when unloaded due to caches, behave roughly linearly over a middle range, and hit a nonlinearity near overload where response times spike or the service locks up entirely.

Be aware that overload can trigger feedback death spirals, such as a service spending ever more CPU logging errors as errors rise, or a JVM entering garbage-collection thrashing where memory management consumes most of the CPU.

Because a service's reaction to overload is very hard to predict from first principles, treat load testing as an invaluable tool for both reliability and capacity planning and require it for most launches.
Capture the lessons learned from past launches in a curated checklist so that novice engineers do not repeat their predecessors' launch mistakes.

Streamline launch reviews by classifying low-risk launches — for example one with no new server binary and a traffic increase under 10% — onto a trivial checklist while subjecting higher-risk launches to the full set of checks.

Expect that a product whose usage grows far beyond early estimates (by more than two orders of magnitude) will eventually require a complete rearchitecture and a costly user migration that slows feature development during the transition.

Operational load — noisy alerts, deployment complexity, and manual maintenance — tends to grow over time unless actively tracked and reduced, so constantly identify and remove sources of operational work to stay under the 50% ops cap.

Enact a churn-reduction policy that prohibits infrastructure teams from releasing backward-incompatible changes until they also provide automated migration of their clients, so that service owners are not forced to run fast just to stay in the same place.

Consider a dedicated launch-coordination role for any company undergoing rapid growth that doubles its product developers every year or two, scales to hundreds of millions of users, and needs reliability despite a high rate of change.

Invest up front in the education and technical orientation of new SREs to accelerate their proficiency and build a robust, balanced skill set, because SRE teams run on trust that on-callers understand the system and can react well under pressure.

Avoid trial-by-fire onboarding that deluges newbies with tickets and alerts, because it trains reaction rather than reasoning, alienates capable engineers, and falsely assumes the job can be learned strictly by doing.

Design concrete, sequential, cumulative learning paths so new SREs see a clear path before them, front-loading the abstract concepts that recur throughout their journey while giving hands-on experience as soon as practical.

Order stack training along a natural sequence — how a query enters the system, frontend serving, mid-tier services, infrastructure, and then debugging and escalation — or group it by similarity of purpose.

Use an on-call learning checklist that enumerates expert contacts, the most useful documentation, the basic knowledge to internalize, and probing comprehension questions with concrete outcomes, rather than encoding procedures and playbooks, which keeps it more future-proof.

Check trainee retention with homework and comprehension questions, and gate progressively deeper production access (read-only, then mutate state) on satisfactorily completing sections of the learning checklist.

Give new SREs targeted project work with partial ownership rather than menial work, splitting their time between learning and projects, with starter projects such as shipping a small feature, adding monitoring to a blind spot, or automating a pain point to build empathy and an appreciation for removing toil.

Train SREs to be reverse engineers who can figure out unfamiliar systems from debugging surfaces, RPC boundaries, and logs; statistical and comparative thinkers who prune the incident decision tree with hypotheses; and improvisers for when standard operating procedures break down.

Architect systems so that factors like kernel version, CPU architecture, binary versions, and traffic mix can each be controlled for and individually analyzed and compared, to support comparative troubleshooting.
Beware analytical traps during outages: being too procedural or carrying too many untested assumptions into decision-making gets you stuck, so learn to zoom out and take a different approach.

Have new SREs reverse-engineer a real production service end-to-end by following the request's RPC path, using multiple discovery methods so no connections are missed, an exercise from which even senior SREs learn by correcting drifts in their own understanding.
Welcome every chance to refamiliarize the team with an ever-changing production system, including learning from the newest members, because production inevitably drifts from everyone's mental model.

Collect and curate teachable postmortems as educational resources and run postmortem reading clubs or 'tales of fail' sessions, because regular study of past outages builds a new SRE's mental map of production and on-call response.

Run regular disaster role-playing exercises (a 'Wheel of Misfortune') in which a game master throws a real or hypothetical scenario at primary and secondary on-call while the team learns, using humorous framing to make it less intimidating so every experience level benefits.

Give new SREs hands-on experience breaking and fixing real production systems before they go on-call, using a live instance diverted from traffic or a fully-featured staging instance under synthetic load, to develop reflexive use of the team's tooling and monitoring.

Run progressive-impairment exercises that start from a known-good configuration, slowly cripple the stack at chosen bottlenecks, and poll participants for predictions before inflicting damage, because such exercises shake out real bugs since systems do not always degrade as gracefully as expected.

Keep on-call documentation fresh by tasking new hires with overhauling the most outdated sections of the learning checklist, peer-reviewed by experts, which harnesses newbie enthusiasm together with senior knowledge.

Let new SREs shadow on-call early by copying incoming pages to them (at first only during business hours) so they observe outages unfold live without time pressure, which builds team trust and lets senior engineers detach when off-call.
Include a newbie as a coauthor, not the sole author, of a postmortem, to avoid creating the impression that postmortems are junior grunt work.
Consider a reverse-shadow step in which the newbie becomes primary on-call while an experienced SRE silently diagnoses in parallel and provides hints and validation as needed.

Treat going on-call as a celebrated rite of passage but not the end of learning: run a regular team learning series on upcoming stack changes (recorded into a training library) and have SREs present their work to developers.
In SRE you must scale your humans faster than you scale your machines.

Operational load falls into three categories — pages (production alerts with a response SLO often in minutes), tickets (customer requests with an SLO in hours to weeks), and ongoing operational responsibilities or toil (often with no defined SLO).
Staff each on-call shift with a single primary engineer (backed by a secondary) to minimize the interruption to the team and to avoid the bystander effect.
Maximize the time engineers spend in cognitive flow ('the zone'), because a disruptive interrupt that breaks flow costs far more than its nominal duration.

In a mixed project and on-call environment, when a person concentrates full-time on interrupts the interrupts stop being interrupts and projects become the distraction, so people are happiest with a balance between the two that varies per engineer.

Assign a real cost to context switches, since a single 20-minute interruption involves two context switches and can cost a couple of hours of productive work, so do not treat engineers as freely-interruptible units of work.

Polarize time so that on any given day a person knows whether they are doing only project work or only interrupts, with each work period as long as possible (ideally a week), to enable sustained concentration.

Never expect a person who is on-call or on primary interrupts to also make progress on high-context-switch project work; write off the on-call week for projects, and escalate to reassign the shift if a project is too important to let slip.

Stop randomly assigning tickets across the whole team, and instead make ticket-handling a dedicated full-time role for a manageable period (two people if the volume demands), to avoid imposing context switches on everyone.
Define ongoing-responsibility roles that anyone can take up, such as a push manager with a formal handover process, so a long-running change need not be shepherded by one person for its entire life.
Discourage working tickets or interrupts when not assigned to them, because doing so to look busy skews the load metrics and can hide an unmanageable queue.

Regularly scrub tickets and pages for root causes — with handoffs and reviews for tickets as well as on-call — and silence a class of interrupt until its root cause is fixed, which both relieves the handler and creates a deadline for the fixer.

Your team sets the level of service it provides, so use policy as powerfully as code to make ticket and interrupt load manageable, striking a balance between respect for the customer and respect for yourself.

Push effort back onto requestors for interrupt steps that do not require your privileges — for example, have the customer prepare the code or config change and submit it for your review — since a customer who wants a task done should expend some effort to get it.
Require that a customer request be meaningful, rational, and accompanied by the information and legwork needed to fulfill it, and in return provide a helpful and timely response.

If you cannot get the attention needed to fix the root cause of a component's interrupts, treat that as a signal the component may not be important and consider giving back the pager, deprecating it, or replacing it.

Relieve an operationally-overloaded team by temporarily embedding a single SRE who focuses on improving the team's practices rather than just emptying the ticket queue, providing a fresh outside perspective, since adding two engineers can provoke defensiveness.

Remind teams that more tickets should not require more SREs: the SRE model adds humans only as system complexity grows, not as load grows, which is how a team escapes the ops-mode trap of scaling headcount with load.

Verify a team's assumption that it is 'too small to worry about scale' by shadowing an on-call session, because the element of scale shapes the strategy, and prepare a young service for explosive growth since a 100-request-per-second service can become 10,000 within a year.

Prioritize a team's problems by their impact on stress levels and identify 'kindling' — emergencies waiting to happen — such as knowledge gaps from overspecialization, quietly-important SRE-built services, deferral in favor of the next big thing, undiagnosed transient alerts, services lacking an SLI/SLO/SLA, reactive capacity plans, rollback-only postmortem actions, and components whose owners SREs disclaim.
Make capacity plans sufficiently forward-looking, because a load test that barely passes today — revealing 1.99 GB against a 2 GB model — does not mean system capacity is adequate.
Ensure postmortem action items address why a failure happened, not merely roll back the specific change that triggered it.
Demonstrate the blameless SRE model by taking ownership of the next postmortem rather than critiquing a team's old postmortems, which would only put them on the defensive.

Reject the Bad Apple Theory that removing the people who make mistakes will keep the system fine, because mistakes are inevitable in any system with multiple subtle interactions; focus the postmortem on where the system misled the on-caller and where cognitive demands were too high.
Sort a team's fires into toil that should not exist and be automated versus acceptable overhead of running the service, and explain to the team why each fire falls into its category.

Treat team health as an ongoing process rather than a one-time heroic fix: restore the right initial conditions and teach the small set of principles needed to make healthy choices, then let the team self-regulate.
Write a service level objective first if one does not exist, because the SLO is the single most important lever for moving a team from reactive ops work to a healthy, long-term SRE focus.

Do not fix identified issues yourself when coaching a team; instead assign the work to a team member, explain how it permanently addresses a postmortem issue, and review their change, so that making changes is not seen as something only other people do.

Always explain your reasoning from first principles, whether or not an explanation is requested, so the team builds a mental model that lets them predict your feedback after you leave, because poorly-explained reasoning gets emulated.
Ask leading questions that prompt the team to reason from basic principles, rather than loaded questions, to reinforce SRE philosophy.
Recognize that SRE is not a command-and-control organization, and that shared culture and values are what produce homogeneous problem-solving approaches across teams by design.

Hold a regular production meeting with compulsory SRE attendance plus major stakeholders and partner product-development teams, to preserve the operations feedback loop, and treat an inability to invite your dev partners as a relationship to be fixed.

Use a real-time collaborative agenda document that anyone in engineering can access to pre-populate bottom-up items and prepare the agenda in parallel and in advance, which is efficient and gives more people a sense of ownership.

Specialization improves technical mastery and reduces cognitive load but risks siloization and loss of the broader picture, so define a crisp team charter of what a team will and, more importantly, will not support.
Diverse teams are better teams: diversity improves collaboration and most other outcomes but demands particular attention to communication and cognitive biases.

Singleton projects usually fail unless the person is exceptional or the problem is trivial, so accomplishing anything significant requires multiple people and therefore good collaboration and communication skills, especially across time zones.

Reward structures that credit each team for building its own solution lead to duplicated, abandoned work, so provide shared infrastructure as products rather than mere toolkits and add cross-team tracking to prevent reinvention.

Merging duplicate efforts into a single shared solution yields development velocity greater than the sum of the separate projects, and a shared long-term vision is the key factor that makes such a merge possible.
Drive adoption of a common solution by recommending it rather than mandating it, declaring it the recommended option instead of forcing teams to switch.

Treat casual, short-term project contributions as useful but costly, because they dilute ownership and leave features unsupported after the contributor leaves, so ensure contributors are genuinely committed with a specific goal to achieve.

Develop projects across sites only when you have to, because cross-site work costs higher action latency and more communication, though done right it yields much higher throughput, while single-site projects risk no one outside the site knowing what you are doing.

Use divide-and-conquer for cross-site projects by splitting the work into many reasonably-sized components each assignable to a small group preferably within one site, with clear deliverables and deadlines, while guarding against Conway's law distorting the software's natural shape.
Orient each project component's goal toward providing some functionality or solving some problem, and consider it complete only once it is fully integrated and used within the main project.
Write things down — design documents and reviews — as a primary technique to offset physical and logical distance and keep the whole team able to follow and influence changes.

Establish team standards and norms: argue each contested decision fully but under a strict time limit, then pick a solution, document it, and move on, using a respected arbitrator when the team cannot agree.
Optimize for making decisions locally where there is a high level of agreement and trust, supported by strong project leaders who provide and enforce the long-term vision.

Recognize there is no substitute for in-person interaction: have project leaders meet the team in person and hold team summits, at a neutral location when neutrality matters, to hash out designs and goals.

Collaborate between product development and SRE as early as the design phase, before any code is committed, because SRE recommendations about architecture and software behavior are difficult or impossible to retrofit later.

In a major migration, let SRE drive the infrastructure design (their domain of extracting and processing data at scale) while developers own the business logic, define the interfaces between them early so each team works independently, sync where they interact, validate the new system by requiring its output to match the old system's exactly, and stand up a production-like test environment to measure performance while business logic is still being developed.

Engage SRE as early as the design phase, because the earlier the engagement the lower the cost to onboard and the more reliable the service is out of the gate, since you avoid spending time unwinding suboptimal design and implementation.

Scale reliability best by providing product-development teams a platform of SRE-validated, reliable, and scalable infrastructure, which removes classes of cognitive load and lets developers focus innovation at the application layer.

Define the set of 'production' aspects SRE cares about — system architecture and dependencies, instrumentation and monitoring, emergency response, capacity planning, change management, and performance (availability, latency, efficiency) — and aim to improve a service along all of them.

When SRE cannot provide full engagement because demand exceeds its bandwidth or a service does not need high reliability, still offer documentation such as a production best-practices guide and consultation as lighter-weight support.

Make a Production Readiness Review a prerequisite before an SRE team takes over a service, using it to verify the service meets production and operational-readiness standards and to improve its reliability before assuming responsibility.

Run the production-readiness engagement in phases — agree on an SLO/SLA and plan changes and training, analyze the service against a checklist and past incidents, prioritize and jointly execute improvements and refactoring, train the SRE team, onboard progressively, and then drive continuous improvement.

Maintain a service-specific production-readiness checklist of best practices — such as whether an update affects too large a fraction of the system at once, whether the service uses the correct serving instance of its dependencies, and whether user-visible failures are instrumented, monitored, and alerted.
Onboard a service by progressively transferring responsibility and ownership while the development team remains available to back up and advise the SRE team as it settles into managing production.

Because active services constantly change with new features, dependencies, and upgrades, the owning SRE team must drive continuous improvement and feed the lessons learned back into shared best practices.
Have SREs work as part of the development team — with highly visible, reviewed work — rather than as an external unit, to ensure effective knowledge sharing.

Apply an early-engagement model for services that add significant new functionality to an SRE-managed system or significantly rewrite an existing one, with SRE participating from the design phase through build and taking over during or after build.

Involve SRE in the design phase to prevent incidents — the best production incidents are those that never happen — and so that SRE shares ownership of any deliberately less-than-ideal trade-offs, minimizing future disputes once the service is in production.

Use launch patterns such as a dark launch, in which a copy of real user traffic is sent to the new service but its responses are discarded, to gain operational insight and resolve issues without impacting existing users.

Aim for a smooth launch, because it keeps the operational burden low and preserves development momentum, whereas a disruptive launch forces emergency changes to code and production and derails future feature work.
