Treat disengaging from a service as a positive outcome when the service has been engineered to be reliable and low-maintenance enough to stay with the development team, and treat early SRE effort on a service that fails to reach projected scale as part of the normal business risk of new projects.

Recognize that a purely review-driven engagement model does not scale, because each onboarding consumes two or three SREs over two or three quarters, production features get reimplemented per service, and fixes and lessons cannot easily be replicated across services — which motivates shared frameworks and a platform.

Build a production platform on frameworks with strong conventions to significantly lower operational overhead, because it enables conformance tests for code structure, dependencies, style, privacy, and security, provides built-in deployment, monitoring, and automation, eases management of many microservices, and can take an idea to production quality in days.

Frameworks give universal support by design: services that cannot warrant full SRE engagement can still use SRE-developed production features, which breaks the SRE staffing barrier, raises baseline service quality, and lets every framework-built service automatically inherit later improvements to the framework.

Frameworks make production-readiness engagements faster and lower-overhead, relying on built-in service features and faster onboarding (often one SRE in a single quarter) to reduce the SRE team's cognitive burden while keeping a high bar on production quality.

A common production platform enables a shared-responsibility model in which SREs own and maintain the platform infrastructure — control systems such as load shedding, overload protection, automation, traffic management, logging, and monitoring — while development teams stay on-call for functional bugs in their application code.

The platform model decouples SRE staffing from service count, because platform teams are staffed to maintain the platform rather than per service and can be shared across products, reducing the number of SREs required per service.

Standardize and encapsulate production best-practice code patterns in frameworks, so that using a framework becomes the recommended, consistent, and relatively simple way to build a production-ready service.

Reliability practice can be compared across industries through four key themes: preparedness and disaster testing, postmortem culture, automation and reduced operational overhead, and structured and rational decision-making.

Treat repetitive reactive work as something to automate away, because automating low-value repeated operations lowers operational overhead and frees engineers to proactively assess and improve the services they support.

Apply automation cautiously where errors are costly, because incorrectly configured automation can inflict enormous damage very quickly — as when a software glitch cost Knight Capital $440M in hours — so the speed of computers becomes a negative when tasks are misconfigured.

Recognize that automation is generally more reliable and repeatable than manual work, producing higher quality and tighter tolerances, and follow the rule of thumb that a response required within about 30 minutes should be automated.
Automate verification of human inputs — for example sanity-checking out-of-range entries and automatically matching a biometric identity — to eliminate whole classes of human error.

Make decisions in a structured, rational way by agreeing the basis for the decision in advance rather than justifying it after the fact, making the inputs clear, stating assumptions explicitly, and letting data win over feelings, hunches, or the opinion of the most-senior person in the room.

Operate on the baseline assumption that everyone on the team has the users' best interests at heart and can figure out how to proceed from the available data, so that decisions are informed rather than prescriptive and made without deference to personal opinion.

Use prescriptive playbook- and checklist-driven decision making for slowly-evolving systems or limited-skill workforces, but rely on open-ended problem solving for rapidly-changing systems whose failure scenarios constantly evolve.

Separate an enforcement function from the execution function to manage risk, so that an independent team monitors for abnormalities, can immediately halt the system, and alone can bring it back up — on the principle that not operating beats operating at a loss.

Weigh velocity against the stakes of failure: where an outage could injure or kill people a conservative approach to reliability is warranted, but where lives are not at risk, error budgets can fund a culture of innovation and calculated risk-taking.

Construct SRE teams so engineers divide their time between operating systems on-call and building tools that make those systems easier to manage, playing both pilot and engineer and codifying operational experience as reusable products.

Found a team or system on a set of general, mostly future-proof axioms, because the core responsibilities — keeping systems reliable, flexible, manageable in emergencies, well monitored, and capacity-planned — stay constant even as scale grows a thousandfold and the specific activities evolve.

Aim for an SRE team that is as compact as possible and operates at a high level of abstraction, relying on backup and failsafe systems and thoughtful APIs while retaining comprehensive day-to-day knowledge of how the systems operate, fail, and recover — the model of a giant aircraft still flown by just two well-supported pilots.

Use an aggregate unavailability metric — the percentage of all operations that failed — rather than outage length for services that can be partially available due to multiple replicas or whose load varies over time.

A live incident state document should record a summary, current status and incident number, the command-post location, and the command hierarchy naming the incident commander plus operations, planning, and communications leads.
The incident state document should be updated on a fixed cadence and at every handoff of the communications-lead role to keep responders aligned.
condition: responders rely on the document as the source of truth, e.g. at least every four hours

statement: An incident should define explicit exit criteria, such as returning to within availability and latency SLOs for a sustained period before declaring the incident over.
The incident document should maintain a running list of open TODOs and filed bugs with their current status so remediation work is tracked during the response.
A postmortem should capture a summary, user/revenue impact, root causes, trigger, resolution, and detection method for the incident.
Postmortem impact should be quantified as the effect on users and revenue rather than described only qualitatively.
Root-cause analysis in a postmortem should use a structured technique such as the Five Whys to surface contributing factors rather than stopping at the first apparent cause.
Postmortem lessons-learned should be separated into what went well, what went wrong, and where the team got lucky (near misses).
The 'where we got lucky' section of a postmortem is for near misses, capturing favorable conditions that prevented a worse outcome but cannot be relied upon.
A postmortem timeline should be a chronological screenplay of the incident, seeded from the incident-management document's timeline and supplemented with other relevant entries.
A postmortem should link supporting evidence such as monitoring dashboards, logs, graphs, and chat transcripts.
Postmortem action items should each be typed by intent (for example prevent, mitigate, or process), assigned an owner, and linked to a tracking bug.
Knee-jerk action items are often too extreme or costly to implement, so judgment is needed to rescope them within a larger context to avoid over-optimizing for a single issue.
Adding narrow monitoring and alerting for a specific failure is weaker than catching the same class of problem earlier with reliable mechanisms such as unit tests in development.
A latent resource leak whose failure rate is negligible under normal load can trigger cascading failure when a sudden traffic surge interacts with the bug.

During cascading failure, directing traffic to a sacrificial cluster while draining the others lets the drained clusters recover and lets responders raise instance counts without servers dying immediately.

Substantially increasing serving capacity (for example to ten times initial capacity) can mitigate a load-driven cascading failure by giving instances enough headroom to do useful work before being restarted.
Restoring traffic to recovered clusters should be ramped gradually (a small percentage at a time) while watching error rates, rather than restored all at once.
A team that is out of practice at responding to rare failure modes such as cascading failure will handle real incidents of that type more slowly and poorly.
Exhausting the availability error budget should trigger a production freeze for a defined period unless an explicit exception is granted, even for unusual circumstances.
A launch coordination checklist should cover the service architecture, including server types, the kinds of client requests, and programmatic client request patterns.
A launch coordination checklist should cover machines and datacenters, including bandwidth, datacenter redundancy such as N+2, network quality-of-service, new domain names, and DNS load balancing.

A launch coordination checklist should cover volume estimates, capacity, and performance, including traffic and bandwidth forecasts, the launch spike, load and end-to-end tests, per-datacenter capacity at maximum latency, impact on other services, and storage capacity.

A launch coordination checklist should cover system reliability and failover, including behavior when a machine, rack, or cluster fails or the network partitions, backend death detection, safe termination and restart, and load-balancing, rate-limiting, timeout, retry, and error-handling behavior, plus backup/restore and disaster recovery.

A launch coordination checklist should cover monitoring and server management, including monitoring internal state and end-to-end behavior, managing alerts, monitoring the monitoring, and avoiding self-inflicted failures such as crashing mail servers by emailing your own alerts.
A launch coordination checklist should cover security, including a security design review and code audit, spam risk, authentication, SSL, prelaunch access control, and blacklists.

A launch coordination checklist should cover automation and manual tasks, including change control for servers, data, and configs, the release process, repeatable builds, canaries under live traffic, and staged rollouts.
A launch coordination checklist should cover growth issues, including spare capacity, alerting on growth, scalability bottlenecks, linear scaling, caching, and data sharding/resharding.
A launch coordination checklist should cover external dependencies, including third-party systems and monitoring, graceful degradation, and avoiding accidentally overrunning third-party services.
A launch coordination checklist should cover schedule and rollout planning, including hard deadlines, external events, riskier launch days, and standard operating procedures.

A regular production meeting should walk a standard agenda: announcements, previous action-item review, outage review, paging and nonpaging events, monitoring changes and silences, planned production changes, resources and utilization, key service metrics versus SLO, and new action items.

condition: when a feature can be hidden or segmented before launch

statement: Organizations should convert each discovered problem into learning that prevents recurrence or speeds detection of similar future problems.

Automated tests and peer reviews embedded in daily work mitigate delivery risk more directly than distant approvals.

condition: when an incident or accident occurs

statement: Internal technology conferences and similar forums can spread skills by making teaching and learning routine across the organization.

condition: when production risk is managed through controlled exercises and recovery capability

statement: State of DevOps research reported that high performers achieved much higher deployment frequency, faster lead time, higher change success, and faster service restoration than low performers.

Developer productivity at scale depends on architecture, technical practices, and cultural norms that let small teams integrate, test, and deploy independently.

DevOps derives practices from Lean, Theory of Constraints, resilience engineering, learning organizations, safety culture, human factors, and high-trust management models.

Testing, deployment, and operations work should become predictable and low-variation even when upstream design work remains uncertain.
Testing, deployment, and operations should happen concurrently with design and development rather than only after a large development batch is complete.
Fast technology flow depends on small batches and building quality into every part of the value stream.

condition: when a value-stream problem is detected

statement: The Third Way requires a generative, high-trust culture that supports disciplined experimentation, risk-taking, and learning from success and failure.

Research cited by the book supports combining continuous integration, testing, deployment, small batches, fast feedback, monitoring, and generative culture to achieve superior outcomes.

Value stream mapping can motivate improvement by helping teams understand end-to-end processes and identify issues to attack.

condition: when funding processes block product flow

statement: A kanban board for technology work should span the full value stream and define done as running successfully in production.

Small batch sizes are a key mechanism for smooth, fast flow.

Continuous deployment represents a technology equivalent of single-piece flow because each committed change can be integrated, tested, and released independently.
condition: when each change can safely pass automated integration, test, and deployment controls

statement: Long deployment lead times often arise from many cross-functional handoffs across testing, environments, infrastructure, networking, security, and approvals.

Improving flow requires continually identifying the system constraint and improving capacity at that constraint rather than optimizing nonconstraints.
Improving a work center before the bottleneck increases bottleneck queueing, while improving after the bottleneck leaves downstream work starved.

condition: when teams wait on test or production environments

statement: Automated, self-service deployment is the countermeasure when code deployment effort constrains deployment flow.
condition: when deployments require long manual, error-prone execution

statement: Automated and parallelized tests are the countermeasure when test setup and execution constrain deployment flow.
condition: when regression testing or test data setup cannot keep pace with development

statement: Loosely coupled architecture is the countermeasure when tight architecture forces many coordination meetings or approvals for small changes.

statement: A mature DevOps flow should move the main constraint toward product discovery and development of good business hypotheses rather than delivery mechanics.

condition: when the activity does not add customer or downstream value

statement: Manual work that can be automated should be made automated, self-served, and available on demand where practical.

statement: Leaders must create real bandwidth and remove competing work when they declare flow improvement important.

statement: Flow improvement should optimize the whole system rather than local departmental metrics or incentives.

condition: when improvement ideas meet resistance

statement: Measurements and rewards should be aligned with system-level flow goals so local teams are not penalized for improving the overall system.
The Second Way aims to create a safer and more resilient system of work through fast feedback from later stages back to earlier stages.

Feedback and feedforward loops should be created across Product, Development, QA, Security, and Operations to detect problems early and clarify cause and effect.
Automated build, integration, and test processes should immediately detect changes that move a system out of a deployable state.
Telemetry should expose component behavior in test and production and make value-stream impacts visible across teams.
Feedback loops should be used both to recover from current problems and to prevent similar future problems.

Teams should design feedback so faster local loops catch implementation problems while slower stakeholder and user loops validate direction and value.
Detecting problems is insufficient; teams must swarm problems with whoever is needed to contain, diagnose, and prevent recurrence.

condition: when a current problem blocks or risks the system of work

condition: when a pull criterion is met for a failing build, test, incident, or stuck work item

condition: when failed tests indicate the system is no longer deployable

statement: Removing unnecessary input requirements and moving information gathering downstream can reduce back-and-forth delays.

statement: Improvement experiments that solve real business problems can attract further business engagement and demand for similar experiments.

statement: Making work visible requires current information and revising measures as target conditions change.
