Logs should preferably be centralized in a common service for search, retention, rotation, and deletion.
Metrics should be collected at every stack layer to understand behavior over time.
An event router should store and aggregate telemetry to support visualization, trending, alerting, anomaly detection, and health checks.
Logs can be transformed into metrics so teams can apply statistical analysis and anomaly detection.
Deployment pipeline telemetry should include test pass/fail events, deployments to each environment, and build/test duration.
Pipeline telemetry can reveal pre-production problems such as unusually slow builds or performance tests before changes reach production.
Telemetry systems should expose self-service APIs for entering and retrieving information rather than depend on ticketed reports.
Monitoring systems should be more available and scalable than the systems they monitor.
Every important feature should generate enough production telemetry to confirm operation and outcomes.
Telemetry should serve developers, Operations, Security, auditors, and product managers through different usage models.
Logging levels should distinguish debugging detail, informational events, potential problems, errors, and fatal termination conditions.
Teams should choose alerting severity by considering whether the condition merits waking someone for response.

Significant application events should log authentication, access, privileged changes, data changes, invalid input, resource limits, health, startup/shutdown, faults, circuit breaker trips, delays, and backups.
Telemetry should support scientific problem solving by showing evidence, relevant changes, candidate causes, and tests of hypotheses.
Public telemetry reduces political blame dynamics and supports institutional learning from incidents.
Fact-based problem solving can reduce MTTR and reinforce a win-win relationship between Development and Operations.
Telemetry libraries and infrastructure should make creating new production metrics easy for Development and Operations.
Adding production telemetry should be simple enough that developers cannot reasonably avoid instrumentation as too much hassle.
Production-change markers should be overlaid on telemetry graphs because many production issues are caused by changes.
Production telemetry created during daily work reveals design and operations problems and increases the number of useful tracked metrics over time.
Telemetry should be radiated through self-service access so stakeholders can inspect service behavior without production access, privileged accounts, or tickets.
Fast, centralized telemetry access gives the value stream a shared view of reality.
Production telemetry should be visible to Development, Operations, Product Management, Security, and other value-stream stakeholders.
Information radiators promote accountability by making current work state and problems visible to teams and stakeholders.
Service status and telemetry transparency can build trust with internal and external customers.
Self-service metrics empower individual and team problem solving and decision making.
Metric tools should let engineers create custom dashboards, compare historical trends, and combine multiple datasets.
Telemetry gaps should be identified and filled when they impede fast incident detection or resolution.
Telemetry coverage should span business, application, infrastructure, client software, and deployment pipeline levels.
Security-relevant faults such as abnormal terminations, application exceptions, and infrastructure errors should be monitored because they can indicate active exploitation.
After every production incident, teams should identify missing telemetry that would have enabled faster detection or recovery.
Peer review during feature development should identify telemetry gaps before production incidents occur.
Application telemetry should measure both service health and progress toward organizational goals.
Business metrics should instrument the user actions that lead to desired outcomes such as revenue, conversion, retention, or engagement.
The meaning of a business metric depends on domain and goal, so the same user behavior can be positive in one product and negative in another.
Top business metrics should be actionable and able to inform product change, experimentation, or A/B testing.
Vanity metrics should be stored if useful but not emphasized or alerted on when they do not guide action.
Every feature should be linked to business outcome metrics early in definition and measured after production deployment.
Business-context periods such as peak sales, financial close, or audits should be visible so risky changes can be scheduled appropriately.
Customer-usage telemetry should feed back to feature teams so they can see whether delivered capabilities are used and achieve goals.
Infrastructure telemetry should allow teams to determine whether database, operating system, storage, network, or other infrastructure is contributing to a problem.
Infrastructure telemetry should be organized by service or application so teams understand which services are affected by infrastructure events.
Dynamic service registration and discovery can replace manual CMDB-style dependency mapping in highly dynamic systems.
Business, application, and infrastructure metrics should be graphed together to accelerate diagnosis of system and customer-impacting problems.
Development and Operations should share business impact metrics, not only technical uptime metrics.
Infrastructure monitoring contributes to continuous delivery by giving all stakeholders visibility and fast feedback on build, test, and deployment outcomes.
Pre-production telemetry is needed to find and fix performance and infrastructure problems before production.
Operational activities such as maintenance or backups should be overlaid on metrics to explain behavior and tune alerts.
Production telemetry can reduce firefighting, stress, and burnout by enabling earlier detection and repair before customer impact.
Telemetry analysis should uncover variances and weak failure signals that can prevent catastrophic failures.
Outlier detection can identify misbehaving nodes by comparing them to the current normal behavior of peer nodes.
condition: when nodes should behave similarly under similar load

statement: Resilient systems can automatically remove or replace misbehaving nodes while logging or notifying engineers.
condition: when the service is engineered to tolerate node replacement

statement: Alerts should focus on actionable variances and outliers to avoid alert fatigue.
Post-incident review should add alerts for indicators that would have predicted or accelerated diagnosis of user-visible outages.
Teams should iterate from severe incidents toward ever-weaker failure signals so problems are found earlier and fewer customers are impacted.
Mean and standard deviation alerts should only be used when the underlying metric distribution supports that interpretation.
Many Operations telemetry datasets are non-Gaussian, making standard-deviation alerting prone to over-alerting, under-alerting, or nonsensical thresholds.
Over-alerting wakes responders for events that do not support useful action, while under-alerting lets customers discover problems first.
Predictive autoscaling should use historical demand patterns when reactive autoscaling cannot provision capacity quickly enough for spikes.
condition: when demand patterns are predictable and instance startup time is significant

statement: Autoscaling should account for post-outage demand drops so capacity is not removed just before demand returns.
condition: when reactive policies shrink capacity after outages

statement: Non-Gaussian user-demand data can still be useful for forecasting when customer behavior is regular and predictable.
Outlier filtering plus forecasting techniques can improve customer experience, availability, and infrastructure cost.
Anomaly detection should be used to find events or items that do not match expected patterns when distributions are non-Gaussian.
Operations teams may need collaboration with statistics, business intelligence, or analytics specialists to detect weak signals in telemetry.
Smoothing techniques such as moving averages can reduce short-term noise and reveal longer-term trends or cycles in time-series telemetry.
condition: when telemetry is a time series

statement: Seasonal and periodic user behavior can be compared to historical norms to detect anomalies such as an unexpected weekday transaction drop.
Nonparametric techniques such as Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests can compare telemetry distributions without assuming normality.
condition: when metric behavior is periodic or distribution assumptions are unsafe

statement: Finding weak failure signals through telemetry analysis creates a safer system of work and improves goal achievement.
Fast, frequent deployment feedback reduces fear and builds confidence for both developers and operators.
Reducing deployment batch size creates safer deployments and better learning.
When the first self-service deployment fails, teams should fix the problem urgently and add telemetry that would confirm recovery and detect recurrence earlier.
condition: when production deployment exposes an unexpected problem

statement: Production telemetry allows teams to decide quickly whether to roll back, fix forward, or disable a feature after deployment problems.
condition: when a deployment impairs service

statement: Peer review, better automated tests, and smaller changes improve deployment outcomes once teams experience production feedback.
Small, frequent production changes are easier to inspect, understand, and recover from than large changes.
Security responsiveness improves when engineers can quickly deploy fixes and receive direct feedback on problems in their code.
Deployment automation must be paired with production telemetry and shared responsibility for value-stream health.
Deployment changes should not be considered done until the changed system operates as designed in production.
Teams should actively monitor feature and service metrics during deployment to detect impairment of the changed service or other services.
Production failures after deployment should trigger rapid service restoration using toggles, rollback, or fix-forward through the pipeline.
Fix-forward can be safe when automated tests, fast deployment, and sufficient telemetry confirm production behavior quickly.
condition: when deployment and validation loops are fast and reliable

statement: Deployment and change events should be overlaid on metric graphs so the value stream can coordinate and recover faster.
Developers, development managers, and architects should share on-call or pager responsibilities for services they build.
Shared pager duty gives upstream engineers visceral feedback on architectural and coding decisions.
Operational incident work should be shared across the value stream so production defects are balanced against new feature work.
A feature is not truly done if it causes excessive escalations or unplanned work in production.
Everyone who touches production code or environments should be reachable for downtime when their work can affect production.
Production feedback brings developers closer to customers and increases buy-in for service health.
Developers should follow their work downstream to observe how downstream teams deploy, run, and support it.
Downstream observation reveals nonfunctional problems in deployability, manageability, operability, and supportability.
Customer and internal-user observation creates empathy and more informed design decisions.
UX-style observation can help codify nonfunctional requirements into a shared backlog for future services.
Operational learnings happen too late when the first true production-condition release occurs after Development considers work complete.
Development groups may need to self-manage services in production before Operations or SRE accepts support responsibility.
condition: when proving a service is stable and supportable

statement: Launch requirements should be defined before services interact with real customers or receive real production traffic.
Ops engineers should consult with product teams to help make services production-ready.
Launch guidance should include defect severity, pager-alert burden, monitoring coverage, architecture, deployment process, and production hygiene.
Production-readiness requirements should emphasize effective monitoring, deterministic deployment, and architecture that supports frequent safe deployment.
Ops reviewers should help feature teams resolve deficiencies and re-engineer services when production-readiness gaps are found.
condition: when launch or handoff review finds gaps

statement: Production readiness should identify revenue, availability, reputation, security, privacy, regulatory, contractual, and compliance risks early.
Compliance and security context should inform the design of the production control environment.
A service handback mechanism lets Operations return support responsibility to Development when a production service becomes too fragile.
condition: when a service is unsupportable or operationally fragile

statement: During handback, Operations should shift from primary support to consulting until the service is production-ready again.
Service handback prevents Operations from being buried by fragile services and preserves capacity for improvement work.
Launch and handoff readiness reviews encode organizational memory from past launches into repeatable safety checks.
Launch readiness should occur before public exposure, while handoff readiness should apply a higher bar before Operations-managed support.
Product teams that work with SRE or Operations early achieve faster production approval and smoother transition.
Helping product teams early should be valued as a long-term investment in service reliability.
Developer self-management of production services creates empathy between upstream and downstream work centers.
Product development should ask whether and why to build a feature before investing in full implementation.
Teams should use the cheapest and fastest experiments possible to validate whether intended features will achieve desired outcomes.
Rapid production experimentation can be valuable even during peak traffic when deployment and release are low risk.
condition: when production changes are fast, safe, and observable

statement: Experimentation has highest value when customer traffic and decision stakes are high, provided release safety supports it.
The faster teams can deploy, release, experiment, and integrate feedback, the faster they can learn against competitors.
A/B testing compares control and treatment cohorts to establish whether a change caused a meaningful outcome difference.
A/B tests can assign business value to performance or design changes by measuring downstream behavior.
Because many seemingly good features have negligible or negative impact, teams should rely on user testing over intuition alone.
Building unvalidated features creates opportunity cost and increases codebase complexity and maintenance cost.
A/B testing should be integrated into feature design, implementation, testing, and deployment.
Fast A/B testing requires on-demand deployments, feature toggles, segmented code exposure, and useful production telemetry.
Experiment frameworks should control the percentage of users exposed to treatments and measure their behavior against controls.
Feature experiments help teams decide whether a feature is worth continued work while it is still underway.
Product owners should frame each feature as a hypothesis that production releases can prove or disprove with real users.
Feature hypotheses should state the change, expected outcome, and measurable confidence threshold for proceeding.
If a feature experiment does not deliver expected outcomes, the roadmap should change toward alternative paths that can achieve those outcomes.
Low experiment frequency causes teams to focus on feature output rather than customer outcomes.
Fast release cycles increase the number of product experiments a team can run and can materially improve visits, engagement, and revenue.
Product teams should maintain top outcome metrics that reflect the customer behavior they are trying to improve.
Daily visibility into experiment results can shift a team from employee mindset to ownership mindset.
Successful digital delivery requires out-experimenting competitors, not only deploying and releasing quickly.
Hypothesis-driven development, funnel metrics, and A/B testing make user experiments safe, easier, and useful for organizational learning.
Review and coordination processes should reduce production-change risk before changes are made.
Late deployment approvals by people far from the work often lengthen lead time and weaken decision quality.
Pull requests can integrate code review, feedback, coordination, and production deployment announcement into daily work.
Peer review should be performed continually as part of daily work rather than periodically as a separate inspection gate.
Development, Operations, and Security should collaborate continuously so system changes are reliable, secure, safe, and as designed.
After major deployment accidents, adding more change-control friction can increase future risk in low-trust command-and-control cultures.
More change-request questions, authorizations, and approval lead time increase friction, batch size, and deployment lead time.
Approval steps by people far from complex work can reduce success likelihood because they know less about the specific problem.
High-performing organizations use clear lightweight change processes that developers trust to move typical approvals quickly.
Heavyweight change processes requiring external boards or senior managers for significant changes have a negative performance impact in cited research.
Change advisory boards should coordinate and govern delivery rather than manually evaluate every change.
External reviewers cannot reliably predict success from brief descriptions or exhaustive code scrutiny in complex systems.
Automated release fitness checks can replace slow senior approval rooms by evaluating system, value-stream, and environment readiness.
Release readiness automation should give clear go/no-go signals and point teams to the failed factor when release is blocked.
Error budgets and release guidelines can let a system self-regulate deployment permission without manual executive approval.
Changes across shared dependencies may need coordination, sequencing, or scheduling so they do not interfere with each other.
condition: when systems or teams share dependencies

statement: Looser architecture reduces the need for cross-team coordination because local changes are less likely to cause global disruptions.
High-risk global infrastructure changes still require technical countermeasures such as redundancy, failover, testing, and simulation.
condition: when changes affect global or shared infrastructure

statement: Peer review should replace external pre-deployment approval where possible because peers close to the work are better positioned to find errors.
Peer review should apply to application, environment, server, network, and database changes, not only source code.
Peer review improves quality while creating cross-training, peer learning, and skill improvement.
Changes should be reviewed before they are committed to trunk or otherwise affect the team or system globally.
Higher-risk areas such as database changes, security-sensitive modules, or poorly tested critical components may require expert or multiple reviews.
condition: when the change area carries higher risk

statement: Review burden and lead time grow nonlinearly with change size, so changes should be kept small.
A change too large to understand after a few readings should be split into smaller changes.
Teams should monitor review statistics or sample reviews to detect rubber-stamping.
condition: when review quality is uncertain

statement: Tool-assisted code review can support trunk-based development and continuous delivery at large scale.
Mandatory code reviews can support readability, ownership consistency, transparency, and cross-team contribution.
More manual testing at the end of a project can backfire by increasing test duration, reducing deployment frequency, and increasing deployment batch size.
Testing should be integrated into daily work and smooth flow instead of concentrated around late change-freeze periods.
Pair programming provides immediate continuous review while work is being performed.
Pair programming can separate tactical implementation from strategic review by using driver and navigator roles.
Pairing people with different specialties transfers skills through shared work.
Pairing can reinforce test-driven development by having one engineer write tests while the other implements code.
Pair programming may be slower in initial coding but can improve defect rates, design quality, maintainability, knowledge flow, and enjoyment.
Every team should own quality rather than rely on separate departments to create it after the fact.
A review process that takes too long creates bottlenecks that prevent simple changes from reaching trunk.
Pair programming can reduce review lead time when asynchronous senior-only review creates intolerable bottlenecks.
condition: when review culture or capacity cannot support timely asynchronous reviews

statement: Code review works only when the culture values reviewing code as highly as writing code.
Peer review effectiveness should be evaluated using production incidents and sampled review artifacts.
A poor pull request lacks enough context for reviewers to understand intent, importance, risk, and implementation thinking.
A strong pull request explains why the change is needed, how it was made, its risks, and its countermeasures.
Pull-request discussions should surface additional risks, better implementation ideas, and stronger mitigations without blame.
If deployment reveals unexpected harm, the incident context and post-mortem links should be added to the related review artifact.
condition: when a reviewed change later contributes to an incident

statement: Bureaucratic approval processes should be re-engineered when they materially increase lead time or risk to organizational objectives.
Teams should measure and reduce mandatory meetings and work tickets required to release software.
Dedicated obstacle-removal efforts can improve flow by removing tools, processes, and approvals that impede work completion.
Governance processes should be challenged with root-cause questioning when their purpose is unclear or their control value no longer fits the work.
If a Development team owns support, integration, availability, and security for a technology, some external adoption approvals may be unnecessary.
condition: when the team accepts full operational responsibility and risk controls

statement: High-trust cultures let change implementers own quality after they have reviewed, tested, and assured themselves that the change will work.
Part IV feedback loops help teams see problems, recover quickly, verify production behavior, meet organizational goals, and learn.
Third Way practices should create learning opportunities quickly, frequently, cheaply, and early.
Complex systems require learning from accidents and failures because static precautions cannot predict all outcomes.
Organizations should become self-diagnosing and self-improving by detecting problems, solving them, and spreading solutions.
Resilience can be designed through loosely coupled components, aggressive timeouts, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation.
Graceful degradation can preserve core service by reducing personalization or expensive functionality under load or dependency failure.
condition: when lower-quality service is preferable to total failure

statement: Chaos engineering can validate resilience by injecting failures into production and pre-production systems.
condition: when services are designed to recover automatically and failure injection is controlled

statement: Running failure experiments during normal working hours lets teams learn and fix resilience weaknesses before real incidents occur.
Learning organizations treat failures, accidents, and mistakes as opportunities for learning rather than punishment.
Incident responses perceived as unjust impede safety investigations and promote fear, bureaucracy, secrecy, evasion, and self-protection.
Human error should be examined as a consequence of system design, tools, and conditions rather than treated as the sole cause of trouble.
Organizations should maximize learning from failure by encouraging actions that expose and share daily-work problems.
Just culture balances accountability and safety by turning incident information into system knowledge and improvement.
Blameless retrospectives should be conducted after significant incidents or accidents once the incident is resolved.
Retrospectives should occur soon enough that memories and cause-effect links have not faded.
Retrospectives should build a multi-perspective timeline, avoid punishment, empower detailed accounts, and create owned countermeasures.
Retrospectives should include people who contributed decisions, detected, responded, diagnosed, were affected, and others interested in learning.
Incident timelines should use chat logs, telemetry, observed effects, investigation paths, and considered resolutions rather than only subjective narratives.
Retrospectives should focus on why an action made sense at the time rather than hindsight blame.
Countermeasures should be concrete system changes rather than advice to be more careful.
Retrospective countermeasures may include new tests, additional telemetry, extra review for risky change classes, or failure rehearsals.
Retrospective notes and artifacts should be published widely in a searchable central location to convert local learning into global learning.
Incident closure may be blocked until a retrospective is completed to ensure learning happens.
condition: when the organization needs a strong learning gate

statement: Public incident retrospectives can increase transparency and customer trust.
Retrospective tooling should make it easy to capture severity, ownership, chat logs, corrective tickets, due dates, customer reports, tags, and history.
Making retrospectives easier to document increases the amount of learning captured, including from lower-severity incidents.
Consistent retrospectives improve culture by increasing information sharing, smart risk taking, and appreciation of learning.
Elite performers are more likely to hold retrospectives consistently and use them to improve work.
Organizations should reduce the stigma of intelligent experimental failure so teams redeploy learning and resources sooner.
As obvious incidents decrease, organizations should lower problem thresholds to keep learning from weaker failure signals.
Weak failure signals in one domain may indicate deeper process ignorance that also affects quality, timeliness, and yield.
Technology work should be treated as experimental because each action is a hypothesis and a source of data.
A rigid standardization mindset can miss ambiguous threats when the work requires experimental evaluation of new information.
Leaders should reinforce that everyone is comfortable with and responsible for surfacing and learning from failures.
High-performing teams may have more absolute failures because they change more frequently, so failure should not automatically be treated as poor performance.
Organizations should not punish high-contribution engineers for mistakes when those mistakes occur in the course of valuable calculated risk-taking.
Teams should define expected failure modes and test that systems fail in controlled and graceful ways.
If teams do not design failure modes, complex systems will produce unpredictable and often dangerous failure modes.
Fault injection and large-scale failure rehearsal should confirm recovery before real accidents occur.
Regular participation in failure exercises can make major external disruptions routine rather than crisis-inducing.
Game days should simulate catastrophic events so teams can practice, remove single points of failure, and create monitoring and failover procedures.
Failure drills should increase in intensity and complexity until they become a normal part of work.
Game days should test business processes and communication, not only technical systems.
Failure rehearsals create relationships and routines that improve real incident response.
Severe outages should be used to improve incident understanding, response, and prevention instead of invalidating DevOps practices.
Incident analysis should build a timeline, identify detection and recovery opportunities, understand system behavior, and maintain blamelessness.
Deep incident analysis should capture multiple perspectives from people working the outage, not just the final technical cause.
Incident improvement programs can organize follow-up around incident response, tool reliability, platform resiliency, and application reliability.
Incident command roles, clear authority, liaison functions, and status cadences can reduce call chaos and improve control during outages.
Blameless post-mortems can drive cultural change when learnings are applied to how work is conducted.
Local discoveries should be captured and shared globally so the whole organization benefits from cumulative experience.
Chat rooms can support fast team communication and can also trigger automation.
ChatOps puts automation in the middle of team conversation to create transparency and documentation of work.
Automation results should be posted back into shared chat so everyone can see what happened.
ChatOps helps new engineers learn daily work patterns from chat logs and observe how work is performed.
Public chat communication makes help-seeking, collaboration, and organizational learning easier than private email.
Operational actions such as deploys, service checks, alert muting, server rotation, rollback, and smoke-log retrieval can be encoded as chat automation.
Repository commits and deployment-pipeline status should be emitted into shared channels to improve transparency.
ChatOps can make Operations work more humane by helping engineers discover problems and help each other quickly.
Organizational standards should be converted from prose documents into executable reusable code where possible.
Executable standards should be stored in searchable shared repositories so teams can find and use them.
Automated blueprints can make policy compliance and consistency a byproduct of normal engineering work.
Compliance improves when policies are expressed as code that teams can execute easily.
Reusable automated processes should become the easiest path so good practices spread without relying on manual governance.
An organization-wide shared source repository is a mechanism for spreading local engineering discoveries across teams.
When shared code or libraries are updated in a common repository, dependent services can receive the change through their deployment pipelines.
condition: Dependent services use the shared artifact and have deployment pipelines that integrate the update.

statement: A single repository gives engineers access to current code and reusable examples without requiring separate coordination for each dependency.

Shared repositories should hold not only application code but also standards, deployment tooling, testing and security tools, pipeline tooling, monitoring tools, tutorials, and reusable operational knowledge.
Encoding organizational knowledge in a shared repository is a strong mechanism for propagating knowledge at scale.
Building from source against the current repository version reduces library-version drift compared with resolving divergent runtime dependencies.
condition: The build process consistently uses the shared source tree as its dependency source.

statement: A single repository can expose accurate dependency relationships, allowing maintainers to identify affected consumers before refactoring shared libraries.
Good code maintainability depends on tools and systems that make cross-team code changes, example discovery, reuse, and dependency migration practical.
Code maintainability supports continuous delivery and reduces technical debt, which can improve developer productivity.
Each shared library should have an accountable owner responsible for keeping the library compiling and passing tests for dependent projects.
Library ownership should include responsibility for migrating consuming projects from one supported version to the next.
Running many production versions of the same framework increases vulnerability exposure, operational burden, and upgrade risk.
When a single source tree is not feasible, an organization-wide package or artifact repository should maintain known-good library and dependency versions.
condition: The organization cannot build everything from one source tree.

statement: Production dependencies should come only from controlled organizational source or package repositories to reduce software supply-chain attack paths.
Shared libraries should include substantial automated tests so those tests serve as executable usage examples for other engineers.
Test-driven development helps keep automated tests aligned with intended system behavior by making tests a living specification.
condition: Teams practice test-driven development.

statement: A shared library is easier to support when a single owner or team is responsible for the knowledge and expertise around it.
Using only one production version of a shared library helps production systems reflect the organization's best current collective knowledge.
Safe shared-library migration requires comprehensive automated regression detection and continuous integration across consuming systems.
Library-specific discussion channels help propagate knowledge because users can answer questions and share patterns beyond the owning team.
Development teams design more operable applications when they follow work downstream and participate in production incident resolution.
Designing for fast flow and deployability should surface non-functional requirements that every production service needs to satisfy.

Operational non-functional requirements should cover telemetry, dependency tracking, graceful degradation, version compatibility, data archiving, log search, request tracing, and centralized runtime configuration.
Codifying operational non-functional requirements makes collective operations knowledge reusable by both new and existing services.
The team building a service is responsible for implementing the operational requirements needed to deploy and run it safely.
Recurring Operations work that cannot be fully automated or made self-service should be standardized, partially automated, and documented.
condition: The Operations activity remains recurring and cannot yet be fully automated or self-service.

statement: Manual server build checklists should be replaced with automated provisioning and post-installation configuration management wherever possible.
exception: Steps that physically require manual work may still need human handoffs.

statement: Non-automatable operational handoffs should be explicitly defined to reduce lead time and error rates.
condition: A work step cannot be automated.

statement: Infrastructure changes should be captured in version control, linked to work records, and applied automatically where the GitOps pattern is used.
condition: The organization manages infrastructure through configuration and work-tracking systems.

statement: Repeatable Operations activities should be modeled as Ops user stories so they can be planned alongside Development work.
condition: The work activity recurs across projects.

statement: Technology choices should be evaluated against organizational goals rather than only local team productivity.
Allowing service teams to choose their own languages and frameworks can support developer productivity in service-oriented architectures.
condition: Developer productivity is a primary goal and teams own small services.

statement: A technology choice becomes a bottleneck when only one team has the expertise needed to change or repair a critical service.
Operations should be able to influence production technology choices or decline support for unsupported platforms when it is accountable for service support.
condition: A functionally oriented Operations group remains responsible for production support.

statement: Without a jointly agreed supported-technology list, teams should inspect production services and dependencies for technologies that create disproportionate failure demand and unplanned work.
condition: No supported-technology list exists across Development and Operations.

statement: Technologies that slow flow, create excess unplanned work, generate support load, or conflict with desired architecture outcomes should be removed from the supported platform set.
Infrastructure platforms should let users self-service required operations without ticket or email handoffs.

An organization does not gain cloud benefits merely by using cloud infrastructure; it must implement essential characteristics such as self-service, broad access, pooled resources, elasticity, and measured service.
Technology guidance works better as accessible, transparent, flexible, community-driven guardrails than as centralized approval governance.
Governance weight should increase for technology decisions with high switching cost, low reversibility, or large blast radius.
Organizations should schedule recurring rituals that reserve Development and Operations time for non-feature improvement work.
Improvement blitzes should focus value-stream teams on solving daily work problems, not on unrestricted product ideation.
Effective improvement blitzes include Development, Operations, and Information Security participation across the value stream.
During an improvement blitz, feature work should be paused so teams can address code, environment, architecture, tooling, or other operational problems they care about.
Having teams demonstrate what they improved at the end of an improvement blitz reinforces debt reduction as valued work.
Improvement blitzes are powerful because they give the workers closest to the problems authority to identify and solve them.
Complex systems require local, continual repair norms because command-and-control management cannot direct every needed improvement.
Regular improvement blitzes and hack weeks help integrate safety, reliability, and learning improvements into the system.
Dedicated organizational learning time should let every technologist both teach and learn through training, workshops, mentoring, and peer exchange.
Operations and Test engineers increasingly need familiarity with development practices such as version control, automated testing, deployment pipelines, configuration management, and automation.
Joint code reviews and small shared problem-solving sessions help Development and Operations transfer skills through daily work.
Development teams can teach Operations by pairing on automated checks that are later integrated into deployment pipelines and monitoring systems.
Learning silos hide knowledge, cause teams to repeat similar experiments and antipatterns, and risk institutional knowledge loss when people leave.
A structured learning loop should align on goals, sense context, run experiments, distill results into insights and metrics, and share learnings for others to reuse.
Learning loops combined with communities and recognition can help disconnected groups become a broader learning ecosystem.
Organizations that want a learning culture should encourage engineers from Development and Operations to attend, speak at, and organize conferences.
Internal technology conferences provide organizational context for learning that external conferences may not supply.
Internal conferences can increase trust, communication, innovation, and improvement of daily work among technologists.
High-performing organizations tend to spread DevOps and Agile through community structures such as communities of practice, grassroots efforts, and reusable proof-of-concept patterns.
Communities of practice can spread technical practices even without formal authority when they use focused improvement efforts, coaching, and explicit adoption paths.
A practice adoption roadmap with measurable levels lowers the barrier for teams that do not know where to start.
Internal coaches accelerate adoption by applying shared tools and techniques directly to product teams' own code and problems.
Visible adoption levels can harness a metrics-oriented culture to motivate teams to improve engineering practices.
Funding internal coaches can institutionalize improvement without relying solely on top-down mandates.
Company-wide fixit events create focused missions that can move long-term culture change to a new plateau.
A learning organization should reserve time to pay down technical debt and build community structures for peer teaching.
Security controls should be integrated into the daily work of Development and Operations instead of being injected at the end of delivery.
Security work should be automated into deployment pipelines wherever possible.
Manual security approvals and acceptance practices should be augmented with automated controls to reduce reliance on separation of duties and change approval gates.
Automated security activities can produce evidence on demand for auditors, assessors, and value-stream participants.
Integrating security into delivery work can improve both security outcomes and the auditability of control effectiveness.
Making security part of everyone's job supports confidentiality, integrity, availability, recovery, and system predictability goals.
A siloed Information Security function with too few specialists cannot scale security engineering without automation and integration into Development and Operations work.
DevOps practices can integrate Information Security objectives across the value stream while preserving development and operational productivity.
Feature teams should engage Information Security early, including during iteration demonstrations.
Security participation in iteration demonstrations gives Infosec business context and allows early feedback while corrections are still cheaper and more flexible.
Compliance-by-demonstration shifts security and compliance complexity earlier in the development process.
Continuous Infosec involvement can reduce reliance on static checklists by applying security expertise throughout development.
Security issues should be tracked in the same work system used by Development and Operations so the work is visible and can be prioritized with other work.
Security incidents and vulnerabilities should be reviewed through postmortems to educate engineers and transfer prevention knowledge.
Security toolchains and approved libraries should be placed in shared version control so they are searchable, reusable, and available in daily DevOps work.
Security-approved authentication, authorization, encryption, logging, and auditing services help teams satisfy common Information Security objectives.
Version control can act as a communication mechanism by making security-relevant changes visible to all parties.
Central shared-service teams should collaborate with Security to operate reusable security platforms needed by Development and Operations.
condition: A centralized shared-services organization exists.

statement: Teams using predefined security libraries or services can avoid repeated module-specific security design reviews.
condition: The predefined module already embodies approved security guidance.

statement: Security training and implementation review are especially useful when teams use approved security tools for the first time.
condition: Teams are adopting the provided tools or libraries for the first time.

statement: Security platforms should provide standard capabilities for authentication, authorization, password management, encryption, and security-specific configuration.
Shared security repositories should include library configurations, secret-management patterns, secure OS packages, secure base builds, integrity monitoring, and centralized logging configuration.
Putting logging and encryption standards in shared repositories makes correct implementation easier for engineers and reduces repeated Security intervention.
Security and Operations should collaborate on secure base cookbooks or images for operating systems, databases, and infrastructure components.
Shared repositories should support monitoring and alerting on changes to security-sensitive modules.
Container base images should be stored in a registry with source versions and secure image hashes.
condition: The organization uses container-based systems.

statement: Container image hashes must be validated whenever images are used or deployed.
condition: A container image is used or deployed.

statement: Late security reviews often produce vulnerability lists that remain unaddressed because problems are found too close to release.
Automated security tests should run in the deployment pipeline alongside other automated tests, preferably on every commit and from early project stages.
Fast security feedback lets Development and Operations detect and correct insecure changes as part of daily work.
Automated security tests should be integrated with static code analysis in the delivery pipeline.
Expressing security tests in frameworks developers already know makes those tests easier to run in normal delivery workflows.
Application security testing must cover error, misuse, and abuse paths rather than only expected user journeys.
Invalid or malicious input scenarios should be tested to reject fraud and common exploit patterns.
Security-focused error-path tests should be automated as unit or functional tests and run continuously in the deployment pipeline.
Static analysis should inspect code before runtime for coding flaws, back doors, banned functions, and potentially malicious code.
Dynamic security analysis should exercise running systems in ways similar to external attackers and can be included in functional testing or production checks.
Build-time dependency scanning should inventory binaries and executables and check them for vulnerabilities or malicious contents.
Developers should sign commits, CI packages should be signed, and package hashes should be recorded centrally for audit.
Developers should receive abuse-prevention design patterns such as rate limits and double-submit protections.
Security teams should change work systems and automation so recurring vulnerabilities are prevented rather than repeatedly fixed.
Security findings should appear in existing developer tools with enough context for the responsible developer to fix them.
Security automation must manage false positives because wasting developer time erodes trust.
Automating scan execution, report interpretation, and assignment preserves Information Security flow and frees specialists for judgment work.
Security guidance should be self-service where possible so teams have the context needed to resolve issues.
A holistic security approach analyzes source code, production environments, and customer-visible behavior.
Early static analysis integrated into the build or development process can reduce the rate of vulnerabilities over time.
Using third-party or open-source components imports both their functionality and their vulnerabilities into the product.
Automation that creates pull-request patches for detected dependency vulnerabilities speeds supply-chain remediation.
Component selection should account for known vulnerabilities, multiple deployed versions, stale versions, and the project's history of fixing vulnerabilities quickly.
Keeping dependencies current is a strong security patching strategy because projects that update dependencies more often tend to remediate vulnerabilities faster.
Open-source project popularity should not be used as a proxy for security characteristics.

High-performing software-supply-chain organizations automate dependency approval and analysis, use composition analysis, enforce governance in CI, manage CI centrally, maintain artifact records, and scan deployed artifacts centrally.
Production environments should be monitored and automatically tested against known-good hardened states, with scan outputs stored and compared to detect undesirable changes.
Security controls fail to detect breaches quickly when monitoring has blind spots or relevant telemetry is not reviewed in daily work.
Security monitoring, logging, and alerting should be deployed across applications and environments and centralized for meaningful analysis and response.
Security telemetry should be integrated into the same tools used by Development, QA, and Operations.
Making production attacks visible to the value stream encourages teams to consider security risks and countermeasures during daily design work.
Applications should emit telemetry for security-relevant user events such as login attempts, password resets, email changes, and payment-information changes.
Ratios of unsuccessful to successful logins can provide early warning of brute-force access attempts.
Important security events should have alerting so teams can detect and correct issues quickly.
Environments need telemetry to detect unauthorized access indicators, especially when infrastructure components are not directly controlled by the organization.
Environment monitoring should cover operating system changes, security group changes, production configuration changes, cloud infrastructure changes, attack attempts, and web-server errors.
Teams should verify that logging configuration sends all required security telemetry to the correct destination.
When attacks are detected, systems should log the event and may block access while retaining source information for mitigation decisions.
Fraud and security responsibilities can be embedded throughout the DevOps value stream rather than isolated in a separate department.
Security metrics should be displayed alongside operational metrics that engineers already review.
Abnormal process terminations and server errors can indicate vulnerability exploitation that requires urgent investigation or patching.
Database syntax errors in production code should receive zero tolerance because they may enable or indicate injection attacks.
SQL injection indicators should generate alerts, and automated tests should prevent uncontrolled user input from reaching database queries.
Showing developers real-time attack telemetry can change how they think about code security while writing software.
Continuous integration and deployment infrastructure is an attack surface that can expose source code or inject malicious application changes if compromised.
Unit tests can be abused as a place to hide malicious code because CI systems run them automatically on commits.
Pipeline security controls are necessary to protect the integrity of applications and environments.
Continuous build and integration servers should be hardened and reproducible through automation from known-good states.
Code changes should be reviewed before merge or at commit time to reduce the risk of CI executing uncontrolled code.
Repositories should detect suspicious API use in test code and trigger quarantine or immediate review when risky patterns appear.
Each CI process should run in an isolated container or virtual machine recreated from a verified base image for every build.
CI systems should use read-only version-control credentials.
Security tools become more useful when they are self-service, API-based, and integrated with normal developer workflow systems.
Developers need training to run security tools and understand their results when security testing is shifted into development workflows.
Security tests integrated into CI/CD on every code check-in make failures visible and actionable to developers.
A secure paved-road pipeline makes compliant deployment easier than bypassing the pipeline.
Failing security tests should stop delivery until the problem is fixed.
Shared accountability works better when teams own what they build and security is built into code rather than inserted later.
Shift-left automated testing reduces dependence on scarce Security personnel for routine testing and deployment decisions.
If the deployment pipeline makes deployments low risk, many changes can rely on automated testing and production monitoring rather than manual approval.
condition: The deployment pipeline has reliable automated controls and proactive monitoring.

statement: Change management should categorize changes by risk so standard, normal, and urgent changes receive different handling.
Low-risk standard changes can be preapproved, automated, and logged for traceability without per-change approval.
condition: The change follows an established approved process and has well-understood impact.

statement: A history of high change success rates and low recovery time can justify recategorizing automated deployments as standard changes.
Automated deployments should be recorded in change management systems and linked to planning records and version-control changes.
Change traceability should remain lightweight and avoid engineering friction beyond useful links to stories, defects, or requirements.
Normal-change requests should be complete, accurate, and supported by automated artifacts such as build manifests, test output, scripts, dry-run results, and machine-readable evidence.
condition: A change still requires manual change-authority review.

statement: A strong record of successful normal changes should be used to seek eventual standard-change classification for automated changes.
condition: The organization still treats these deployments as normal changes.

statement: Separation of duty has traditionally reduced fraud and mistake risk by requiring independent review and promotion of changes.
As software complexity and deployment frequency increase, teams need faster visibility into deployment outcomes.
Traditional handoff-based separation of duty can slow feedback, weaken engineer ownership of quality, and reduce organizational learning.
Pair programming, continuous inspection of code check-ins, and code review can provide control evidence comparable to separation-of-duty objectives.
Compliance scope can be contained by physically and logically separating regulated environments and assigning a cross-functional team to own them.
condition: A regulation allows the organization to define and isolate the in-scope environment.

statement: DevOps organizations can satisfy compliance requirements, but low-trust control mechanisms can damage high-performing team behaviors.
Rigid separation can prevent full-stack visibility and create fear around deployment and maintenance.
A platform modernization effort should begin from customer needs, including regulators, internal users, analysts, and external customers.
Teams should deliver value iteratively to maximize learning and reduce transformation risk.
Transformation teams should avoid replicating legacy systems simply because those systems are familiar.
Segmenting users by needs and functionality can provide thin deployment slices for experimentation and iteration.
An MVP for critical modernization should be a minimum viable experience rather than merely the smallest possible feature set.
Standardizing on proven enterprise tools can help engineers contribute across teams and move between teams faster.
CI/CD pipelines enable incremental releases that reduce cycle time and release risk.
Pipelines can enforce regulatory and compliance controls by blocking releases when required checks fail.
A shared delivery pipeline lets product teams focus on feature delivery instead of each team rebuilding delivery infrastructure.
DevOps teams must help bridge the knowledge gap between modern engineering practices and auditor expectations.
Traditional audit evidence methods such as server samples, screenshots, and CSV exports do not map cleanly to infrastructure as code, autoscaling, and deployment pipelines.
Organizations should create alternative audit evidence methods that clearly show controls are operating effectively.
Auditors should be involved iteratively in control design so audit evidence needs are known before production operation.
Telemetry systems can let auditors self-serve evidence for specific time ranges instead of requesting manual samples.
Modern audit logging, chat rooms, and deployment pipelines create operational transparency that should be translated into auditor-recognizable evidence.
Engineering control requirements should be derived from the actual regulatory text rather than from inherited audit rituals.
Compliance, Security, and DevOps teams should jointly decide how each control prevents, detects, or corrects problems.
A control can be implemented as version-controlled configuration or as a monitoring control depending on the regulatory requirement.
Audit evidence should be linked to the control requirement in the logging or telemetry framework.
Documentation that narrates risks, controls, attestations, and artifacts helps auditors understand how DevOps controls satisfy requirements.
Code review, approval, and separation of duty may not detect deliberate fraud when a perpetrator has sufficient means, motive, and opportunity.
Production telemetry and regular operations review can detect fraud that code review fails to catch.
Telemetry-based controls can reduce the perceived need for additional separation layers or change review boards.
Integrating Information Security objectives into daily value-stream work improves prevention, detection, recovery, and audit preparation.
DevOps transformations require cultural, management, technical, and architectural changes rather than tooling changes alone.
A DevOps transformation requires a coalition spanning business leadership, Product Management, Development, QA, Operations, Information Security, and other technology-originating functions.
Small teams should be enabled to develop and validate code independently while still deploying safely to customers.
Postponing improvements and accepting daily workarounds creates risk for technology organizations.
DevOps is relevant to organizations that must increase flow of planned technology work while maintaining quality, reliability, and security.
High software delivery performance depends on automation, strategic process design, trust, and information flow.
Smart automation, flexible processes, and good communication help organizations adapt under disruptive conditions.
Higher activity metrics can hide exhaustion and are not sufficient evidence of sustainable productivity.
Productivity should be measured holistically rather than through hours worked or commit counts alone.
Developer productivity measurement should combine at least three dimensions such as well-being, performance, activity, collaboration, and flow.
Adding metrics from different productivity dimensions gives leaders better decision information than adding more activity metrics.
Productivity metrics should expose sustainability, tool-system health, and tradeoffs that teams are making.
Technology capability should be embedded close to where customer problems are solved.
Tools and organizational structure are important but insufficient for sustained improvement, architectural evolution, culture change, and teamwork.
High performance starts with leadership creating psychological safety across different backgrounds and perspectives.
Teams need resources, capacity, and encouragement to experiment and learn together safely and systematically.
DevOps work should be understood as intentionally reducing friction between organizational silos.
Bottlenecks move after improvement, so organizations must continually reevaluate where friction currently limits flow.
Optimizing only pipeline automation can leave other organizational friction points unresolved.
Legacy organizations must deliberately adopt new operating habits because older systemic habits can repeatedly pull transformations backward.
Lean treats shorter lead time and smaller batch size as key predictors of quality, customer satisfaction, and employee happiness.
Lean practice emphasizes customer value, systems thinking, constancy of purpose, scientific thinking, flow and pull, quality at the source, humility, and respect for individuals.
Agile emphasizes frequent delivery of working software, small motivated teams, high-trust management, and small batch sizes.
Continuous delivery uses a deployment pipeline to keep code and infrastructure in a deployable state.
Improvement work should become habitual daily work through iterative, incremental, scientific problem solving toward a shared direction.
Product teams should test business hypotheses before making large feature investments.
High deployment rates make late-cycle QA and Information Security turnaround times untenable.
Reducing batch size, reducing work in process, and shortening feedback loops can break chronic conflicts in value streams.
DevOps applies the same flow and feedback principles to optimize the IT value stream from business need to customer-facing service.
Many handoffs create queues, and queues greatly extend lead time even when the actual work is short.
As resource utilization approaches full capacity, waiting time increases nonlinearly.
Value-added work can represent only a tiny fraction of lead time when work waits across multiple busy work centers.
Human error should be treated as a signal of deeper system vulnerabilities rather than as the primary explanation for failure.
Explaining what people should have done does not explain why their action seemed reasonable at the time.
Organizations improve safety by continually seeking vulnerabilities rather than simply telling people to be more careful.
An Andon pull should trigger rapid local resolution first and stop the broader line only if the issue is not resolved in time.
Commercial off-the-shelf software can be brought under version control by replacing opaque installers with reproducible install artifacts and environment-specific configuration separation.
condition: The organization must deploy complex vendor software reproducibly.

statement: Application configuration should be transformed into version-controlled artifacts wherever possible.
Postmortem facilitators should explicitly frame the meeting as blameless and avoid speculation about what people should have done.
A postmortem corrective action should have an owner and be treated as a top priority after the meeting.
Incident timelines should include detection, discovery channel, restoration time, participants, and external communications.
Complex-incident timelines should capture multiple contributing events, troubleshooting paths, actor perspectives, and cause-effect hypotheses.
Postmortems should collect both human and technical contributing factors without allowing participants to deny another participant's observed factor.
Postmortem analysis should avoid prematurely converging on a single root cause.
Postmortem corrective actions should either prevent recurrence or improve detection and recovery.
Postmortem improvement plans should favor the smallest incremental steps that achieve the desired outcome over large delayed changes.
Lower-priority postmortem ideas should still receive owners so they can inform future countermeasures if similar problems recur.
Incident reviews should agree on severity, downtime, time to detect, time to resolve, and organizational impact metrics.
Blamelessness means examining the surrounding conditions that made an action possible, not avoiding responsibility.
Removing blame reduces fear and enables more honest incident learning.
Chaos engineering tools can deliberately simulate increasingly severe failures so systems are engineered to handle them.
Latency injection helps verify that dependent services respond appropriately to service degradation.
Conformity and security automation can identify or terminate cloud resources that violate operational or security standards.
Health-check automation can find unhealthy instances and remove them if owners do not correct root causes in time.
Automated cleanup of unused cloud resources reduces clutter and waste.
Public service-health dashboards reduce support load by helping users distinguish local problems from service-wide incidents.
Status pages let providers communicate outages through one broadcast channel instead of repeated one-to-one support updates.
Real-time incident visibility builds customer trust for SaaS services that customers depend on.
